v-p-menon: Vappala Pangunni Menon was born on 30 September 1893 in Kerala, the son of a school headmaster, Chunangad Shankara Menon. He dropped out of formal education, never earning a high school diploma or a college degree, and worked as a railway stoker, a coal miner and a clerk for a tobacco company in Bangalore. He then joined the Imperial Secretariat Service, becoming a superintendent in the Reforms Office in 1930 and rising to joint secretary to the Government of India by 1941. Encouraged by Edwin Montagu, he became the highest serving Indian officer in British India.

Menon was joint secretary to the Simla Conference in June 1945 and in 1946 became Political Reforms Commissioner to the Viceroy. As political adviser to Lord Louis Mountbatten, he proposed to Mountbatten, Jawaharlal Nehru and Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel the Muslim League's plan to partition India into two independent nations, India and Pakistan, after the interim government collapsed. Under Patel he became the envoy to the princes. When Hanwant Singh, Maharaja of Jodhpur, pointed a pistol at him after signing his accession, Menon told him he would be making a very serious mistake.

On 17 September 1947 he delivered India's protest against Junagadh's accession to Pakistan to its dewan, Sir Shah Nawaz Bhutto. He drafted and negotiated the Standstill Agreement with Hyderabad, and on 26 October flew to Jammu to secure the signature of Maharaja Hari Singh on the accession of Jammu and Kashmir. In May 1948 a meeting he initiated led the Rajpramukhs of the princely unions to sign new Instruments of Accession, and he signed the Tripura Merger Agreement for the Governor-General.

After his time as secretary, Menon was briefly Governor of Odisha, then called Orissa, in 1951. He wrote The Story of the Integration of Indian States and Transfer of Power, an account of the partition. He later joined the free-market Swatantra Party but never contested elections. He had been made Rao Bahadur, CIE in 1941 and CSI in 1946, but in 1948 he refused a knighthood, saying that with independence he had entered the service of the new Indian government; according to his grandson, he privately said he could not accept it for having caused the partition of his country.
v-weapons: Vergeltungswaffen means retaliatory or reprisal weapons, and the V-weapons were counted among the so-called Wunderwaffen of Nazi Germany. A strategic bombing purpose for the A4 rocket, later the V-2, was put forward as early as 28 June 1940 at a meeting between the army ordnance chief Emil Leeb and Walther von Brauchitsch. After the relative failure of the Baedeker Raids of 1942, work on both the flying bomb and the rocket was speeded up with Britain as the target. On 29 September 1943 Albert Speer publicly promised retribution for the bombing of German cities by a secret weapon. A third weapon, the V-3 cannon, was built to fire on London but never did.

Launch sites for the V-1 were built in northern France along the coast from Calais to Le Havre from October 1943, and the first attack on London came on 13 June 1944, a week after the Normandy landings. Of the 9,251 V-1s fired at Britain, 2,515 reached London, killing 6,184 civilians and injuring 17,981. By late August a million and a half people had left the city, though better countermeasures later brought many back.

The first V-2 was fired from near The Hague on 8 September 1944 and struck Chiswick. Arriving faster than sound and without warning, the rockets could hardly be intercepted; one killed 168 people at the Woolworths store in New Cross Road on 25 November 1944. Of the 1,115 V-2s fired at Britain, most at London, they killed an estimated 2,754 people there. V-2s were also fired at Antwerp, to deny the Allies its port, and at Liège: 2,342 V-weapons fell within 16 kilometres of Antwerp alone.

The campaign ended in March 1945; the last V-2 landed in Kent on 27 March, and a V-1 that struck a Hertfordshire field on 29 March was the last enemy action on British soil. In all the V-weapons killed about 18,000 people, mostly civilians. Their effect in lives was smaller than their makers hoped or their victims feared, but at the height of the campaign 20,000 houses a day were damaged, causing a housing crisis in south-east England. Thomas Pynchon's novel Gravity's Rainbow takes the V-2 attack on London as its theme.
vaal-river: The Vaal River rises near Breyten in Mpumalanga, east of Johannesburg and only about 240 kilometres from the Indian Ocean, and flows westwards to meet the Orange River southwest of Kimberley in the Northern Cape. It forms the border between Mpumalanga, Gauteng and North West Province on its north bank and the Free State on its south, and is the longest river wholly within South Africa. Vaal is a Dutch name, later Afrikaans, translated from an earlier Kora Khoekhoe name. Both Vaal and the Khoekhoe ǀHai mean drab or dull, alluding to the colour of its silt-laden waters in flood.

At its height in the mid-19th century the river formed the northern border of Moshoeshoe I's Basotho kingdom, and it then became the boundary between two Boer republics, the South African Republic and the Orange Free State. The name Transvaal means beyond the Vaal, reckoned from the Cape Colony and Natal, the main areas of European settlement, which lay to the south.

The gold rush of the late 19th century drew people to the Witwatersrand, whose growing population first used groundwater from the Zuurbekom Wells before the Vaal became its main source. Private schemes such as the Sivewright Concession of 1887 supplied expensive water. The Rand Water Board, founded in 1903 and fully operating from 1905, took over supply, and its works include the barrage of 1914 to 1924, the Vereeniging Pumping Station of 1924 and the Vaal Dam, completed in 1938.

Because its runoff is erratic, large dams hold its water, and transfer schemes bring more from other catchments: the Tugela-Vaal scheme was completed in 1974, and the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, under a treaty signed on 24 October 1987, was launched in 1997. The river supplies industry in the Greater Johannesburg area and part of the Free State, supports irrigation and serves about 12 million consumers in Gauteng and nearby. About 50 kilometres are navigable, with boating and yachting around Deneysville.
vaballathus: Lucius Julius Aurelius Septimius Vaballathus was born and raised in Palmyra, an oasis settlement in the Syrian Desert, in about 259, the son of the king of kings Odaenathus and his second wife, Zenobia. His name is the Latinized form of the Palmyrene Wahballāt, “Gift of Allāt”. Because the Arabian goddess Allat was identified with Athena, he used Athenodorus as the Greek form. He had a half-brother, Hairan I, who reigned as co-king of kings with their father.

In 267 a relative of his father, perhaps a cousin named Maeonius, murdered Odaenathus and Hairan I. The unreliable Historia Augusta lists Maeonius among the Thirty Tyrants, which is most likely an invention; according to Zonaras he was executed immediately. The succession passed to Vaballathus, who was made king at the age of eight, while his mother Zenobia ruled as regent.

At first the emperor Aurelian recognised him, perhaps because Aurelian was engaged against the Gallic Empire in the west. Early coins issued under Vaballathus’s name acknowledge Aurelian as emperor. The two probably spent most of their reign at Antioch. In October 270 a Palmyrene army of 70,000 invaded Roman Egypt and proclaimed Zenobia queen of Egypt, and the Roman general Tenagino Probus was besieged and killed at the fortress of Babylon by the Palmyrene general Zabdas. In 271 Septimius Zabbai and Zabdas campaigned in Anatolia, subduing Galatia and occupying Ancyra, the farthest extent of Palmyrene expansion. Aurelian then vanished from the coinage, and Zenobia and Vaballathus took the titles Augusta and Augustus.

In 272 Aurelian crossed the Bosporus and advanced through Anatolia while the general Marcus Aurelius Probus regained Egypt. Aurelian defeated Zenobia at the Battle of Immae near Antioch, took Antioch and defeated the Palmyrenes at Emesa. During a siege of Palmyra Zenobia left to seek help from the Sasanian Empire, but the Romans arrested her near the Euphrates, and the city surrendered. Vaballathus, his mother and her council were taken to Emesa and tried; most high officials were executed.

The fates of Zenobia and Vaballathus are uncertain. According to Zosimus, Vaballathus died on the way to Rome, which has been neither confirmed nor disproved. Other sources imply that both were marched in Aurelian’s triumph and then allowed to live, as Aurelian treated the Gallic emperors Tetricus I and II. In 273 a revolt led by Septimius Apsaios proclaimed a relative of Zenobia, Septimius Antiochus, as Augustus, and Aurelian razed Palmyra, ending its ascendancy over Roman Asia Minor.
vaclav-havel: Havel was born in Prague on 5 October 1936 into a wealthy family known in Czechoslovakia for its entrepreneurial and cultural achievements. His grandfather Vácslav Havel built an entertainment complex on Wenceslas Square, and his father, Václav Maria Havel, developed the Barrandov Terraces, beside which his uncle Miloš Havel built one of the largest film studios in Europe. Because of his bourgeois background his educational opportunities were limited under the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. In the early 1950s he began a four-year apprenticeship as a chemical laboratory assistant while taking evening classes at a gymnasium.

After military service from 1957 to 1959, Havel found work in Prague's theatre world, first as a stagehand and then at the Theatre on Balustrade. His first full-length play performed in public was The Garden Party in 1963. In works such as The Garden Party and The Memorandum he used an absurdist style to criticise the communist system.

After the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in August 1968 and the suppression of the Prague Spring he was banned from the theatre and became more politically active. He worked at the Krakonoš brewery in Trutnov, an experience he drew on in his play Audience; it and two other plays featuring the character Ferdinand Vaněk circulated in samizdat. He helped found several dissident initiatives, including Charter 77, came under surveillance by the StB secret police and spent several periods as a political prisoner, the longest nearly four years, between 1979 and 1983.

His Civic Forum played a major role in the Velvet Revolution of 1989. On 29 December 1989 the Federal Assembly voted unanimously to make him President of Czechoslovakia. He had long insisted that change should come through autonomous civic initiatives rather than official institutions. He was re-elected in 1990 and again as the first president of the Czech Republic after Czechoslovakia dissolved on 31 December 1992.

Havel was instrumental in dismantling the Warsaw Pact and in the eastward enlargement of NATO. After leaving office in 2003 he remained a public intellectual, and from 1997 he hosted the annual conference Forum 2000. He died on 18 December 2011 at the age of 75 at his country home in Hrádeček. His political philosophy combined anti-consumerism, humanitarianism, environmentalism, civil activism and direct democracy. The international airport in Prague was renamed Václav Havel Airport Prague in 2012.
vadodara: Vadodara lies on the fertile plain between the Mahi and Narmada rivers in central Gujarat, at an elevation of 39 m. The Vishwamitri river, which frequently dries up in summer, runs through it. The city is the administrative headquarters of Vadodara district. Its name is said to come from the abundance of banyan (vad) trees, and by tradition it is a corrupt form of the Sanskrit vatodara, meaning "in the belly of the banyan tree".

The city was once called Chandanavati after Raja Chandan of the Dod Parmar Rajputs, and its capital was known as Virakshetra, the Land of Warriors. Early English travellers and merchants of the 15th century call the town Baroda, and the official name was changed to Vadodara in 1974.

At Akota, now a suburb, excavations have found microlith deposits showing habitation no later than 1000 BCE. By the first centuries CE Akota, known in antiquity as Aṅkoṭṭaka, was a commercial town with well-built brick houses and far-reaching trade links. It flourished under the Maitraka dynasty, and a large hoard of Jain bronzes, including images of tirthankaras, shows that it was a centre of Jainism. Under the Chaulukya dynasty Vadodara gained importance: a plate dated 1077 mentions a battle on the bank of the Vishvamitri, and by then it was called a pura, or city, and the main centre of Jainism in the area had moved there.

Under the Delhi Sultanate the city was home to Afghan amirs known as the Amir-i Sadgan, who revolted in 1344 against Muhammad bin Tughluq; he defeated them at Bharuch in 1345. Muzaffar Shah I, founder of the Gujarat Sultanate, made his son Firuz Khan governor of Vadodara, and Firuz claimed the throne after 1411 but gave up his claim on being forgiven. After Akbar conquered Gujarat in 1573 he gave Vadodara to Nawab Aurang Khan. In the late 1600s Maratha and Koli raids increased, and Kolis looted the city for two days in 1705.

The 2011 census counted 1,670,806 people in the Vadodara Municipal Corporation, which was founded in 1951, and about 3.5 million in the urban agglomeration. Gujarati is the first language of 71.37 per cent of residents, and Hinduism is the main religion. Vadodara is known as the Cultural City and the City of Art. It has landmarks such as the Laxmi Vilas Palace, the residence of the Maratha Gaekwad dynasty, and the Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda.

Industry grew after oil and natural gas were found in the area, and the Gujarat Refinery, begun in 1963, was the third public-sector refinery in India. The city lies on the main rail and road routes linking Mumbai with Delhi and Ahmedabad.
vaduz-castle: The counts of Werdenberg-Sargans are presumed to have been the builders of the castle, which gave its name to the town of Vaduz, the capital of Liechtenstein, and overlooks it from an adjacent old hilltop. The oldest parts are the bergfried, or keep, built in the 12th century, and parts of the eastern side. The tower stands on ground measuring 12 by 13 metres, and at the ground floor its walls are up to 4 metres thick. The original entrance lay on the courtyard side at a height of 11 metres above the ground.

The chapel of St. Anna was presumably built in the Middle Ages as well, and its main altar is late-gothic. In the Swabian War of 1499 the castle was burned by the Swiss Confederacy. Its western side was later expanded by Count Kaspar von Hohenems, who is dated 1613 to 1640.

The princely family of Liechtenstein acquired Vaduz Castle in 1712, when it purchased the countship of Vaduz. At this time Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, combined the countship with the Lordship of Schellenberg, which the Liechtensteins had purchased in 1699, to form the present Principality of Liechtenstein. The castle was therefore tied to the creation of the state from the start of the family's ownership.

A major restoration took place between 1904 and 1920, and the castle was worked on again in the early 1920s during the reign of Prince Johann II. It was expanded in the early 1930s by Prince Franz Joseph II. Since 1938 it has been the primary residence of the Princely Family, and it is not open to the public because the family still lives there.
vagharshapat: Vagharshapat lies about 18 kilometres west of Yerevan in the basin of the Kasagh River, in the north-eastern end of the Ararat plain, at about 853 metres above sea level. The area was inhabited from the 3rd millennium BCE. The first written record is in the inscriptions of the Urartian king Rusa II, who opened a water canal there, and the most probable site of the ancient city is Shresh Hill near the Kasagh River. According to the 5th-century writer Movses Khorenatsi, the place was first called Artimed and was later rebuilt as Vardgesavan during the reign of King Orontes I.

In the first half of the 2nd century CE the Arsacid king Vagharsh I of Armenia renovated the old town of Vardgesavan and renamed it Vagharshapat. It was the capital of the Arsacid Kingdom of Armenia from 120 to 330. After Armenia adopted Christianity as a state religion in 301, the city became the seat of the Armenian Catholicosate and was gradually called Ejmiatsin, after its Mother Cathedral. The name means the descent of the Only-Begotten, for a vision of Jesus that Gregory the Illuminator had on the spot. The political capital moved to Dvin in 336, and the seat of the Catholicosate followed in 452.

Vagharshapat remained the country's most important city until the fall of the Arsacid Kingdom in 428, and the first manuscript library in Armenia was founded there in 480. Arabs conquered it in 658. It revived briefly under the Bagratid Kingdom, was overrun by the Byzantines in 1045 and by the Seljuks in 1064, and became part of the Ilkhanate in the 13th century. From 1502 to 1828 it was under Persian rule, with short periods of Ottoman rule, and it passed to the Russian Empire by the Treaty of Turkmenchay on 21 February 1828. In 1833 two visitors described it as a village of about 500 mud cabins.

Vagharshapat is the fifth largest city in Armenia and a suburb of Yerevan in effect. It was officially named Echmiatsin from 1945 to 1995 and is still commonly called Ejmiatsin. It is the seat of the Armenian Apostolic Church and is known as Armenia's spiritual capital. In 2000 the churches of Vagharshapat and the ruins of Zvartnots Cathedral were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Etchmiadzin Cathedral was built in 301 to 303 and enlarged in 480, 618 and 1658. The Churches of Saint Hripsime, built in 618, and Saint Gayane, built in 630, also stand there.
vaisakhi: Vaisakhi, also known as Baisakhi, marks the first day of the month of Vaisakh and is traditionally observed on 13 or 14 April. It is a spring harvest festival, primarily in Punjab and northern India, and the date of the Indian solar new year. The word derives from the name of the month Vaishakha. Historically it was one of the major annual market occasions in northern India. It began as a grain harvest festival for Hindus, and its observance predates the creation of Sikhism, but it gained a historical association with the Sikhs after the inauguration of the Khalsa.

Many Hindus bathe in sacred rivers such as the Ganges, Jhelum and Kaveri, because they believe the river goddess Ganga descended to earth on this day, and they visit temples and give charity. One of the largest fairs in India is at Haridwar, where around 5 million pilgrims bathe at Brahm Kund. For Sikhs it marks the birth of the Khalsa order, founded by Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, on 13 April 1699, and is called Khalsa Sajna Diwas. Sikhs hold kirtans, visit gurdwaras, hold nagar kirtan processions and raise the Nishan Sahib flag, with special celebrations at Anandpur Sahib, Talwandi Sabo and the Golden Temple in Amritsar.

Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja of the Sikh Empire in April 1801, timed to coincide with Vaisakhi, creating a unified political state. Vaisakhi was also the day on which the British Indian Army officer Reginald Dyer ordered his troops to fire into a protesting crowd in Amritsar, the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, which proved influential to the history of the Indian independence movement. In western Punjab, Muslims used to observe it as a harvest festival, but the policies of Zia-ul-Haq led to the end of that observance. Pilgrims visit Sikh sites in Pakistan such as Panja Sahib, and in Vancouver a parade first held in 1979 attracts up to 300,000 people.
vaishnava-jana-to: The poem is a pad, a compact lyric that turns on a refrain sung back by a group, and it is written in Gujarati, the language people of the region spoke, rather than Sanskrit. It is missing from the earliest 17th-century manuscript collections of Narsinh Mehta's lyrics. The oldest known manuscript containing it, at the B. J. Institute in Ahmedabad, is dated 1835, though K. K. Shastri reported examining an early 18th-century one. A 19th-century claim that the poet Dalpatram wrote it was dismissed by comparing that manuscript's date with the start of his literary career.

The poem defines a Vaishnava, a devotee of Vishnu, by conduct alone: empathy for the pain of others, honesty, restraint, humility, freedom from greed and lust, detachment from possessions and devotion to God, with no test of caste, community or gender. The scholar Shukla-Bhatt stresses that it ties empathy to a duty to relieve suffering without pride. Steven Rosen reads it as expressing jīva-dayā, actively doing good to others, and Charlotte Vaudeville as a lay ideal of sanctity.

Gandhi made the poem central to his spiritual practice. It was sung daily at his ashrams, during the Salt March in 1930, during his fasts and at Kasturba Gandhi's cremation in 1944, and its opening stanza stands on the title page of the Ashram Bhajanavali. He said that even if he forgot the Bhagavad Gita this hymn would keep him going, and in his weekly Navajivan he cited it against untouchability, arguing that a Vaishnava is defined by non-violence and sympathy, not caste.

The tune now familiar is not the traditional morning setting. Narayan Khare, musician at the Sabarmati ashram, set it in the 1920s in Mishra Khamaj, an evening raga, to carry it beyond Gujarat. It closes Vijay Bhatt's film Narsi Bhagat of 1940 and Richard Attenborough's Gandhi, entered the concert repertoire of M. S. Subbulakshmi, and has been performed as qawwali and in hip-hop.
vaishnavism: The early emergence of Vaishnavism is unclear, and the evidence is scanty. In the Rig Veda Vishnu is a benevolent solar deity mentioned in only a few hymns. Scholars hypothesise that various regional non-Vedic religions, particularly the Bhagavata cults of Vāsudeva-Krishna and Gopala-Krishna and the Pancaratra cult of Narayana, fused with one another and with the worship of Vishnu.

The tradition took its settled form when it developed the doctrine of avatars, in which the different non-Vedic deities are revered as distinct incarnations of the one supreme god Vishnu. The earliest scriptural evidence of Vaishnava bhagavatas is an inscription of 115 BCE, in which Heliodoros, ambassador of the Greco-Bactrian king Amtalikita, calls himself a bhagavata of Vasudeva.

Most of the Gupta kings, beginning with Chandragupta II, were known as Parama Bhagavatas. After the Alchon Huns invaded around 500 CE the Gupta Empire fragmented and collapsed, and the new regional powers of central and northern India, such as the Maukharis and the Vardhanas, preferred Shaivism. Vaishnavism remained strong mainly in South India and Kashmir. The Alvars, poet-saints whose name means those immersed in God, travelled singing the praises of Vishnu and established temple sites such as Srirangam. Their poems were compiled as the Divya Prabhandham.

The Bhakti movement began among Vaishnavas of South India in the 7th century, spread north through Karnataka and Maharashtra, and was widely accepted across India by the 15th century. Vaishnava sampradayas grew under teachers such as Ramanuja, Nimbarka, Madhva and Vallabha, and bhakti poets and teachers such as Namdev, Ramananda, Surdas, Tulsidas and Chaitanya Mahaprabhu extended its reach. These teachers rejected Shankara's Advaita Vedanta and built their theology on the devotion of the Alvars. The ISKCON movement, founded by A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada in 1966, spread Vaishnavism widely beyond India.

Vaishnavism centres on devotion to Vishnu and his avatars, among them Rama and Krishna. Its teaching is that his avatars descend to empower the good and fight evil, restoring dharma. Its texts include the Vedas, the Upanishads, the Bhagavad Gita, the Pancharatra texts, the Divya Prabhandham and the Bhagavata Purana, and the epics Ramayana and Mahabharata carry its philosophy in stories. Its traditions are grouped in four sampradayas, which emerged in the early centuries of the 2nd millennium CE.

They are the Sri Sampradaya of Ramanuja, the Brahma Sampradaya of Madhvacharya, the Rudra Sampradaya of Vishnuswami and Vallabhacharya, and the Kumaras Sampradaya of Nimbarka. Their philosophies range from the qualified non-dualism of Ramanuja to the dualism of Madhva. Vaishnavas mark the forehead with a tilaka of sandalwood paste, each sampradaya in its own style, and an initiate receives a mantra from a guru to repeat as japa. Pilgrimage sites include Srirangam, Tirupati, Vrindavan, Mathura, Ayodhya and Puri.
vaison-la-romaine: Vaison-la-Romaine lies in the Vaucluse department, in the Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur region. The Roman ruins stand in the valley on the banks of the Ouvèze, which is crossed by a Roman bridge of the 1st century CE, while the medieval town stands high on a rocky hill. The area was inhabited in the Bronze Age. At the end of the 4th century BCE Vaison became the capital of a Celtic tribe, the Vocontii, centred on the oppidum in the upper city.

After the Roman conquest of 125–118 BCE in the wars against the Salyes, the Vocontii kept a degree of autonomy. They had two capitals, Luc-en-Diois, apparently the religious centre, and Vaison, named Vasio Julia Vocontiorum. Early building was probably done by Vocontian aristocrats who moved down from the oppidum and set their houses along the river. Large public monuments, including a theatre, a bridge, aqueducts and thermal baths, were begun in the second half of the 1st century. The city was at its finest in the 2nd century, when it covered up to 75 hectares and was one of the richest in Gallia Narbonensis.

Pillaging and burning in 276 were followed by recovery. A bishopric existed from the 4th century, and councils met there in 442 and 529. Invasions by the Burgundians in the 5th century ruined the city, and the theatre's benches began to be reused as Christian tombstones. Vaison was taken by the Ostrogoths in 527 and by Chlothar I, King of the Franks, in 545. In the 12th century the counts of Provence, who had refortified the upper town, quarrelled with the bishops, each of whom held half the town, until a treaty of 1251 negotiated by the future Pope Clement IV. From the 18th century most of the population moved back down to the plain by the river.

The Roman ruins lie in two main areas, La Villasse and Puymin. Several large town houses have been excavated, among them the House of the Dolphin, the House of the Laurelled Apollo, the House of the Arbour and the House of the Peacock, which must have belonged to Vocontian aristocrats who owned estates in the region. The apse of the Church of St. Quenin seems to date from the 8th century. A market authorized by Pope Sixtus IV in 1483 is still held on Tuesdays.
vajiravudh: Vajiravudh was the son of King Chulalongkorn and the queen Saovabha Phongsri. He was first taught in the royal palace in Thai and English. In late 1893 his father, prompted by the Franco-Siamese crisis and a wish to modernise Siam's army and navy, sent him to Britain to study military science. After the death of his half-brother Crown Prince Vajirunhis in January 1895 he became crown prince. He studied at the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, was commissioned as a captain in the Durham Light Infantry, and read law and history at Christ Church, Oxford, though appendicitis kept him from graduating in 1901. In 1902 he represented his father at the coronation of King Edward VII. He returned to Siam in 1903.

Vajiravudh succeeded on 23 October 1910 and was crowned formally on 28 November 1911, with royal guests from Europe and Japan. His first act was to found the Royal Pages College, a boarding school on the model of Eton and Harrow, in place of a royal monastery. He set up the Wild Tiger Corps in 1911, a paramilitary force outside the army that grew to 4,000 men in a year and angered army officers. He changed the era of the calendar to the Buddhist Era in 1912 and in 1917 founded Chulalongkorn University, the first university in Siam. A plot by young officers to overthrow the monarchy, planned for 1 April, was uncovered; he commuted the death sentences and released several plotters.

On 22 July 1917 he declared war on Germany and Austria-Hungary, and he used the war to promote Siamese nationalism, replacing the elephant flag with a tricolour. Siamese troops reached Europe late in the war and did little fighting, but participation opened the way to revising the unequal treaties of the 19th century. Rice shortages, a silver crisis and loans from Britain strained the treasury, and in 1925 he dissolved the Nakorn Sri Thammarat Regiment and merged provinces to cut costs. He also wrote plays, novels and translations, among them three Shakespeare plays.

In 1924 Vajiravudh promulgated the Law of Succession, which became the code for later Chakri successions. He fell ill in November 1925, and died on 26 November, about two hours after his only child, Princess Bejaratana, was born to Suvadhana. The throne passed to his brother Prajadhipok. Some writers regard him as the father of Thai nationalism, which Phibunsongkhram and Sarit Thanarat later built upon, while others see that view as a later political construct. He also introduced the use of the name Rama for the Chakri kings.
vajrayana: Vajrayana means the Diamond Vehicle or Thunderbolt Vehicle; it is also called Mantrayana, Tantrayana and Indo-Tibetan Buddhism. In medieval India the first terms for it were Mantranaya and Mantrayana. According to David B. Gray, it grew out of tantric traditions that had emerged within Hinduism in the first millennium CE and strongly influenced Mahayana Buddhism in South Asia. Alexis Sanderson holds that its literature developed as royal courts sponsored both Buddhism and Shaivism. The tradition is associated with wandering yogis called mahasiddhas, who used methods very different from those of the monasteries, including practice on charnel grounds. Tibetan tradition holds that the Buddha taught the tantras to a few people only.

Vajrayana rests on the philosophy of the Madhyamaka and Yogacara schools of Mahayana Buddhism, and it keeps the aim of becoming a fully awakened Buddha for the benefit of all beings. It claims that its methods give a faster path to that goal. They include mantras, mandalas, mudras, the visualisation of deities and rituals such as the goma fire ritual. Its central practice is deity yoga, meditation on a chosen deity, and the tradition also knows formless practices such as Mahamudra and Dzogchen.

Teachings pass from teacher to student through initiation, and the guide, a lama or vajracharya, is considered indispensable. Practitioners keep tantric vows called samaya. Some rituals traditionally used taboo substances such as blood and alcohol, which are related to the non-dual nature of a Buddha's wisdom, and some of these are now replaced by milder ones such as yogurt. The vajra, a thunderbolt weapon of the god Indra, stands for the indestructible nature of things.

Tantric teaching reached Tang China in the first half of the 7th century, and the masters Subhakarasimha, Vajrabodhi and Amoghavajra translated texts and founded the Zhenyan tradition. In Japan it lives on in the Shingon and Tendai schools. Tibet adopted Vajrayana on a full scale after the Samye debate, in which the Indian scholar Kamalasila defeated the Chan scholar Moheyan. Bengal under the Pala dynasty was a thriving centre, and Atisa helped to revive Buddhism in Tibet. Srivijaya was a major centre of esoteric learning, and the Borobudur complex reflects tantric or proto-tantric influence. Today Vajrayana exists chiefly as Indo-Tibetan Buddhism and Japanese Esoteric Buddhism, and Newar Buddhism in Nepal preserves many Sanskrit tantric texts.
vakataka-dynasty: The Vakatakas are believed to have ruled a state that stretched from the southern edges of Malwa and Gujarat in the north to the Tungabhadra River in the south, and from the Arabian Sea in the west to the edges of Chhattisgarh in the east. Scholars disagree about where the family began. Ramaprasad Chanda pointed to an inscription at Amaravati, dated to around the middle of the third century CE, that mentions a householder named Vakataka, and V. V. Mirashi developed this into a theory of a Deccan origin.

Ajay Mitra Shastri instead placed the homeland in the Vindhya region, on the evidence of Puranic traditions. The epigraphist K. V. Ramesh argues that the name is a Sanskritisation of a local place-name meaning forest, and that the family was of local, non-Brahmin origin.

Almost nothing is known of the founder Vindhyashakti. The Ajanta inscription of Cave XVI calls him the banner of the Vakataka family and says he added to his power by fighting great battles and had a large cavalry. His son Pravarasena I was the first Vakataka ruler to call himself Samrat, or universal ruler, and he fought wars with the Naga kings. He performed several Vedic sacrifices, including four horse sacrifices.

According to the Puranas he had four sons, and it is generally believed that the family then split into four branches, of which only two are known: the Pravarapura-Nandivardhana branch, which kept marriage ties with the Imperial Guptas, and the Vatsagulma branch, founded by his son Sarvasena, with its capital at Vatsagulma, the present Washim.

The Gupta emperor Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavatigupta into the Nandivardhana branch, and after the early death of her husband Rudrasena II she acted as regent for her two sons. Her son Pravarasena II composed the Setubandha in Maharashtri Prakrit, founded a new capital at Pravarapura and left the largest number of copperplate grants of any Vakataka ruler, seventeen in all. The Vatsagulma king Harishena, who reigned c. 475–500, is said by the Ajanta inscription to have conquered Avanti, Kosala, Kalinga, Andhra, Lata, Trikuta and Kuntala.

Under Harishena, caves XVI, XVII and XIX at Ajanta, two viharas and a chaitya, were excavated and decorated with painting and sculpture, and the art historian Walter M. Spink attributes most of the rock-cut monuments of Ajanta to his reign.

The end of the dynasty is unknown. Two further rulers followed Harishena, and the Kalachuri of Mahismati probably defeated them. Dandin's Dashakumaracharita, written about 125 years after the fall, tells of a son of Harishena who gave himself up to pleasure and was killed in a battle on the Wardha, while a Kadamba record suggests that the Kadambas annexed the kingdom. No Vakataka coins have been found.
vakhsh-river: The Vakhsh is a Central Asian river and one of the main rivers of Tajikistan, known also as the Surkhob in north-central Tajikistan and as the Kyzyl-Suu in Kyrgyzstan. It flows through the Pamirs, through very mountainous territory that often confines it to narrow channels within deep gorges. Some of the largest glaciers in Tajikistan, including the Fedchenko and Abramov glaciers, drain into it, the Fedchenko being the longest glacier in the world outside the polar regions. Its largest tributaries are the Muksu and the Obikhingou.

After leaving the Pamirs the river crosses the fertile lowlands of south-western Tajikistan and ends by flowing into the Panj, on the border of Tajikistan and Afghanistan, to form the Amu Darya. Its catchment area is 39,100 square kilometres, and it contributes about 25% of the Amu Darya's flow. Because it is fed mostly by melting snow and glaciers, its flow varies greatly with the season: winter flow averages around 150 cubic metres per second, while summer flow can exceed 1,500.

Soviet leaders stressed the development of under-developed regions such as the Tajik Soviet Socialist Republic, and strategic aims added weight to this, especially in the Second World War, when industry was evacuated eastward from the German front. Industry was to be fuelled by Tajikistan's hydropower. The Vakhsh Valley Canal Project, completed in 1933, expanded farmland along the lower reaches before any dam existed.

Dam building began only in the 1950s. The Perepadnaya power station was commissioned in 1959 and the Golovnaya Dam in 1963. The Nurek Dam was built between 1961 and 1980, and the Baipaza Dam was completed in 1983. Transmission lines over the Pamirs would have been prohibitively expensive, so the Soviet Union built industries near the dams, among them the Tajik Aluminum Company plant, chemical plants, nitrogen fertilizer factories and cotton gins. Reservoirs also supplied irrigation for cotton, vineyards and orchards, and in the 1960s tunnels carried water to other valleys.

Five dams stand on the river: the Nurek, the second tallest in the world, with the Baipaza, Sangtuda 1, Sangtuda 2 and Golovnaya downstream. Hydroelectricity powers aluminium production at Tursunzoda. About 85% of the water taken from the Vakhsh goes to irrigation. The Tigrovaya Balka Nature Reserve, at the confluence of the Vakhsh and the Panj, was the last habitat of the now-extinct Caspian tiger in the former USSR.

In the Soviet system the upstream republic released water in summer and exported power to the downstream republics of Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan along the Amu Darya, which supplied oil and gas in winter. Intensive agriculture has left the river polluted with fertilizers, pesticides and salts.
vakhtang-i-of-iberia: Vakhtang I Gorgasali, of the Chosroid dynasty, was king of Iberia, known natively as Kartli, in eastern Georgia. Dating his reign is problematic, and scholars give different years. The main source is the Life of Vakhtang Gorgasali, a vita attributed to Juansher, which mixes history and legend into an epic narrative. According to it, he succeeded his father Mihrdat V at the age of seven, with his mother Sagdukht, a Christianized Persian Sagdukht as regent, and at sixteen led a victorious war against the Ossetians. He later took part in the campaigns of the Great King against the Hephthalites and against the Roman Empire.

Resenting Iranian encroachment, Vakhtang turned towards the Roman government and married Helena, said to be a daughter or relative of Emperor Zeno. With Constantinople's permission he raised the bishop of Mtskheta to the rank of catholicos and sent him with twelve new bishops to be consecrated at Antioch, over the opposition of the deposed bishop Mikel. His pro-Roman policy alienated nobles who sought Iranian support. In 482 he executed his powerful vassal Varsken of Gogarene, who had put to death his Christian wife Shushanik, and so confronted his Iranian suzerain.

With Armenian princes under Vahan Mamikonian he fought Iranian forces, but the allies were routed and Iranian punitive expeditions ravaged Iberia in 483 and 484, forcing him to flee to Lazica. Peace was restored after the death of Peroz, and Vakhtang resumed his reign. Later, when Kavadh I summoned him to join a campaign against Rome, he refused and Iranian forces invaded. At about sixty he spent his last years in war and exile, appealing in vain for Roman help. According to the Life he was shot by a renegade slave through a gap in his armour and was buried at the cathedral of Mtskheta.

His eldest son Dachi succeeded him and returned to Iranian allegiance, while Leon and Mihrdat received provinces in the south-west, where Leon's descendants, the Guaramids, kept a pro-Roman orientation. Vakhtang became one of the most popular figures in Georgian history, the subject of folk poems and legends about his strength and piety, and the Georgian Orthodox Church canonised him as a saint. Tradition credits him with founding Tbilisi after his falcon chased a pheasant into a hot spring, and a monument of 1967 by Elguja Amashukeli stands on the Metekhi cliff above the city.
vakhtang-vi-of-kartli: Vakhtang VI, of the royal Bagrationi dynasty, was born on 15 September 1675, the son of Prince Levan. From 1703 to 1714 he ruled as regent for his absent uncle George XI and his brother Kaikhosro. In those years he launched reforms, revived the economy and culture, reorganised the administration and tried to strengthen royal authority. In 1707 to 1709 he substantially revised the legal code, known as Vakhtang’s code, which served as a basis of the Georgian feudal system until the Russian annexation.

In 1712 Shah Husayn summoned Vakhtang to be confirmed as ruler of Kartli but required him to become a Muslim. He refused and was imprisoned, and his brother Jesse, who complied, was put in his place in 1714. In captivity Vakhtang sought help from Christian monarchs, sending his uncle Sulkhan-Saba Orbeliani to Louis XIV of France. When this failed he reluctantly converted in 1716, taking the name Husayn-Qoli Khan, and was appointed commander-in-chief of the Persian armies. After seven years in Persia he returned in 1719 to stop raids by the Lezgin tribes of Dagestan, and made progress until the Persian government recalled him in the winter of 1721.

He then made secret contact with Tsar Peter the Great, who led an army down the Caspian in July 1722. In September Vakhtang encamped at Ganja with a Georgian-Armenian army of 40,000 to join him, but Peter fell ill and returned to Russia. Abandoned, Vakhtang went back to Tbilisi. The shah authorised Constantine II of Kakheti to take Kartli, and in May 1723 Constantine marched in. Vakhtang was expelled and submitted to the Ottomans, who instead gave the throne to Jesse. In the invasions by Turkey, Persia, Dagestanis and Afghans, three-fourths of the population of Georgia was destroyed.

In July 1724 Vakhtang crossed the Caucasus to Russia with his family and a retinue of 1,200. Peter had died, and his successor Catherine I gave no real help but granted a pension and estates. In 1734 he set out to recover his lands with the cooperation of the shah, but fell ill on the way and died at Astrakhan on 26 March 1737.

His political choices have sometimes been criticised, but his scholarly work is regarded as the crowning merit of his reign. In 1709 he founded the first printing press in Georgia and the Caucasus, which printed Shota Rustaveli’s The Knight in the Panther’s Skin with his own commentary, and the Gospels, Acts and Psalms. He translated the fables Kalila and Demna from Persian, and chaired a commission that compiled the Georgian chronicles. Among his descendants was Pyotr Bagration.
val-daran: Aran is an autonomous administrative entity, formerly counted as a comarca, in northwest Catalonia in the Pyrenees, in the province of Lleida, with an area of 620.47 square kilometres. Its capital is Vielha e Mijaran. It is the only contiguous part of Catalonia on the northern side of the Pyrenees, so it holds the only Catalan rivers that flow into the Atlantic, and its climate is Atlantic rather than Mediterranean. The Garonne rises on the Pla de Beret near the Port de la Bonaigua, while the Noguera Pallaresa, whose source is only a hundred metres away, flows the opposite way to the Mediterranean. The name comes from Basque haran, meaning valley.

In 1313 James II of Aragon granted the valley administrative and political autonomy, whose legal details are set out in a Latin manuscript called the Querimonia. It was a reward for the Aranese pledging allegiance to him in a dispute with the kingdoms of France and Mallorca over control of the valley. In 1411 the Catalan parliament confirmed it as part of the Principality of Catalonia at the request of the Syndic of Aran. This status survived the Nueva Planta decrees of 1707 to 1716 but was suppressed in 1834, when the valley was joined to the new Province of Lleida.

On 19 October 1944 guerrillas of the Communist Party of Spain invaded the valley to try to bring down the Spanish dictatorship. They held several villages until 27 October, when they withdrew to France after Franco sent reinforcements to Vielha. Until the Vielha tunnel opened in 1948, the valley had no direct winter link to the south side of the mountains.

Aranese is the standardised form of the local Gascon variety of Occitan, and has been taught regularly in schools since 1984. In 1990 the Parliament of Catalonia restored Aran's special status, reestablishing the Conselh Generau, granting a degree of home rule and declaring Occitan an official language. A law of 2015 increased the council's powers and recognised Aran as an Occitan national reality. The valley is divided into six terçons, meaning thirds, an arrangement dating from the 15th century, and is headed by the Síndic d'Aran. Its main economic activity is tourism, based on winter ski resorts and summer visitors.
val-di-chiana: The Val di Chiana, formerly the Clanis Valley, is a tectonic valley of central Italy in the provinces of Arezzo and Siena in Tuscany and of Perugia and Terni in Umbria. It runs about 104 kilometres from north to south between the plains of Arezzo and Orvieto, with a valley floor of about 2,300 square kilometres and a mean elevation of around 405 metres. It is bounded to the north-east by the Tuscan pre-Apennines, reaches Lake Trasimeno to the south-east and rises to 1,148 metres on Monte Cetona in the west.

The valley formed mainly in the Miocene and was later almost entirely submerged by the Pliocene sea. About 150,000 years ago the Arno, which had drained part of it, found its present course towards Florence. Since 1780 the watershed has lain at Chiusi Scalo, dividing a Tuscan part, drained to the Arno by the Canale Maestro della Chiana, from a Roman part drained to the Tiber by the Chiani.

The Clanis, a tributary of the Tiber, was navigable, and the ancient Italic peoples and the Etruscans used it to reach Rome and the Tyrrhenian Sea; Pliny the Elder wrote of the valley's beauty and its farming. Boats could travel from Arezzo to the Tiber until the middle of the 11th century, when a great dam built in 1052–1055 in the Orvieto area, on the orders of the Holy Roman Emperor and Pope Leo IX, flooded the valley.

In 1338 the Republic of Florence ordered the people of Arezzo to cut a canal through the rock to drain the resulting lake towards the Arno, though the mills of the Arezzo monastery of Ss. Flora and Lucilla held back the outflow with a dam 12 metres high. Leonardo da Vinci drew a map of the lake, and Goethe later praised the tilled fields of the valley in his Italian Journey. Human works have since made the valley floor flat and raised it by several metres.

The valley is known for its local products, among them Chianina cattle, the original ingredient of the Bistecca alla Fiorentina, the giant garlic Aglione della Valdichiana, a DOP product since 2019, and the wines Vinsanto and Grechetto Valdichiana Toscana DOC.
val-dossola: The Ossola lies north of Lago Maggiore and is made up of the main valley, the Ossola proper, and its side valleys, among them Anzasca, Antrona, Bognanco, Divedro, Antigorio, Formazza, Isorno and Vigezzo. The Pennine Alps close it to the west and the Lepontine Alps to the north and east. Its highest point is the Nordend, a peak of the Monte Rosa Massif and the highest summit of Piedmont; other important mountains are the Pizzo d'Andolla, the Monte Leone and the Corno Cieco.
The name has been explained in many ways, most likely as Celtic for high lands. The valley's German name, Eschental, and its Walser name, Eschetaal, mean valley of the ash trees.

In 1944, with the Allies held south of the Apennines and Benito Mussolini's Italian Social Republic in control of all Northern Italy, Italian partisans led by the Committee of National Liberation of Upper Italy rose behind the German lines. The rising produced several provisional partisan governments across Northern Italy, of which the Free Republic of Ossola was the most prominent. It was officially recognised by Switzerland and by Allied consulates there. Within a few weeks German reinforcements crushed the uprising, and the valley was not freed until the final offensives of 1945.

The Ossola belongs to the Province of Verbano-Cusio-Ossola in the region of Piedmont. Besides Domodossola its main towns are Villadossola, Crevoladossola, Ornavasso and Mergozzo. It holds the Alpe Veglia and Alpe Devero Natural Park and the Alta Valle Antrona Natural Park, and part of the Val Grande National Park, the largest wilderness area in Italy.
valais: Valais is essentially coextensive with the valley of the Rhône from its headwaters to Lake Geneva, between the Pennine Alps and the Bernese Alps. It borders Vaud and Bern to the north, Uri and Ticino to the east, Italy to the south and France to the west. The canton is traditionally divided into Lower, Central and Upper Valais. The French-speaking Lower and Central regions are more populous, while Upper Valais is German-speaking, with the linguistic border at Pfynwald. It is among the driest regions of Switzerland in its central valley and also has some of the snowiest peaks, such as Monte Rosa and the Finsteraarhorn.

The Romans called the upper Rhône valley Vallis Poenina and conquered it after the Battle of Octodurus, now Martigny, in 57 BCE. A tradition traced to the middle of the 8th century holds that the Theban legion was martyred at Agaunum, now Saint-Maurice, around 285 or 302. From 888 the land belonged to the kingdom of Transjurane Burgundy, which passed to the Holy Roman Empire in 1032.

In 999 King Rudolph III of Burgundy gave all temporal rights and privileges to the Bishop of Sion, who was later styled prefect and count of Valais. The count-bishops struggled to defend their territory against the house of Zähringen and then the dukes of Savoy, so that medieval Valais is closely bound up with the history of the diocese of Sion. Savoy won most of the land west of Sion, Lower Valais, while Upper Valais was held by many feudal lords, among them the lords of Raron and the counts of Visp.

Valais became an associate member of the Swiss Confederation in 1529. It resisted the Protestant Reformation and stayed Roman Catholic, and in 1628 it became a republic under the guidance of the prince-bishop of Sion. It entered the Confederation fully as a canton in 1815. The Simplon Railway reached it in 1878 and the Lötschberg Railway in 1913.

Sion is the capital and largest city, and French and German are the official languages. The wine industry is the largest in Switzerland, with vineyards on terraces above the Rhône, and water from the glaciers is carried to the fields in small channels called bisses or Suonen. Hydroelectric plants, including the Grande Dixence dam, supply a large share of Swiss electricity, and the resorts of Zermatt, Verbier and Saas-Fee draw many visitors. Monuments include the Valère Basilica and the territorial Abbey of Saint-Maurice, which dates from the 6th century.
valdemar-i-of-denmark: Valdemar was born on 14 January 1131, the son of Canute Lavard, Duke of Schleswig, who was murdered by Magnus Nielsen days before his birth. His mother, Ingeborg of Kiev, named him after her grandfather, Grand Prince Vladimir Monomakh. He was raised at Ringsted in the household of the nobleman Asser Rig, together with Asser's sons Absalon, later an archbishop, and Esbern Snare, later royal chancellor. The two became his foster brothers, and Absalon and Valdemar swore blood brotherhood, as their fathers had.

In 1146 King Eric III abdicated and civil war broke out. Valdemar contended with Sweyn III Grathe and Canute V, and joined Canute to be recognised as co-king. In July 1157 the three agreed to divide the country. Canute was killed at the Bloodfeast of Roskilde in August 1157, and Valdemar defeated Sweyn at the Battle of Grathe Heath on 23 October 1157, after which he was the sole king.

In 1158 Absalon became bishop of Roskilde and Valdemar's chief adviser. The king rebuilt war-torn Denmark, strengthened the Dannevirke and built Sønderborg Castle. At Absalon's urging he made war on the Wends, who were raiding the Danish coasts and who outnumbered the Danes more than two to one. Using ships that carried cavalry, the Danes conquered Rügen, and their influence reached Pomerania and the Obotrite confederacy. In 1175 Valdemar built Vordingborg Castle as a base for raids on the German coast.

In 1180 the people of Scania rose, demanding governors from their own province and refusing taxes and tithes. Valdemar crushed them at the Battle of Dysiaa, but conceded that Scanians should replace the governors from Jutland, and he had them make gifts to the church instead of tithes.

Valdemar died on 12 May 1182. His reign saw the rise of Denmark, which reached its medieval height under his son Valdemar II. His son Canute VI improved his use of amphibious assault. By his wife Sophia of Minsk he had nine children; his daughter Ingeborg married King Philip II of France.
valdemar-ii-of-denmark: Valdemar was the second son of King Valdemar I of Denmark and Sophia of Polotsk. He was 12 when his father died, and he was named duke of Southern Jutland. His regent, Bishop Valdemar Knudsen, an illegitimate son of King Canute V, plotted after becoming archbishop of Bremen in 1192 to overthrow Valdemar's elder brother, King Canute VI, with German help. Duke Valdemar invited him to Aabenraa and the bishop fled to Norway. In 1193 King Canute VI captured him, and he stayed in captivity until 1206. Duke Valdemar then defeated and captured Count Adolf III of Holstein at the Battle of Stellau in 1201. In November 1202 Canute VI died childless.

Valdemar was proclaimed king at the Jutland Assembly. The Holy Roman Empire was torn between Otto IV of the House of Guelf and King Philip of the House of Hohenstaufen, and Valdemar allied himself with Otto against Philip. He conquered Lybeck and Holstein early in his reign. His support for a pretender to the Norwegian throne, Erling Steinvegg, led to the second Bagler War, which lasted until 1208 and left the Norwegian king owing allegiance to Denmark.

In 1219 the Livonian Knights, hard pressed in the eastern Baltic, turned to him, and Pope Honorius III made his invasion of Estonia a crusade. The Estonian chiefs agreed to accept him as overlord, but on 15 June 1219 thousands of Estonians broke into the Danish camp during mass. Vitslav of Rügen attacked them from the rear, and the Danes won the Battle of Lindanise. Legend says that a red banner with a white cross, the Dannebrog, fell from the sky. Valdemar ordered a fortress built at Reval, around which the city of Tallinn grew.

In 1223 Count Henry I of Schwerin abducted Valdemar and his eldest son while hunting on the island of Lyø. To secure his release Valdemar had to acknowledge the German territories that had broken away and pay 44,000 silver marks. The pope voided his oath, but a series of defeats ending at the Battle of Bornhöved on 22 July 1227 confirmed the loss of Denmark's north German lands.

Valdemar then turned to domestic affairs. He instituted a feudal system, which increased the power of the noble families. He had laws gathered for Jutland, Zealand and Skåne, which were Denmark's legal code until 1683 and outlawed trial by ordeal and trial by combat. The Code of Jutland was approved at Vordingborg Castle in 1241, shortly before Valdemar died there on 28 March 1241. He was buried next to his first wife, Queen Dagmar, at Ringsted. Since 1912 15 June has officially been Valdemarsdag, one of Denmark's flag days.
valdemar-iv-of-denmark: Valdemar was the youngest son of King Christopher II of Denmark and Euphemia of Pomerania. After his father's defeats and the death and imprisonment of his older brothers at the hands of the Holsteiners, he spent his youth in exile at the court of Emperor Louis IV in Bavaria, acting as a pretender. After Niels Ebbesen and his warriors assassinated Gerhard III, Count of Holstein-Rendsburg, Valdemar was proclaimed king at the Viborg Assembly on 24 June 1340. Through his marriage to Helvig of Schleswig he controlled about a quarter of Jutland north of the Kongeå.

Under Christopher II Denmark had gone bankrupt and been mortgaged out in parcels. Valdemar paid off the mortgage on the rest of northern Jutland with taxes from peasants above the Kongeå, and in 1344 he recovered North Friesland. The bishop of Roskilde gave him Copenhagen Castle and town, and he was the first Danish king to rule from Copenhagen. For 19,000 marks he gave up Danish Estonia to the Teutonic Knights, to pay mortgages on more important parts of Denmark. In 1346 he took back Vordingborg Castle, headquarters of the Holsteiners, and by 1347 he had thrown out the Germans.

In 1349 the Black Death arrived, and general figures for 1349 to 1350 range between 33 and 66 percent of the people of Denmark. Valdemar refused to reduce taxes the following year though fewer peasants farmed less land, and uprisings flared in the following years. In 1360 he forced King Magnus of Sweden to give up Helsingborg and for all intents regained Scania, also capturing Halland and Blekinge.

In 1361 Valdemar invaded Gotland and defeated the Gotlanders in front of Visby, killing 1800 men. Visby belonged to the Hanseatic League, and in 1362 the Hansa states, Sweden and Norway allied against him. They captured and pillaged Copenhagen and, with rebellious nobles in Jutland, forced him out of Denmark at Easter in 1368. He signed the Treaty of Stralsund in 1370, acknowledging the Hansa's rights in the herring trade and its tax exemptions, and returned to Denmark after four years.

Valdemar died at Gurre Castle in North Zealand on 24 October 1375 and was buried at Sorø Abbey. His heavy taxation and his usurpation of rights long held by noble families led to uprisings throughout his reign, and the great landed families of Jutland opposed him bitterly. He expanded royal power on the basis of his military prowess and a loyal nobility that became the foundation of Danish rulers until 1440. His grandson Olaf II, son of his daughter Margaret and Haakon VI of Norway, was elected as his successor.
valdivia: Valdivia stands in southern Chile where the Calle-Calle, Cau-Cau and Cruces rivers join to form the Valdivia River, which reaches the Pacific at Corral Bay about 15 km to the west. The city was built on a river terrace of hardened volcanic sand and later spread over adjoining wetlands. The river network made it a trade centre even before the Spanish arrived. It lies in a depression in the Chilean Coast Range, where the Nazca Plate is subducted beneath the South American Plate. Archaeological discoveries at Monte Verde, less than 200 km to the south, suggest that people lived in the region from about 12,000 to 11,800 BCE.

The first European to visit the estuary was the Genoese captain Juan Bautista Pastene, who took possession of it in 1544 in the name of Charles V and named the river after Pedro de Valdivia, Governor of Chile. In the 17th century the Dutch, at war with Spain, planned a base there to attack the Viceroy of Peru. Hendrik Brouwer died on 7 August 1643 before he reached Valdivia, and Elias Herckman occupied its ruins that year and renamed it Brouwershaven. The Dutch found no gold, and the hostility of the native people forced them to leave on 28 October 1643.

In 1645 the Viceroy of Peru, Pedro Álvarez de Toledo y Leiva, repopulated and fortified the city, sending seventeen ships filled with building materials and supplies. Chile could not secure it, being at war with the Mapuche, so the Viceroyalty of Peru administered it directly until 1740. Corral Bay became one of the most fortified of its time, with 17 forts.

Valdivia's original site was repopulated in 1684. In the mid-1840s German immigrants began to settle, and German influence still shows in the city, whose Instituto Alemán Carlos Anwandter was founded in 1858. 5 the most powerful ever recorded, struck Valdivia hardest. About 2 m of subsidence permanently flooded pastures and created new wetlands.

Valdivia is the capital of the Los Ríos Region and of Valdivia Province, and the commune had 170,043 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Its best-known historical landmarks are the Torreones, two towers of the Spanish city wall, and the forts of Corral Bay, since nearly all other colonial buildings were destroyed by fires and earthquakes. The Universidad Austral de Chile, founded in 1954, has its main campus on Isla Teja. The city celebrates the Semana Valdiviana each February, whose parade of ships began in the 17th century as a protest against the Spanish authorities.
vale-of-glamorgan: The Vale of Glamorgan lies immediately west of Cardiff between the M4 motorway and the Severn Estuary. The county borough covers 33,097 hectares and has 53 kilometres of coastline. The district that gives it its name is slightly larger and generally low-lying, extending from the River Kenfig in the west to the Rhymney in the east, with the Pennant Sandstone scarp forming its northern boundary. The highest point is Tair Onen, east of Cowbridge, at 137.3 metres. The yellow-grey cliffs of the Glamorgan Heritage Coast, between Gileston and Ogmore-by-Sea, are formed of Liassic limestone, shale and Carboniferous Limestone and hold traces of Jurassic sea creatures such as ammonites.

Calcium carbonate in the soil allows crops to be grown that would be difficult elsewhere in Wales. In earlier centuries limestone was taken by sloops across the Bristol Channel to North Cornish ports such as Bude, Boscastle and Port Isaac to fertilise Cornwall's poor slate soils, and hard Devonian slate came back as a roofing material. The coast faces west and takes the brunt of the Atlantic gales, which created ideal conditions for deliberate shipwrecking along it. Nash Point, Southerndown and Ogmore-by-Sea have some of the highest numbers of shipwreck victims on the Welsh coast.

Between the 11th century and 1536 the area was part of the Lordship of Glamorgan. The village of Cosmeston, near Penarth, grew up around a fortified manor house built about the 12th century by the De Costentin family, who came from the Cotentin peninsula in northern France and were among the first Norman invaders of Wales after William the Conqueror's invasion of England in 1066. The village would have consisted of small thatched stone round houses. In 1974 the Vale of Glamorgan Borough was created as a second-tier district of the new county of South Glamorgan, with a population of 103,000, and in April 1996 it became a county borough, a unitary authority.

The Vale of Glamorgan is a county borough in the south-east of Wales, bordering Bridgend, Cardiff, Rhondda Cynon Taf and the Bristol Channel. The largest town is Barry, and others include Penarth, Llantwit Major and Cowbridge. Its economy rests largely on agriculture and chemicals, with chemical industries east of the port of Barry and beef and dairy farming inland. Sites include the medieval wall paintings in St Cadoc's Church at Llancarfan, St Donat's Castle and Cosmeston Medieval Village. Cardiff Airport lies near Rhoose.
valencia: Valencia lies on the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula, fronting the Gulf of Valencia, on the highly fertile alluvial silts of the floodplain formed in the lower course of the Turia River. When the Romans founded it in 138 BCE it stood on the alluvial plain several kilometres from the sea. Its Latin name was Valentia, meaning strength or valour, and Livy says the colony was founded by Roman soldiers who had fought the Lusitanian rebel Viriatus.

Founded around 138 BCE as Valentia Edetanorum, Valencia is one of the oldest cities in Spain. It later became part of the Visigothic Kingdom and surrendered to the Moors around 714. In the wake of the fitna of al-Andalus it became the head of the independent Taifa of Valencia, which saw notable urban development. The Jewish poet and philosopher Solomon ibn Gabirol spent his last years there.

After Toledo fell in 1085 the territory became a protectorate of El Cid. A revolt in 1092 handed the city to the Almoravids, and in 1094 El Cid took it by force and established his own principality. With the Aragonese Christian conquest of 1238 Valencia became the capital of the Kingdom of Valencia. Its trade with the Iberian Peninsula and Italian ports made it thrive in the 15th century, and by the end of that century it had become one of the largest European cities. The University of Valencia was founded in 1499.

Between 1521 and 1522 the Revolt of the Brotherhoods plunged the kingdom into civil war, and Muslim vassals were forced to convert in 1526 at the behest of Charles V. Its economy suffered a crisis after the expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609. The city became a major silk-manufacturing centre in the 18th century. During the Spanish Civil War it was the provisional seat of the Spanish Government from 1936 to 1937.

Valencia is the capital and largest city of the Valencian Community and of the province of the same name, and the third most populous city in Spain. Valencian and Spanish are the official languages. Its historic centre is among the largest in Spain, and its monuments include Valencia Cathedral, the Torres de Serrans, the Torres de Quart and the Lonja de la Seda, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1996. The Falles festival, held in March, was recognised by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage in 2016.
valenciennes: In 923 Valenciennes passed to the Duchy of Lower Lotharingia, which depended on the Holy Roman Empire. In 1259 it hosted a General Chapter of the Dominican Order, attended by Thomas Aquinas, which set out a programme of studies that made philosophy part of Dominican training. In 1306 the book of the author Marguerite Porete, The Mirror of the Simple Souls, was burned in the Place d'Armes as heretical.

Emperor Charles V came to the city in 1524. About 1560 it became an early centre of Calvinism, and in 1562, on the day called the Journée des Mals Brûlés, a mob freed Protestants condemned to be burned, the first act of resistance to the persecution of Protestants in the Spanish Netherlands.

The Beeldenstorm of 1566 reached Valenciennes on 24 August, further south than any other city, and the city fell to repression after a siege ended on 23 March 1567. One victim was Guido de Bres, author of the Belgic Confession. Louis of Nassau took the city on 21 May 1572, but the Duke of Alba retook it in early June.

The French besieged it in 1656, and in 1677 the armies of Louis XIV, led by Vauban, captured it. The Treaty of Nijmegen of 1678 gave France Valenciennes and the southern part of Hainaut, roughly cutting the former county in half. The First Coalition besieged it in 1793, and Germany occupied it in 1914 until British forces drove the German army out in the Battle of Valenciennes in 1918.

Valenciennes is a commune on the Scheldt in the Nord department and a subprefecture of it. The Hindenburg Line ran through it in the World War I, and the city was again almost completely destroyed in the World War II and rebuilt in concrete.

Surviving monuments include the façade of the Hôtel de Ville, the Basilica of Notre-Dame du Saint-Cordon, to which a pilgrimage is made each year, the Maison Espagnole, a relic of the Spanish occupation that ended in 1678, and the Dodenne Tower, part of the medieval fortifications that Charles V ordered reduced. The city has long been known for lace, and until the 1970s its main industries were steel and textiles. Among those born there are the painter Jean-Antoine Watteau, the chronicler Jean Froissart and Baldwin I, the first Latin Emperor of Constantinople.
valens: Valens and his elder brother Valentinian were born, in 328 and 321 respectively, to an Illyrian family at Cibalae (Vinkovci) in Pannonia Secunda. Both were Christians of different sects: Valentinian a Nicene Christian, Valens an Arian of the Homoean kind. After Jovian's death in February 364, Valentinian was acclaimed augustus, and, since he needed help with so large an empire and the soldiers demanded a second augustus, he named Valens co-emperor on 28 March. The brothers divided the empire at Mediana: Valens took the east, from Greece and the Balkans through Anatolia and Egypt to the Sasanian border.

In September 365, while Valens was away, Procopius, a maternal cousin of Julian, declared himself augustus. Valens first despaired and considered abdication, but after about eight months his generals defeated Procopius, who was executed on 27 May 366. Valens then fought the Goths across the Danube in 367 and 369, winning the title Gothicus Maximus, and agreed to a treaty with Athanaric in early 370. He also supported the Armenian prince Pap against Persian intervention and put down revolts of the Isaurians and of the Saracens under Queen Mavia.

He is described as a capable administrator who lightened the burden of taxation, but also as indecisive and fearful, and his suspicion of plots led to treason trials and executions that stained his reputation. In religion he favoured a compromise between Nicene Christianity and its rivals. He inaugurated the Aqueduct of Valens in Constantinople, and became senior augustus in 375, when Valentinian died.

In 376 the Visigoths under Fritigern, displaced by the Huns, asked Valens for asylum, and he allowed them across the Danube, hoping to recruit them. Further groups crossed uncontrolled, corrupt Roman officials took bribes instead of disarming the Goths and charged exorbitant prices for food, and in early 377 the Goths revolted. Valens advanced without waiting for his nephew Gratian's western army and was killed on 9 August 378 at the Battle of Adrianople; two-thirds of the eastern army lay dead.

Ammianus Marcellinus gives two accounts of his end: an arrow wound, or burning in a hut where he had been carried. He was deified as Divus Valens. Ammianus saw it as the worst Roman defeat since Edessa, and Rufinus called it the beginning of evils for the Roman Empire. A. H. M. Jones judged him undistinguished as a general but a conscientious administrator, careful of the humble.
valentin-gomez-farias: José María Valentín Gómez Farías was born in Guadalajara, Jalisco, on 14 February 1781, the son of José Lugardo Gómez de la Vara and María Josefa Martínez y Farías. He studied medicine at the university of his home city, learned French and read the Enlightenment works that circulated secretly in New Spain. His dissertation was so marked by them that it drew the attention of the Mexican Inquisition, though no action was taken, and he opened a successful practice in Guadalajara. He was elected to the congress of 1821, supported Agustín de Iturbide's election as emperor and turned against him when Iturbide dissolved the body.

Gómez Farías was elected in March 1833 together with Antonio López Santa Anna, with whom he was to share the presidency. Santa Anna was away from the capital, so when Manuel Gómez Pedraza's term ended on 1 April power passed to Gómez Farías, which has been suspected as a ploy by Santa Anna to gauge opinion on his intended reforms. The campaign against the Catholic Church that followed lifted the legal obligation to pay tithes nationally on 27 October 1833 and the legal obligation to keep monastic vows on 6 November. On 17 December it gave the government the patronato, the power to appoint to the church hierarchy. Clergy were forbidden to teach, and the University of Mexico, which the church ran, was closed.

The congress also passed the Ley del Caso on 23 June 1833, which authorised the arrest and six years of exile of fifty-one people considered enemies of the government. Gómez Farías opposed it, wishing to be more moderate. Reformers had hoped the loss of tithes would starve the church, but most people kept paying them. Backlash grew, and in April 1834 Santa Anna took action. Congress was dissolved, the patronato annulled and the university restored, and the exiles were allowed to return. Gómez Farías moved to New Orleans.

Gómez Farías returned to Mexico in 1838 and led the failed federalist revolt of 1840. He served as minister of finance in 1846 and was elected again in December 1846 with Santa Anna, in the midst of the Mexican–American War. In January 1847 his administration nationalized and sold church lands to fund the war, which met controversy and sparked conservative revolts, and Santa Anna again deposed him. In 1856 he was elected to the congress that inaugurated La Reforma, which led to the Constitution of 1857, and he died on 5 July 1858, during the Reform War.
valentin-submarine-pens: Bombing by the Royal Air Force and the United States Army Air Forces had sharply reduced the output of German shipyards, so bomb-proof production sites were built, among them Nordsee III on Helgoland, Fink II and Elbe II in Hamburg and Kilian in Kiel. Under the codename Valentin a factory was to rise directly on the Weser between the Bremen suburbs of Rekum and Farge, for the final assembly of Type XXI submarines: three boats from April 1945, then at least 14 a month from August 1945. The Organisation Todt designed and oversaw the work, with Marineoberbaurat Edo Meiners in overall charge.

The bunker is around 426 metres long and 97 metres wide at its widest, with walls 4.5 metres thick and a height of 22.5 to 27 metres. Its roof was made of large reinforced concrete arches lifted into place and filled around with concrete; most of it is 4.5 metres thick, part of it 7 metres. Inside were 13 assembly bays, each for one stage of the work, on boats delivered by barge in eight prefabricated sections. The last bay was a dry dock for leak tests, and finished boats were to leave through a sliding bomb-proof door to the river.

Most of the 10,000–12,000 people who built Valentin were slave workers held in seven camps nearby, among them the Bremen-Farge camp, the largest subcamp of the Neuengamme concentration camp, where some prisoners were housed in an empty underground fuel tank. They were mainly foreign concentration camp inmates and Russian, Polish and French prisoners of war, made to work 12-hour shifts around the clock. Only 553 victims, mostly Frenchmen, have been identified; the dead may have numbered 6,000 or more, since the names of the Polish and Russian dead were not recorded.

By March 1945 the factory was 90% complete. On 27 March 1945 Lancaster bombers of 617 Squadron attacked it with Tallboy and Grand Slam bombs; two Grand Slams broke through the thinner west part of the roof and brought down around 1,000 tons of debris. The site was abandoned, and the British Army's XXX Corps occupied the area four weeks later. After the war Project Ruby tested penetration bombs on it, the German Navy used it as a storage depot from 1960 to 2010, and in 1983 a memorial by the Bremen artist Fritz Stein, Vernichtung durch Arbeit (Extermination through labour), was put up.
valentin-vodnik: Valentin Vodnik was born on 3 February 1758 in Zgornja Šiška, now a suburb of Ljubljana, then part of the Habsburg monarchy. His family was a relatively well-to-do peasant and artisan one. He became a Franciscan and studied in Ljubljana, Novo Mesto and Gorizia, finishing his studies in 1782.

He then served as a priest in Ljubljana, in the Upper Carniolan village of Sora, in Bled and in Ribnica. In 1793 he returned to Ljubljana and joined the circle of Sigmund Zois, where several figures of the Slovenian Enlightenment gathered. Zois remained his sponsor until his own death. In 1797 Vodnik became a professor at the lyceum in Ljubljana.

Vodnik wrote poetry in Slovene, which he called Carniolan. His first poems appeared in Marko Pohlin's collections of Slovene folk songs. His verse was simple, patriotic and often satirical. One of his best-known poems, Dramilo (A Pick-me-up), appeals to Slovenes to be proud of their land, language and heritage. His first collection, Pesme za pokušino (Poems for Sampling), appeared in 1806. He also edited Lublanske novice, the first Slovenian newspaper, issued twice a week from 1797 to 1800.

He wrote grammars and textbooks, the first Slovene-language cookbook, Kuharske bukve (1799), and a translation of a midwifery manual by Johann Matoschek, Babištvo (1818). He worked with Zois on the origin of the Julian Alps and kept a mineral collection of 338 specimens. In his own writing he used his Upper Carniolan dialect, adding words and grammar from other Slovene dialects and replacing German expressions with local ones, so as to be understood more widely.

In 1809 Vodnik wrote the poem Ilirija oživljena, praising Napoleon Bonaparte for establishing the Illyrian Provinces. During the short French administration he helped persuade the authorities to promote Slovene in education, culture and administration. After Austrian rule returned in 1813 most of these reforms in language policy were kept, but Vodnik was viewed with mistrust, retired and removed from public life. He died in Ljubljana on 8 January 1819, aged 60.

He is generally regarded as the first real poet in Slovene and the first journalist. He helped younger writers, among them France Prešeren, who wrote two elegies for him. A monument to him was erected in 1889, and a coin marked the 250th anniversary of his birth in January 2008. His cookbook was developed into Slovenska kuharica (1868) by Magdalena Pleiweis.
valentinian-i: Valentinian was born at Cibalae in southern Pannonia into a family of Illyro-Roman origin. He and his younger brother Valens were the sons of Gratianus, nicknamed Funarius, a military officer noted for his wrestling skills, who served as comes Africae and later comes Britanniarum. Valentinian joined the army in the late 330s. Later he served as a tribune under the Caesar Julian in Gaul, but after a failed attempt to intercept Alemannic raiders he and a colleague were blamed and cashiered. He then lived on the family estate at Sirmium, and the sources disagree about whether he left Julian's service over pagan sacrifices or was simply dismissed.

After Jovian's death the officials meeting at Nicaea rejected other candidates and settled on Valentinian as a man well qualified and nearby. He accepted the acclamation on 25 or 26 February 364 and, to forestall a succession crisis, named his brother Valens co-Augustus at Constantinople on 28 March. Valens took the East, while Valentinian held Italy, Gaul and Illyricum, with his court at Milan.

In 365 the Alemanni crossed the Rhine, and Valentinian stayed in Gaul rather than march east. In 368 he crossed the Rhine and the Main with his son Gratian and fought the Alemanni at the Battle of Solicinium, a Roman victory with heavy losses. He built and refurbished fortifications along the Rhine's west bank. In 367 the Great Conspiracy struck Britain, and he sent Theodosius, who restored order there, and later put down the revolt of Firmus in Africa. In 373 the Roman commander Marcellianus murdered the Quadic king Gabinius at a banquet, which brought the Quadi and Sarmatians into war.

Valentinian crossed the Danube into Quadi territory in 374 and wintered at Savaria. He reached Brigetio on 17 November 375 and received a Quadi deputation, who insisted that the Roman forts built in their lands had caused the conflict. Enraged, he shouted abuse at the envoys and suffered a fatal stroke. His sons Gratian and Valentinian II succeeded him in the West. Ammianus calls him violent, hostile to the educated and reportedly cruel to servants, yet also an able painter and sculptor. Modern historians such as Michael Grant nonetheless rate him a superb soldier and conscientious worker who tolerated differences of religious opinion.
valentinian-ii: Valentinian was born to Emperor Valentinian I and his second wife Justina, and had three sisters: Galla, Grata and Justa. His half-brother Gratian had shared the imperial title with their father since 367.
