When the elder Valentinian died on campaign in Pannonia in 375, the leading generals and officials, among them Merobaudes, Petronius Probus, Equitius and Cerealis, did not acknowledge Gratian. They brought the four-year-old boy to Aquincum and named him augustus on 22 November 375. Historians suggest that the army and its Frankish general Merobaudes were concerned about Gratian's limited military skill and expected to command in the child's name.

Gratian had to accommodate the generals who supported his half-brother. Valentinian was nominally ruler of Italy and North Africa, but Gratian in fact governed the whole West and Valentinian issued no laws. At Milan the boy grew up under the pro-Arian influence of Justina and the court, which brought conflict with the Nicene bishop Ambrose. In 384 Valentinian refused the petition of the pagan senators, led by Aurelius Symmachus, to restore the Altar of Victory. In 385 Ambrose declined an order to hand over the Portian Basilica for the court's Easter service, and the people of Milan rallied to him.

After Magnus Maximus killed Gratian in 383, Maximus crossed the Alps in 386 to 387 and threatened Milan. Valentinian and Justina fled to Theodosius I in Thessalonica, who married Valentinian's sister Galla and marched west in 388 to defeat Maximus. The restored emperor was installed at Vienne in Gaul.

Theodosius appointed his own supporters in the West, and modern scholars suspect he never meant Valentinian to rule, since he planned for his sons to succeed. When Theodosius returned east, the Frankish general Arbogast became guardian of Valentinian and commander in the western provinces. A chronicler wrote that the emperor was shut up in the palace and reduced almost below the position of a private person.

Valentinian tried to dismiss Arbogast, who publicly tore up the order. On 15 May 392 the emperor was found hanged in his residence at Vienne. Arbogast maintained it was suicide; many sources believe he had the young man murdered, ancient historians were divided, and some modern scholars lean toward suicide.

Ambrose's eulogy, the only contemporary Western source, is ambiguous. The body was taken to Milan and laid in a porphyry sarcophagus beside Gratian, and Valentinian was deified. Arbogast then raised Eugenius, and Theodosius defeated both at the Battle of the Frigidus in 394. Valentinian's reign foreshadowed the fifth century, when young emperors were controlled by powerful generals and officials.
valentinian-iii: Valentinian was born at Ravenna on 2 July 419, the only son of Galla Placidia and Constantius III. Through his mother he descended from Theodosius I and Valentinian I, and he was nephew of the emperor Honorius and cousin of the eastern emperor Theodosius II. After Constantius died in 421, court intrigue forced Galla Placidia to flee with her children to Constantinople. When Honorius died in 423 and Joannes took power in Rome, Theodosius named the five-year-old Valentinian caesar for the West in October 424 and betrothed him to his daughter Licinia Eudoxia. After Joannes was defeated, the eastern official Helion installed Valentinian as augustus in Rome on 23 October 425, at the age of six.

Under his mother's influence the early reign saw victories over the Visigoths in Gaul and over the Franks along the Rhine, and the Huns left Pannonia Valeria. A struggle among the generals Felix, Bonifatius and Aetius troubled it: Aetius had Felix killed in 430, and Bonifatius, who had brought in the Vandals, was beaten and fled. Valentinian made peace with the Vandal king Gaiseric in 435. He married Licinia Eudoxia in 437 at Constantinople, and the regency ended, but policy remained in the hands of Aetius. The Vandals took Carthage on 19 October 439, a major blow because taxes and food from Africa supported Rome. In 444 the government taxed sales and the senatorial class to pay for troops.

In 451 Aetius gathered a coalition and defeated Attila at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 Attila invaded Italy and destroyed Aquileia. Valentinian sent Pope Leo I and two senators to negotiate, and plague, famine and an attack by the eastern emperor Marcian on Hun homelands made Attila withdraw.

Egged on by the senator Petronius Maximus and his chamberlain Heraclius, Valentinian killed Aetius with his own hands on 21 September 454. A counsellor reportedly told him that he had cut off his right hand with his left. On 16 March 455 two of Aetius's followers, Optelas and Thraustelas, killed him on the Campus Martius. Petronius Maximus was proclaimed emperor and died after eleven weeks, and Gaiseric's Vandals then sacked Rome for two weeks. By Valentinian's death almost all of North Africa, western Spain and most of Gaul had left Roman control. He is described as spoiled and pleasure-loving, yet devoted to religion, and Edward Gibbon and J. B. Bury judged him unfavourably.
valka: Valka is a town and the centre of Valka Municipality in the Vidzeme region of Latvia, on the border with Estonia, along both banks of the river Pedele. Its German name is Walk and its Estonian counterpart is Valga. The two towns are twins, separated by the national border but using the slogan One Town, Two Countries. With the expansion of the Schengen Agreement and the abolition of border controls between Estonia and Latvia in 2007, the border crossing-points were removed and roads and fences opened. A joint public bus service was planned to link the twin towns.

The town of Walk was first mentioned in 1286, and from 1419 it was the seat of the Landtag of the Livonian Confederation. The Polish-Lithuanian king Stefan Batory granted it city rights in 1584. It gained importance only at the end of the 19th century, when the Vidzeme teachers' seminary, founded by Jānis Cimze, operated there and an important railway junction developed. The first narrow-gauge railway line in the territory of modern Latvia ran from Valka to the Estonian city of Pärnu.

On 15 November 1917 the Latvian Provisional National Council made the decision in Valka to proclaim the independent Republic of Latvia, and the red-white-red flag of Latvia was raised there for the first time. The town became the subject of a dispute between the newly formed Latvian and Estonian states. On 1 July 1920 it was divided between them as a compromise, and the border was marked out by an international jury headed by the British colonel Stephen George Tallents.
vallabhbhai-patel: Vallabhbhai Jhaverbhai Patel, one of the six children of Jhaverbhai Patel and Ladba, was born in Nadiad, Gujarat, and raised in the Gujarati countryside. His date of birth was never officially recorded; he entered 31 October on his matriculation examination papers. He belonged to the Patidars, specifically the Leva Patel community of central Gujarat, and he became a successful lawyer.

In September 1917 Patel spoke at Borsad in support of Mahatma Gandhi's petition demanding swaraj, and a month later he met Gandhi for the first time. He became secretary of the Gujarat Sabha, fought the forced servitude known as veth and organised relief after plague and famine in Kheda. When the Kheda peasants' plea for exemption from taxation was refused, Patel volunteered to lead the struggle.

He toured the villages and urged complete unity and non-violence, and when tax revenue was withheld and the government sent police to seize property, he organised volunteers to help villagers hide valuables. The government agreed to suspend taxes for a year and scaled back the rate. In 1920 Patel was elected president of the Gujarat Pradesh Congress Committee, which he led until 1945.

From 1934 he was the Congress's main fundraiser and chairman of its Central Parliamentary Board. He was arrested in 1940 and imprisoned for nine months, and he opposed the Cripps mission of 1942. In 1946, realising that rejecting the Cabinet Mission plan of 16 May would leave only the Muslim League to form a government, he lobbied the Congress Working Committee to accept it.

As the first Home Minister he organised relief for partition refugees, and with V. P. Menon he lobbied the princes from 6 August 1947, offering favourable terms such as privy purses, while not ruling out force. All but three of the 565 states acceded willingly; Jammu and Kashmir, Junagadh and Hyderabad did not. He was also a senior figure in the Constituent Assembly and is remembered as a founder of the All India Services.

Patel sparred with Jawaharlal Nehru over Kashmir and the states, but on 30 January 1948 Gandhi told him not to leave the government, and he was the last man to speak with Gandhi privately before his assassination. His health declined through 1949 and he died on 15 December 1950. His commitment to national integration earned him the name Iron Man of India. The Statue of Unity, about 182 metres (597 ft) high, was dedicated to him on 31 October 2018.
valladolid: Valladolid lies at about 735 metres above sea level in the centre of the Meseta Norte, where the Pisuerga and Esgueva rivers meet 15 km before they join the Duero. It is surrounded by winegrowing areas. The Vaccaei, a Celtic tribe, were the first people documented as a stable presence in this part of the middle Duero valley. The origin of the name is uncertain. One theory derives it from a Celtiberian expression meaning valley of waters, and another from the Arabic Balad al-Walid, city of al-Walid. In medieval texts the town is called Vallisoletum, sunny valley.

After the Muslim invasion of 711 the district stayed thinly settled until the Christians secured the whole Duero basin at the battle of Simancas in 939. In 1072 Alfonso VI of León and Castile gave the lordship of Valladolid to Count Pedro Ansúrez, who with his wife Eylo Alfónsez led the foundation of the town. The town grew rapidly in the 12th and 13th centuries, helped by commercial privileges from Alfonso VIII and Alfonso X, and the university dates from 1241. The earliest documented Jewish community dates to 1221.

Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon married in the city in 1469, and by the 15th century it was a residence of the kings of Castile. Christopher Columbus died there in 1506. In 1550 and 1551 the town held what is described as the first moral debate in European history on the treatment of indigenous peoples by conquerors. A fire in 1561 destroyed part of the city. Valladolid served briefly as the capital of the Hispanic Monarchy from 1601 to 1606 under the Duke of Lerma, valido of Philip III, before the court returned to Madrid.

Valladolid is the capital of the province of Valladolid and the seat of the government and parliament of the autonomous community of Castile and León, with a population of 299,816. Since the 1950s it has been an industrial centre, with an automotive industry that began with the founding of FASA-Renault in 1953. Its Holy Week processions and the Valladolid International Film Festival are held each year, and in 2019 it was recognised as a City of Film by UNESCO's Creative Cities Network.
valladolid-debate: Bartolomé de las Casas, a Dominican friar and Bishop of Chiapas, had worked for years against forced conversion and the treatment of Indigenous people in the encomiendas. His efforts influenced the papal bull Sublimis Deus of 1537, which declared them rational beings, and he was instrumental in the New Laws of 1542, designed to end the encomienda system. Moved by him and others, King Charles I in 1550 ordered further military expansion to stop until the question was examined, and assembled a junta of doctors and theologians at the Colegio de San Gregorio in Valladolid to hear both sides.

The arguments stayed largely theoretical. Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda, drawing on Aristotle and the humanist tradition and on his Latin dialogue Democrates Alter, gave four grounds for just war: that some Indigenous peoples were by nature unable to govern themselves and needed Spanish masters, that cannibalism and human sacrifice were crimes against nature to be stopped, and that the natives must be converted. Colonists and landowners who profited from the encomienda took up his case.

Las Casas answered with his own Latin Apologia, written in the late 1540s. He argued that Aristotle's barbarian and natural slave did not fit peoples fully capable of reason, who should be brought to Christianity without force, and cited Saint Augustine and Saint John Chrysostom against coercion. Human sacrifice was wrong, he held, but war should be avoided by every possible means.

The judges dispersed without a joint ruling. Of their individual opinions only that of Doctor Anaya survives; he approved conquest to spread Christianity but only for the good of the Indians and not for gold. Both men claimed victory and neither got what he wanted: the conquests went on, Pedro de Valdivia fighting in Chile in the early 1550s and expansion being allowed again in May 1556, while the New Laws stood. Sepúlveda's arguments fed the policy of war by fire and blood adopted in 1585 during the Chichimeca War, but his works were not published in Spain again in his lifetime. The ideas of Las Casas influenced Philip II and the move from encomiendas to reducciones.
valladolid-yucatan: Valladolid lies in the eastern region of the Mexican state of Yucatán and is the seat of Valladolid Municipality. It stands about 170 km east of the state capital Mérida, 40 km east of Chichén Itzá and 150 km west of Cancún. Its Maya name is Sakiʼ. It was named after Valladolid, then the capital of Spain. It lies inland, in a hot climate with a rainy season from June to October.

The Spanish city was established on 27 May 1543 by the nephew of the conquistador Francisco de Montejo, at some distance from its present site, beside a lagoon in the municipality of Tizimín. The early settlers complained of mosquitoes and humidity and asked for the city to be moved inland. On 24 March 1545 it was relocated to its present site, on a Maya town whose buildings were dismantled so that the stones could be reused for the colonial town. The Maya rose the following year, but the revolt was put down with extra Spanish troops from Mérida.

In 1705 local Maya rebelled again and killed a number of town officials who had taken refuge in the cathedral. After the revolt was suppressed the cathedral was judged irreparably profaned and was demolished. A new one was built the next year, and it still stands. It faces north, unlike most colonial churches in Yucatán, which face east.

The city had 15,000 inhabitants in 1840. In January 1847 Maya rioted and killed some eighty whites; after a Maya noble was shot by firing squad the riot turned into a general uprising led by Jacinto Pat, batab of Tihosuco, and Cecilio Chi of Ichmul. Valladolid was the scene of intense fighting in the Caste War of Yucatán. Ladino forces were forced to abandon it on 14 March 1848, and half were killed in an ambush before reaching Mérida. Maya rebels sacked it, and it was recaptured later in the war. Until the early 20th century it was the third-largest city of the peninsula, after Mérida and Campeche, with a prosperous Criollo population, and was nicknamed the Sultana of the East.

Sights include the Convent of San Bernardino de Siena, built by Franciscan missionaries between 1552 and 1560, which is linked to the centre by the 16th-century Calzada de los Frailes, and the Church of Saint Servatius on the main square. The Cenote Zací, a freshwater sinkhole, lies close to the centre. Valladolid belongs to the federal Pueblos Mágicos programme and is a base for visiting Chichén Itzá, Ekʼ Balam and Cenote Ik Kil. Its regional dishes include cochinita pibil, lomitos de Valladolid and longaniza sausage.
valletta: Valletta lies between the Grand Harbour to the east and Marsamxett Harbour to the west, on the Sciberras peninsula. The peninsula's older names include Xagħret Mewwija, from the Arab period, and Sceberras, which recent scholarship derives from a Punic phrase meaning the headland or the middle peninsula. Before the city was built, the only structure on it was a small watchtower of 1488 dedicated to Saint Elmo.

The Order of Saint John had proposed building a city on the peninsula as early as 1524. In 1552 the watchtower was replaced by the larger Fort Saint Elmo, which fell to the Ottomans in the Great Siege of 1565 before the Order won the siege with Sicilian reinforcements. The victorious Grand Master Jean de Valette at once set out to build a fortified city that would bind the Knights to the island. Pope Pius V sent his military architect Francesco Laparelli to design it, and Philip II of Spain sent substantial money. De Valette laid the foundation stone on 28 March 1566, in what later became Our Lady of Victories Church. He died on 21 August 1568, aged 74, before the city was finished.

Laparelli laid the city out on a rectangular grid of wide, straight streets, a departure from the winding streets of medieval Maltese towns. After his death in 1570 the Maltese architect Girolamo Cassar oversaw the work. The city was mostly complete by the early 1570s, and it became the capital on 18 March 1571, when Grand Master Pierre de Monte moved from Fort St Angelo in Birgu to the Grandmaster's Palace. Seven auberges for the Order's Langues were finished by the 1580s. Under Grand Master Pinto, in the 18th century, many buildings were rebuilt in Baroque style.

The French invaded in 1798 and expelled the Order, and French troops held Valletta until they capitulated to the British in September 1800. Under British rule most of the fortifications were spared demolition and survive largely intact. The Malta Railway to Mdina opened in 1883 and closed in 1931. German and Italian air raids in the Second World War caused great destruction, including the loss of the Royal Opera House.

Valletta is the capital of Malta and one of its 68 council areas, with a population of 5,157 in 2021. It is Baroque in character, with 320 monuments in an area of 0.55 square kilometres, and is noted for its bastions, palaces, gardens and churches. The whole city has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1980, and it was European Capital of Culture in 2018.
valley-of-elah: The Valley of Elah, Emeq HaElah in Hebrew and Wadi es-Sunt in Arabic, is a long, shallow valley in the Shephelah. Its Hebrew name, the valley of the terebinth, comes from the large, shady terebinth trees that grow there, the Arabic one from the white acacia. Near Sokho on its western side stands an ancient terebinth 17 m high, with a trunk 5.2 m round and a canopy at least 23 m across, which marks the valley's upper end. The hilltop ruin of Adullam rises at its south-eastern end.

The valley is best known from the story in the Hebrew Bible of David's victory over Goliath (1 Samuel 17), and its archaeological sites include those identified as the towns of Azekah and Sokho named in that chapter. In 2009 Yosef Garfinkel uncovered a fortified Iron Age II city at Khirbet Qeiyafa, on its north side, dated sometime between 1050 and 915 BCE and identified with Shaaraim of 1 Samuel 17:52. Its fortifications have been said to support the biblical account of a United Monarchy that was more than a tribal chiefdom; others are sceptical and suggest a Judahite or Canaanite fortress.

In the late 19th century Claude Conder and Herbert Kitchener described it as one of the most fertile districts in Palestine: an open, flat vale about half a mile across, covered with corn, with a pebbled watercourse down its centre, terebinths and solitary oaks along its course, and stony hills of brushwood on either side.

A large satellite relay station with about 120 dishes has stood in the valley since the early 1970s. A plan for shale oil extraction in the region, opposed by groups such as the Green Zionist Alliance and Save Adullam, was blocked by a zoning committee in 2014, and in July 2019 the valley came under the Israel Nature and Parks Authority, owing to its historical importance and to limit the spread of Beit Shemesh to the north. Its wildlife includes the mountain gazelle, the Egyptian mongoose and the Greek tortoise.
valley-of-mexico: The Valley of Mexico, called Anahuac in Nahuatl, meaning Land Between the Waters, is a large natural basin on the highland plateau of central Mexico, in the Trans-Mexican Volcanic Belt. It is about 125 kilometres long and 75 kilometres wide and covers roughly 9,600 square kilometres, with a minimum elevation of 2,200 metres, surrounded by mountains and volcanoes that reach over 5,000 metres. It is an endorheic basin, with no natural outlet to the sea. Historically it held five shallow, interconnected lakes, Zumpango, Xaltocan, Xochimilco, Chalco and the largest, Texcoco, which together covered about 1,500 square kilometres. The northern lakes, near Texcoco, were saline and the southern ones fresh.

The valley has been inhabited for at least 12,000 years. The oldest known settlement is Tlapacoya, on the former edge of Lake Chalco. Tlatilco, on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, was a large agricultural village that flourished in the Middle Pre-Classic period, and Cuicuilco in the far south was later covered by lava from the Xitle volcano.

Teotihuacan became an organised village around 800 BCE and reached its height after about 200 BCE, when it had about 125,000 inhabitants. In the early eighth century, with the rise of the Toltecs, the population shifted to Tula. After the Toltec decline in the thirteenth century people moved back to the lakes, and about fifty small city-states arose around the shores, all claiming Toltec descent. The largest, Tenochtitlan, had more than 150,000 inhabitants.

The Aztec Empire, from 1325 to 1521, ruled from Tenochtitlan. The Aztecs built dikes to control flooding and to separate the saline northern lakes from the fresh water of the south, and the city-states maintained chinampas, aqueducts and dikes. When Spanish explorers arrived in 1519 the valley held about one million people.

After the conquest in 1521 the Spaniards rebuilt Tenochtitlan as Mexico City. Floods, including one in 1555 and the Great Flood of 1629, led to the desagüe, a drainage project pursued through the colonial period, with the Nochistongo canal begun in 1605 by Enrico Martínez and later the Grand Canal. Drainage was officially completed under Porfirio Díaz in 1894.

The lakes have almost entirely disappeared, and the valley is now almost entirely occupied by Mexico City, the capital of Mexico. The metropolitan area, which also covers parts of the State of Mexico, Hidalgo, Tlaxcala and Puebla, has about 21 million inhabitants. The valley drains through artificial canals to the Tula River and on to the Gulf of Mexico. It lies in an earthquake-prone zone. The five aquifers beneath the valley supply most of Mexico City's drinking water, and the city has sunk into the old lake floor as groundwater has been extracted.
valley-of-oaxaca: Also called the Central Valleys of Oaxaca, the valley lies within the Sierra Madre in the present-day state of Oaxaca. It is shaped like a distorted, almost upside-down Y, whose arms bear their own names: the Etla arm to the north-west, the Valle Grande to the south and the Tlacolula arm to the east. In administrative use the region comprises the districts of Etla, Centro, Zaachila, Zimatlán, Ocotlán, Tlacolula and Ejutla.

In the Formative period San José Mogote, in the Etla arm, grew from a permanent farming village into a community where high rank was held by birth. Tilcajete in the Valle Grande and Yegüih in the Tlacolula arm were centres of the same time, and their shared ceramic styles suggest close contact; the valley's people also dealt with the Olmec, though what effect this had is unclear. In the Late Formative the population moved to the hilltop of Monte Albán, which had about 5,200 people by 400 BCE and about 17,200 two centuries later, while the older centres were abandoned.

Monte Albán became the capital of a Zapotec state that spread into the highlands and towards the Pacific lowlands. In the Early Classic it dealt closely with Teotihuacan, whose visitors appear on its monuments and which had a Zapotec quarter. Its decline seems to follow Teotihuacan's collapse, as Cuilpan, Zaachila, Lambityeco and Mitla asserted their autonomy, and by about 900 the old capital had been abandoned.

In the Postclassic the Zapotec valley often fell under the Mixtec state to the west. Aztec forces under Moctezuma Ilhuicamina invaded in 1450, and in 1486 an Aztec garrison was set on the hill of Huaxyácac to enforce tribute; the Zapotec were conquered under Ahuitzotl between 1497 and 1502, though not completely. On 25 November 1521 Francisco de Oruzco arrived to claim the valley for Hernán Cortés, who was made Marqués del Valle de Oaxaca.

The Spanish settlement of Segura de la Frontera, later Nueva Antequera, was made a royal city in 1532 by Emperor Charles V and is now the city of Oaxaca, the state capital, in the middle of the valley. Monte Albán, Mitla, San José Mogote and Yagul are among its archaeological sites.
valley-of-the-kings: The valley lies within the Theban Necropolis and has two main sections: the East Valley, where most of the royal tombs are, and the West Valley, also called the Valley of the Monkeys. The Theban hills are dominated by the peak of al-Qurn, known to the Egyptians as ta dehent, the Peak.

Its pyramid shape probably echoed the pyramids of the Old Kingdom. The site's isolation allowed special tomb police, the Medjay, to guard it. Its official ancient name was The Great and Majestic Necropolis of the Millions of Years of the Pharaoh in the West of Thebes. The rock is limestone interspersed with marl, and violent flash floods dump debris into the tombs.

At the start of the Eighteenth Dynasty only kings were buried in large tombs in the valley, and non-royal people lay in small chambers near their masters. Tombs of the Eighteenth Dynasty vary in plan, such as Hatshepsut's, which winds down more than 200 metres, but a bent axis became usual, as in the tombs of Thutmose III and Thutmose IV.

Later tombs straightened, and Ramesses III's and Ramesses IX's tombs have a straight axis. The early tombs were decorated with the Amduat, describing the sun god's journey through the twelve hours of the night, and from Horemheb's time with the Book of Gates. Seti I's KV17 is usually regarded as the finest tomb, and Ramesses II built a massive tomb, KV7.

By the end of the New Kingdom Egypt was in decline, and the valley was heavily plundered. Papyri from the late Twentieth Dynasty record trials of tomb robbers, and one describes the robbery of the tomb of Ramesses VI. In the Twenty-first Dynasty the priests of Amun opened most of the tombs and moved the mummies into a few tombs, later most of them to a single cache near Deir el-Bahari. Ancient visitors left more than 2,100 Greek and Latin graffiti, the earliest dated to 278 BCE. In Coptic times some tombs served as churches, stables and houses.

Napoleon's expedition drew maps and plans of the known tombs in 1799, and in 1827 Wilkinson painted the KV numbers over the entrances of 21 open tombs. The numbers now run from KV1, of Ramesses VII, to KV64, found in 2011, and 65 tombs and chambers are known. Only eleven have been completely recorded. Tutankhamun's tomb, discovered in 1922, drew wide attention, and in 1979 the valley became a UNESCO World Heritage Site with the rest of the Theban Necropolis. Eighteen tombs can be opened, rarely at the same time, and Ay's is the only open tomb in the West Valley.
valmiera: Valmiera is the second largest city of the historical Vidzeme region, with an area of 19.35 square kilometres. It lies on both banks of the Gauja River, at the crossroads of several important roads, 107 kilometres north-east of Riga and 50 km south of the border with Estonia. The site is one of the longest-inhabited in Latvia, and archaeological evidence indicates it was occupied 9,000 years ago. The name may derive from the Old German given name Waldemar or the Slavic name Vladimir, and the town may have been named after Vladimir Mstislavich, prince of Pskov, or after King Valdemar II of Denmark.

After the partition of Tālava in 1224 the trade roads along the Gauja passed to the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, who built a castle that is now known as Valmiera Castle. After the Battle of Saule in 1236 the castle and nearby lands became the property of the newly established Livonian Order. Valmiera was first mentioned as a town in a chronicle of 1323. It belonged to the Hanseatic League from the 14th to the 16th centuries, which brought significant trade, and several regional assemblies, or landtags, were held there in the same period.

The Livonian War left the town heavily devastated in 1583, and it was incorporated into the Duchy of Livonia. After the Polish-Swedish war of 1622 it was managed by the Swedish Lord High Chancellor Axel Oxenstierna. It was destroyed and burned down in the Great Northern War in 1702 and then devastated by plague. In 1738 the first seminary of the Moravian Church was opened there, and in 1785 Valmiera became the centre of a district. The first bridge over the Gauja was built in 1865, and the Riga to St Petersburg railway reached the town in 1899, bringing new factories.

In 1906 Latvians won 18 of 24 seats in the municipal elections, and the local doctor Georgs Apinis was elected mayor. In the Second World War German troops captured the town on 4 July 1941, and in October 1941 209 Jews from Valmiera and the surrounding area were murdered in local forests. The Red Army recaptured it on 24 September 1944, by which time almost all the buildings at the centre had been destroyed. Valmiera is an industrial centre, with food processing, fibreglass production, metalworking and woodworking.
valparaiso: Valparaíso lies in central Chile, about 120 kilometres north-west of Santiago, on dozens of steep hillsides overlooking the Pacific Ocean. Its proximity to the Peru–Chile Trench, which stores large amounts of energy and sometimes ruptures in violent earthquakes, makes it vulnerable to them. The August 1906 earthquake devastated the city and killed nearly 3,000 people, and the 1730 Valparaíso earthquake and the 1985 Algarrobo earthquake were also significant. Residents are called porteños, Spanish for 'port dwellers'.

The first identifiable people of the bay were the Picunche, known for their agriculture. Spanish explorers arrived in 1536 aboard the Santiaguillo, a supply ship sent by Diego de Almagro for his expedition. Its commander, Juan de Saavedra, named the town after his native village of Valparaíso de Arriba in Cuenca Province, Spain; the town's original name was Alimapu or Quintil. Through the colonial period it remained a small village of a few houses and a church, attacked at times by English privateers, among them Francis Drake with the Golden Hind in 1578 and Richard Hawkins with the Dainty in 1594. Drake's sack of the town gave rise to the legend of the Cueva del Pirata.

The Chilean Navy has had its headquarters in the city since 1817. In the second half of the 19th century Valparaíso was a major stopover for ships travelling between the Atlantic and Pacific oceans by the Straits of Magellan, and in its golden age it drew many European immigrants and was known to sailors as Little San Francisco. It acquired Latin America's oldest stock exchange, the continent's first volunteer fire department, Chile's first public library and El Mercurio de Valparaíso, the oldest newspaper in the Spanish language in continuous publication. The opening of the Panama Canal in 1914 reduced ship traffic and dealt a serious blow to the port economy.

Valparaíso is the seat of the National Congress of Chile, which has met there since 1990, and the capital of the Valparaíso Region. Its historic quarter, a labyrinth of cobbled alleys and colourful buildings on the hills, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. Sixteen funiculars, called ascensores, remain, fifteen of them public and national monuments. The commune had 284,938 inhabitants at the 2024 census, within a Greater Valparaíso metropolitan area of 951,311.
valsad: Valsad is a town and municipality in the Valsad district of Gujarat, and the district headquarters. It lies north of Vapi and shares borders with Maharashtra and the union territory of Daman to the south. The old city is about 4 km inland from the Arabian Sea, at an average elevation of 13 metres. The name derives from the Gujarati vad-saal, meaning covered by banyan trees, or a place where banyan and sal trees grow. In the British era it was known as Bulsar. Rainfall is very heavy from June to September under the south-west monsoon, and little or none falls from October to May.

Valsad is known for its historical Parsi community, and the town was once a hub for Parsis. Udvada, in the district, is described as the primary and oldest Parsi fire temple in India. The family of Farrokh Bulsara, known as Freddie Mercury, originated from Valsad, and so did the family of Field Marshal Sam Manekshaw. The railway station building dates from 1925, and the Callian Baug, an urban park, was given to the municipality in 1929 by Motilal Callianji in memory of his father and opened in 1931. Morarji Desai, later Prime Minister of India, and the lawyer and freedom fighter Bhulabhai Desai are among the notable people of the town.

The 2011 census gave the metropolitan area a population of 170,060. The main language is Gujarati, with Hindi, Marathi and English also spoken, and most people are Hindu, with Islam, Christianity, Jainism, Zoroastrianism and Buddhism also followed. Valsad lies on the New Delhi to Mumbai main railway line. The district has chemical, textile and paper industries, centred on Vapi, and is also a horticulture region. Nearby sights include Tithal Beach, the Tadkeshwar Mahadev Temple at Abrama, Parnera Hill and Dharampur Palace.
valtellina: The Valtellina, also called the Valtelline and in German Veltlin, borders Switzerland and was a key Alpine pass between northern Italy and Germany. Control of it was much sought after, particularly during the Thirty Years' War, because it formed an important part of the Spanish Road. Its most important town is Sondrio. The official language is Italian, and the Valtellinese variety of Lombard is also spoken.

The Romans conquered the region in 16 BCE. By the 5th century it was Christian, with about ten rural churches with baptisteries under the Diocese of Como. The Lombards gained control after 720, and about fifty years later Charlemagne gave the valley to the Saint Denis Monastery near Paris, after which it returned to the Bishop of Como. In the 16th, 17th and 18th centuries it belonged to the Three Leagues, a mutual-defence region independent of Switzerland that is now the Swiss canton of Graubünden.

During the Thirty Years' War it was a theatre of military and diplomatic struggle between France, the Habsburg powers and local authorities, culminating in the Valtellina War of 1620 to 1626. Between 1618 and 1620 a court of the anti-Habsburg Protestants of the Leagues convicted a number of Catholics, often in absentia, and the Catholic arch-priest Nicolò Rusca of Sondrio died under torture. These judgments led to a conspiracy to drive the Protestants out, led by Giacomo Robustelli of the Planta family.

On the evening of 18 and 19 July 1620 rebels, supported by Austrian and Italian troops, marched into Tirano and killed Protestants there and then in Teglio, Sondrio and further down the valley. Between 500 and 600 people were killed that night and over the following four days, and nearly all Protestants were driven out of the valley. In February 1623 France, Savoy and Venice signed the Treaty of Paris to expel the Spanish forces from the territory.

On 10 October 1797 the Valtellina revolted against Graubünden with French support and joined the Cisalpine Republic. After 1815 it formed part of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia in the Austrian Empire, and with Lombardy it passed to the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1859 and to the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. The Ferrovia della Valtellina, electrified in 1902, was the world's first mainline electrified railway.

The valley is known for its ski centres, hot spring spas, bresaola, cheeses and wines, made mainly from the Chiavennasca grape, the local Nebbiolo. The Bernina Line of the Rhaetian Railway links Tirano with St. Moritz in Switzerland. At the Rock Engraving Park in Grosio stands the Rupe Magna, a large rock with more than 5,000 engraved figures dating from between the 4th and 1st millennia BCE.
van-fortress: The fortress stands on the steep-sided bluff on which Tushpa, the Urartian capital, was centred, just west of the modern city of Van in the Van Province of Turkey. Built by the kingdom of Urartu between the 9th and 7th centuries BCE, it is the largest of a number of similar strongholds cut into hillsides and outcrops across the kingdom, in the region where present-day Armenia, Turkey and Iran meet. Such fortresses served to control the surrounding region rather than to hold off foreign armies. At Van the lower parts of the walls were of unmortared basalt and the rest of mud brick.

Carved into the rock of the citadel is a chamber 20 metres long and 9 metres wide known as the royal stable, or Siršini, where, according to inscriptions found there, oxen and sheep were kept for sacrifice to the Urartian gods. In the 5th century BCE Xerxes the Great had a trilingual inscription cut on a smoothed face of the rock about 20 metres above the ground, in a niche his father Darius had carved and left blank. It survives in near perfect condition, in three columns of 27 lines in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian. After Urartu the fortress passed in turn to the Medes, Achaemenids, Armenians, Parthians, Romans, Sassanid Persians, Byzantines, Arabs, Seljuks, Safavids, Afsharids, Ottomans and Russians.

The ancient ruins lie outside the modern city and carry walls built in the medieval period. An American expedition led by Silva Tipple New Lake worked there in 1938–40, but most of its finds and field records were lost when the S.S. Athenia sank in 1940.
vandalic-war: The Vandals, allied with the Alans, crossed the Straits of Gibraltar in May 429 at the call of the Roman governor Bonifacius, reportedly 80,000 in all. They took Carthage in October 439, and a treaty of 442 gave them the rich provinces of Zeugitana and Byzacena as their own possessions. Under King Geiseric their fleet raided across the Mediterranean and sacked Rome in 455. Unlike other Germanic kingdoms, the Vandals replaced the Roman order rather than continuing it, and being adherents of Arianism they persecuted the Chalcedonian majority, especially under Huneric and Gunthamund. Relations with Constantinople were often friendly under Thrasamund.

In 530 Gelimer overthrew the pro-Roman king Hilderic after a defeat by the local chief Antalas. Justinian I took this as a pretext to intervene, once he had secured peace with Sassanid Persia in 532. Revolts in Sardinia, under the governor Godas, and in Tripolitania, under Pudentius, distracted Gelimer, and he sent the bulk of the Vandal navy and army under his brother Tzazo to Sardinia.

Belisarius, whose secretary Procopius wrote the main narrative, sailed from Constantinople around 21 June 533. At Methone 500 men died of dysentery from badly baked bread. The army landed at Caputvada in early September, catching Gelimer by surprise. Belisarius presented himself as a liberator of the Latin-speaking population and punished soldiers who stole fruit, so that the army won the local people over. At Ad Decimum on 13 September Gelimer's plan to encircle the Romans nearly succeeded, but Belisarius drove the Vandals into flight and entered Carthage on 15 September, where the citizens welcomed him. He sat on Gelimer's throne and ate the dinner that Gelimer had ordered, then set about repairing the walls.

In December Gelimer advanced from Bulla Regia, joined by Tzazo's army, and met the Romans at Tricamarum, a cavalry battle in which Tzazo was killed. Gelimer fled to a remote mountain fortress, where he was blockaded until he surrendered in the spring.

Officers hoping for advancement told Justinian that Belisarius meant to set up his own kingdom, and Belisarius chose to return. He brought Gelimer, many captured Vandals, who were enrolled in five regiments as the Vandals of Justinian, and the royal treasury, which included objects looted from Rome eighty years earlier. He was given a triumph, the first in Constantinople since its foundation. Africa was restored to imperial rule as a praetorian prefecture, though control scarcely reached beyond the old kingdom. It was the first war of Justinian's attempt to reassert Roman sovereignty over the lost western provinces.
vande-mataram: Bankim Chandra Chatterjee was one of the earliest graduates of the newly founded Calcutta University and served the colonial government as a Deputy Collector and then a Deputy Magistrate. He was much interested in the Revolt of 1857 and the Sanyasi Rebellion, and at about the same time the administration was trying to promote God Save the King as an anthem for Indian subjects, which nationalists disliked. The idea of the poem is generally believed to have come to him around 1876, while he was still an official.

He wrote it at Chinsura, on the Hooghly river, in a spontaneous session, using words from Sanskrit and Bengali. It was published in 1882 in his novel Anandamath, which is set during the Sannyasi Rebellion and has been noted for its pro-British sentiments. Jadunath Bhattacharya was asked to set a tune to it soon after it was written.

The poem became one of the most popular songs of protest in the independence movement. Rabindranath Tagore sang it at the Calcutta session of the Indian National Congress in 1896, and the Congress adopted it in 1905 as a salutation to Mother India. The colonial government banned the book and made public recital a crime, but crowds repeatedly sang it in front of officials. On 20 May 1906 more than ten thousand Hindus and Muslims marched at Barisal behind Vande Mataram flags, and in 1907 Bhikaiji Cama's early flag of India, made in Stuttgart, carried the words.

In 1937 a Congress committee of Maulana Azad, Jawaharlal Nehru, Subhas Chandra Bose, Acharya Deva and Tagore recommended using only the first two stanzas, because later stanzas refer to the Hindu goddess Durga; Tagore wrote that the song could not unite all communities, and the Muslim League opposed it. On 24 January 1950 the Constituent Assembly, with Rajendra Prasad presiding, resolved that it should be honoured equally with Jana Gana Mana. Sri Aurobindo's prose translation appeared in Karmayogin on 20 November 1909, and the oldest surviving recordings date from 1907.
vanga: The kingdom of Vanga emerged in the lower Ganges delta during the Northern Black Polished Ware period. Its lands took in the many islands of the delta and the Sundarbans mangrove forest, and in Bangladesh they reached the present Khulna, Barisal and Dhaka divisions and areas east of the Old Brahmaputra. Its neighbours included Pundravardhana to the north and Magadha, Anga and Suhma to the west. Ancient texts name subdivisions such as Upa Vanga, corresponding to Jessore and the forests of the Sundarbans, and Anuttara Vanga around Barisal.

Ancient Indian records describe Vanga as a hub of sailors, and its fleet controlled many of the delta's islands. The Arthashastra of Kautilya records it as an administrative unit, and the poet Kalidasa describes it as a naval power. Indian and Greco-Roman writers mention the region's war elephants, and it was probably the centre of the Gangaridai of the Greco-Roman authors. According to the story of Prince Vijaya, the son of King Sinhabahu was expelled with 700 followers for violent deeds and sailed across the Bay of Bengal in the 5th century BCE to found the Kingdom of Tambapanni in Sri Lanka.

The exact capital is not known. Chandraketugarh, with continuous remains from the Pre-Mauryan to the Pala-Sena period, is considered a major city, and Jain texts name Tamralipta as the capital. Most of its rulers remain unknown, and after the 2nd century BCE the territory passed under successive powers, among them the Mauryans, the Guptas, the Palas, the Chandras and the Senas. After the Guptas, Bengal was divided into the kingdoms of Gauda and Vanga, with Kotalipara as a centre of the Vanga kings.

In the Mahabharata the founders of Vanga, Anga, Kalinga, Pundra and Suhma are sons of King Bali, and the Vangas fight with elephants on the side of the Kauravas. The Ramayana names Vanga as an ally of Ayodhya. The name lived on as Vangala, Vangaladesha in a Chola inscription and Bangalah after the Muslim conquest, precursors of Banga and Bangla. Chandraketugarh, Tamralipta and Wari-Bateshwar are its main archaeological sites.
vani: Vani is a town in the Imereti region of western Georgia, on the Sulori river, a tributary of the Rioni, 41 kilometres southwest of the regional capital Kutaisi. Systematic archaeological studies by Nino Khoshtaria and Otar Lordkipanidze in the Vani environs since 1947 revealed the remnants of a rich city of the ancient power of Colchis. The name of the ancient settlement is still unknown.

Four distinct stages of uninterrupted occupation have been identified. The first, from the 8th to the 7th century BCE, is presumed to have been a major cultic centre. The second, from the end of the 7th and beginning of the 6th century to the first half of the 4th century BCE, is represented by cultural layers, remains of wooden structures, sacrificial altars cut into the rocky ground and rich burials. Vani is assumed to have been the centre of a political-administrative unit of the kingdom of Colchis in this stage.

The third phase, from the second half of the 4th to the first half of the 3rd century BCE, is represented largely by rich burials and the remains of stone structures. To the fourth, from the 3rd to the middle of the 1st century BCE, belong defensive walls, the so-called small gate, sanctuaries and cultic buildings and the remains of a foundry for casting bronze statues. Vani is assumed to have been a temple-city in these centuries. According to the archaeological data the city was destroyed in the middle of the 1st century BCE, and it declined to a village.

Vani was officially granted the status of a town only in 1981. It is the administrative centre of the Municipality of Vani, which also comprises 40 neighbouring villages. A museum founded in 1985 exhibits unique pieces from ancient Colchis.
vannes: The name comes from the Veneti, a seafaring Celtic people of south-western Armorica who engaged in cross-Channel trade for thousands of years. Julius Caesar's fleet defeated them in 56 BCE in front of Locmariaquer, and many were then slaughtered or sold into slavery. The Romans settled a town called Darioritum where the Veneti had lived, and late in the 1st century BCE the Ramparts of Vannes were established as fortifications.

From the 5th to the 7th century the remaining Gauls were displaced or assimilated by Britons driven out of Britain by the Anglo-Saxons. Under the Breton name Gwened the town was the centre of an independent principality or kingdom called Bro-Wened or Bro-Ereg, whose dynasty claimed descent from Caradog Strongarm. The diocese was erected in the 5th century and the Council of Vannes was held there in 461. The realm was permanently joined with Domnonia under King Saint Judicaël around 635.

In 1342 Vannes was besieged four times in the Breton War of Succession. It was the capital of the duchy of Brittany in the 14th and 15th centuries: Duke John IV heavily fortified the city and its ramparts, and both John V and Francis I were born at the Château de l'Hermine. The Franco-English Tournament of Vannes took place in 1381. The Parlement of Brittany sat there from 1675 to 1690. In 1759 a large French army assembled at Vannes for a planned invasion of Britain, but could not sail after the naval defeat at the Battle of Quiberon Bay. In 1795 French forces based there repelled a British-Royalist invasion through Quiberon.

Vannes lies on the Gulf of Morbihan at the mouth of two rivers, the Marle and the Vincin, about 100 kilometres north-west of Nantes. Its inhabitants are called Vannetais. Its sights include the Gothic Cathedral of St Peter, the Château Gaillard, now an archaeological museum, the Musée de la Cohue and the old city walls with their medieval gates, such as the Porte Calmont and the Tour du Connétable. The old town has many timber-framed houses.
vansda-national-park: The park, also known as Bansda National Park, lies in the Vansda tehsil about 65 km east of Chikhali on National Highway 48 and about 80 km northeast of Valsad. It represents the thick woodlands of the Dangs and southern Gujarat and lies in the Western Ghats of the Sahyadri range. The town of Vansda, which gives the park its name, is a trading centre for the surrounding area, where most people are adivasis. The Vansda–Waghai state highway and the narrow gauge railway from Waghai to Billimora both run through the park.

The forest holds 443 species of flowering plants, among them teak, sisam, mahudo and groves of katas bamboo, with orchids along the Ambika. Its mammals include the Indian leopard, dhole, striped hyena, four-horned antelope, spotted and barking deer, pangolin and Indian giant squirrel, as well as pythons, cobras, kraits and Russell's viper. About 155 species of birds have been recorded, including the Malabar trogon and great Indian black woodpecker, and about 121 species of spider.

No trees have been felled in the forest since 1952, and it was established as a national park in 1979. A rusty-spotted cat was seen at a mango plantation in the park in 1992. In February 2020 dholes were sighted, and camera traps confirmed two in May 2020, the first time in 50 years that the species had been confirmed in Gujarat.

The Bengal tiger is reported to be extinct in the state, but tigers live where Gujarat borders Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, so the forest remains a potential habitat. Besides its botanical garden, visitors come for the Gira Waterfalls, local tribal life and the birds, and the Gujarat government has built a campsite at Kilad.
vanua-levu: Vanua Levu, once known as Sandalwood Island, has an area of about 5,587 square kilometres. The main part of the island is shaped like a tall, thin triangle 30 to 50 kilometres wide and 180 kilometres long, pointing north-east to Udu Point, the northernmost in the Fiji chain, and a long peninsula runs out from its south-eastern side into the Koro Sea. The island is rough and hilly and ringed by coral reefs, among them the Cakaulevu Reef off the northern shore. A rugged mountain range divides it and forms much of the boundary between the provinces of Cakaudrove and Macuata. The southern coasts are wet, while the north has a dry climate for eight months of the year, which suits sugar cane.

The island was settled about 3,100 years ago, the settlers living in houses raised above the reefs on the shore. Between 1250 and 1350 the Pacific sea level fell by about 30 centimetres, exposing the reef tops, killing much of the shellfish and lowering the water table below the roots of crops. Scarcity brought conflict, and people moved from seaside villages to fortified villages on mountaintops, which were occupied until about 1870, the last clear sign of warfare dating to about 1860.

Abel Tasman was the first known European to sight Vanua Levu, in 1643, and William Bligh passed it in 1789 after the mutiny on the Bounty. Traders began cutting sandalwood in the Bua Bay area around 1805, but the supply was exhausted by 1815. Settlers from Australia and New Zealand established coconut plantations near Savusavu in the 1860s, and Savusavu became a major centre of the copra trade until the Great Depression of the 1930s collapsed the price. In the same period Indians founded the town of Labasa.

Vanua Levu is divided into the provinces of Bua, Macuata and Cakaudrove, which together form the Northern Division of Fiji. With the Lau Islands it belongs to the Tovata Confederacy, one of the three traditional alliances of Fiji's chiefs, whose paramount chief, the Tui Cakau, is based on nearby Taveuni. The main towns are Labasa, a centre of the sugar industry, and Savusavu. Sugar cane and copra remain the main crops.
vanuaaku-pati: Walter Lini founded the party on 17 August 1971 as the New Hebridean Cultural Association, and it took the name New Hebrides National Party later that year. It was one of two parties formed as the islands moved towards independence: the National Party had the support of British interests, while the rival Union of New Hebrides Communities was backed by French interests. The party won the elections of 1975, and after its renaming in 1977 Lini became chief minister following the pre-independence elections of 1979.

Lini remained prime minister until 1991, when the party split and he was among those who left it. It lost its hold on government but stayed strong, and in the following decade two of its members, Donald Kalpokas and Edward Natapei, served as prime minister. Its seats then fell from 18 in 1998 to 14 in 2002 and 8 in 2004, a setback that forced Natapei to resign. After a further split it reunited in December 2004 and backed the government of Walter Lini's brother Ham Lini.

In September 2008 it won 11 of the 52 seats, becoming the largest party in Parliament, and Natapei returned as prime minister until a vote of no confidence removed him on 2 December 2010. Joe Natuman of the party became prime minister in 2014 for about a year. After the 2020 election its new leader, Bob Loughman, was appointed prime minister and held the office until August 2022, when he asked the President to dissolve Parliament to avoid a vote of no confidence; after the snap election the party went into opposition.
The name means Party of My Land or Party of Our Land, from the word vanua. The party supports socialist economic policies and draws most of its support from English speakers.
vanuatu: Vanuatu is a Y-shaped archipelago of about 83 relatively small islands of volcanic origin, 65 of them inhabited, with about 1,300 kilometres between the most northern and southern islands. It lies 1,750 km east of northern Australia and 540 km northeast of New Caledonia. The largest island is Espiritu Santo, and the highest point is Mount Tabwemasana, at 1,879 metres. Most islands are steep, with unstable soils and little permanent freshwater. There are several active volcanoes, including Lopevi and Mount Yasur, and volcanic activity is common.

The history before European colonisation is mostly obscure, since no written sources predate contact and little archaeological work has been done. Evidence gathered since the 1980s supports the settlement of the islands about 3,000 years ago, between roughly 1100 BCE and 700 BCE, by people almost certainly of the Lapita culture. Notable Lapita sites include Teouma on Éfaté, which has a large ancient cemetery containing the remains of 94 individuals. Sites on Éfaté, Lelepa and Eretoka are associated with the 16th–17th century chief or chiefs called Roy Mata, a title possibly held by different men over several generations, who according to oral tradition united local clans and presided over an era of peace.

The first Europeans to visit were a Spanish expedition led by the Portuguese navigator Fernandes de Queirós, who reached Espíritu Santo in 1606 and claimed the archipelago for Spain as La Austrialia del Espíritu Santo. James Cook named it the New Hebrides in 1774, after the Hebrides of Scotland. In the 1880s France and the United Kingdom claimed parts of it, and in 1906 they agreed to manage it jointly as an Anglo-French condominium. An independence movement arose in the 1970s, and the Republic of Vanuatu was founded in 1980. The name combines vanua, meaning land or home, and tu, to stand; the first prime minister, Walter Lini, said it was meant to connote a country that has stood alone.

Vanuatu is a parliamentary democracy with a written constitution, and its capital is Port Vila on Efate. The official languages are Bislama, English and French, and Bislama, a creole with a mostly English-derived vocabulary, is the lingua franca. The Lapita sites became the country's first UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008. A national Council of Chiefs, the Malvatu Mauri, advises the government on culture and language, and chiefs remain leading figures at village level. The country is a member of the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Pacific Islands Forum.
vapheio: The site lies on the right bank of the Eurotas, some 8 kilometres south of Sparta. Its tholos, or beehive tomb, has a walled approach about 30 metres long leading to a vaulted chamber some 10 metres across, in the floor of which the grave itself was cut. The tomb suffered considerable damage in the decades after it was dug, and during conservation work in 1962 its walls were restored to a height of about 6 metres.

Besides the cups, the grave held a large number of carved gem seals and amethyst beads, with objects of gold, silver, bronze, iron, lead, amber and crystal. Its 43 seals make it the largest find of Mycenaean and Minoan seals in the Aegean, and the princely figure buried there seems to have worn them on his wrists. Many are so close in style and subject to Minoan seals that archaeologists cannot tell whether they were made locally or brought from Crete; Sinclair Hood held that the finer ones were broadly Cretan and the cruder ones mainland work. The pottery dates the burial, but the gold and seals may have been old when buried.

The two cups show different ways of catching bulls, perhaps for the bull-leaping of Minoan Crete or for sacrifice. On one a cow is used to lure a bull, which is then roped by a rear leg; on the other bulls are driven into nets while one escapes, shoving its catchers aside. The netting scene has been compared with the capture of bulls for sacrifice in Plato's dialogue Critias. Marcus Niebuhr Tod called the pair perhaps the most perfect surviving works of Mycenaean or Minoan art.

Scholars had long seen that the cups were probably by different artists. Ellen Davis argued that one was made on mainland Greece, and Hood agreed; the usual view now is that the finer seduction cup is Cretan and the other Mycenaean. In Aegean archaeology the name Vapheio cup is now used for the shape itself, found in pottery as well as metalwork.
vaps-movement: The movement was founded in 1929 out of associations of veterans of the Estonian War of Independence of 1918–1920, and was led by former officers. Andres Larka was its figurehead and presidential candidate, Artur Sirk its leading figure. Early support came from campaigns to help veterans financially and to redistribute land once held by the Baltic German nobility. It was anti-communist and called for a more authoritarian and nationalist government; moderate members such as Johan Pitka gradually left.

Members, called Vaps, wore a black beret and used the Roman salute, and the movement published its own newspaper, Võitlus (The Struggle). After Socialists broke up one of its meetings it formed a paramilitary wing, the Korrapidajate Üksused, under Captain Heinrich-Balduin Dunkel. It welcomed Hitler's rise to power but later tried to distance itself from Nazism, rejecting racial ideology and criticising the persecution of Jews, though Sirk made antisemitic statements and Võitlus at times attacked Jews as conspirators. It kept good relations with the Finnish Lapua Movement.

Estonia's constitution of 1920 let 25 thousand citizens force a referendum on a draft law. After weaker centre-right proposals failed, the Vaps proposal for a strong presidency won 72.7 percent of the vote in October 1933, although the government of Jaan Tõnisson had banned the movement under a state of emergency before the vote. Early in 1934 it won absolute majorities in the local elections of the three largest cities. The coup of Konstantin Päts in 1934 prevented its expected victory in the presidential election. On 6 May 1936, 150 members went on trial and 143 were sentenced to long prison terms; they were amnestied in 1938, by which time the movement had lost most of its support.
varanasi: Varanasi lies on the left, crescent-shaped bank of the Ganges, in the south-east of Uttar Pradesh, 121 kilometres downstream of Prayagraj. Traditional etymology links the name to two tributaries that bound the old city, the Varuna and the Assi. The city is known for its ghats, steps leading down the steep bank, where pilgrims perform rituals. At the Manikarnika and Harishchandra ghats Hindus cremate their dead, and the genealogy registers of Hindu families are kept in the city.

According to Hindu scriptures, Shiva founded Varanasi under its name Kashi. Excavations in 2014 found artefacts dating to 800 BCE, and digs nearby at Aktha and Ramnagar found objects from 1800 BCE. Kashi was a kingdom of the first millennium BCE, and the Buddha gave his first teaching at Sarnath. In the 8th century Adi Shankara established the worship of Shiva as an official sect of the city. In 1033 Ahmad Nialtagin, a subordinate of Mahmud of Ghazni, raided it and partly destroyed temples, but withdrew by midday because of the threat of local resistance.

Bhakti figures born there in the mid-second millennium include Kabir, Ravidas and Tulsidas, who wrote the Ramcharitmanas in Awadhi. Guru Nanak visited in 1507. The Benares Estate was established near the city in 1740, in the Mughal province of Awadh, and in 1775 the East India Company acquired Benares under the Treaty of Faizabad. It passed through the Ceded and Conquered Provinces in 1805, the North-Western Provinces in 1836 and the United Provinces in 1902, and became part of Uttar Pradesh in 1950.

The Kashi Vishwanath Temple and the Sankat Mochan Hanuman Temple are among its notable shrines, and the Jantar Mantar observatory of 1737 stands above the ghats. Jonathan Duncan founded the Benares Sanskrit College in 1791, and Annie Besant and Madan Mohan Malviya founded the Banaras Hindu University in 1916. The city is a centre of silk weaving and carpets, and of music: the Benares gharana of tabla playing was developed there.
varangian-guard: Men from Kievan Rus' were the earliest Varangians in Byzantine service. A treaty of 874 after a period of hostilities obliged the Rus' to provide men, and Varangians are recorded as mercenaries in 911. In 988 Basil II asked Vladimir I of Kiev for help to defend his throne, and under an earlier treaty Vladimir sent 6,000 men, taking the chance to rid himself of unruly warriors he could not pay. In exchange he received Basil's sister Anna in marriage and agreed to convert to Christianity. Basil distrusted the native guardsmen, whose loyalties often shifted, and kept the Varangians as his personal guard.

In 989 these men landed at Chrysopolis with Basil II and defeated the rebel Bardas Phokas, who died of a stroke on the field. The guard served extensively in southern Italy in the 11th century, winning the Battle of Cannae in 1018, and in the reconquest of Sicily under George Maniakes in 1038, where Harald Hardrada was a prominent member. At Manzikert in 1071 virtually all the emperor's guards fell around him. Until the late 11th century the guard was almost entirely Norse, with so many Swedish men enlisting that a medieval Swedish law forbade anyone to inherit while staying in Greece.

After the Norman conquest of England many Anglo-Saxons joined, and by the time of Alexios Komnenos the guard was largely recruited from them and others who had suffered at the hands of the Vikings and Normans. The Varangians helped John II Komnenos win at Beroia in 1122, and they defended Constantinople in the Fourth Crusade. By the late 13th century most were assimilated, though the guard lasted to at least the mid-14th century and up to 3,000 are said to have stood in the city in 1453.

The Varangians swore an oath of loyalty to the emperor, performed ceremonial duties as retainers and acclaimers, and carried out some police duties in cases of treason and conspiracy. They were headed by an officer called the akolouthos, usually a native Byzantine. Their main weapon was the broad-bladed Dane axe, and Byzantine writers called them axe-bearing barbarians. They were used in battle at critical moments.

Their loyalty became a trope of Byzantine writers such as Anna Komnene, but it attached to the office and not the man: in 969 they knelt to John Tzimiskes after he killed Nikephoros II. Snorri Sturluson says that on an emperor's death the Varangians could take as much gold as they could carry, but Byzantine sources do not mention it and modern historians doubt it. Their service is also recorded on Scandinavian runestones, such as the Greece Runestones raised by former members or in their memory.
varangians: The word Varangian comes through Greek and Old East Slavic from Old Norse væringi, probably meaning a sworn companion, extended to a foreigner who has taken service with a new lord by a treaty of fealty. Geography leads many to argue that most Varangians who settled in the lands of the eastern Baltic and modern Russia came from the area of modern Sweden. It has also been argued that the word does not appear in primary sources until the eleventh century, and that the name Rus' had earlier been used broadly for Scandinavians.

The Primary Chronicle first mentions Varangians as exacting tribute from Slavic and Finnic tribes in 859. In the 9th century the Rus' operated the Volga route to the Middle East, selling furs, honey and slaves and receiving Arabic silver dirhams; hoards of Baghdad-minted coins have been found in Sweden, particularly on Gotland. Later the Dnieper and Dniester routes overtook it in importance. Ahmad ibn Fadlan described the Rus' he met on the Volga in 921 and 922. Raids included an expedition of 913 on 500 ships that pillaged Gorgan, and a capture of Barda in 943.

Raiding and trade also led to Constantinople. The Rus' attacked it from Kiev in 860, though the result is disputed, and rulers of Kiev launched a naval expedition in 907, an abortive campaign in 941 and, under Sviatoslav I, an invasion of the Balkans in 968 to 971. Militarily the Varangians were usually beaten by Byzantine forces, partly through Greek fire. From at least the early 10th century many served as mercenaries in the Byzantine army, forming the Varangian Guard.

The Varangian Guard served as bodyguard of the emperors from the 10th to the 14th century. It kept an almost entirely Norse character until the late 11th century, and after the Norman Conquest of England it increasingly took in Anglo-Saxons. By the late 13th century its members were largely assimilated to the Byzantines. In Sweden, the Västgötalagen declared that no one could inherit while staying in Greece, a measure meant to curb enlistment.

Most Varangians converted from Norse paganism to Orthodox Christianity, culminating in the Christianization of Kievan Rus' in 988. As the Viking Age declined, the flow of Scandinavians to Rus' stopped and they gradually assimilated into Slavic culture by the late 11th century. Runestones in Sweden, such as the Greece Runestones, commemorate those who died abroad.
vardan-mamikonian: Vardan Mamikonian was born around 387 in Ashtishat in the Taron region, the son of Hamazasp Mamikonian and Sahakanoysh, a daughter of Patriarch Sahak of Armenia. He was educated at Vagharshapat in the school founded by Sahak and Mesrop Mashtots. After his father's death he became head of the Mamikonian family, which held the hereditary office of sparapet, supreme commander of the Armenian armed forces.

In 420 he went to Constantinople with Mashtots and was appointed stratelates of Byzantine Armenia by Theodosius II. In 422 he went to Ctesiphon, where the Sasanian king Bahram V recognised him as sparapet of the Kingdom of Armenia. He kept the title after the kingdom was abolished in 428.

Conditions worsened after Yazdegerd II came to the throne in 439, with heavier taxes and obligations on Armenia and its nobility. In 442 he sent the Armenian cavalry under Vardan east against the Huns. In 449 he issued an edict imposing Zoroastrianism. The Armenian elite met at Artaxata under the marzpan Vasak Siwni and declared loyalty to the Sasanian state and to their Christian faith. Yazdegerd summoned the nakharars to Ctesiphon and forced them to convert, then released most of them after an attack from the east.

On their return Vardan and most of the nobles repudiated their conversion, though Yeghishe and Ghazar Parpetsi give conflicting accounts of his first apostasy and of how the rebellion of 450 began. Vardan became its leader, and he and his allies swore an oath and took fortresses and settlements. They won a major victory in the summer of 450 and allied with the northern Huns, but an embassy to Byzantium for aid failed. A pro-Persian party of nobles opposed him.

A large Sasanian army with the Immortals and war elephants marched against the rebels in the summer of 451. On 2 June Vardan's army fought at Avarayr near Maku. Followers of Vasak Siwni deserted during the battle, and Vardan and most of the Armenian nobility died. The aftermath is not wholly clear, but Yazdegerd seems to have withdrawn his troops, alarmed by Persian losses, and imprisoned Vasak. Many of Vardan's surviving supporters were imprisoned in Iran and released over the following years.

In 481 a new rebellion under his nephew Vahan Mamikonian won recognition of Armenian religious rights and autonomy by the Treaty of Nvarsak in 484. Vardan is venerated as a saint by the Armenian Apostolic, Armenian Catholic and Armenian Evangelical churches, and his feast falls on the last Thursday before Great Lent. The Armenian-American fraternal organization Knights of Vartan bears his name.
vardar: The Vardar is 388 kilometres long, of which 76 are in Greece, and drains an area of around 25,000 square kilometres. It rises at Vrutok, a few kilometres south-west of Gostivar in North Macedonia, and passes through Gostivar, Skopje and Veles. It crosses the Greek border near Gevgelija and flows by Polykastro and Axioupoli, meaning town on the Axios, before emptying into the Thermaic Gulf west of Thessaloniki. Its basin makes up two-thirds of the territory of North Macedonia. Its valley has fertile land in the Polog region, around Gevgelija and in the Thessaloniki regional unit, and mountains surround the river elsewhere.

The oldest known name of the river is Axios, mentioned by Homer as the home of the Paeonians, allies of Troy. The name Vardários was sometimes used by the ancient Greeks in the 3rd century BCE and widely in the Byzantine era, and the modern Vardar probably descends from it. The name may come from Thracian, though Dardanian, Paeonian, Ancient Macedonian and Greek were also spoken in the lands the river drains. Vardarios may derive from a Proto-Indo-European form meaning black water, and Axios may have meant dark or not shining. The Albanian author Pjetër Bogdani used the form Asi.

Under the Ottoman Empire the river became well known, and in Turkey it remains the inspiration for many folk songs, the best-known being Vardar Ovasi. It appears on the coat of arms of Skopje, which is part of the city's flag.

Together with the Loudias and the Haliacmon, the Vardar forms a large delta at the Axios-Loudias-Aliakmonas National Park. Greek National Road 1 and the M1 and E75 run within the valley along the river's length as far as near Skopje. A prevailing northerly ravine wind, the Vardaris or Vardarec, blows down the valley, usually as a breeze. When it meets the mountains between North Macedonia and Greece it gathers great momentum and brings cold conditions to Thessaloniki and the delta, especially in winter, when pressure over eastern Europe is higher than over the Aegean.
vardzia: Vardzia was excavated from the slopes of Erusheti Mountain on the left bank of the Kura River, thirty kilometres from Aspindza. Four building phases have been identified. The first, under Giorgi III (1156-1184), laid out the site and dug the first cave dwellings. The second, between his death and the marriage of his successor Tamar in 1186, saw the Church of the Dormition carved and decorated. The third, until the Battle of Basian around 1203, added many dwellings, the defences, the water supply and the irrigation network. The fourth was a partial rebuilding after heavy damage in the earthquake of 1283.

Chronicles say the monastery held large amounts of silver, gold and precious stones, and that it escaped the Mongol invaders in the 1290s. The belltower and southern portal were built in the late 13th and early 14th centuries. The Safavid chronicler Hasan Beg Rumlu described its sack by the Persians under Shah Tahmasp I in 1551. After the Ottomans arrived in 1578 the monks departed and the site was abandoned.

The caves stretch some five hundred metres along the cliff in up to nineteen tiers, and the main lower site holds about 500 caves at an elevation of thirteen hundred metres. The eastern part has seventy-nine cave dwellings with 242 rooms, including six chapels, a pharmacy and twenty-five wine cellars, where 185 wine jars sunk into the floor show the importance of viticulture. The western part has forty houses with 165 rooms, a refectory with a bakery and a forge. A 3.5 km aqueduct brought water from Zeda Vardzia, and the complex had access tunnels and provision for defence.

The Church of the Dormition measures 8.2 by 14.5 metres and rises to 9.2 metres. Its paintings, executed in secco, are of crucial significance in the development of medieval Georgian mural painting. A donor portrait commemorates Rati I Surameli, and portraits of Giorgi III and Tamar hold a model of the church. Tamar lacks the ribbon of a married woman, which helps date the paintings to between 1184 and 1186. Since 1985 the site has formed part of the Vardzia Historical-Architectural Museum-Reserve, and Vardzia-Khertvisi was submitted for UNESCO World Heritage listing in 1999.
variolation: In China, where the British sinologist Joseph Needham dates the first variolation to between 1567 and 1572, scabs from mild cases were dried, ground into powder and puffed up the nostril through a silver blowpipe, the right for boys and the left for girls. The Kangxi Emperor had his children and his troops inoculated. In Bengal, according to accounts of 1768, practitioners called Tikadars rubbed dried scabs into needle pricks in the arm; claims that the practice was ancient in India are disputed. In Sennar in Sudan, mothers bargained over a sick child's pustules in a custom known as buying the smallpox.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, scarred by smallpox in 1715, met the practice in Constantinople and in 1718 had her five-year-old son variolated, supervised by the embassy doctor Charles Maitland. In 1721 Maitland variolated six condemned prisoners at Newgate, promised freedom if they survived, and the royal family then promoted the procedure. In Boston that year, during an outbreak, Cotton Mather, who had learned of it from an enslaved West African named Onesimus, backed the surgeon Zabdiel Boylston, who variolated 300 people of whom six died, while 1,000 of the 6,000 who caught smallpox naturally died.

Doctors made the procedure harder by adding severe bloodletting and deep incisions. Robert Sutton, a Suffolk surgeon, advertised a secret new method from 1762, and by 1770 his family had treated over 300,000 patients; it rested on a shallow scratch, mild donors and no bleeding. In 1769 Thomas Dimsdale variolated Catherine the Great, her son Grand Duke Paul and over 140 courtiers, and in 1775 George Washington ordered the Continental Army variolated.

Its great drawback was that the variolated could spread smallpox to others, and these cases came to outweigh its benefits. After Edward Jenner vaccinated James Phipps with cowpox in 1796 and published evidence that his vaccine was safer, variolation declined, and Russia banned it in 1805, the first country to do so. It lingered in remote places: during the World Health Organization's eradication campaign, vaccination teams found variolators in Pakistan and Afghanistan and confiscated their samples. John Haygarth's plan of 1793 to exterminate smallpox from Britain was impractical in its time, but with vaccination in place of variolation it was very like the strategy that campaign adopted.
vasai: Vasai, also written Bassein and known in Portuguese as Baçaim, lies in the Palghar district of Maharashtra, partitioned out of the Thane district in August 2014. It forms part of the Vasai-Virar twin cities in the Konkan division. The name derives from the Sanskrit waas, meaning dwelling or residence. It was recorded as Baxay by Barbosa in 1514, became Baçaim under the Portuguese, Bajipur under the Marathas and Bassein under the British, and took the Marathi name Vasai again after the British Raj ended.

The history of Vasai is traced to the Puranic ages. Greek, Arab, Persian and Roman traders came to this coast, and the Greek merchant Cosma Indicopleustes is known to have visited the area in the 6th century and the Chinese traveller Xuanzang in 640. Historians connect the district with the Chalukya dynasty, then the Silhara dynasty of Konkan and the Seuna dynasty, under which it was a district head from 1184 to 1318. The Gujarat Sultanate later conquered it and named it Basai.

The Portuguese valued it as a trading centre on the Arabian Sea and a place for a shipyard and for crops such as rice, sugarcane and cotton. Nuno da Cunha assembled 150 ships and 4,000 men against Malik Tokan, who was fortifying Basai with 14,000 men. The Treaty of Bassein, signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon São Mateus, gave the Portuguese the village, its territories and islands, including Bombay. Baçaim became the northern capital of Portuguese territories in India, with the Court of the North in its fort. By 1674 the Portuguese had built two colleges, four convent schools and fifteen churches in its territories.

Marathas under Chimaji Appa, brother of Peshwa Baji Rao, took the fort after the Battle of Vasai, and the Portuguese surrendered on 16 May 1739. Bombay, held by the British, was by then overtaking the town as the region's economic centre. The British took Bassein on 11 December 1780, during the First Anglo-Maratha War. The Peshwa Baji Rao II took refuge there in 1801, and the Treaty of Bassein, signed on 31 December 1802, was a decisive step in the dissolution of the Maratha Empire.

Vasai lies within the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Its eastern part is industrial, with about 12,000 industrial units, and the station at Vasai Road is a major rail junction. Its fort, Bassein Fort, also known as Saint Sebastian's Fort, is the main tourist attraction. Other sites include the Vajreshwari Temple and St. Francis Xavier's Church.
vasco-da-gama: Vasco da Gama was born in Sines, a seaport on the Alentejo coast of southwest Portugal. His father, Estêvão da Gama, had served as a knight of the household of Ferdinand, Duke of Viseu, rose in the ranks of the military Order of Santiago and was civil governor of Sines until 1478. Portuguese ships had worked down the African coast since the early 15th century, and Bartolomeu Dias had found the South Atlantic westerlies in 1487.

On 8 July 1497 da Gama left Lisbon with four ships and a crew of 170.
