The earliest settlement is thought to have stood at the source of the Volkhov, where Ryurikovo Gorodishche was founded in the 9th century. By 930 the elite residences outside that fort had merged at the present site, and reliably dated archaeological layers there begin in the 930s. The name was first given to the detinets, or kremlin, and later extended to the whole city.

The Nikon Chronicle, a late source, mentions the city under 859, in connection with the death of the elder Gostomysl, while the Primary Chronicle in the Laurentian Codex has it under 862. The city's charter accepts 859, a date proposed by the historian Mikhail Tikhomirov in 1959. Lying on the route from the Varangians to the Greeks, Novgorod became the second most important city of Kievan Rus', and the eldest son of the ruling Kievan prince was customarily sent to rule it.

In 1136 the Novgorodians dismissed their prince, Vsevolod Mstislavich, and this year traditionally begins the Novgorod Republic, which lasted until 1478. It was a city-state dominated by a small group of wealthy merchant and noble families, unusual in Russia, where princes typically held supreme authority. It controlled much of the Russian North, from the Gulf of Finland to the Ural Mountains, traded with the Hanseatic League, whose kontor there was the Peterhof, and was one of Europe's largest cities at its peak in the 14th century.

Ivan III abolished some elective offices after the incorporation into the Russian state. In 1570 the oprichniki of Ivan IV sacked the city, and the historian Ruslan Skrynnikov counted 2,170-2,180 recorded deaths, a figure he did not consider final. After the capital moved to Saint Petersburg in 1712 Novgorod lost its commercial importance.

German forces occupied the city from 19 August 1941 until the Red Army liberated it on 20 January 1944, by which time only 40 of 2,346 residential buildings were undamaged and 65 architectural monuments had been destroyed or badly damaged. Its chief monuments and those of its surroundings were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1992. It is the administrative centre of Novgorod Oblast, and the population was 224,286 in the 2021 census. Archaeological research has been systematic since 1932.
veliky-ustyug: Veliky Ustyug stands near the confluence of the Sukhona, flowing from the west, and the Yug, flowing from the south. Below the junction the rivers form the Northern Dvina. The name Ustyug means the mouth of the Yug, and by the late 15th century it had become Veliky, or Great, Ustyug. The first recorded settlement was the monastic settlement at Gleden, where the Troitsko-Gledensky Monastery now stands. The historic centre lies on the high left bank of the Sukhona, in an area that was once a posad, a craftsmen's quarter outside the fortress.

A chronicle first mentions the town in 1207, and the Mikhaylo-Arkhangelsky Monastery was founded in 1212. It belonged to the Vladimir-Suzdal Principality, while neighbouring lands such as Totma were colonised by Novgorod, so it formed the only obstacle to Novgorod's trade with the north along the Sukhona and the Northern Dvina. Clashes between Novgorod and Ustyug became regular, especially in the 14th century. The Grand Duchy of Moscow annexed the town in 1328. The Mongol invasion did not directly affect it, and in the second half of the 13th century it grew rapidly with refugees from central Russia.

In 1450 Dmitry Shemyaka took the town during his war with his cousin Vasily II of Moscow, drowned in the Sukhona the citizens who refused to accept him as prince, and held it for two years. Polish troops besieged the town in 1613, during the Time of Troubles, but never took it. At the junction of important trade routes it became a significant commercial and industrial centre in the 16th and 17th centuries. It was also known for silver filigree, birch bark fretwork and niello, for its own Ustyug icon painting and for tiles.

Veliky Ustyug lost its key role as a river port when trade between China and western Europe was diverted to the Baltic after the founding of Saint Petersburg in 1703. It has preserved almost all of its architectural monuments, with churches and cathedrals of the 17th and early 18th centuries, among them the Assumption Cathedral, built between 1619 and 1659. The museum director Nikolay Bekryashev, from 1924 to 1938, persuaded the authorities to hand old churches to the museum rather than demolish them. Many of the town's heritage buildings stand on the left bank of the Sukhona. In Vologda Oblast, it is mostly known for tourism.
velleius-paterculus: Few details of Velleius' life are known with certainty, and even his first name is uncertain: Priscian calls him Marcus, but the first printed edition of 1520 calls him Publius and elsewhere Gaius. Most of what is known comes from his own brief account in his history. He was born into a noble Campanian family, though the place of his birth is unknown, and was a great-great-great-grandson of Minatus Magius of Aeculanum in Samnium, who received the Roman franchise for his actions during the Social War. His uncle Capito sat in the Roman Senate.

As a young man Velleius served as a military tribune in Rome's eastern provinces. In 2 CE he was with the army of Gaius Caesar and witnessed his meeting with Phraates V of Parthia on the banks of the Euphrates. Two years later he was a cavalry prefect in the command of Tiberius in Germania, and he remained a senior member of Tiberius' staff until 12 CE. He was elected quaestor, filling the office in 7 CE. Augustus designated him and his brother Magius Celer for the praetorship before he died, and the two were formally elected under Tiberius and served in 15 CE.
He was among the friends of Sejanus, whom he praises in his writing. There is no evidence that he outlived his friend's downfall by long, and it seems likely that he shared his fate.

His Roman history, in two books, was apparently conceived as a universal history. The first book runs from the aftermath of the Trojan War to the destruction of Carthage in 146 BCE and is missing several portions, including its beginning. The second, intact, runs from the age of the Gracchi to 30 CE. It is the only connected narrative of much of that period, since Livy's books on the late Republic are lost, and it is especially detailed from the death of Caesar to that of Augustus. It consists largely of highlights and character portraits, and its showy rhetoric is typical of Silver Age Latin; judgements of its quality vary considerably.

The work seems to have been little known in antiquity. A badly damaged manuscript found at Murbach Abbey in Alsace in 1515, since lost, formed the basis of the first printed edition, published by Beatus Rhenanus in 1520.
velletri: Velletri lies about 40 km to the south-east of the centre of Rome, in the Alban Hills of Lazio. Its northern territory stands on the southern foothills of the Colli Albani range, formed about 150,000 years ago after the collapse of the volcano Laziale, while its southern boundary reaches the Pontine Marshes, whose reclamation began under Pope Pius VI and was completed under Benito Mussolini. The square of the Trivium in the old town stands at 332 metres above sea level, and the climate is mild and very rainy.

The Latin term for a swamp was Velia, and the name Velitrae is thought to come from the same root. Tradition says the town came into conflict with Rome under Ancus Marcius, the fourth king of Rome, who besieged it after the Volsci plundered Roman territory; its elders surrendered and a treaty of peace and friendship followed. Its massive Volscian walls were razed in 338 BCE as a punishment after the final Roman conquest, and they were not rebuilt until the Middle Ages.

Velletri declined after it was sacked by Alaric the Goth in 410 CE. It was a bishopric, and after the Byzantine reconquest of Italy it became an imperial city. In 592 Pope Gregory I joined the Diocese of Tres Tabernae to that of Velletri. In the Middle Ages it was one of the few free cities of Lazio, and its motto, Est mihi libertas papalis et imperialis, claims liberty from both pope and empire. The bell tower of Santa Maria in Trivio was raised in 1353 in thanks for deliverance from the plague of 1348.

During the War of the Austrian Succession (1740-1748), Bourbon troops defeated the Austrian Habsburgs at the Battle of Velletri. After the French Revolution the town rebelled and was proclaimed a republic, which lasted until 1814. In 1849 Giuseppe Garibaldi defeated a Bourbon Neapolitan force there, but the Roman Republic was overwhelmed soon after. Fierce fighting took place around the town in 1944, after the Anglo-American landing at Anzio.

Velletri is an Italian comune in the Metropolitan City of Rome. Its Cathedral of St Clement was built in the 4th century over a pagan temple and rebuilt in 1659-1662. The Oreste Nardini Civic Archaeological Museum holds the Sarcophagus of the Labors of Hercules, of the 2nd century. The bronze sheets of Velletri, found in 1784 within the Church of St Francis, are kept at the National Archaeological Museum of Naples. The surrounding country is known for its wine, and the town was a regular stop between Rome and Naples on the Grand Tour.
vellore: Vellore lies on the banks of the Palar River in the Palar basin, surrounded by the Javadi Hills, an extension of the Eastern Ghats, about 135 kilometres west of Chennai. It is the administrative headquarters of Vellore district. According to one legend the name comes from the many babul trees, called velan trees locally, that surrounded the region; another story says the god Murugan, with the epithet Velan, came to the place in anger. Because of its importance and its position relative to Madras it has also been called the Second Madras.

The recorded history of Vellore goes back to the ninth century, as a Chola inscription in the Annamalaiyar Temple at Tiruvannamalai shows. Many dynasties dominated it, among them the Pallava dynasty, the Medieval Cholas, the Rashtrakuta dynasty, the Sambuvaraya chieftains, Vijayanagar, the Nawabs of the Carnatic and the British. The fort and the Jalakandeswarar Temple inside it date from the Vijayanagara period; because records are lacking, the fort's exact date of building is not known. The Aravidus lost Vellore to the Bijapur Sultan before the Marathas captured it in 1676 after a siege of four and a half months. It passed to the British in 1760, and the fort withstood Hyder Ali's siege from 1780 to 1782.

After Tipu Sultan was killed at Sringapatam, the British exiled his surviving children and their households to Vellore Fort, where they took part in the mutiny of 1806. In 1805 the new commander of the Madras Army, General Sir John Cradock, had approved regulations on uniform and appearance: Hindus were forbidden religious marks on the forehead on duty, Muslims had to shave their beards, and a new headdress with a leather cockade offended upper-caste sepoys, for whom leather was a taboo. Many sepoys came to believe their officers meant to convert them to Christianity.

Vellore Fort, a Monument of National Importance managed by the Archaeological Survey of India, has a broad moat, granite ramparts broken by round towers, and within it a church, a mosque and a Hindu temple. Tipu Sultan's family and the last king of Sri Lanka, Vikrama Rajasinha, were held there as prisoners. The Christian Medical College and Hospital, founded in 1900 by the American medical missionary Ida S. Scudder, has grown into an institution of international standing. Vellore is also a centre of the leather industry.
veluwe: The Veluwe is a forest-rich ridge of hills of 1,100 km2 that includes woodland, heath, some small lakes and the largest sand drifts in Europe. It is the largest push moraine complex in the Netherlands, stretching 60 km from north to south and reaching heights of up to 110 metres. It was formed by the Saalian glacial during the Pleistocene, some 200,000 years ago, when glaciers about 200 metres thick pushed the sand deposits of the Rhine and Maas delta sideways. Because the hills are sand, rain water disappears quickly and flows tens of metres below the surface to the edges, where it emerges again.

Originally a string of swamps surrounded the Veluwe, heavily populated with game such as deer and wild boar, which found rich vegetation there. Its name comes from Proto-Germanic words for pale or fallow and for island, and it corresponds to fallow lands in English. It was probably used in contrast with the fertile good lands of the Betuwe to the south. The sparsely populated and infertile Veluwe is the traditional linguistic boundary between the Low Franconian dialects to the west and south and the Low Saxon dialects further north and east.

The region has 21 municipalities, among them Apeldoorn, Arnhem, Ede, Harderwijk and Wageningen. Its coniferous and deciduous forests hold some 500 plant species and animals such as wild boar, roe, red and fallow deer, pine martens, red foxes and badgers. Since the 1990s many plans have restored wetlands by blocking drainage systems built by farmers over the previous 150 years. By 2012 nine wildlife overpasses, each about 50 metres wide, had been built to reconnect parts of the Veluwe separated by roads, towns and farmland.

The Veluwe is a tourist destination, especially for Dutch people on short holidays, with more than 500 campsites and bungalow parks, four zoos and over 50 museums, including the Kröller-Müller art museum. The royal palace Het Loo stands at Apeldoorn, and the National Sports Centre Papendal, an Olympic training facility, lies near Arnhem.
velvet-revolution: The Communist Party seized power in Czechoslovakia on 25 February 1948, and no official opposition parties operated afterwards. Dissidents, notably those of Charter 77, published home-made periodicals, and the secret police persecuted them. People were blacklisted for signing Charter 77, supporting Alexander Dubček during the Prague Spring, promoting religion or having family in the West, and as all schools, media and businesses belonged to the state the rules were easy to enforce. By the late 1980s discontent with living standards had grown, and the changes in neighbouring countries, among them the fall of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989, encouraged protest.

On 17 November 1989, International Students' Day, about 15,000 people joined a demonstration in Prague, which marked the fiftieth anniversary of the killing of the student Jan Opletal by the Nazi authorities. Riot police stopped the marchers on Národní Street and attacked them. A false report that a student, Martin Šmíd, had been killed spread the next day and persuaded hesitant citizens to join the protests. Students and theatres went on strike, and on 19 November Václav Havel and other dissidents founded the Civic Forum in Prague, with Public Against Violence formed the same day in Bratislava.

The number of protesters in Prague grew from 200,000 to an estimated 500,000 by 20 November. The entire Presidium of the Communist Party, including General Secretary Miloš Jakeš, resigned on 24 November, and on 27 November a two-hour general strike took place across the country, supported by a reported 75 per cent of the population. The Federal Assembly then removed the constitutional provision for the party's leading role. On 10 December President Gustáv Husák swore in the first government in 41 years not dominated by the Communist Party, and resigned.

Havel was elected president of Czechoslovakia on 29 December 1989, and Alexander Dubček became speaker of the federal parliament the day before. Havel negotiated the removal of about 73,500 Soviet troops, who left within months. Free elections in June 1990 were the first democratic ones since 1946, and Czechoslovakia split peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia on 31 December 1992. The name Velvet Revolution was coined by Rita Klímová, the dissidents' English translator. Slovaks have called the events the Gentle Revolution. Some theorists, among them Jaroslav Krejčí, argue it was not a true revolution because it involved no illegitimate violence.
vemork: Construction began in 1906 under the newly founded Norsk hydro-elektrisk Kvælstofaktieselskab, the forerunner of Norsk Hydro, at the Rjukan Falls in what is now Tinn Municipality. The works were so costly that they had to be financed from abroad. When the station opened in 1911, after four years of building, its capacity of 108 megawatts made it the largest power plant in the world. Ten 6-megawatt generating sets were supplied by Voith and AEG and by Escher Wyss and Oerlikon.

The plant was built to power a factory making artificial fertiliser by fixing nitrogen, using a method invented by Kristian Birkeland. Norsk Hydro later added a unit producing concentrated heavy water by electrolysis, an offshoot of the hydrogen production then used for the Haber process. Production began in December 1934, and it was the first plant in the world to make heavy water in quantity. In 1940 the French government bought the whole available stock; Germany had also offered to buy it, but the Norwegian government, told of its possible military use, handed it to a French agent who smuggled it out through England.

Under the German occupation at least five attacks were launched to deny the Germans heavy water for an atomic bomb. Four Norwegian agents of the Special Operations Executive parachuted in on 18 October 1942 for the reconnaissance operation Grouse. On 19 November 1942 the British Operation Freshman, using two Halifax bombers towing gliders, failed when three of the aircraft crashed; the survivors were captured and executed by the Germans.

The six agents of Gunnerside joined the Grouse team and on the night of 28 February to 1 March 1943 destroyed the heavy-water section and 500 kg of heavy water. An American air raid on 16 November 1943 did little damage, and on 20 February 1944 the Norwegian resistance sank the ferry D/F Hydro carrying a shipment to Germany. The Germans later proved to have been further from a bomb than feared.

Heavy-water production ended in 1971, when a new power station opened inside the mountain behind the old one. The old building has been the Norwegian Industrial Workers Museum since 1988, with exhibitions on the sabotage and the early Norwegian labour movement. The raid has been retold in a 1948 film with several of the saboteurs, in Knut Haukelid's account Skis Against the Atom, and in the 1965 film The Heroes of Telemark. In 2026 the site was added to the European Film Academy's Treasures of European Film Culture.
venantius-fortunatus: Venantius Fortunatus was born at Duplavis, near Treviso in Veneto, and grew up during the Roman reconquest of Italy. Historians disagree about where he spent his childhood. D. Tardi suggests that his family moved to Aquileia after the troubles that followed the death of King Theoderic, while Judith George argues that it never did, since the poet speaks of Duplavis more than of any other place. Sometime in the 550s or 60s he went to Ravenna, where he received a classical education in the Roman manner and became familiar with poets such as Virgil, Horace, Ovid, Statius and Martial, as well as Christian writers including Arator, Claudian and Coelius Sedulius.

Fortunatus moved to Metz in the spring of 566, probably intending to become a poet at the Merovingian court. He gave two reasons for his winding route through Italy, Austria, Germany and France: the adventures of a wandering minstrel, and a wish to venerate Saint Martin at Tours. At Metz he performed a poem for the whole court at the marriage of King Sigibert and Queen Brunhild, and nobles and bishops then sought verse from him. He visited King Charibert in Paris until Charibert's death in 567 or 568, and later went to Poitiers, where he met Radegund.

He became her close friend and wrote many poems in her honour and in support of her political campaigns. Gregory of Tours, installed as bishop in 573, became a patron, and in 580 Fortunatus wrote a poem defending him against charges of treason at the court of King Chilperic. He was ordained around 576 and stayed at Poitiers, succeeding Bishop Plato about 599 to 600.

Fortunatus left eleven books of Latin poetry, including epitaphs, panegyrics, georgics, consolations and religious verse, arranged chronologically and by the importance of the subject. He wrote four major panegyrics for Merovingian kings. The wedding poem for Sigibert and Brunhild tells how Cupid brought the couple together, in the manner of the classical poets. Scholars differ on the poem for Chilperic, which praises a headstrong king as gracious and merciful: some see an attempt to please a new patron, others a gentle hint of how an ideal king should rule, made to help Gregory.

His long narrative poem Vita S. Martini and a verse life of Radegund belong to his other work. His hymns Pange lingua and Vexilla Regis prodeunt entered the liturgy; the latter honours a relic of the True Cross sent to Radegund by the Byzantine Emperor Justin II. He wrote as Latin verse moved from quantitative metre towards accentual forms, and his poems give a view of the Merovingian court that sometimes differs from Gregory's account.
vendel: Vendel lies in Tierp Municipality in Uppland and overlooks Vendelsjön, a long stretch of water near the Vendel river, which joins the river Fyris. It was the site of an ancient royal estate belonging to Uppsala öd, the network of estates that provided income for the medieval Swedish kings. Vendel Church was probably begun in the Romanesque style in the latter half of the 13th century and was given brick vaults around 1450. It is best known for its murals by Johannes Iwan, who worked in Uppland in the 15th century.

Between 1881 and 1883 the Swedish archaeologist Hjalmar Stolpe uncovered 14 graves in and just beyond the south-east corner of the churchyard. Several were burials in boats up to 9 m long, identified by their many ship rivets, and they held fine swords and other weapons, helmets, cauldrons, chains, beads, shields and tools, with many animal sacrifices, mainly horses. One later grave, Grave 3, held an important set of bridle mounts. The graves date from the later 6th to the 8th century.

The helmets from Graves 1, 12 and 14 carry die-stamped plaques of warriors like those on the helmet from the early 7th-century ship burial at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk. The shield from Grave 12 has a stamped metal strip that is die-linked to an equivalent piece at Sutton Hoo, which points to a direct connection between the armourers who made the two sets of objects. The Sutton Hoo burial is often associated with King Rædwald of East Anglia. A companion cemetery lies at Valsgärde in the same region.

At nearby Husby stands a large mound that local tradition calls Ottarshögen, after Ottar or Ohthere, a figure also named in the epic Beowulf. An excavation in 1917 found the remains of a powerful man buried at the beginning of the 6th century, the time of Ohthere; other graves of that date linked with his family lie at Old Uppsala. Vendel has also given its name to the Vendel style in art.
venetian-arsenal: The Arsenal is described as one of the earliest large-scale industrial enterprises in history. A Byzantine-style establishment may have existed there as early as the 8th century, and the present structure is usually said to have been begun in 1104 under Ordelafo Faliero, although no evidence supports so precise a date. It certainly existed by the early 13th century. At first the state dockyard maintained naval ships that had been built privately. The much larger Arsenale Nuovo of 1320 made it possible to build and maintain the whole state navy and the larger merchant ships in one place, and the Arsenal became an important centre of rope manufacture, with housing for its workers growing up outside the walls.

High walls and guards shielded the Arsenal, a 2-mile rampart enclosing it, and each area produced a particular prefabricated part or other supply, such as munitions, rope and rigging. The wood came from an exclusive forest owned by the Arsenal in the Montello hills. Venice replaced the Roman hull-first practice with a frame-first system, which was faster and used less timber. Production was divided into framing, planking and cabins, and final assembly, with standardised, interchangeable parts, and a canal carried galleys along as they were built. The Arsenal often held up to 100 galleys in different stages of construction and maintenance, and a finished galley could be fitted out, armed and provisioned in as little as a day.

Its staff also developed firearms early, beginning with bombards in the 1370s, and the condottiere Bartolomeo Colleoni is usually credited with mounting its lighter artillery on carriages. In the late 16th century its designers produced the galleass, used at Lepanto in 1571, and the galleon. The main gate, the Porta Magna, built around 1460, was among the first works of Venetian Renaissance architecture, modelled on the Arch of the Sergii at Pula. In 1593 Galileo became a consultant, advising on rowing, instruments and ballistics.

Dante mentioned the Arsenal in the Inferno, likening the boiling pitch of the damned to the pitch used there on unsound vessels. By 1450 over 3,000 Venetian merchant ships were in operation, and the government spent almost 10% of its revenues on the fleet, which underpinned Venice's control of Mediterranean trade and the palaces and art it paid for. Significant parts of the Arsenal were destroyed under Napoleonic rule and rebuilt for use as a naval base. Parts have since served as a research centre, a venue of the Venice Biennale, a historic boat preservation centre and the operations centre of the MOSE flood barrier. Venice also built a network of smaller arsenals in the Aegean, Epirus, the Peloponnese and Crete.
venetian-dalmatia: Venice had fought the Croats and other Slavs of the coast for the eastern Adriatic since the 7th and 8th centuries. Around 1000 an expedition under Doge Pietro II Orseolo secured Venetian suzerainty over coastal Istria and Dalmatia, and he named himself Duke of Dalmatia. The coastal cities then changed hands repeatedly between Venice, the Croatian kings and the Kingdom of Hungary; the crusaders of the Fourth Crusade took Zadar for Venice in 1202, and by the Treaty of Zadar of 18 February 1358 Venice lost the whole coast to King Louis the Great of Hungary.

During the Hungarian civil war between King Sigismund and the House of Anjou, the losing contender, Ladislaus of Naples, sold his rights on Dalmatia to Venice for 100,000 ducats. Sigismund tried to recover the territory, but Venice defeated his troops at the Battle of Motta in 1412. Dubrovnik, as the Republic of Ragusa, stayed outside Venetian rule, and the southernmost part of the coast was known as Venetian Albania.

Dalmatia formed part of the Stato da Màr. Its cities were run by magistrates under the Provveditore Generale in Dalmazia e Albania, who usually sat at Zadar. In the Ottoman–Venetian wars that began in 1499 the Ottoman Empire took the Croatian lands of the hinterland between Skradin and Obrovac, without taking the Venetian cities. Dalmatians served Venice as sailors, oltramarini infantry, cappelletti cavalry and militia: more than 9,000 were in the Venetian fleet at Lepanto.

In the Cretan War the Ottomans took Novigrad in 1646, but the Venetian commander Leonardo Foscolo retook it and seized Klis, and the peace of 1669 left Venetian territory in Dalmatia three times larger. In the Morean War Venice took Sinj on 30 September 1686, Herceg Novi in 1687 and Knin on 11 September 1688, which fixed much of the later border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Treaty of Passarowitz added Sinj and Imotski along the line named after Sebastiano Mocenigo.

By the late 18th century the name Dalmatia had come to mean only the Venetian territory. When Napoleon Bonaparte dissolved the republic in 1797, the Habsburgs annexed its Dalmatian lands. The area passed to the French client Kingdom of Italy in 1805 and to the Illyrian Provinces in 1809, and after Napoleon's defeat the Austrian Empire made it the Kingdom of Dalmatia in 1815.
venetian-ghetto: The Ghetto lies in the Cannaregio sestiere of Venice and is divided into the Ghetto Nuovo and the adjacent Ghetto Vecchio. The names refer to older and newer foundry sites that had gone out of use before the Ghetto was created, so in terms of Jewish residence the Ghetto Nuovo is the older. The origin of the word ghetto is disputed. Theories derive it from the Venetian word for foundry, from the Italian gettare, to throw, from borghetto, or from the Hebrew get, a divorce document. The linguist Anatoly Liberman concluded in 2009 that all of them are speculative.

Jews had been allowed in Venice only for visits of at most fifteen days a year, but after the defeat of the Republic by the League of Cambrai in 1509 they settled throughout the city. On 29 March 1516 the Senate decreed that all Jews must move into the Ghetto Nuovo, citing what it called misdemeanours and detestable acts. The Ghetto was joined to the rest of the city by two bridges that were open only by day.

Its gates were opened at the ringing of the marangona, the largest bell of St Mark's Campanile, and locked in the evening, with guards paid for by the Jewish residents. Jews could not own real estate, but they could hold a permanent lease, the jus gazaka, and had to pay the high rents in perpetuity. In 1555 Venice had 160,208 inhabitants, including 923 Jews, who were mainly merchants.

Between 1541 and 1633 the Ghetto Vecchio and the Ghetto Nuovo were enlarged to house a growing immigration, though the Jewish community of Venice did not exceed 5,000 until the early seventeenth century. It never became a single Venetian Jewish people. Four of its five synagogues served separate groups: the Scuola Grande Tedesca the German, the Scuola Italiana the Italian, the Scuola Spagnola the Spanish and Portuguese, and the Scuola Levantina the Levantine Sephardi. The Venetian Republic dissolved itself on 12 May 1797 under French occupation, and the Ghetto's separation from the city ended on 11 July. In the 19th century it was renamed the Contrada dell'unione.

The Ghetto is still a centre of Jewish life in Venice, though few Jews live there because the area has become expensive. Two of the five synagogues are still used for worship, and the Jewish Community Museum offers guided tours. Notable residents of the Ghetto included the scholar Leon of Modena and his disciple Sara Copia Sullam, who wrote, debated by letter and hosted a salon.
venetic: Venetic is an extinct centum Indo-European language spoken by the Veneti in north-eastern Italy, in Veneto and Friuli, and in part of modern Slovenia, between the Po Delta and the southern fringe of the Alps. It is associated with the Este culture. The Romans called its speakers Veneti and the Greeks Enetoi, and local varieties included Alpine Venetic, Este Venetic and Padua Venetic. The language is attested by over 300 short inscriptions from the 6th to the 1st century BCE, written in a variety of the Northern Italic alphabet, similar to the Etruscan alphabet. Inscriptions dedicating offerings to the goddess Reitia are a primary source.

Venetic had about six, possibly seven, noun cases and four conjugations, similar to Latin. About 60 words are known, some borrowed from Latin or Etruscan. Many show a clear Indo-European origin, such as vhraterei, to the brother. Its sound changes resemble those of Latin: the labiovelar kʷ was preserved, as in ekvon, horse, and in the enclitic -kve, and, related to Latin -que. The scholars most prominent in studying the inscriptions are Pauli, Krahe, Pellegrini, Prosdocimi and Lejeune.

Its relationship to Latin, Germanic, Celtic and the other Italic languages is debated. Some linguists class it with Proto-Italic in a Proto-Italo-Venetic group, and Eric P. Hamp argued in 1954 that it was closer to Latino-Faliscan than to Osco-Umbrian. Others think it split off from the core of Italic early, and in 2016 Peter Schrijver argued that Venetic and Italic together form one sub-branch of an Italo-Celtic branch. In the period of Latin-Venetic bilingual inscriptions, 150–50 BCE, the language was flooded with Latin loanwords, and the shift to Latin is thought to have been well under way by then. It became extinct around the 1st century.
veneto: Veneto covers 18,398.9 square kilometres in the north-east of Italy. It is bordered by Friuli-Venezia Giulia to the east, Emilia-Romagna to the south, Lombardy to the west and Trentino-Alto Adige/Südtirol to the north, and in its northernmost corner it touches Austria. The climate is continental on the plains and milder along the Adriatic coast, around Lake Garda and in the hills. Rainfall is scarce near the river Po, about 750 millimetres a year, and much greater in the Prealps. The region is divided into seven provinces: Belluno, Padua, Rovigo, Treviso, Venice, Verona and Vicenza.

Between the 2nd and 1st millennium BCE the region was inhabited by the Euganei. Ancient historians derived the Veneti from Paphlagonia in Anatolia, led by Prince Antenor, a comrade of Aeneas, at the time of the fall of Troy, which may have been an attempt to link Venetic origins with the legend of Roman origins in Troy. Other historians link them with the Celts. In the 3rd century BCE the Veneti sided with Rome, and during the Second Punic War they sent soldiers against Hannibal, some of whom were killed at the Battle of Cannae in 216 BCE. The region remained part of the Roman Empire until the 5th century CE.

By the middle of the 8th century the Franks controlled the mainland, which became part of the Carolingian Empire. When invaders threatened the wealth of the mainland, part of the population took refuge on islands in the lagoon, where Venice arose. It became an independent maritime republic ruled by an elected doge, and it ruled the region until 1797. Napoleon's armies conquered Veneto in 1805–1806, and after the Congress of Vienna of 1814–1815 it formed the eastern half of the Kingdom of Lombardy–Venetia within the Austrian Empire. The region joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1866 after the Third Italian War of Independence and a plebiscite.

Veneto is one of the 20 regions of Italy, with 4,857,460 inhabitants. Venice is the capital and Verona the largest city. Most inhabitants speak Venetian as well as Italian. The regional Statute, first promulgated on 22 May 1971, speaks of the Venetian people, though the region does not have the special statute of its neighbours Friuli-Venezia Giulia and Trentino-Alto Adige. Under Austrian rule the agricultural economy suffered, and nearly 3 million Venetians left between 1861 and 1961, many for Brazil and Argentina. Millions of people of Venetian descent now live abroad, especially in southern Brazil, where places such as Nova Veneza and Nova Treviso recall their origin.
venezuelan-war-of-independence: The French invasion of Spain in 1808 and the rule of Joseph Bonaparte left a power vacuum in Spain's American possessions. On 19 April 1810 the municipal council of Caracas deposed the Captain-General Vicente Emparán and set up a junta, which at first upheld the rights of Ferdinand VII. A faction led by Francisco de Miranda and the young Criollo aristocrat Simón Bolívar soon pressed for full independence. Maracaibo Province, Guayana Province and the district of Coro never recognised the junta, and civil war began between its supporters and royalists.

The First Republic, short of funds and blockaded, was struck by an earthquake on 26 March 1812. Miranda, given dictatorial powers, could not halt Captain Domingo de Monteverde and signed an armistice on 25 July 1812. With New Granadan backing, Bolívar led the Admirable Campaign of 1813, issued his Decree of War to the Death in Trujillo, and entered Caracas on 6 August 1813, while Santiago Mariño and Manuel Piar fought in the east. In 1814 the llanero caudillo José Tomás Boves, raising the pardos against the Second Republic, defeated them, and after Boves's death Francisco Tomás Morales captured and executed José Félix Ribas.

In 1815 Ferdinand VII sent Pablo Morillo with the largest expedition Spain had ever dispatched to the Americas. Bolívar sought help in Jamaica and then in Haiti, where President Alexandre Pétion supported him. From 1817 the republicans held Angostura, where Bolívar had Piar court-martialled and executed, while British veterans formed what became the British Legion and José Antonio Páez fought in the llanos of Apure. The war settled into a stalemate, the royalists holding the populous north.

In 1819 Bolívar and Francisco de Paula Santander invaded New Granada and crushed Spanish power there at Boyacá. On 17 December 1819 the Congress of Angostura proclaimed the union of Venezuela and New Granada as the Republic of Colombia, confirmed at the Congress of Cúcuta in 1821. After Carabobo only Cumaná and Puerto Cabello remained royalist, and Puerto Cabello capitulated in October 1823, the year a Spanish fleet was beaten at the Battle of Lake Maracaibo. Venezuelan troops then fought on with Gran Colombia's army in Ecuador, Peru and Bolivia.
veni-creator-spiritus: Veni Creator Spiritus, Latin for Come, Creator Spirit, is an invocation of the Holy Ghost. Several variants of the text exist: the original ninth-century version and a classicised revision published in 1632 under Pope Urban VIII. The original is used in some Protestant churches and certain Catholic religious orders, and the revision in most secular Catholic parishes. The hymn calls on the Comforter, the gift of God Most High, the fount of life, fire, love and spiritual anointing, and asks for light for the senses, love for the hearts and strength for the weakness of the body. It ends with a doxology to the Father, the Son and the Spirit.

In the Catholic Church the hymn is sung at Terce and Vespers on the feast of Pentecost. It also marks solemn occasions: the College of Cardinals entering the Sistine Chapel for a papal conclave, the consecration of bishops, the ordination of priests, confirmation, the dedication of churches, the convening of synods or councils, the coronation of monarchs and the Red Mass that opens the judicial year. It is traditional to chant it on New Year's Day to obtain a plenary indulgence.

It has been used in Anglican liturgies since the ordinal of 1550. John Cosin's translation, Come Holy Ghost, our souls inspire, was written for the coronation of Charles I of Great Britain in 1625 and has been sung at every British coronation since. At the coronation of Charles III and Camilla in 2023 it was sung for the first time also in Irish Gaelic, Scots Gaelic and Welsh. Thomas Cranmer's version appeared in the 1550 ordinal, and John Dryden's Creator Spirit, by whose aid was published in 1693.

Martin Luther based his Pentecost chorale Komm, Gott Schöpfer, Heiliger Geist on the hymn, published in 1524 with a melody derived from the chant. Heinrich Bone published a German paraphrase in 1845. There have been more than fifty English translations and paraphrases since the sixteenth century.

Composers have set the hymn in many forms. They include Marc-Antoine Charpentier, with five settings, Johann Sebastian Bach, who harmonised Luther's chorale and built organ preludes on its tune, Hector Berlioz, César Franck, Anton Bruckner, Maurice Duruflé and Karol Szymanowski. Gustav Mahler set the Latin text in Part I of his Symphony No. 8 in E-flat major, completed in 1906, and Paul Hindemith ended his Concerto for Organ and Orchestra with a Phantasy on it in 1962.
venice: Venice is built on an archipelago of more than a hundred islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, an enclosed bay of about 550 square kilometres between the mouths of the Po and the Piave. The islands are separated by canals and linked by several hundred bridges, and the historic centre is divided into six districts, or sestieri. Those who sought refuge on the islands of Torcello, Iesolo and Malamocco learned to drive closely spaced piles of alder trunks into the mud until they reached compressed clay, and laid plates of Istrian limestone on top. Subsidence contributes to the seasonal acqua alta, when the lowest surfaces are covered at high tide.

No surviving record deals directly with the founding of Venice. Tradition and the evidence have led several historians to agree that the first inhabitants were refugees from nearby Roman cities such as Padua, Aquileia, Treviso, Altinum and Concordia, and from the countryside, fleeing Germanic and Hun invasions. The traditional founding is the dedication of the church of San Giacomo on the islet of Rialto, said to have taken place at noon on 25 March 421. The city was the capital of the Republic of Venice from 810 to 1797, when Napoleon ended its sovereignty, and in 1866 it became part of the Kingdom of Italy.

Early prosperity probably owed much to the trade in slaves captured in central Europe and sold to North Africa and the Levant. The city later controlled a vast sea empire and was considered the first real international financial centre, reaching its fullest prominence in the 14th century. The Venetian Arsenal, the base of its naval power, is considered by several historians to be the first factory in history. Its population was 60,000 in 1000, 80,000 in 1200, between 110,000 and 180,000 in 1300, and approached 200,000 by 1600.

The municipality had 254,850 residents in 2021, of whom 50,434 lived in the historic island city. Within the historic centre transport remains entirely on water or on foot, and the gondola survives mainly for tourists and ceremonies. The lagoon and the city were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Marco Polo and Giacomo Casanova were Venetian writers, and the composers Tomaso Albinoni and Antonio Vivaldi were born there.
venice-commission: The Commission was created in 1990, after the fall of the Berlin Wall, when Central and Eastern Europe urgently needed constitutional assistance. The Italian minister Antonio Mario La Pergola conceived the idea of a group of constitutional experts and chose the name from his conviction that lasting democracies could be built only in a constitutional framework based on the rule of law. The Italian foreign minister Gianni De Michelis formally proposed it at a conference at the Giorgio Cini Foundation in Venice on 31 March and 1 April 1989.

The Committee of Ministers approved its creation as a partial agreement at a session in Venice on 19 and 20 January 1990. On 10 May 1990 ministers from 18 countries adopted its statute, and La Pergola became its first president. All member states of the Council of Europe soon joined, and since 2002 non-European states can also become full members.

The members are senior academics, particularly in constitutional or international law, supreme or constitutional court judges, or members of national parliaments. They sit in their individual capacity and are appointed for four years by the participating countries. Its secretariat is at the Council of Europe's headquarters in Strasbourg. Its main work is to give constitutional assistance in the form of opinions on draft constitutions, amendments or other legislation.

For an opinion the Commission appoints a working group of rapporteurs, which visits the country and meets the political actors, then prepares a draft that the Commission adopts at a plenary session. The opinions are not binding but are mostly followed. The Commission describes its approach as non-directive and based on dialogue. Its code of good practice in electoral matters was adopted in October 2002.

At the request of the European Union the Commission played an important role in developing and interpreting the constitutional law of Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, Serbia and Montenegro and Kosovo. In 2009 it drew rare news coverage with its opinion that blasphemy should not be illegal. In Opinion 833/2015, on changes to the Polish Constitutional Tribunal, it found that a new quorum of 13 judges out of 15 went beyond established standards. Russia was a member from 1996 until 2022, when it was expelled from both the Council of Europe and the Commission after its invasion of Ukraine.
venkatapati-raya: Venkatapati Raya was born around 1540, the fourth and youngest son of Emperor Tirumala Deva Raya and his queen Vengalamba. Before he succeeded his older brother, Emperor Sriranga Deva Raya, in January 1586, he served as governor of Chandragiri and viceroy of the Tamil country. He was the third emperor of the Aravidu dynasty, and his reign of nearly three decades saw a revival in the strength and prosperity of the Vijayanagara Empire.

In 1588 he went to war with the sultanates of Golkonda and Bijapur and recovered some of the lands his predecessor had lost. His general Kasturi Ranga Nayaka and his son Yachama Nayaka met the combined sultanate army on the upper bank of the river Pennar. Accounts put that army at more than 120,000 men with artillery, and say the battle lasted eight hours and cost the sultanates more than 50,000 dead, among them the generals Rustam Khan and Khasim Khan. Quarrels among the emperor's nobles prevented a further advance into Golkonda. In 1605 and 1606 his forces under Jagadeva Row, aided by the Tanjore prince Raghunatha, repulsed a Golkonda siege of Penukonda and forced Sultan Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah to withdraw.

He also put down revolts at home. The Nayak of Gingee was imprisoned after rising in 1586. In 1601 Chennappa Nayaka defeated Lingama Nayaka of Vellore at Munnali and captured the Vellore Fort, and Yachama Nayaka led an expedition into the Madurai province. Around 1592 the capital moved from Penukonda to Chandragiri, and after 1604 to Vellore. In the north he eased taxes and revived farming. In 1608 the Dutch sought leave to set up a factory at Pulicat, which his favourite queen Gobburi Obayama ruled.

Venkatapati had several queens but no son. Distrusting an infant that Queen Bayamma presented as her own, which accounts describe as the child of a Brahmin servant, he named Sriranga II, son of his brother Rama, as his successor. His death in October 1614 began a succession crisis that lasted four years, during which some nayakas stopped sending tribute and Bijapur and Golkonda encroached further on the empire.
venlo: Roman and Celtic coins have been found at Venlo. It was speculated to be the settlement called Sablones on the Roman road between Maastricht and Xanten, though what little evidence there is goes against this. Documents of the 9th century mention it as a trade post, and it became one of the more important ones in the Meuse-Rhine area. It received city rights in 1343 and joined the Hanseatic League in 1375.

Because of its strategic importance Venlo was besieged several times, the most significant siege being that of 1702, carried out by Menno van Coehoorn. By the Treaty of 1713 it was incorporated into the Generaliteitslanden of the United Provinces, and after the Napoleonic Wars it became part of the United Kingdom of the Netherlands. At the start of the Belgian Revolution of 1830 Venlo, like most of Limburg, sided with the Belgian rebels and was then Belgium's northernmost fortress. In 1839 King William I signed the Treaty of London recognising Belgian independence, and Belgium gave up parts of Limburg, including Venlo, to the Dutch. From 1839 to 1866 the city was completely surrounded by the territory of the German Confederation without belonging to it.

On 9 November 1939 two British Intelligence Service agents were kidnapped by the Sicherheitsdienst in the Venlo Incident, which the Nazis used to link Britain to Georg Elser's failed attempt on Hitler's life the day before and to justify the invasion of the Netherlands on 10 May 1940. Between 13 October and 19 November 1944 bombing raids on the road and railway bridges over the Meuse killed about 300 people and destroyed much of the historic city, though the Stadhuis and the Römer house survived. Allied forces liberated Venlo from the east.

Venlo lies in the province of Limburg, close to the German border. In 2001 the municipalities of Belfeld and Tegelen were merged into it, and Arcen en Velden followed in 2010. It is linked to Germany by two motorways and by a junction railway station. Greenport Venlo is one of five designated Greenports in the Netherlands and its second largest concentration of horticulture. Higher education is provided by Fontys University of Applied Sciences, the HAS University of Applied Sciences and Maastricht University Campus Venlo, and the city hosted Floriade 2012, a horticultural exhibition.
venta-belgarum: The name is Celtic: Venta comes from a Common Brittonic word meaning market, and Roman writers called the town Venta Belgarum, the Venta of the Belgae, to tell it apart from other tribal markets such as Venta Silurum and Venta Icenorum. The settlement was apparently founded around 70 CE, partly on the site of Oram's Arbour, which had been abandoned for some years. The Belgae had probably held several hill forts nearby, among them St Catherine's Hill and Worthy Down, and the Romans moved them to the new tribal capital once the area was pacified.

The River Itchen was diverted and a street grid laid out. In the first years of the province Venta was less important than Silchester and Chichester, but it outgrew both by the later 2nd century. A bank and ditch were dug round it in that century, and stone walls followed early in the 3rd, when the town covered 58 hectares. It had fine townhouses, temples and public buildings; the forum-basilica seems to have held a temple to Jupiter, Juno and Minerva, and another temple honoured the Celtic horse goddess Epona. Large cemeteries lay to the north, at Lankhills, and to the east.

From the mid-4th century building stopped, houses fell into disrepair and the drains failed, and people gathered on the higher, drier ground. Yet the defences were strengthened, and men were buried wearing military-style belts. The historian David Nash Ford identifies the town with Cair Guinntguic, one of the 28 cities of Britain in the History of the Britons of Nennius. After the Roman withdrawal in 410, town life seems to have ended around 450, though a small administrative centre may have lasted on the site of the later Anglo-Saxon palace. Cemeteries of the 6th and 7th centuries suggest that settlement revived.
ventspils: Ventspils lies in the historical region of Courland in north-western Latvia, where the Venta river reaches the Baltic Sea. Its name means castle on the Venta, after the castle that the Livonian Order built beside the river. Historically it was known as Windau in German. In the Russian Empire it was called Vindava or Vindau, and the form Ventspils has been used since the Second World War. Its harbour does not freeze, which has made it an important port.

The town grew up around the Livonian Order's castle and was chartered in 1314. It became an important merchant city of the Hanseatic League. Under the Duchy of Courland it flourished as a shipbuilding centre, where 44 warships and 79 trading ships were built, and the duke's fleet that set out to colonise Gambia and Tobago sailed from Ventspils. Metal, amber and wood-working shops also contributed to its growth. The Polish-Swedish War and the Great Northern War destroyed the town, and a plague in 1711 killed most of the remaining inhabitants. After the Third Partition of Poland-Lithuania in 1795 it came under the Russian Empire.

Shipbuilding and trade did not matter again until about 1850. The port was modernised in the 1890s and linked to Moscow by rail, and it became one of the most profitable ports of Imperial Russia, with a yearly profit of 130 million rubles by 1913. The population grew from 7,000 in 1897 to 29,000 in 1913, then fell by almost half during the German occupation of 1915 to 1919.

The Red Army set up a base in 1939, and the city was under Soviet occupation from 1940 and German occupation from 1941 to 1944. In Soviet times an oil pipeline was built to the port, which became the USSR's leading port for crude oil export.

Ventspils is the sixth-largest city of Latvia, and it remains an ice-free port from which oil and other minerals from Russia are loaded. It has an international airport and a high technology park. The Old Town keeps 17th-century storehouses near the Market Square, and a house built in 1646 at the crossing of Tirgus and Skolas Streets is among the oldest of its type in Latvia. The city hosts the Sea Festival every July, and since 2006 an International Writers' and Translators' House has stood in the former City Hall of 1850. Ventspils University College is among its institutions of higher education.
venus-de-milo: The Venus de Milo is made of Parian marble and stands over 2 metres high, larger than life size. The flesh is polished smooth, while chisel marks remain on other surfaces. The drapery is more elaborately carved on the right than on the left, and the back is less finely finished, which suggests the figure was meant to be seen only from the front. The body is realistic, but the head is more idealised, with small eyes and mouth and slightly open lips. Stylistically it combines classical elements, such as the strong brow and nose, with Hellenistic ones, such as the shape of the torso and the deeply carved drapery.

A Greek farmer found the statue on 8 April 1820 on the island of Milos, then part of the Ottoman Empire. Olivier Voutier, a French sailor interested in archaeology, witnessed the discovery. A hand holding an apple, an arm fragment and two herms were found alongside it. The Comte de Marcellus bought the statue as it was being loaded onto a ship for another buyer. Louis XVIII had it installed in the Louvre, unrestored.

The goddess has usually been identified as Aphrodite holding the apple of discord, though other proposals include Amphitrite, a Muse, Nemesis and Sappho. In the 19th century the consensus placed her in the fourth century BCE. In 1893 Adolf Furtwängler argued that she was late Hellenistic, a dating widely accepted since. The original position of the arms is still uncertain; Wilhelm Fröhner suggested in 1876 that the right hand held the slipping drapery and the left an apple.

Within a few years of the discovery, according to Kenneth Clark, the statue took the central place once held by the Venus de' Medici. In the 19th century it was distributed in plaster casts, photographs and bronze copies. In 1964 it was exhibited in Tokyo and Kyoto, the only time it has left France since the Louvre acquired it. More than 70 poems have been written about it, and René Magritte and Salvador Dalí took it up in the 20th century. Martin Robertson thinks its reputation owes more to propaganda than to artistic merit.
venustiano-carranza: José Venustiano Carranza de la Garza was born on 29 December 1859 in Cuatro Ciénegas, Coahuila, into a prosperous cattle-ranching family of Basque descent. His father, Jesús Carranza Neira, fought on the Liberal side in the Reform War and against the French intervention, and Benito Juárez rewarded him with land that became the basis of the family's fortune. Venustiano entered politics in 1887 as municipal president of Cuatro Ciénegas and served as a senator for his state under Porfirio Díaz.

He grew disillusioned with Díaz's authoritarian rule and backed Francisco Madero in 1910. Madero made him minister of war on 3 May 1911, though he had contributed little to the rebellion, and as governor of Coahuila from 1911 he pursued reforms of the judiciary, tax laws and workplace safety, and invested in education.

When Madero was murdered in February 1913, Carranza issued the Plan of Guadalupe against Huerta and, as Primer Jefe, forged a northern coalition, the Constitutionalists. After Huerta fell in July 1914 the coalition split: the Convention of Aguascalientes rejected Carranza, and Pancho Villa allied with Emiliano Zapata. Álvaro Obregón's loyalty, the oil-rich Gulf Coast and the ports of Veracruz and Tampico gave Carranza the means to win, and Obregón defeated Villa at Celaya in April 1915.

The convention at Querétaro met in December 1916, with 85 delegates close to Carranza and 132 radicals who insisted on land reform. Article 27 of the new constitution declared that private property had been created by the Nation, which could regulate it. The constitution was proclaimed on 5 February 1917, and Carranza became constitutional president in May. He achieved little change in office, and kept Mexico neutral in the First World War. He ordered Zapata's assassination in 1919.

In 1920 Carranza endorsed the obscure diplomat Ignacio Bonillas as his successor. Obregón, Plutarco Elías Calles and Adolfo de la Huerta issued the Plan of Agua Prieta, and Carranza fled the capital and was assassinated, on 21 May 1920. The Sonoran leaders left him out of the official memory of the Revolution, but his remains were reburied in the Monument to the Revolution in 1942.
venutius: Venutius first appears in the record in about 51 CE as the husband of Cartimandua, queen of the Brigantes. Some scholars have suggested that he belonged to the Carvetii, a tribe that probably formed part of the Brigantian confederation. At that time the British resistance leader Caratacus, defeated in Wales by Publius Ostorius Scapula, fled north to the Brigantes and was handed over to the Romans by Cartimandua. The kingdom was nominally independent, but Tacitus says that Cartimandua and Venutius were loyal to Rome and "defended by Roman power".

After the capture of Caratacus, Venutius became the most prominent leader of resistance to the Roman occupation. Cartimandua had married his armour-bearer, Vellocatus, and raised him to the kingship in Venutius's place. At first Venutius sought only to overthrow his former wife, and turned against her Roman protectors later. Rome defended its client queen, and his revolt was defeated by Caesius Nasica while Aulus Didius Gallus was governor, between 52 and 57 CE.

When Venutius rose again in 69, the Romans could send Cartimandua only auxiliary troops; she was evacuated and he took the kingdom. The revolt may have had wider effects. Tacitus says that Vespasian, once emperor, had to recover Britain, and that Britain had been abandoned when only just pacified, though some take this to refer to Agricola's later conquests in Caledonia. Nothing is recorded of Venutius after Vespasian's accession. Quintus Petillius Cerialis, governor from 71 to 74, campaigned against the Brigantes, yet they were not fully subdued for many decades: Agricola appears to have fought in their territory, and both Juvenal and the Greek geographer Pausanias refer to warfare against them in the first half of the second century.
veracruz: Veracruz, officially the Free and Sovereign State of Veracruz de Ignacio de la Llave, is one of the 31 states that with Mexico City make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico. It lies in eastern Mexico and borders Tamaulipas, San Luis Potosí, Hidalgo, Puebla, Oaxaca, Chiapas and Tabasco. It is a crescent-shaped strip between the Sierra Madre Oriental and the Gulf of Mexico, about 650 kilometres from north to south with an average width of about 100 kilometres, and covers 78,815 square kilometres. Its coastline runs for 690 kilometres, and the land rises from coastal plains to the Pico de Orizaba, at 5,636 metres Mexico's highest peak.
The state is divided into 212 municipalities. The suffix of its name honours Ignacio de la Llave y Segura Zevallos, governor in 1855 to 1857 and again in 1861 to 1863.

Before the Spanish arrival the region was populated mainly by four Indigenous groups: the Huastecs and Otomis in the north, the Totonacs in the centre-north and the Olmecs in the south. Archaeological remains survive at Cempoala, El Tajín, San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán and Tres Zapotes, among other sites.

Hernán Cortés and his expedition founded Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz on 18 May 1519, the first Spanish town in what is now Mexico. By doing so Cortés overthrew the authority of the governor of Cuba, Diego Velázquez, and claimed authority directly from the Spanish Crown. During the Mexican War of Independence much of the state backed the insurgents, who held most of it for the rest of the war, although the commercial class of the port did not support them.

In 1905 more than 5,000 workers of the El Valle Nacional company struck, and strikes at factories in Rio Blanco and Orizaba led to violence in January 1907. No major battles of the Mexican Revolution were fought in the state, but in 1917 Venustiano Carranza temporarily moved the federal government there.

The capital is Xalapa-Enríquez, usually called Xalapa. Other large cities include Veracruz, Boca del Río, Coatzacoalcos, Córdoba, Minatitlán, Orizaba and Poza Rica. Its economy has long rested on agriculture and petroleum, and the Laguna Verde Nuclear Power Plant lies in Alto Lucero.
veracruz-city: Veracruz, also known as Heroica Veracruz, is the municipal seat of the municipality of Veracruz on the Gulf of Mexico, 90 km (56 mi) south-east of the state capital Xalapa. The area is flat, at an average altitude of ten metres above sea level, with a tropical savanna climate and a wet season that lasts from June to October. Part of the city extends into the neighbouring municipality of Boca del Río.

The name comes from the Latin Vera Crux, True Cross. Hernán Cortés founded the settlement of Villa Rica on Good Friday, 22 April 1519, and dedicated it to the True Cross. It was the first Spanish settlement on the mainland of the Americas to receive a coat of arms. The Spanish captain Juan de Grijalva, with Bernal Díaz del Castillo, had first arrived in 1518 at the island later known as San Juan de Ulúa.

In the colonial period the port was the most important in New Spain, and its merchants formed a mercantile class larger and at times wealthier than that of Mexico City. Turkeys, corn, beans, avocados and cotton were exported to Spain, and fava beans, wheat, rice, cattle, pigs, fabric and wine came in return. From the mid sixteenth century gold and silver were the chief exports, carried on the treasure ships of the Spanish treasure fleet. This wealth attracted pirates, mostly from Britain and Holland, such as Francis Drake and John Hawkins, and Fort San Juan de Ulúa was built against them.

After independence in 1821 the city twice earned the title of Heroic City, for its defence against a French attack during the Pastry War and against American forces in 1847. In the Mexican–American War the siege continued until 27 March 1847, when General Juan Morales began to negotiate with General Winfield Scott, and on the 29th the city and San Juan de Ulúa were occupied. About five thousand prisoners and four hundred pieces of artillery were taken. American forces attacked and occupied the port again between April and November 1914, during the Mexican Revolution, in a dispute with President Victoriano Huerta, and the city gained its fourth title.

Veracruz is the most populous city of its state, with 537,952 inhabitants at the 2020 census. The Port of Veracruz is the oldest and largest in Mexico, and its economy has recovered since the later twentieth century. Its culture blends indigenous, Spanish and Afro-Caribbean elements, seen in its son jarocho music and its cuisine, including red snapper Veracruz-style. The Veracruz Carnaval has been held every year since 1866, in the reign of Maximilian I.
veraguas-province: Veraguas lies in the centre-west of Panama and covers 10,587.6 square kilometres. It is the only Panamanian province with coastlines on both the Caribbean Sea and the Pacific Ocean, but most of its people live on the Pacific side, and the Caribbean coast is mostly uninhabited. It is said that the name comes from the indigenous word Veracua or Viragua, though other theories exist. The province is divided into 12 districts, subdivided into 104 corregimientos, and had 259,791 inhabitants in 2023.

Veraguas was originally inhabited by the Veraguas culture. Christopher Columbus explored it on his fourth voyage and tried to establish the first colony on the new Spanish mainland, but failed because of resistance from Indigenous peoples. Diego de Nicuesa also tried to found a colony and failed, which led him to create a colony from which to fight the Indigenous population, which he named Nombre de Dios.

The capital, Santiago de Veraguas, was founded about 1636. A province called Veraguas that contained Santiago, but whose boundaries changed over time, existed in Gran Colombia, in the Republic of New Granada and at times during the Panama State era.

The people of Veraguas are mainly of Spanish and Indigenous origin and are known as campesinos. The province has forests, mountains, coasts and islands, with more than 200 varieties of orchids and more than 400 species of birds. Its national parks include Coiba National Park, which has the largest coral reef on the Pacific coast of America, Cerro Hoya National Park on the Azuero Peninsula and Santa Fe National Park, a forest in the north. The church of San Francisco de la Montaña, in Baroque style, dates from 1727 and was declared a National Historical Monument on 27 January 1937.
vercingetorix: Vercingetorix belonged to the Arverni, a people of what is now Auvergne. Their king Bituitus was decisively defeated by Rome in 121 BCE, and the Arverni later abandoned kingship for an oligarchy like that of their rivals the Aedui. Vercingetorix was probably born at their chief town Gergovia. His birth year is inferred from Caesar calling him a young man in 52 BCE, and scholars place it in the 80s or 70s BCE. His father Celtillus was murdered by fellow aristocrats, around 70 to 60 BCE, for trying to restore kingship. His name probably means supreme king of warriors and may be a title rather than a birth name. Nearly all that is known comes from Caesar, who describes him through a Roman lens.

In early 52 BCE, after the Carnutes massacred Romans at Cenabum, Vercingetorix tried to raise the Arverni, but his uncle Gobannitio and other aristocrats exiled him. He rallied countryside followers, retook Gergovia and was proclaimed king. About ten peoples joined, and he imposed harsh discipline. When Caesar took Vellaunodunum, Cenabum and Noviodunum, Vercingetorix adopted scorched-earth tactics, but the Romans stormed Avaricum, where only about 800 of the reported inhabitants escaped. At Gergovia he drove Caesar back, one of only three recorded Roman defeats of the Gallic Wars. The Aedui then joined him, and an assembly at Bibracte made him sole commander.

A cavalry defeat sent him into the Mandubian town of Alesia, which Caesar surrounded with siege works. The Gauls expelled women, children and the old, whom Caesar refused to admit; they starved between the lines. A relief army failed in three assaults, and Vercingetorix accepted responsibility, saying the war had been fought for collective freedom, and offered himself to spare his people.

Plutarch has him ride out in fine armour, circle Caesar and sit at his feet; Cassius Dio, thought more plausible, says he hoped for pardon because of past friendship with Caesar. He was held six years in the Tullianum, shown in Caesar's triumph in 46 BCE and executed there, possibly by strangulation. Zecchini suggests Caesar could not appear pro-Gallic while Roman opinion was hostile to the Gauls.

Largely forgotten in the Middle Ages, Vercingetorix was rediscovered in the 16th century. In 19th-century France, especially after 1871, he became a symbol of national identity and of the noble loser. Napoleon III financed excavations at Alesia and commissioned a bronze statue there by Aimé Millet. Painters such as Lionel Royer in 1899 fixed the image of the Gaul throwing down his weapons.
verdun: Verdun stands on both banks of the Meuse in the north of the Meuse department, in Grand Est. It lies 225 km from Paris and 184 km from Strasbourg, and is the largest city of the department, although the prefecture is Bar-le-Duc, 47 km to the south. The Gauls founded it, and its Latin name, Verodunum, is a latinisation of a Gaulish place name meaning strong fort. In 486 it refused to yield to the Franks after their victory in the Franco-Roman War and was besieged by King Clovis I.

Verdun became a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire in 1374, and with Toul and Metz it formed the Three Bishoprics. A large bastioned citadel was built from 1624 to 1636 on the site of the Abbey of Saint Vanne. In 1670 Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban visited and drew up a scheme to fortify the whole city; much of it was carried out in the following decades, and some elements were finished only after the Napoleonic Wars, when the citadel held British prisoners of war.

In the War of the First Coalition the fortress was captured on 20 August 1792 by the Prussians, who opened the path to Paris but abandoned Verdun after the Battle of Valmy. In the Franco-Prussian War it was the last French fortress to surrender, in 1870. A new system followed, a ring of 22 polygonal forts up to 8 kilometres from the city and an inner ring of 6.

The battle of 1916 began on 21 February with a bombardment by over 1,000 German guns commanded by Erich von Falkenhayn. The Germans took Douaumont on 25 February; Philippe Pétain then organised the defence and kept open the supply road from Bar-le-Duc, which became known as the Voie Sacrée. Fort Vaux fell on 7 June, and the Anglo-French offensive on the Somme from 1 July drew the Germans away. Estimates put the dead at 143,000 Germans and 162,440 French. French counter-attacks under Robert Nivelle regained the forts by the end of the year.

The Châtel Gate is the only surviving part of the medieval walls, and the 17th-century Citadel is still in military hands, though its tunnels can be visited. Verdun Cathedral was consecrated in 1147, and the Episcopal Palace was built in the 18th century by Robert de Cotte. On the battlefield stand French and German cemeteries; the largest is the French National Cemetery and Douaumont Ossuary, which holds roughly 130,000 unidentified remains. In 1916 King George V awarded the city the Military Cross.
vere-bird: Bird was born in a poor area of St John's, the capital of Antigua. Unlike most of his political contemporaries, such as the lawyers Norman Manley of Jamaica and Grantley Herbert Adams of Barbados or the scholar Eric Williams of Trinidad, he had little formal education beyond St John's Boys School. He served for two years as an officer in the Salvation Army, leaving it, he said, because of the way landowners treated black Antiguans and Barbudans.

Bird was an executive member of the Antigua Trades and Labour Union from its formation in 1939 and its president by 1943, leading the fight for better pay and conditions against the white sugar planters; he won workers paid annual holidays and campaigned to end the rule that only property owners could stand for election. Under universal adult suffrage, introduced in 1951, the union's Antigua Labour Party won every seat in the legislature in each election until 1967. Bird received the trade and production portfolio in 1956, became Chief Minister on 1 January 1960 and Premier when associated statehood came in 1967.

A split in the union in 1967 and rioting in 1968 broke the party's hold, and in 1971 Bird lost both the government and the seat he had held for 25 years to George Walter's Progressive Labour Movement. He returned in 1976 after campaigning against early independence, then won in 1980 with independence as his platform, and became Prime Minister of Antigua and Barbuda on 1 November 1981. In 1984 his party won every Antiguan seat. A supporter of the West Indies Federation, he joined Errol Barrow and Forbes Burnham in creating the Caribbean Free Trade Association in 1965, the forerunner of Caricom.

Failing health and troubles within the government led Bird to resign on 9 March 1994, and his son Lester Bird succeeded him. That year he was made a Knight of the Order of the National Hero. Critics accused his government of corruption and cronyism and of treating politics as a family business, and the author Jamaica Kincaid compared it to the dictatorship of François Duvalier in Haiti in A Small Place; his supporters answered that he had freed Antigua from the colonial sugar planters. He died in St John's on 28 June 1999, aged 88, and Coolidge International Airport has borne his name since 1985.
verica: Verica's coinage presents him as a son of Commius and king of the Atrebates, a tribe that was probably Belgic. His predecessors are likely to have influenced a wide area covering Berkshire, Surrey, western Kent, Sussex, Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. The distribution of his own coins shows a much smaller kingdom, limited to modern Sussex and east Hampshire, with its capital in or near the later Roman town of Noviomagus Reginorum, the modern Chichester. He succeeded his elder brother Eppillus in about 15 CE.

He may also have ruled the northern Atrebatic kingdom at Calleva Atrebatum, the modern Silchester. Rome recognised him as rex, and he appears to have had friendly trading and diplomatic links with the empire, perhaps in an attempt to restore the kingdom to its former strength. Unlike those of nearby areas, the hillforts in the core of his kingdom show no sign of refortification, which implies that its inhabitants were well disposed to Rome.

The Catuvellauni pressed on his territory from the east. Epaticcus, brother of Cunobelinus, conquered Calleva in about 25 CE. After the death of Epaticcus about 35 CE Verica regained some territory, but Caratacus, the son of Cunobelinus, conquered the entire kingdom some time after 40 CE. By the time of his expulsion the kingdom had been reduced to a core around Chichester and the Manhood Peninsula.

Dio Cassius records that a Berikos, widely taken to be Verica, fled to the emperor Claudius because of a revolt, and Suetonius mentions British demands that Rome return certain deserters. His ties with Rome have been used to argue that the invasion landed on the south coast and not at the traditional site of Richborough in Kent. He may have been restored afterwards, but this is not attested, and a new ruler of the region, Cogidubnus, soon appeared; he may have been Verica's heir.

Most scholars take Verica to have been a man. The archaeologist Miles Russell has argued that Verica was a woman, citing the ending of the name and the horsewomen on the coinage. Roger Tomlin disputes this, since no female client ruler is known to have used the title rex, and Daphne Nash notes that some coins show Verica with an Adam's apple and in male priestly dress.
verkhovna-rada: The word Rada means council. The institution originated in the time of Kievan Rus', when it was a council of boyars and of the higher clergy. In the 17th and 18th centuries the Zaporozhian Cossacks used the term for the meetings where major decisions were made, and they elected new councils by popular vote. The Ukrainian People's Republic had a Central Rada between 17 March 1917 and 29 April 1918. The present name comes from the Soviet practice of calling national and republican parliaments Supreme Soviets, a term localised in the Ukrainian SSR as Verkhovna Rada.

The Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR was set up under the 1937 constitution, with its first elections on 26 June 1938 and its first session in Kyiv from 25 to 28 July 1938. Its first chairman was Mykhailo Burmystenko. During the Second World War its Presidium was evacuated to Saratov, and it returned to Kyiv in 1944.

The first partially free elections were held on 4 March 1990. The Communist Party remained in control, but a Democratic Bloc that included the People's Movement of Ukraine (Rukh) was formed. The new parliament issued the Declaration of State Sovereignty on 16 July 1990 and declared independence on 24 August 1991, under its chairman Leonid Kravchuk. A national referendum overwhelmingly supported the act on 1 December 1991. The Constitution of Ukraine was adopted on 28 June 1996.

The Verkhovna Rada is the sole body of legislative power. It has 450 deputies, elected by equal and direct universal suffrage by secret ballot, and it elects a chairman and two deputy chairmen from among its members. It adopts laws, amends the constitution, approves the state budget, appoints the prime minister, ratifies treaties and declares war and peace. Bills are usually considered in three readings, and the president must sign a law before it is promulgated. Electoral systems have varied: all seats were filled in single-member districts in 1990 and 1994, half in 1998 and 2002, and by party lists alone in 2006 and 2007.

The parliament meets in a neo-classical building on Mykhaila Hrushevsky Street in Kyiv, designed by Volodymyr Zabolotny after a competition in 1936. It was built from 1936 to 1938, destroyed in the Second World War and rebuilt from 1945 to 1947.
veronica-gambara: Veronica Gambara was born in Pralboino, in Lombardy, one of the seven children of Count Gianfrancesco da Gambara and Alda Pio da Carpi. Her family included learned women: her great-aunts were the humanist poets Ginevre and Isotta Nogarola, and she was a niece of Emilia Pia, the principal female speaker of Castiglione's Il Cortegiano. She received a humanist education in Latin, Greek, philosophy, theology and scripture.

In 1502, at the age of 17, she began writing to Pietro Bembo, the leading neo-Petrarchan poet, who became her poetic mentor two years later when she started sending him her compositions. In 1509 she married her cousin, the count of Correggio, a widower of 50, at Amalfi. Their sons Ippolito and Girolamo were born in 1510 and 1511.

After her husband's death in 1518 she took charge of the state, including the management of Correggio's condottieri, and of the education of her two sons and her step-daughter Costanza. Under her rule the small court became something of a salon, visited by Gian Giorgio Trissino, Marcantonio Flaminio, Ludovico Ariosto and Titian as well as Bembo.

Correggio had been aligned with King Francis I of France, but she allied it with Emperor Charles V. She received him at her estate in 1530, when he signed a treaty guaranteeing that Correggio would not again be besieged, and again in 1533. The treaty was broken in 1538 when Galeotto Pico II, Count of Mirandola and Concordia, attacked the town; she organised a successful defence, and between 1546 and 1550 saw that Charles V paid for better fortifications. She died at Correggio on 13 June 1550.

About 80 of her poems and 150 of her letters survive. Little of her verse was printed in her lifetime, but it circulated in manuscript and was known throughout Italy by 1530. She wrote mainly in Italian, in four groups: political poems, devotional poems, Virgilian pastoral and love poems to her husband. The political poems express an idea of Italy as a single entity centuries before unification. Most are sonnets, with madrigals, ballads and stanze in ottava rima, and she also wrote in Latin, including an ode greeting Charles V in 1530.

Besides Bembo she corresponded with Bernardo Tasso, Matteo Bandello and Pietro Aretino, who later slandered her as a laureated harlot, an attack she ignored. In a letter of 1549 to Ludovico Rosso she admits exhaustion with her duties and a wish to retire to a solitary life in the country. A complete English translation of her poems appeared in 2014.
versailles: The Palace of Versailles stands in the north-western part of the commune of Versailles, about 16 kilometres south-west of Paris, in the Yvelines department.
