The name covers both the main building and the wider estate, which includes the Grand Trianon, the Petit Trianon, the Grand Canal and the park. The palace covers about 63,154 square metres and contains roughly 2,300 rooms. The park now covers 815 hectares, compared with more than 8,000 hectares before the French Revolution.

The site is first mentioned in 1038 in an abbey charter. In the 16th century the land belonged to the Gondi family, and Louis XIII bought part of it in 1623 and the rest in 1632. In 1668 and 1669, after the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle, Louis XIV decided to turn Versailles into a full royal residence. From 1668 to 1671 the architect Louis Le Vau encased Louis XIII's château on three sides in a new building known as the enveloppe, which gave an Italianate façade towards the gardens.

Louis XIV used the palace to promote himself and to centralise royal power, beginning with nighttime festivals in the gardens in 1664, 1668 and 1674. The king, the court and the government lived there permanently from 6 May 1682 until 6 October 1789, except during the Regency years of 1715 to 1723. Jules Hardouin-Mansart enlarged the palace in the 1680s, and Ange-Jacques Gabriel remodelled the Ministers' Wings in the 1770s.

Napoleon considered making Versailles his residence but abandoned the idea because of the cost, and had the Grand Trianon restored in 1810. Louis XVIII and Charles X did not live there either. In June 1919, after six months of negotiations, the Treaty of Versailles was signed in the Hall of Mirrors.

The palace is owned by the French state and has been run since 1995 as a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture. It houses the National Museum of the History of France. Restoration work began in 1892 under the first conservator, Pierre de Nolhac, and John D. Rockefeller Jr. gave funds for it between 1925 and 1928. The restoration of the Hall of Mirrors was completed in 2006.
vertumnus: In Roman religion Vertumnus, also written Vortumnus or Vertimnus, was the god of seasons, change and plant growth, together with gardens and fruit trees. His name most likely derives from the Etruscan Voltumna, and its Latin form was probably shaped by the verb vertere, meaning to change. Ancient writers explained the name by sound resemblances, which show how his function was understood. Ovid, writing on the Roman calendar, recalls a time when the Forum was still a reedy swamp and the god was not yet called Vertumnus from damming back the river.

Varro was convinced that Vortumnus was Etruscan and a major god, and Propertius, the main literary source for the god, also says he came from Volsinii. A temple to him stood on the Aventine Hill by 264 BCE, the year Volsinii, the Etruscan Velzna, fell to the Romans. His festival, the Vertumnalia, was held on 13 August.

Propertius describes a bronze statue of Vortumnus made by Mamurius Veturius, who was also credited with the twelve ritual shields, the ancilia, of the priests of Mars known as the Salii. It replaced an ancient maple statue said to have been brought to Rome in the time of Romulus. The statue stood in a simple shrine in the Vicus Tuscus near the Forum Romanum and was decorated according to the changing seasons. In Propertius's poem the statue speaks in the first person to a passer-by.

The god could change his form at will. In Ovid's Metamorphoses he gains entry to the orchard of Pomona by disguising himself as an old woman. He then tells the tale of Iphis and Anaxarete as a warning of the dangers of rejecting a suitor, and so wins her. The tale has been called the first exclusively Latin tale. The base of the statue was found in 1549, perhaps still in place, but has since been lost. An inscription recorded a restoration under Diocletian and Maximian in the early 4th century CE.

The story of Vertumnus and Pomona appealed to European sculptors and painters from the 16th to the 18th century, since it set youthful female beauty against an aged crone and carried a disguised erotic subtext. It was woven into tapestries, among them a mid-16th-century Brussels piece in Lisbon, and François Boucher supplied designs for a Gobelins series of 1775 to 1778. Camille Claudel made a marble Vertumnus and Pomona in 1905, and Joseph Brodsky wrote a poem about the god. Modern readers differ on the episode: David Littlefield finds a movement from rape to mutual desire, while Roxanne Gentilcore reads deception and veiled threat in it.
verulamium: Verulamium lay south-west of the modern city of St Albans in Hertfordshire, about a day's walk from London, on the Roman road Watling Street, which was realigned in medieval times to bring trade to St Albans. The pre-Roman settlement of the Catuvellauni was founded by Tasciovanus, who minted coins there. Its Brittonic name has been reconstructed as *Uerulāmion, perhaps meaning of the broad hand, and it was among the first places in Britain recorded by name.

The Roman town became a municipium around 50 CE, its citizens holding Latin Rights, a lesser status than that of a colonia. A black ash layer found by archaeologists confirms the written record of its burning on Boudica's orders. Rebuilt, it grew steadily, and by the early 3rd century it covered about 125 acres behind a deep ditch and wall. Fires in 155 and around 250 damaged the forum, basilica and theatre, and the town was rebuilt in stone rather than timber at least twice. A wax tablet of 21 October 62 CE found in London records a contract to carry twenty loads of provisions from Verulamium. Roman occupation ended between 400 and 450.

St Albans Abbey and its Anglo-Saxon settlement grew up on a hill outside the walls, near a Roman cemetery. In the eighth century the Saxon inhabitants of St Albans still knew the old town as Verulamacæstir or Vaeclingscæstir. Its ruins were quarried for medieval St Albans, and Roman brick and stone are visible in the Norman abbey. Sir Francis Bacon built Verulam House within the walls and in 1618 took the title Baron Verulam.

Much of the site is a scheduled monument, and a large part of the Roman city lies unexcavated under park and farmland, where ploughing has damaged buried buildings. Visible remains include parts of the walls, a hypocaust under a mosaic floor and a theatre with a stage. The Verulamium Museum, founded after the excavations of Mortimer Wheeler and Tessa Wheeler in the 1930s, stands on part of the forum site and holds mosaics, pottery, jewellery, coins and the Verulamium Forum inscription.
verviers: Verviers lies roughly halfway between Liège and the German border. It is the centre of an agglomeration that includes Dison and Pepinster, the second biggest in the province of Liège. Water has played an important part in its economy, first in the development of its textile industry and later of its tourist industry. Many fountains have been built in the city, and it is called Wallonia's Water Capital. Flint and bone fragments and Roman coins found in the area attest to early settlement.

After the Romans failed to hold back Germanic tribes in the 4th century, Clovis's Salian Franks occupied the region at the end of the 5th. The Verviers area was forested and became a hunting ground for the Merovingian kings, who kept a vicus in neighbouring Theux, and monks of the nearby Abbey of Stavelot slowly made it Christian. Late in the 10th century Charles the Simple ceded the Marquisate of Franchimont to Notker of Liège, who was consolidating the Prince-Bishopric of Liège. Liège took direct control of the marquisate in 1014, and Frederick Barbarossa and Pope Adrian IV confirmed this in 1155.

A textile industry in the area is first mentioned in the 15th century. The Eighty Years War in the neighbouring Netherlands helped the cloth industry to replace the older metallurgical works. The town stayed modest in size until 1651, when the expansion of its fulleries led to its recognition as one of the prince-bishopric's bonnes villes, or main cities. The annexation of Liège to France in 1795 caused a steep economic decline and unprecedented poverty.

The city's fortunes rose after the Battle of Waterloo in 1815. William Cockerill, who brought his knowledge of the machines of British industry, introduced mechanisation to the factories of Iwan Simonis. Roads were paved, gas lighting was installed, and the city doubled in size during the Industrial Revolution. Verviers lay at the eastern end of the sillon industriel, the industrial backbone of Wallonia. After the First World War it could share with Bradford the title of Wool Capital of the World. Its factories could not face international competition from the 1950s and closed one after another. The Wool and Fashion Tourist Centre now stands in a former factory, and the Grand Theatre was built at the end of the 19th century.
vespasiano-gonzaga: Vespasiano was born on 6 December 1531 at Fondi, a Colonna fief in southern Latium, the son of Isabella Colonna and the condottiero Louis "Rodomonte" Gonzaga, Lord of Palazzolo. Soon orphaned, he was brought up by his aunt Giulia Gonzaga, who had moved to Naples to escape attempts by other members of the Colonna family to kill him and take the fiefs he had inherited from his mother. Through his mother's second marriage, in 1534, to Philip de Lannoy, 2nd Prince of Sulmona, he was the elder half-brother of the later princes Charles and Horace de Lannoy.

At the age of eleven he was sent to the Spanish royal court to complete his education under Philip II, to whom he was distantly related through common descent from the kings of Aragon. Philip found in him one of his most faithful advisers and made him a Grandee of Spain. Besides soldiering and engineering he was a diplomat and a writer.

In 1556 he began his chief project, the town of Sabbioneta between Mantua and Parma, whose name, sandy, comes from the sandy banks of the Po on which it rose. Designed on the Renaissance principles of the ideal city, it was finished in 1591. At the Spanish court he had met Rudolf II of Habsburg, and it was through Rudolf's personal support that Sabbioneta was declared an autonomous duchy.

Vespasiano married three times: first Diana Folch de Cardona, who died in 1559; then Anna d'Aragona y Folch de Cardona, who died in 1567; and finally Margherita Gonzaga, a daughter of Cesare I Gonzaga, Lord of Guastalla. His only son, Luigi, died in 1580 at the age of 14; the writer Aldous Huxley claimed that Vespasiano kicked him to death for failing to touch his cap to him in the street. Vespasiano died at Sabbioneta on 26 February 1591, and his estate passed to his surviving daughter Isabella, wife of Luigi Carafa, 4th Prince of Stigliano. He is remembered as a patron of the arts and as the founder of Sabbioneta.
vexin: The Vexin is a plateau on the right bank of the Seine, crossed by the valleys of the Epte and the Andelle, running roughly from Pontoise to Romilly-sur-Andelle near Rouen. Its name comes from the Gaulish tribe now known as the Veliocasses, whose chief city was Rouen. The French Vexin is a limestone plateau covered with loam, about 40 by 35 kilometres, at 100 to 140 metres, rising to 216 metres at the Buttes de Rosne. Its main road, the Route Nationale 14 from Paris to Rouen, follows a Roman road, the Chaussée Jules César.

The division of 911 came with the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte, by which King Charles the Simple ceded land to the Norman leader Rollo. In 1031 Duke Robert I of Normandy received the French Vexin for helping King Henry I, but in 1082 King Philip I took it back. Both sides fortified the Epte valley, at Gisors, Château-sur-Epte, Trie-Château and La Roche-Guyon, yet the region suffered over a century of pillage. Philip II took Gisors in 1193 and annexed the French Vexin to the royal domain in 1195.

A time of peace followed: in 1332 Pontoise had 2,150 fiscal hearths. The Hundred Years' War, the Black Death, which killed 1,000 people in Pontoise in 1348, and the Jacquerie left the land deserted, and the English held the Vexin from 1419 until 1449. During the Wars of Religion it was a stronghold of the Catholic League, and Pontoise opened its gates only after Henry IV abjured Protestantism in 1594. In the late 19th century Pissarro, Monet, Cézanne and van Gogh painted its landscapes, and in August 1944 fighting at Fontenay-Saint-Père cost an estimated 2,500 civilian lives.

The old county is shared by five departments, Val-d'Oise, Yvelines, Oise, Eure and Seine-Maritime, and its chief towns are Pontoise, Vernon, Meulan-en-Yvelines, Gisors and Les Andelys. The plateau remains largely agricultural. Since 1995 most rural communes of the French Vexin have formed the French Vexin Regional Natural Park, headquartered in Théméricourt.
via-aemilia: To the Romans of the republican period northern Italy was Gallia Cisalpina, inhabited by Celtic tribes from Gaul who had colonised it in the 4th and 5th centuries BCE. Its great plain, the Pianura Padana, held the best agricultural land of the peninsula and offered the Romans room for mass colonisation. They subdued the Gauls in hard campaigns in the late 3rd century BCE, and the Via Flaminia was completed by 220 BCE. Hannibal's invasion between 218 and 203 BCE overturned Roman control, and tribes such as the Insubres and the Boii rebelled and joined him. Only in 189 BCE were the rebels pacified enough for work on the Via Aemilia to begin.

The Roman method was to build a road straight through newly conquered land and then plant colonies of civilians or veterans along it, on plots confiscated from the defeated peoples. The Via Aemilia followed this plan: Bononia was founded in 189 BCE, and Mutina, Regium and Parma in 183 BCE. The consul Marcus Aemilius Lepidus completed it in 187 BCE and it was named after him. It ran largely in a straight line for 176 Roman miles, about 260 km, north-west from Rimini to Piacenza, partly on elevated embankments and partly over an older road system. It crossed many tributaries of the Po, among them the Rubicon near Rimini and the Trebbia near Piacenza, and joined the Via Flaminia at Rimini.

Piacenza became the key road hub of the plain: the Via Postumia linked it to Aquileia in 148 BCE, and in 109 BCE the consul Marcus Aemilius Scaurus completed the Via Aemilia Scaura to Genoa and Pisa. Augustus rebuilt the road in 2 BCE from Rimini to the Trebbia, as a milestone found in the bed of the Reno records.

The road launched intensive Roman colonisation of the plain, which became the most populous and economically important part of Italy. By the time of the Second Triumvirate, Romanisation was so complete that Gallia Cisalpina was abolished and absorbed into Italia. The road gave its name to the region, already called Aemilia by the time Augustus took sole power; around 7 BCE, when he divided Italia into eleven regions, the eighth was first named Padus and later Aemilia.

Several Roman bridges remain, among them the Ponte di Tiberio at Rimini, begun by Augustus and completed by Tiberius, which still carries its two dedicatory inscriptions. The modern State Road 9 is still officially called Via Emilia and in many places lies directly over the Roman road. Its inhabitants are today called Emiliani.
via-augusta: Augustus stayed in Hispania between 16 and 13 BCE, as part of a reorganisation of its provinces that aimed at new cities, roads to connect them and land for veteran soldiers. The model was the network of roads that Marcus Vipsanius Agrippa had laid out in Gaul in 20–19 BCE. Augustus ordered the rebuilding of the older Via Herculea, which ran from the Pyrenees to Carthago Nova, and its extension to Gades, using what remained of roads of the Roman Republic. The work was carried out between 8 and 2 BCE, and many milestones bearing his name have been found along it.

The historian Pierre Sillières, who has supervised excavations to trace its route, describes it as more a system of roads than a single road. It ran from the Coll de Pertús pass in the Pyrenees south and south-west to the upper Baetis, where an arch, the Ianus Augusti, stood on the border between Baetica and Tarraconensis, and from which the milestones to Gades were numbered. It was usually four to six metres wide, with sections of ten or fourteen metres, and pavements only near cities. Continuing the Via Julia Augusta, Via Aemilia and Via Flaminia, it formed part of a chain of roads joining Rome to the Atlantic.

Built by legionaries as a military road, it served mainly for general communication and trade, and helped cities such as Valentia, Saguntum, Lucentum, Saetabis and Ilici to grow. In 90 CE Domitian restored a dilapidated stretch near Corduba. The Moors of southern Spain still used it in the 10th century, calling it al-Racif, and parts of it served traffic until they were paved in the 1920s. The N-340 road and the A-7 highway follow much of its course, and remains include the Arc de Berà north of Tarragona, the Alcantarilla bridge near Utrera and paving in Valencia's Almoina museum.
via-cassia: The Via Cassia, the Way of Cassius, was an important Roman road that left the Via Flaminia near the Milvian Bridge, close to Rome. It passed not far from Veii and crossed Etruria, running through Baccanae, Sutrium, Volsinii, Clusium, Arretium, Florentia, Pistoria and Luca before joining the Via Aurelia at Luna. The date of its construction is uncertain. It cannot be earlier than 187 BCE, when the consul Gaius Flaminius built a road from Bononia to Arretium, which must have coincided with a portion of the later Via Cassia. No ancient writer mentions it before Cicero, who in 45 BCE speaks of three roads from Rome to Mutina: the Flaminia, the Aurelia and the Cassia.

The Via Cassia met other important roads. At the eleventh mile the Via Clodia diverged to the north-north-west. At Sette Vene another road, probably the Via Annia, branched off to Falerii. At Sutrium the Via Ciminia split off and later rejoined the main road. A milestone of 124 CE records repairs made by Hadrian from the boundary of the territory of Clusium to Florentia, a distance of 86 miles, or 138 kilometres.

In late antiquity the Via Amerina branched from the Via Cassia near Baccanae, ran north through Falerii, Tuder and Perusia and rejoined the Cassia at Clusium. When the raids of Faroald, the Lombard Duke of Spoleto, cut the Via Flaminia, which was the lifeline between Rome and Ravenna, the Via Amerina was improved and fortified at intervals. This work was among the last road-building carried out in Italy in late antiquity. A modern account calls the road the communications core of imperial Italy and the chief support to the claim that imperial Italy was still extant.

Several Roman bridges still stand along the road, among them the Ponte San Lorenzo and the Ponte San Nicolao. The road was also used as part of the route of the individual road race in cycling at the 1960 Summer Olympics in Rome.
via-egnatia: The Via Egnatia crossed the Roman provinces of Illyricum, Macedonia and Thracia, in what is now Albania, Greece, North Macedonia and European Turkey. From Dyrrachium, today Durrës, it followed the river Genusus, now the Shkumbin, over the Candaviae mountains and on to the highlands around Lake Ohrid. It then turned south through high mountain passes to the northern coast of the Aegean at Thessalonica, and from there ran through Thrace to Byzantium.

The main literary source for its building is Strabo's Geographica, together with milestones found along the route. Bilingual inscriptions on the milestones record that Gnaeus Egnatius, proconsul of Macedonia, ordered its construction, and the road presumably took its name from him. The exact date is uncertain. It may have replaced an earlier military road from Illyria to Byzantium, described by Polybius and Cicero, which the Romans built over or improved.

The road was built to link a chain of Roman colonies stretching from the Adriatic to the Bosphorus. Its western end lay almost directly opposite the end of the Via Appia, so the colonies of the southern Balkans had a direct connection to Rome. Until a more northerly route across Illyria was opened under Augustus, it was Rome's main link with its empire in the eastern Mediterranean. It was repaired and extended several times but suffered long periods of neglect during Rome's civil wars.

It figured in several moments of Roman history. The armies of Julius Caesar and Pompey marched along it in Caesar's civil war, and Mark Antony and Octavian pursued Cassius and Brutus along it to the Battle of Philippi. The Apostle Paul used it on his second missionary journey, travelling from Philippi to Thessalonica. Surviving milestones record that the emperor Trajan carried out extensive repairs before his campaign of 113 against the Parthians.

By the 5th century CE the road had largely fallen out of use because of violent instability in the region, and a historian of that century noted that its western sections were barely passable. It revived as a key road of the Eastern Roman Empire. Procopius records repairs by the emperor Justinian I in the 6th century, though the road was said to be almost unusable in wet weather. Almost all Byzantine overland trade with western Europe used it, and armies of the Crusades travelling east by land followed it to Constantinople. A modern Greek highway, the Egnatia Odos, takes its name from the road. The Aromanians call the old road Calea Mare, the Big Road.
via-francigena: The Via Francigena, also known as Francisca or Romea, runs from Canterbury in England through France and Switzerland to Rome, and then on to Apulia, where ports served those embarking for the Holy Land. In medieval times it was the main pilgrimage route to Rome for those wishing to visit the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul. It was first documented as the Lombard Way and was called the Iter Francorum, the Frankish Route, in the Itinerarium sancti Willibaldi of 725. The name Via Francigena is first mentioned in the Actum Clusio, a parchment of 876 in the abbey of San Salvatore at Monte Amiata in Tuscany.

It was never a single road like a Roman road, paved with stone blocks and supplied with changes of horses. It comprised several possible routes that shifted over the centuries as trade and pilgrimage waxed and waned, and travellers might use any of three or four crossings of the Alps and Apennines. The Lombards financed the maintenance and security of the section through their territories as a trading route north from Rome. Unlike Roman roads it relied on abbeys rather than connecting cities.

Around 990 Sigeric, Archbishop of Canterbury, travelled to Rome to receive his pallium and back. He recorded only the return journey, in 80 stages averaging about 20 kilometres a day, a total of some 1,700 kilometres. From Canterbury it ran by Dover, Wissant, Arras, Reims, Besançon, Lausanne and the Great St Bernard Pass to Aosta, then by Vercelli, Pavia, Lucca, San Gimignano, Siena, Viterbo and Sutri to Rome. Later itineraries include that of Nikolás Bergsson in 1154 and of Philip Augustus of France in 1191. From Rome the road followed the Via Appia or the Via Latina to Benevento, and then the Via Traiana to Troia, Bari, Brindisi and Otranto.

The route was identified and mapped on the ground in the late 1980s and early 1990s by the anthropologist Giovanni Caselli. In 1994 the Via Francigena was designated a Cultural Route, and in 2004 a Major Cultural Route. The zero milestone stands at the south porch of Canterbury Cathedral. In France the route is signed as GR145, and it crosses the Swiss cantons of Vaud and Valais and the Italian regions of Aosta Valley, Piedmont, Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna, Tuscany and Lazio. In November 2009 the Italian government launched a project to recover the Italian leg. Pilgrims still travel the route on foot, on horseback or by bicycle, with an estimated 50,000 walking it in 2022.
via-regia: The road ran west to east through the centre of the Holy Roman Empire, from the Rhine at Mainz-Kastel to Frankfurt am Main, where the King of the Romans was elected, then by Hanau, the imperial palace at Gelnhausen, Fulda and Eisenach to Erfurt, a centre of woad production. It crossed the Saale between Bad Kösen and Naumburg to Leipzig, and its eastern part led through Upper Lusatia by Bautzen and Görlitz to Wrocław in Silesia. Its origins go back to the 8th and 9th centuries, and it is first recorded as strata regia in a document of Margrave Henry III of Meissen in 1252.

After imperial power in central Germany gave way to the Saxon House of Wettin following the Battle of Lucka in 1307, the road lost its royal status. Its section between Frankfurt and Leipzig carried on as the Hohe Straße, or High Road, under the control of territorial lords such as the Bohemian Crown, the Saxon electors, the Abbey of Fulda and the Archbishopric of Mainz, who levied tolls.

Flemish blankets came from the west and wood, pelts, wax and honey from the east, while the middle section handled the woad of the Thuringian Basin and the mining products of the Saxon Ore Mountains. The road linked the great trade fairs of Frankfurt and Leipzig. Pilgrims to the shrine of Aachen Cathedral used it in large numbers, and there are records of pilgrims to Santiago de Compostela at towns along it. Armies used it too, and battles were fought near it at Breitenfeld in 1631, Lützen in 1632, Rossbach in 1757, Jena-Auerstedt in 1806 and Leipzig in 1813.

The road declined after Napoleon's defeat, when the Congress of Vienna took much of Lusatia from the Kingdom of Saxony and Leipzig's toll ended. Parts of the route are followed today by the German federal roads B7, B87 and B6 and by Polish national road 94 towards Kraków. In 2005 the Council of Europe named the Via Regia a Major Cultural Route, describing it as a link of 4,500 km across eight European countries.
vibo-valentia: Vibo Valentia was originally the Greek colony of Hipponion, founded, probably in the late seventh century BCE, by settlers from Locri, a principal city of the region on the Ionian Sea. Its city wall, 7 km in circumference, enclosed the hill and ran down to the port. It had cylindrical towers at intervals, and its monumental size testifies to the wealth of the city and the wars it fought. Diodorus Siculus reports that Dionysius the Elder, tyrant of Syracuse, took the city in 388 BCE and deported its whole population. The people returned in 378 BCE with Carthaginian help, and Hipponion later came under the Bruttii, who controlled most of present Calabria.

After the town fell to Rome its name was Latinised to Hipponium, and it became a Roman colony as Vibo Valentia. It prospered in the late Republic and early Empire, and Cicero had a villa there. A diocese was established in 451 and suppressed in 1083, when it was incorporated into the Diocese of Mileto. The town was almost completely abandoned after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. In 1070 the Normans built a castle on the site of the old acropolis, and in 1235 Frederick II, Holy Roman emperor and king of Sicily, established a new city with the name of Monteleone.

The town took back its old Roman name only in 1928, having been called Monteleone di Calabria from 1861. It is the capital of the province of Vibo Valentia and a commune of 30,753 inhabitants, near the Tyrrhenian Sea, with the harbour of Vibo Marina important to its economy. About 350 metres of the Greek walls survive, including the foundations of eight towers, each with an estimated height of 10 metres. The Norman-Hohenstaufen castle, built of materials from nearby Greek temples and damaged by the earthquake of 1783, houses a state museum. The cathedral, dedicated to Santa Maria Maggiore e San Leoluca, was built in the ninth century over a Byzantine basilica.
vicente-cerna-y-cerna: Vicente Cerna y Cerna was born on 22 January 1815 in Ipala, Chiquimula, where he later served as corregidor. A friend and comrade of Rafael Carrera, he rose as an officer of the caudillo's army. As a colonel he commanded one of the Guatemalan battalions at the Battle of La Arada, fought near Chiquimula on 2 February 1851 against an invading army of El Salvador and Honduras, which Carrera's forces defeated with 125 casualties against more than 1,500 on the other side. In 1854 he was among those who signed the act declaring Carrera president for life.

In 1863, as a brigadier general, Cerna led an army of Hondurans, Salvadorians and Guatemalans formed by Carrera into Honduras. His forces took Cucuyagua on 10 June 1863 and Los Llanos de Santa Rosa on 15 June, occupied Gracias a Dios and declared José María Medina president of Honduras, then marched on the capital, Comayagua, against the interim president José Francisco Montes Fonseca, whose forces set the town on fire before fleeing. After Carrera's victory over the Salvadorian leader Gerardo Barrios that year, Cerna was made a field marshal, a rank also given to Serapio Cruz and José Víctor Zavala.

Cerna became president on 24 May 1865, after Carrera's death, although Guatemala's leaders would have preferred Zavala. Church and state remained closely bound under the Concordat of 1852, and liberals were prosecuted and sent into exile, among them those who later began the Liberal Revolution. His victory over Zavala in the election of 1869 brought charges of fraud, and from then on his government faced constant uprisings.

Liberal writers such as Alfonso Enrique Barrientos later described it as an archaic regime that concentrated all power in him. With reinforcements sent by the Mexican president Benito Juárez, the liberal forces defeated his troops at Totonicapán on 23 June and at San Lucas Sacatepequez in June 1871. He died on 27 June 1885.
vicente-filisola: Filísola was born Vincenzo Filizzola in the Kingdom of Naples, at Ravello or nearby Rivello, and his family moved to Spain while he was a child. He enlisted in the Spanish army on 17 March 1804 and fought in the Peninsular War. Sent to New Spain in 1811, he served as a royalist officer against the insurgency and joined the circle of Agustín de Iturbide. In 1821 he led the 13th Division of the Army of the Three Guarantees, about 1,500 men, and on 24 September 1821 entered Mexico City ahead of the main army and took it over from the last royalist authorities.

Filísola entered Guatemala City on 12 June 1822 at the invitation of its council and became captain general on 23 June, relying on the Conservative merchant elite for money and auxiliary troops. San Salvador, under José Matías Delgado and Manuel José Arce, rejected annexation. He opened a campaign with about 2,000 men in November 1822, fought around El Guayabal and Guazapa on 14 January 1823 and entered San Salvador on 9 February. News of the Plan of Casa Mata ended the occupation. He convened the congress on 29 March, it opened on 29 June, and the Mexican division left in August by way of Chiapas, which stayed with Mexico.

In 1831 he received a contract to settle 600 families in East Texas, which he never fulfilled. In 1836 he had charge of the slow main body with the supply train, held up by flooded rivers. After Antonio López de Santa Anna was captured at San Jacinto on 21 April 1836, a council of war under Filísola weighed fighting on. José de Urrea argued for it, but Filísola obeyed the captive Santa Anna's order to withdraw and led about 4,000 men back to Matamoros. Urrea replaced him on 12 June.

Denounced as a coward and traitor, and blamed by Santa Anna himself, Filísola defended his conduct in a Representación, printed in English by the Republic of Texas in 1837 as Evacuation of Texas, and was acquitted by court-martial in June 1841. After the peace of 1848 he presided over the Supreme Tribunal of War and Navy and published his two-volume Memorias para la historia de la guerra de Tejas, now among the most important Mexican sources for 1835 to 1837. He died of cholera in Mexico City on 23 July 1850 and was buried at the cemetery of Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles.
vicente-guerrero: Vicente Guerrero was born in Tixtla, a town in the Sierra Madre del Sur about 100 kilometres inland from Acapulco. He worked in his father's mule-driven freight business, which took him across Mexico and exposed him to ideas of independence. He joined the insurgent army of José María Morelos in late 1810. Because he spoke Nahuatl, he was able to recruit support among Indigenous communities, and in a speech at Tlapa in 1815 he argued for citizenship to be extended to Indigenous people.

After Morelos was captured and executed in December 1815, Guerrero became one of the last major insurgent commanders in the field. From 1816 to 1821 he kept the war alive by guerrilla warfare in the Tierra Caliente, refusing viceregal offers of pardon even when his father carried an appeal for him to surrender.

In 1821 Guerrero held the royalist commander Agustín de Iturbide to a stalemate and appealed to him to join the cause of independence. The Plan of Iguala of 24 February 1821 proclaimed independence and a constitutional monarchy, kept the place of the Catholic Church and made all inhabitants citizens without distinction of European, African or Indian origins. Their combined forces entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821. In 1823 Guerrero joined the rising against Emperor Iturbide, and he was afterwards named one of the ruling triumvirate.

The September 1828 election, decided by the state legislatures, went to Manuel Gómez Pedraza, with Guerrero second. Antonio López de Santa Anna rose in support of Guerrero, fighting broke out in Mexico City, and Gómez Pedraza resigned and went into exile. Guerrero took office on 1 April 1829 with the conservative Anastasio Bustamante as vice president. Facing an empty treasury and a Spanish attempt at reconquest, he used extraordinary powers to abolish slavery across almost all of Mexico in September 1829, though he exempted Texas on 2 December 1829 under pressure from settlers.

Bustamante's rebellion began on 4 December 1829, and Guerrero was deposed on 17 December. He withdrew to the south and fought through 1830. In January 1831 the Italian captain Francisco Picaluga, who was paid 50,000 pesos by the government, invited him aboard his ship at Acapulco and handed him to federal troops. After a court-martial he was shot at Cuilapam on 14 February 1831, an act the liberal press called judicial murder.

His remains were returned to Mexico City in 1842. The state of Guerrero is named for him, and his reported reply to his father, La Patria es Primero, is written in gold inside the Chamber of Deputies.
vicenza: Vicenza lies at the northern base of Monte Berico, where it straddles the River Bacchiglione, about 60 kilometres west of Venice. Three of its bridges over the Bacchiglione and the Retrone are of Roman origin, and isolated arches of a Roman aqueduct stand outside the Porta Santa Croce.

The site was settled by the Italic Euganei and then by the Paleo-Veneti in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE. In 157 BCE the city was a de facto Roman centre, called Vicetia or Vincentia, 'victorious', and its citizens received Roman citizenship in 49 BCE. It was known for agriculture, brickworks, a marble quarry and wool. The city recovered from raids after the Ostrogoth conquest in 489, was soon taken by the Byzantine Empire, and was later a Lombard and Frankish centre.

Magyar raiders destroyed Vicenza in 899. In 1001 Otto III handed the government to the bishop, but the commune soon separated from episcopal authority and joined the Lombard League against Frederick I Barbarossa. Frederick II sacked it in 1237. In 1311 it submitted to the Scaligeri lords of Verona. It came under Venetian rule in 1404, and in 1496 the podestà Antonio Bernardo expelled the Jews. After 1797 it passed to Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy and then to Austria, rose against Austria in 1848, and was annexed to Italy after the Third Italian War of Independence. It was the most damaged city in Veneto in Allied bombing in the Second World War.

Twenty-three buildings by Andrea Palladio stand in Vicenza, among them the Basilica Palladiana in the Piazza dei Signori and the Teatro Olimpico, begun in 1580, the year he died. UNESCO inscribed the city as a World Heritage Site in 1994 and extended the listing in 1996 to the Palladian villas of the Veneto. Textile, steel and jewellery industries are central to its economy.
viceroy-of-kush: The former Kingdom of Kerma in Nubia was a province of ancient Egypt from the 16th century BCE to the 11th century BCE, ruled by a viceroy who reported directly to the pharaoh. The office's first titles were King's Son of the Southern Countries and King's Son, Overseer of the Southern Foreign Countries. By the reign of Thutmose IV the title King's Son of Kush appears, and it then became standard.

The viceroy oversaw the land north of the Third Cataract, divided into Wawat in the north, centred at Aniba, and Kush in the south, centred at Soleb during the 18th Dynasty and later at Amara West. Two deputies, a number of scribes, an overseer of cattle and the priests of local temples of Egyptian building assisted him. Paintings in the tomb of Amenhotep Huy in the Theban necropolis show a viceroy at work, overseeing the collection and counting of tribute and its delivery by boat to the pharaoh at Thebes.

The title seems to have lapsed after Piankh, who led an unsuccessful campaign against his rebellious predecessor Pinehesy, and Piankh's successor Herihor. After them it is rarely attested, and then outside Nubia: Neskhons, wife of Pinedjem II, was named Superintendent of Southern Foreign Lands and Viceroy of Kush for reasons that are unclear. In the later 22nd Dynasty and one of its Upper Egyptian branches, often called the 23rd Dynasty, the title appears often again, apparently for important officials, several of them royal, stationed at Elephantine on Egypt's southern border rather than for governors of Nubia. Modern lists of the viceroys rest mainly on George Reisner's, supplemented by Frédéric Payraudeau's research on Theban officials.
viceroyalty-of-new-spain: After the Spanish conquest of the Aztec Empire in 1521, Hernán Cortés named the territory New Spain and set the capital, Mexico City, on the site of Tenochtitlan. The Kingdom of New Spain was established on 18 August 1521 under the Crown of Castile. It was a kingdom and not a colony, subject to the monarch in Spain, who held sovereignty and property rights over it. With the political and economic importance of the conquest, the crown asserted direct control, and on 12 October 1535 it created the viceroyalty by royal decree, appointing as viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, an aristocrat loyal to the monarch rather than to Cortés. Peru followed as the second viceroyalty in 1542.

The viceroy lived in Mexico City and was appointed by the monarch, but most matters were handled by local bodies, first among them the audiencias, which were superior tribunals with administrative and legislative functions and answered to the Council of the Indies. Second-level divisions were the captaincies general: Santo Domingo (1535), the Philippines (1565), Puerto Rico (1580), Cuba (1608), Guatemala (1609) and Yucatán (1617). Spanish Florida and Spanish Louisiana were governorates. Through the Patronato real the crown oversaw the Church in everything but doctrine.

Early on, conquistadors received grants of native tribute and labour known as encomiendas, modelled on the tribute and corvée labour that the Mexica rulers had demanded. In practice the system often intensified exploitation. The discovery of silver at Zacatecas in the 1540s drew Spanish miners and crown officials, and silver mining enriched both the colony and the crown. Acapulco was the American terminus of the transpacific trade with the Philippines by the Manila galleon. Mexico City was the seat of the viceroy, the archbishop, the Inquisition and the merchants' guild.

The history of mainland New Spain spans three hundred years, from the conquest of 1519-1521 to the Mexican War of Independence of 1810-1821. In the eighteenth century the Bourbon Reforms created intendancies, increased the military presence and centralised royal authority, and the Jesuits were expelled.

At its widest extent the crown claimed all of modern Mexico and Central America except Panama, most of the United States west of the Mississippi, the Floridas, the Spanish West Indies, and the Philippines, the Mariana Islands and the Caroline Islands, though it did not control large parts of this. After Napoleon's invasion of Iberia in 1808 and the forced abdication of Charles IV, a crisis ended the government of Viceroy José de Iturrigaray. The viceroyalty was dissolved in 1821 and the Mexican Empire was established, with Agustín de Iturbide crowned emperor.
viceroyalty-of-peru: Francisco Pizarro and his conquistadors arrived in Peru in 1532, and the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire is traditionally dated from the encounter at Cajamarca on 16 November 1532. Atahualpa was taken prisoner and executed on 26 July 1533. Pizarro founded Lima on 18 January 1535 as the City of the Kings. The conquerors then fell into conflict among themselves, and to end it King Charles I of Spain signed the New Laws in Barcelona on 20 November 1542. They established the Viceroyalty, officially the Kingdom of Peru, in place of the governorships of New Castile and New Toledo, and moved the seat of the Audiencia of Panama to Lima.

After almost forty years of administrative disorder, Viceroy Francisco de Toledo established between 1569 and 1581 the political and administrative framework that governed for many years. Between 1580 and 1650 large-scale mining took hold, with the silver of Potosí refined by amalgamation using mercury from Huancavelica. Silver production peaked in 1610. In the Bourbon period the viceroyalty lost territory: New Granada was created in 1717 and re-established permanently in 1740, and the Río de la Plata in 1776. Lima lost its place as the economic centre, though Peru remained the Crown's most valuable asset in South America.

Viceroy José Fernando de Abascal made Peru the centre of the royalist counter-revolution, and all attempts at independence, such as the Cuzco Rebellion of 1814, were suppressed. The Capitulation of Ayacucho, signed on 9 December 1824, ended the royalist military effort, and the last strongholds, the Real Felipe Fortress at Callao and the Chiloé Archipelago, fell in 1826.

The rest of the viceroyalty depended administratively on Lima, whose University of San Marcos, founded in 1551, is the oldest institution of higher education on the American continent. The economy rested on silver, mined by contract and free wage labourers and by the mita, a system of unfree labour inherited from pre-Hispanic times. A census by the last quipucamayoc recorded 12 million inhabitants of Inca Peru, and under Toledo, 45 years later, the figure was 1,100,000 Indians, a loss attributed largely to smallpox and other Eurasian diseases. Inca cities were rebuilt as Spanish towns around a plaza, and the Church was prominent: in the 17th century, Lima, with 26,000 inhabitants, had nineteen churches and monasteries.
vichy: Vichy is a city in the department of Allier, on the river Allier, with about 25,000 inhabitants. Its mineral springs are rich in trace elements such as lithium and fluorine and high in sodium bicarbonate. They owe their warmth to volcanic activity in the nearby Massif Central, and about 289 springs have been charted in the town and its surroundings. The name is the French form of the Occitan Vichèi, of uncertain etymology; one proposal derives it from a Latin Vippiacus, after a landowner presumably called Vippius. The cold soup vichyssoise is named after the town.

The first known settlement was founded by Roman legionaries in 52 BCE, who found the hot springs on their way south after their defeat at Gergovia by the Gauls under Vercingetorix. They called the township Aquae Calidae, "Hot Waters". In 1344 John II of France ceded the fiefdom to Peter I, Duke of Bourbon, and by 1374 it was wholly in the House of Bourbon's hands. A Celestinian monastery was founded in 1410. By the end of the 16th century the baths drew patients from the noble and wealthy classes, and the marquise de Sévigné, a patient in 1676 and 1677, popularised them in her letters.

Napoleon III's stays between 1861 and 1866 transformed the town: dikes were built along the Allier, 13 hectares of gardens replaced the marshes, chalets and pavilions were built for his court, and a large casino opened in 1865. The Opera House and the Hall of Springs were inaugurated in 1903. Vichy welcomed 40,000 curistes in 1900 and nearly 100,000 just before the First World War, and thermal life reached its height in the 1930s.

After the defeat of 1940 the French government fled Paris and, finding Clermont-Ferrand too cramped, moved to Vichy on 1 July. The town lay in the unoccupied zone and had the second largest hotel capacity in the country. On 9 and 10 July, 670 of the 846 members of the Senate and Chamber of Deputies voted full powers to Philippe Pétain. The new regime called itself the French State but became known as Vichy France. Germany occupied the Free Zone in November 1942. The city was liberated without bloodshed on 26 August 1944.

In 2021 Vichy became part of the transnational UNESCO World Heritage Site Great Spa Towns of Europe. Vichy Pastilles are octagonal candies made from the soda in the spring waters, and the name Vichy is used for a brand of the L'Oréal company. A term of the war years must not be confused with its inhabitants: partisans of the Pétain regime are called Vichyste, while residents are Vichyssois.
victimae-paschali-laudes: Before the Council of Trent (1545–1563) many feasts had sequences of their own, and some sixteen different Easter sequences were in use. Victimæ paschali laudes was one of only four medieval sequences kept in the Roman Missal of the Tridentine Mass published in 1570, beside Veni Sancte Spiritus for Pentecost, Lauda Sion for Corpus Christi and Dies irae for the Requiem Mass; Pope Benedict XIII added a fifth, Stabat Mater, in 1727.

The 1570 missal also changed the text. It deleted a section beginning Credendum est, which made a pejorative reference to the Jews, replaced praecedet suos (his own) with praecedet vos (you), and added Amen and Alleluia at the end. In this form it remains one of the few sequences still in liturgical use today.

The text was set by many composers, most of them of the Renaissance and Baroque, among them Busnois, Josquin, Lassus, Willaert, Hans Buchner, Palestrina, Byrd, Perosi and Fernando de las Infantas; the French composer Jehan Revert wrote a setting for four-part choir and organ. Chorales derived from the sequence include the 12th-century Christ ist erstanden and Martin Luther's Christ lag in Todes Banden.

It is often sung in Jane E. Leeson's metrical paraphrase, which opens Christ the Lord is risen today Its verses move from the Lamb who bled for the sheep and the strife of Death and Life to Mary telling of the empty tomb and the angels, and close with a prayer to Christ as King of victory. It is sung to several tunes, among them Victimae Paschali and St George's Windsor, or with alleluias to Easter Hymn or Llanfair.
victor-amadeus-i-duke-of-savoy: Victor Amadeus was born in Turin, the second son of Charles Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy, and Catalina Micaela of Spain, a daughter of King Philip II of Spain. He spent much of his childhood at his grandfather's court in Madrid, until the king's death in 1598, when he was eleven. As a second son he was not expected to rule. That changed when his elder brother, Filippo Emanuele, died in 1605, and he became heir to the duchy and received the homage of the court at Racconigi on 21 January 1607. In 1619 he married Christine Marie of France, a daughter of Henry IV of France and Marie de' Medici.

He became Duke of Savoy on the death of his father, on 26 July 1630. Charles Emmanuel's policies had left Savoy's relations with both France and Spain unstable, and troops were needed to defend the duchy. Money was lacking to recruit mercenaries or train local soldiers, and Victor Amadeus signed a peace treaty with Spain. Under the Treaty of Cherasco, Savoy was forced to give Pinerolo to France, which gave France a strategic route into the heart of Savoyard territory and on into the rest of Italy. His successors resented the loss and worked for decades to regain it.

Afterwards, under the direction of Cardinal Richelieu, he tried to create an anti-Spanish league in Italy. He won two victories against the Spanish, at the Battle of Tornavento in 1636 and at the Battle of Mombaldone on 8 September 1637. He was also known as the Lion of Susa.

On 25 September 1637 he fell ill after a dinner given by the Duke of Créqui. A prominent Savoyard noble who attended, Count Augusto Manfredo Scaglia di Verrua, died the same week, which aroused suspicions of poisoning and created uncertainty in Savoyard–French relations. Victor Amadeus was carried to Vercelli, where he died on 7 October, aged 50. His elder son, Francis Hyacinth, succeeded him but died the next year, and the younger, Charles Emmanuel II, followed. Christine served as regent from 1637 to 1663.
victor-amadeus-ii: Victor Amadeus was born in Turin on 14 May 1666, the only child of Charles Emmanuel II and Marie Jeanne Baptiste of Nemours. His father died in June 1675, and his mother ruled as regent, known at court as Madame Royale, until he banished her from the state's affairs in 1684. She had tried to arrange his marriage to his first cousin Infanta Isabel Luísa of Portugal, which would have kept her permanently in control; he refused, and the plan came to nothing. Under pressure from Louis XIV and his mother he instead married Anne Marie d'Orléans, by proxy at Versailles on 10 April 1684 and in person on 6 May.

Under his mother's regency Savoy had been a French satellite. At Louis XIV's urging Victor Amadeus began a persecution of the Vaudois in 1685, but his alliances with England and the Dutch Republic in the Nine Years' War forced him to stop in 1688, and in 1694 he granted an Edict of Toleration. He broke with France by joining the Grand Alliance in that war, and he enlarged his army from about 8,500 to more than 24,000. In the War of the Spanish Succession he changed sides again, joining the Grand Alliance in 1703. Turin was besieged in 1706 and saved in September by the combined forces of Victor Amadeus and Prince Eugene of Savoy.

He reformed the state. In 1696 he set up a system of intendants on the French model to collect taxes and keep order, and in 1697 he began a land survey, the Perequazione, of the holdings and privileges of the Church and nobility. In 1717 he created separate secretaries for war, internal affairs and foreign affairs. He established a select militia in 1690 and overhauled it in 1714, and from 1713 began a navy. He was crowned King of Sicily at Palermo on 24 December 1713, and after objections from an alliance of four nations he exchanged it in 1720 for the poorer kingdom of Sardinia.

In 1730 Victor Amadeus married Anna Canalis di Cumiana, and in September abdicated in favour of his son Charles Emmanuel III. After a stroke in 1731 he wished to resume the throne, and his son had him arrested and held at Moncalieri. He died on 31 October 1732. He reigned for over 55 years, the longest of any Savoyard ruler, and left a cultural mark on Turin, remodelling the Royal Palace and the Palace of Venaria and building the Basilica of Superga.
victor-amadeus-iii-of-sardinia: Victor Amadeus was born on 26 June 1726 at the Royal Palace of Turin, the eldest son of King Charles Emmanuel III and his second wife, Polyxena of Hesse-Rotenburg. He was styled Duke of Savoy from birth until he succeeded to the throne. His education was entrusted to Gerdil Giacinto Sigismondo, with particular emphasis on military training. He is said to have been privately conservative, and his father felt him unsuitable to hold power.

On 31 May 1750 at Oulx he married Infanta Maria Antonia of Spain, youngest daughter of Philip V of Spain and Elisabeth Farnese. The marriage was arranged by her half-brother Ferdinand VI and served to strengthen relations between Madrid and Turin after the War of the Austrian Succession. The couple had twelve children, among them the later kings Charles Emmanuel IV, Victor Emmanuel I and Charles Felix.

Victor Amadeus succeeded on 20 February 1773 and began by working on bureaucratic and military matters. On the advice of the bourgeoisie and aristocracy he set up two new cultural state institutions. He had the port of Nice improved and dams and the road of the Côte built. In 1785 he created the Società Agraria di Torino, and he encouraged the extension of the Orto Botanico dell'Università di Torino. Although politically conservative, he carried out numerous administrative reforms until he declared war on Revolutionary France in 1792. At the outbreak of the Revolution he gave his sons-in-law, the Counts of Artois and Provence, shelter in his kingdom. On 21 May 1793 he established the Gold Medal of Military Valour.

In April 1796 the French under Napoleon Bonaparte beat the Piedmontese army at Montenotte (12 April), Millesimo (13–14 April) and Mondovì (21 April). On 26 April they proclaimed the Republic of Alba in the occupied territories, and two days later, by the Armistice of Cherasco, it was ceded back to Victor Amadeus. On 15 May he was forced to sign the Treaty of Paris, abandoning the First Coalition. He ceded the fortresses of Cuneo, Ceva, Alessandria and Tortona, allowed French armies free passage towards Italy, and gave up Nice and Savoy.

He died on 16 October 1796 at the Castle of Moncalieri after an attack of apoplexy, leaving an economically struggling kingdom, and was buried at the Basilica of Superga in Turin. In 1786 he had moved the remains of many of his ancestors and kinsmen there.
victor-emmanuel-i-of-sardinia: Victor Emmanuel was born on 24 July 1759 at the Royal Palace of Turin, the second son of King Victor Amadeus III of Sardinia and Maria Antonia Ferdinanda of Spain. He was known from birth as the Duke of Aosta. His father took part from 1792 to 1796 in the struggle of the old powers against revolutionary France, was defeated and made peace by the Treaty of Paris. In 1789 Victor Emmanuel married Archduchess Maria Teresa of Austria-Este, with whom he had seven children, including the future Empress of Austria.

His elder brother Charles Emmanuel IV, who succeeded their father, faced a French occupation and then annexation of his mainland territories from December 1798 and withdrew to Sardinia, the only part of his domains the French had not conquered. He took little interest in ruling it. When his wife died in 1802 he abdicated in favour of his younger brother.

Victor Emmanuel took the throne on 4 June 1802 and ruled from Cagliari for twelve years. During this time he constituted the Carabinieri, a gendarmerie corps that still exists as one of the main branches of the Italian armed forces. After Napoleon's defeat in 1814 he returned to Turin, and the Congress of Vienna reconstituted his realm and added the territories of the former Republic of Genoa. He also wished to annex Monaco, but it became only a protectorate of his kingdom.

He abolished the freedoms granted by the Napoleonic codes and restored a fiercely oppressive rule: he brought back the Regie Costituzioni of Victor Amadeus II and the Jus commune, strengthened customs barriers, refused to grant a liberal constitution, entrusted education to the Church and reintroduced laws on labour and justice that discriminated against Jews and Waldensians. He also nurtured expansionist ambitions in Lombardy, which brought conflict with Austria.

In March 1821 a liberal revolution, largely the work of the Carbonari, broke out in Italy, and it seemed that the anti-Austrian attitude of the revolutionaries matched the king's own. On 11 March the king met the council of the crown, which included his distant cousin Charles Albert. He would not grant a liberal constitution and abdicated the next day, 12 March 1821, in favour of his brother Charles Felix. Because Charles Felix was in Modena, Victor Emmanuel entrusted the regency to Charles Albert in the meantime.

He lived in several cities until 1824, when he returned to the Castle of Moncalieri, where he died on 10 January. He is buried in the Basilica of Superga. As a descendant of Henrietta of England he also carried the Jacobite claim to the thrones of England and Scotland.
victor-emmanuel-ii: Victor Emmanuel was born in the Palazzo Carignano in Turin, the eldest son of Carlo Alberto, Prince of Carignano, who in 1831 succeeded a distant cousin as King of Sardinia. He spent some years of his youth in Florence and showed an early interest in politics, the military and sports. In 1842 he married his cousin Adelaide of Austria, and they had eight children. He fought in the front line under his father in the First Italian War of Independence, at Pastrengo, Santa Lucia, Goito and Custoza.

Charles Albert abdicated in 1849 after defeat by the Austrians at the Battle of Novara, and Victor Emmanuel obtained a favourable armistice at Vignale from the Austrian commander Radetzky. When the Chamber of Deputies refused to ratify it, he dismissed his Prime Minister, Claudio Gabriele de Launay, and appointed Massimo D'Azeglio; after new elections the peace was accepted. In 1849 he also suppressed a revolt in Genoa. In 1852 he appointed Camillo Benso, Count of Cavour, who modernised the kingdom for war, and in 1855 Sardinia joined Britain and France in the Crimean War, which gave it a place at the peace conference.

At Plombières in 1858 Cavour and Napoleon III agreed that France would receive Nice and Savoy in return for help against Austria. After the campaign of 1859 Napoleon III made a separate treaty at Villafranca, giving Piedmont only Lombardy and leaving Venetia to Austria; Cavour resigned, then returned, and the Treaty of Turin of March 1860 gave France Nice and Savoy. Plebiscites joined Tuscany, Modena, Parma and Romagna to Piedmont-Sardinia. The king's forces defeated the papal army at Castelfidardo, and he was excommunicated. He met Garibaldi at Teano and received control of the south, and on 17 March 1861 he was proclaimed first King of Italy, keeping his old numeral and making Turin the capital.

In 1866 he allied with Prussia and received Veneto after the Austrian defeat in Germany. After the French withdrew in 1870 he entered Rome on 20 September, and the capital was set up there on 2 July 1871, with the Quirinal Palace as the royal residence, after a temporary move to Florence in 1864. His part in day-to-day government gradually dwindled, as ministers in practice became responsible to Parliament.

Victor Emmanuel died in Rome in 1878, after envoys of Pope Pius IX had lifted his excommunication and he had received last rites. He was buried in the Pantheon and succeeded by his son Umberto I. Italians gave him the epithet Padre della Patria, Father of the Fatherland, and he became the symbol of the Risorgimento. The Victor Emmanuel II Monument in Rome, containing the Altare della Patria, was built in his honour.
victor-emmanuel-iii: Victor Emmanuel was born in Naples on 11 November 1869, the son of Umberto I and Margherita of Savoy, who were first cousins. On 24 October 1896 he married Princess Elena of Montenegro, and on 29 July 1900 he became king at the age of 30, after his father was assassinated by an anarchist. The Statuto Albertino left the king considerable residual powers, among them the right to appoint a prime minister who lacked a majority in the Chamber of Deputies.

The first fourteen years of the reign were dominated by the prime minister Giovanni Giolitti, who pursued industrialisation and brought in universal male suffrage. When the First World War began Italy stayed neutral, then signed the secret Treaty of London in April 1915. The Chamber forced Antonio Salandra to resign, but the king declined his resignation and personally decided that Italy would enter the war. Victory brought Trento, Trieste and South Tyrol, and he was called the King of Victory.

In 1922 Benito Mussolini led the March on Rome. Prime Minister Luigi Facta drafted a decree of martial law, but the king, after some hesitation, refused to sign it, doubting that the army could contain the rising without a civil war. He then appointed Mussolini. He took no action against the regime's abuses, among them the murder of Giacomo Matteotti in 1924, though critics held that he could have dismissed Mussolini then. In 1936 he took the crown of Emperor of Ethiopia after the invasion that the League of Nations condemned, and in 1939 that of King of the Albanians; he also stayed silent when racial laws were issued.

In 1939 he held back Mussolini from entering the war, telling Count Galeazzo Ciano that Italy was in no condition to wage war, but he gave him sweeping powers in June 1940. After the Allied invasion of Sicily he dismissed Mussolini in July 1943 and appointed Pietro Badoglio. The armistice of Cassibile followed in September, and the king fled to Brindisi. After the liberation of Rome in June 1944 he transferred most of his powers to his son Umberto.

He abdicated on 9 May 1946 in favour of Umberto II, hoping to strengthen the monarchy before the referendum of 1946, which established the Republic. He went into exile in Alexandria, where he died on 28 December 1947. His decisions to take the crowns of Ethiopia and Albania and his silence over Fascist abuses are held to have proved fatal to the monarchy.
victor-horta: Victor Horta was born in Ghent on 6 January 1861, the son of a master shoemaker who considered craftsmanship a high form of art. He began studying music at the Royal Conservatory of Ghent but was expelled for misbehaviour and went to the Royal Academy of Fine Arts there. At seventeen he moved to Paris and worked for the architect Jules Debuysson.

After his father died in 1880 he returned to Belgium, settled in Brussels and studied architecture at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts, where he became friends with Paul Hankar and was taken on as an assistant by his professor Alphonse Balat, architect to King Leopold II. With Balat he worked on the Royal Greenhouses of Laeken, his first use of glass and iron. He admired the theorist Eugène Viollet-le-Duc throughout his life.

Horta's breakthrough came in 1892, when he was commissioned to design a house for the scientist Émile Tassel. The Hôtel Tassel, completed in 1893, has a fairly traditional stone facade, but the interior is built around an open central stairway, with curling lines modelled on vines and flowers repeated in the ironwork, floor tiles, glass and painted walls. It is widely recognised as one of the first appearances of Art Nouveau in architecture.

Further town houses followed: the Hôtel Solvay for Armand Solvay, the Hôtel van Eetvelde with its winter garden, and his own house and studio. In 1896 to 1899 he built the Maison du Peuple for the Belgian Workers' Party, a functional steel structure with a hall seating over 2,000, demolished in 1965 despite a petition by over 700 architects.

After about 1900 his buildings became simpler, and after he returned from the United States in 1919 he abandoned organic forms for geometrical ones. His later works include the Centre for Fine Arts in Brussels, built between 1923 and 1929, and Brussels-Central railway station. He was named a baron by King Albert I in 1932. He died on 8 September 1947, still working on the station, which was completed by his colleagues led by Maxime Brunfaut and opened on 4 October 1952.

The novel element in Horta's houses was his search for maximum transparency and light on the narrow building sites of Brussels, achieved with large windows, skylights, mirrors and open floor plans. He designed furniture and details to match each house, down to the bronze doorbell of the Hôtel Solvay.

His curving vegetal forms influenced Hector Guimard in Paris, and he is also considered a precursor of modern architecture. After Art Nouveau lost favour, many of his buildings were abandoned or destroyed. In 2000 UNESCO listed four of his Brussels town houses: the Hôtel Tassel, the Hôtel Solvay, the Hôtel van Eetvelde and the Horta House, now the Horta Museum.
victor-hugo: Victor-Marie Hugo was born on 26 February 1802 in Besançon, the youngest son of Joseph Léopold Sigisbert Hugo, a general in the Napoleonic army, and Sophie Trébuchet. His father was an atheist and an ardent supporter of the Republic, while his mother was loyal to the deposed dynasty. Because his father was an officer, the family moved often from posting to posting. In 1810 his father was made Count Hugo de Cogolludo y Sigüenza by Joseph Bonaparte, then King of Spain, though the Spanish title seems not to have been legally recognised in France.

In his youth Hugo resolved to be Chateaubriand or nothing, and his life came to parallel that of the older writer in many ways. Like him, he furthered the cause of Romanticism, became involved in politics and was forced into exile. He married Adèle Foucher in October 1822.

Hugo published his first novel, Hans of Iceland, in 1823 and his second, Bug-Jargal, in 1826. His five volumes of poetry between 1829 and 1840 cemented his reputation as one of the great elegiac and lyric poets of his time. The Hunchback of Notre-Dame appeared in 1831 and Les Misérables in 1862. He was at the forefront of Romanticism with his play Cromwell and his drama Hernani. After three unsuccessful attempts he was elected to the Académie française in 1841, and he wrote the libretto of Louise Bertin's opera La Esmeralda in 1836.

Politically he moved from royalism toward republicanism. Louis Philippe I appointed him a peer of France in 1845, where he spoke against the death penalty and social injustice and for freedom of the press. Elected in 1848 to the National Assembly of the Second Republic as a conservative, he broke with the conservatives in 1849 with a speech calling for an end to misery and poverty. His campaign to abolish the death penalty was known internationally.

When Louis Napoleon seized complete power in 1851, Hugo openly declared him a traitor to France. He moved to Brussels, then to Jersey, from which he was expelled for supporting the newspaper L'Homme. He settled at Hauteville House in Saint Peter Port, Guernsey, in self-imposed exile from October 1855 until 1870. He returned to Paris in 1870 and was hailed as a national hero. He lost a bid for re-election to the National Assembly in 1872 and was elected to the new Senate on 30 January 1876.

Hugo died on 22 May 1885, aged 83. He was given a state funeral in the Panthéon of Paris, attended by over two million people, the largest in French history. He produced more than 4,000 drawings, with about 3,000 surviving. His portrait was placed on French currency.
victor-paz-estenssoro: Paz Estenssoro was born on 2 October 1907 to a landowning family in Tarija; his father was a banker. He spent his childhood in Tarija and Oruro and studied economics and law at the Higher University of San Andrés in La Paz, receiving a law degree in 1927. He began work at the Ministry of Finance in 1932, fought in the Chaco War, where he reached the rank of artillery sergeant, and started a teaching career in 1939.

In 1941 he co-founded the Movimiento Nacionalista Revolucionario with Hernán Siles Zuazo and others. He became finance minister under Colonel Gualberto Villarroel but was forced out and went into exile in Argentina. He ran for president in 1947, finishing third, and again in 1951, when the MNR won although suffrage was limited to a small, propertied part of the population. The government of Mamerto Urriolagoitía annulled the result, and the MNR came to power after a popular revolution the next year.

In his first government, from 1952 to 1956, Paz Estenssoro extended the vote to all adult citizens, natives and illiterates included, nationalised the largest tin-mining concerns and began a land distribution programme. Much of the old military was dismantled and reorganised as an arm of the party, while armed workers and peasants, overseen largely by Juan Lechín of the Bolivian Workers' Center, became a counterweight. Barred from a consecutive term, he served as ambassador in London while Siles governed, then won the 1960 election with Lechín as his running mate.

The second administration saw dissent and political violence. Paz Estenssoro leaned on the reconstituted army, expelled Lechín and amended the constitution to run again in 1964, choosing General René Barrientos as his running mate. On 4 November 1964 Barrientos and Alfredo Ovando led a coup that overthrew him, and he went into a long exile in Lima.

He backed Hugo Banzer's coup of 1971, but Banzer broke with the MNR in 1974 and exiled him, and he taught history at the University of California, Los Angeles and the University of New Mexico. In 1985 he came second to Banzer, yet Congress elected him because no candidate had 50 percent. Through Decree 21060 he curbed hyperinflation: unions were repressed, 30,000 miners were removed from state payrolls, and a curfew and mass arrests of union leaders followed. The New Economic Policy, run largely by Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada, turned a statist economy towards privatisation, though poverty persisted. He retired in 1989 and died on 7 June 2001, after complications from surgery on his leg.
victor-raul-haya-de-la-torre: Haya de la Torre was born in Trujillo on 22 February 1895 into an aristocratic family. At the National University of Trujillo, where he studied literature from 1913, he befriended the poet César Vallejo in the circle later called the North Group. In 1919 he supported the workers' campaign for the eight-hour day and was elected president of the Peruvian Student Federation, and in 1922 the González Prada popular universities, night schools for workers, took shape. Banished by Augusto B. Leguía, he reached Mexico City on 16 November 1923 as secretary to José Vasconcelos, and founded APRA there on 7 May 1924.

Returning in 1930, he founded the Peruvian Aprista Party and lost the 1931 presidential election to Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro. He was arrested, and an APRA rising in Trujillo in 1932 was harshly repressed: over 6,000 were executed before the ruins of Chan Chan. The party was banned, and after an APRA member assassinated Sánchez Cerro on 30 April 1933 Haya lived in hiding until the party returned to legality in 1945, when it backed José Luis Bustamante y Rivero. After Manuel A. Odría's coup of 1948 he took refuge in the Colombian embassy, a case that became a reference in international law, and left Peru in 1954.

In 1956 he backed Manuel Prado Ugarteche, beginning the so-called coexistence, in which a party once clearly anti-oligarchic supported an oligarchic regime. He came first in 1962 with 33 per cent, but the armed forces vetoed him and overthrew Prado; in 1963 he lost to Fernando Belaúnde, and his party's alliance with Odría then controlled Congress and limited Belaúnde's agrarian reform. Under the military government he trained young leaders, among them Alan García. Elected to the Constituent Assembly of 1978 with over one million votes, he presided over it for a salary of one sol de oro.

Suffering from lung cancer, Haya signed the constitution on his deathbed on 12 July 1979 and died on 2 August at his home in the Ate District. He is buried in Trujillo under a rock inscribed Here lies the light. His thought began close to Marxism but parted from Leninism: he held that imperialism was the highest stage of capitalism, that capitalism was an inevitable phase that had to mature before it could be surpassed, and that the young proletariat of Latin America could not yet make that revolution.
victor-schoelcher: He was born in Paris on 22 July 1804, the son of Marc Schœlcher, who owned a porcelain factory, and Victoire Jacob. He left the Lycée Louis-le-Grand after a year to work in the family factory. In his teens he opposed the Bourbon monarchy while frequenting the literary and political salons of Paris.

In 1828 his father sent him on an eighteen-month trip to America as the firm’s representative. He visited Mexico, Cuba and the southern United States, learned much about slavery and began writing against it. On his return in 1830 he published Des noirs in the Revue de Paris, which proposed gradual abolition.

After inheriting the business in 1832 he sold it to devote himself to abolitionism. He went to the West Indies in 1840 to study the results of abolition in the British colonies, then to Egypt, Greece and Turkey to study Muslim slavery, and to Senegal and Gambia between September 1847 and January 1848. His travels convinced him to demand immediate emancipation, and in 1842 he published Des colonies françaises: Abolition immédiate de l’esclavage.

After the revolution of February 1848 he reached Paris from Senegal on 3 March. The next day François Arago, Minister of the Navy and Colonies in the provisional government, appointed him under-secretary of state for the colonies and president of a commission to draft the abolition. He argued that waiting for the National Assembly could lead to revolt and bloodshed in the colonies. He wrote the decree of 27 April 1848, which abolished slavery in all French colonies and granted citizenship to the emancipated.

He was elected deputy for Martinique in 1848 and for Guadeloupe in 1850. On 2 December 1851, the day Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte seized power, he was among the few deputies at the barricades. Exiled, he settled in London in 1852, wrote a biography of Handel and published works against Napoleon III, and refused the amnesty of 1859.

He returned to France in August 1870, organised an artillery legion in the defence of Paris and in 1871 again sat for Martinique. During the Paris Commune he tried unsuccessfully to mediate and was briefly imprisoned by the communards. He was elected senator for life in December 1875 and published a biography of Toussaint Louverture in 1889. He died on 25 December 1893 at Houilles, aged 89.

He left his money and collection to Guadeloupe, now in the Schœlcher Museum at Pointe-à-Pitre. His remains were moved to the Panthéon on 20 May 1949, together with those of his father and of Félix Éboué. The commune of Case-Navire in Martinique took his name in 1888. Statues of him in Martinique were destroyed in 2020 and 2021 in protests against colonial memory.
victor-turner: Victor Witter Turner was born in Glasgow, the son of Norman Turner, an electrical engineer, and Violet Turner, a repertory actress who founded the Scottish National Players. He first studied poetry and classics at University College London. In 1941 he was drafted into the war and served as a noncombatant until 1944, and during that time he met and married Edith Brocklesby Davis, who was serving as a land girl. Turner went back to University College in 1946 with a new focus on anthropology, and he later pursued graduate studies at Manchester University.

Turner worked in Zambia, then Northern Rhodesia, as research officer for the Rhodes-Livingstone Institute, and there began his lifelong study of the Ndembu people. He completed his doctorate at the University of Manchester in 1955. Like many Manchester anthropologists of his time he was concerned with conflict, and he developed the concept of social drama to account for the symbolism of conflict and crisis resolution among Ndembu villagers. As a professor at the University of Chicago in the late 1950s he began to apply his study of ritual and rites of passage to world religions and the lives of religious heroes. He and his wife converted to Catholicism in 1958.

His books include The Forest of Symbols (1967), The Drums of Affliction (1968), The Ritual Process (1969), Dramas, Fields, and Metaphors (1974), From Ritual to Theatre (1982) and The Anthropology of Performance (1986). With Edith L. B. Turner he wrote Image and Pilgrimage in Christian Culture (1978).

Turner took up Arnold van Gennep's threefold structure of rites of passage, which has a pre-liminal phase of separation, a liminal phase of transition and a post-liminal phase of reincorporation, and he expanded the theory of the liminal phase. In liminality, he noted, individuals are betwixt and between: they no longer belong to the society they came from and have not yet been reincorporated into it. He described liminality as a limbo, an ambiguous period marked by humility, seclusion, tests, sexual ambiguity and communitas. His work, with that of Clifford Geertz and others, is often called symbolic and interpretive anthropology.

Turner died on 18 December 1983 in Charlottesville, Virginia. His widow Edith went on to her own career as an anthropologist and developed his anthropology of experience in a publication on communitas. His work on liminality and performance strongly influenced performance studies, through his friendship and collaboration with Richard Schechner, with whom he explored the relationship between ritual and theatre. The Society for Humanistic Anthropology awards the Victor Turner Prize in Ethnographic Writing each year, and the first winner, in 1990, was Kirin Narayan.
victoria-and-albert-museum: The museum traces its origins to the Government School of Design, set up by the British government in 1832 at Somerset House in London for the direct application of the arts to manufactures. The government feared that poor art education was restricting the growth and export potential of British industry. The school included a museum that held plaster casts of ancient sculptures and architectural features for teaching. By February 1854 discussions were under way to move it to Brompton, where Prince Albert was planning a group of institutions as a legacy of the Great Exhibition, nicknamed Albertopolis by the press.

Henry Cole persuaded the authorities to rename Brompton as South Kensington, and in 1857 the museum moved there as the South Kensington Museum. Queen Victoria opened it on 20 June 1857. In its first fifty years it formed part of the national system of art education, and its School of Design component became the National Art Training School, later the Royal College of Art. Aston Webb won the competition of 1891 to design the Cromwell Road front, and at the foundation stone ceremony on 17 May 1899 the new name was announced.

In the Second World War many objects were sent to quarries, a country house and tunnels near two tube stations, while the Raphael Cartoons were bricked up in the basement. After the war the Britain Can Make It exhibition of 1946 drew nearly one and a half million visitors. The fifteen British galleries were rebuilt and reopened in 2001, and the Medieval and Renaissance galleries opened in November 2009.

The collection spans 5,000 years and numbers about 2.83 million objects. It holds the largest ceramics collection in the world, with over 80,000 objects, and more than 53,000 textiles. Its sculpture collection is the most comprehensive holding of post-classical European sculpture, and the Asia collection exceeds 160,000 objects, with South Asian art the most important in the West. The Jameel Gallery of Islamic Art, opened in 2006, has the Ardabil Carpet as its centrepiece.

The museum also houses the National Art Library and, since 2004, the RIBA Drawings and Archives Collection. Until 1983 it was controlled directly by a government department; it is now a non-departmental public body, and entrance is free. Besides South Kensington it includes Young V&A, V&A Dundee, which opened in September 2018, and the V&A Wedgwood Collection, acquired in 2014.
