victoriano-huerta: Huerta was born in Colotlán, Jalisco, to parents reported as ethnically Huichol, and identified himself as indigenous. He learned to read at the local priest's school, and chose a military career as the only way out of poverty. With the support of General Donato Guerra he entered the military academy at Chapultepec in 1872 and excelled at mathematics. Commissioned into the Corps of Engineers in 1877, he rose under the patronage of General Manuel González, and spent nine years on topographical surveys in Puebla and Veracruz. His hero was Napoleon, and he supported Porfirio Díaz as a strongman Mexico needed.

In 1911 he commanded the escort that took Díaz into exile. Under the interim president Francisco León de la Barra he fought Emiliano Zapata in Morelos, burning villages, which hindered Francisco I. Madero's later efforts at conciliation. In 1912 he defeated Pascual Orozco's rebellion at Rellano and became a national military hero.

In February 1913 a conspiracy of Félix Díaz, Bernardo Reyes and Manuel Mondragón began the Ten Tragic Days in Mexico City. Madero put Huerta in command, and Huerta secretly joined the plotters. The United States Ambassador, Henry Lane Wilson, took an active part, and the Embassy Pact provided for the exile of Madero and his vice president and for Huerta's takeover. Madero and José María Pino Suárez were seized on 18 February; Pedro Lascuráin held the presidency for under an hour and handed it to Huerta. Four days later Madero and Pino Suárez were shot by officers of the rurales, assumed to be acting on his orders.

The incoming Wilson administration in the United States refused to recognise the regime. Huerta suspended payment of the foreign debt, borrowed at a high rate and forced banks to issue paper money, which brought inflation. He resisted the United States landing at Veracruz in 1914, a stance even his opponents shared. The Constitutionalist Army won at the Battle of Zacatecas, and Huerta resigned in July 1914 and left for Spain, 17 months into his presidency.

Huerta reached the United States in April 1915 and dealt with the German naval agent Franz von Rintelen on a plan to regain power. He was arrested in June 1915 as he travelled to meet Orozco, held at Fort Bliss, and died in custody in January 1916, perhaps of cirrhosis or cancer; poisoning was widely suspected. Mexican historiography calls him the demon of the Revolution, and he is still known as El Chacal and El Usurpador.
victorinus: Marcus Piavonius Victorinus came from a wealthy Gallic family and served as a soldier under Postumus, the first of the Gallic emperors. He showed considerable ability. He held the post of tribune of the praetorians in 266 or 267 and rose swiftly to become co-consul with Postumus in 268, and Postumus may then have made him praetorian prefect. Shortly after Postumus put down the rebellion of Laelianus in 269, his own troops murdered him and appointed Marius emperor in his place.

After engineering the death of Marius, Victorinus was declared emperor by the troops at Augusta Treverorum, now Trier, in the autumn of 269. His chief concern was to keep the western provinces from submitting to the central Roman government, but in his first weeks only Gaul, Germania and Britain recognised him. Hispania deserted the Gallic Empire and declared for Claudius Gothicus, who sent his general Placidianus to south-eastern Gaul. Placidianus took Cularo, now Grenoble, but went no further.

His presence led the city of Augustodunum, now Autun, to abandon Victorinus and announce for Claudius. Victorinus marched south and besieged it; it fell after seven months, and his troops plundered and destroyed it. He returned in triumph to Cologne. Why Claudius did not allow Placidianus to relieve Autun is unknown, but it is speculated that he was fully engaged against the Alamanni in Italy or the Goths in the Balkans and did not want a second theatre of war in Gaul.

Victorinus was murdered at Cologne in early 271 by one of his officers, Attitianus, whose wife he had supposedly seduced. Because the motive was personal and not political, his mother, Victoria, whom some sources call Vitruvia, was able to keep power. She arranged his deification and, after a large payment to the troops, the appointment of Tetricus I as his successor. Another commander, apparently proclaimed as Domitianus II, was soon eliminated.

The Historia Augusta, a dubious source, lists Victorinus among the Thirty Tyrants. It also describes a Victorinus Junior, allegedly his son, whom the family proclaimed emperor on the day of his father's murder and whom the troops killed immediately; it says both were buried in marble tombs near Cologne.
victory-stele-of-naram-sin: The stele dates to about 2254–2218 BCE, in the time of the Akkadian Empire. Carved in pinkish limestone, it is now about two metres high, though estimates of its original height range up to three metres, and it carries cuneiform inscriptions in Akkadian and Elamite. The scene runs diagonally up a steep slope rather than in the horizontal registers usual for conquest scenes: ordered Akkadian troops march over the broken defenders, while the king stands at the top, far larger than anyone else, with every figure looking up to him. A tree native to the area stands between the two groups and places the battle in a particular spot.

Naram-Sin wears a horned helmet, which in Akkadian art of the time marked a god, and the stele thus presents him as a god-king. He tramples a dead enemy, has stabbed another in the neck with a spear, and the Lullubi are shown thrown from the mountainside, fleeing and begging for mercy. Above the peak are sun-stars standing for the god Shamash; there were three, but damage to the stone has left only two visible. The fragmentary Akkadian inscription over the king's head reads in part: "Sidur and Sutuni, princes of the Lullubi, gathered together and they made war against me."

The stele is believed to have stood first at Sippar. About 1,000 years after it was carved, the Elamite king Shutruk-Nakhunte took it after the pillage of Sippar and kept its old inscription, adding one in Elamite over the mountain in which he says that at the order of the god Inshushinak he defeated Sippar, carried the stele off to the land of Elam and set it up there as an offering to the god. In 1898 the French archaeologist Jacques de Morgan excavated it at Susa, and it was moved to the Louvre in Paris.
victual-brothers: The Victual Brothers, in German Vitalienbrüder, were a loosely organised guild of privateers who later turned to piracy. The Dukes of Mecklenburg hired them in 1392 in the struggle of Queen Margaret I of Denmark against Albert of Mecklenburg, who had been King of Sweden since 1364. Margaret had imprisoned Albert and his son Eric to subdue Sweden, and her forces were besieging Stockholm. The blockade runners who shipped provisions into the city took their name from the Latin victualia, meaning provisions.

Their main naval enemy in 1392 was the Hanseatic town of Lübeck, which supported Denmark. The rest of the Hanseatic League at first supported the brotherhood, since most of its towns did not want a victory for Denmark. The Brothers had safe harbours at Rostock, Ribnitz, Wismar and Stralsund.

The Brothers soon turned to open piracy and coastal plunder. They sacked Bergen in 1393 and took Malmö in 1394, occupied parts of Frisia and Schleswig, and plundered Turku, Vyborg and other castles. In 1394 they occupied Gotland and made Visby their headquarters, and they also operated from the Turku archipelago, where the castle's chief, Knut Bosson, supported them. Maritime trade in the Baltic virtually collapsed and the herring industry suffered. Queen Margaret even sought to charter English ships from King Richard II against them.

From 1395 Margaret gained the upper hand, uniting Denmark, Sweden and Norway in the Kalmar Union. Albert pledged Gotland to the Teutonic Order, and an army under the Grand Master Konrad von Jungingen drove the Brothers off the island in 1398. Those who remained at sea called themselves Likedeelers, meaning equal sharers, who shared with the poor coastal population. They worked from the Schlei, the mouth of the Ems and Friesland, and raided Brabant, France and as far south as Spain.

Their best-known leader was Klaus Störtebeker, who first appears in the record as a Victual Brother around 1394. His name in Low German means Down the beakerful, and he allegedly earned it by swallowing four litres of beer without taking the beaker from his mouth, though it may simply be a family name from Wismar. In 1401 the Hamburg warship Die Bunte Kuh, leading a small fleet under Simon of Utrecht, caught up with his forces near Heligoland. After a running battle of three days Störtebeker and his crew were overpowered and executed.

Raiding did not end with him. In 1429, about 28 years later, members of the Victual Brothers plundered Bergen and burned it to the ground, and until about 1440 trade in the North and Baltic Seas remained in danger of attack by the Likedeelers.
vidarbha: Vidarbha forms the eastern part of the state of Maharashtra in central India and comprises the Amravati and Nagpur divisions, with eleven districts. It lies on the northern part of the Deccan Plateau and borders Madhya Pradesh to the north, Chhattisgarh to the east, Telangana to the south and the Marathwada and Uttar Maharashtra regions to the west. The terrain is largely flat, the Satpura Range lies to the north, and large basaltic formations belong to the volcanic Deccan Traps. It lies in the rain shadow of the Western Ghats and receives little rainfall. The census of 2011 counted 23,003,179 people, 21.3 percent of the population of Maharashtra on 31.6 percent of its area.

In the Mahabharata and other Puranic scriptures, Rukmini, the wife of Krishna, was born to Bhishmaka, king of the kingdom of Vidarbha. The region was part of the Satavahana Empire in the 1st and 2nd centuries CE, as coins found at Pauni show. Coins and inscriptions of the Paramara king Jagadeva, son of Udayaditya, who reigned c. 1060 to 1086, have been found in its northern parts. In the medieval period it formed part of the Berar Subah, according to the Ain-i-Akbari.

Sambhaji, son of Shivaji, captured the region in 1680. In 1724, after a battle at Buldana, Asaf Jah defeated the Mughal governor and declared independence, later becoming the Nizam of Hyderabad; most of the region came under his nominal rule, while the Marathas kept the administration and the right to collect chauth. After the defeat of the Marathas in 1803 it passed to the British East India Company, and in 1857 the British Empire took control. After independence it was part of the Central Provinces and Berar, and most of it joined Bombay State in 1957 and then Maharashtra.

Nagpur is the largest city, and other major towns include Amravati, Akola, Chandrapur, Yavatmal and Gondia. Marathi is the first language of about 73.72 percent of the population, in its Varhadi and Zadi dialects, with Hindi, Urdu, Gondi and other languages. Oranges and cotton are the main crops, and coal and manganese are the chief minerals. The Tadoba Andhari Tiger Reserve is the oldest national park in Maharashtra. A movement for a separate state of Vidarbha began in the 1930s, citing the region's perceived neglect by the government of Maharashtra; parties differ on it, and the economist Shrikant Jichkar argued that it was not sustainable.
vidin: Vidin lies on the southern bank of the Danube in north-western Bulgaria, close to the borders with Romania and Serbia. It is the westernmost important Bulgarian Danube port, and its hinterland is fertile and known for its wines. The town grew on the site of an old Celtic settlement called Dunonia, a name meaning fortified hill. The Romans built a fort, Bononia, on the Danubian Limes, around which a town developed that became one of the important centres of the province of Upper Moesia. Slavs who settled there called it Badin or Bdin, the source of the modern name.

In the Middle Ages Vidin was a bishop's seat and the capital of a large province of the First Bulgarian Empire. Between 971 and 976 it was the centre of the possessions of the future emperor Samuil. In 1003 Basil II took it after an eight-month siege, thanks to the betrayal of the local bishop. Under the Second Bulgarian Empire its despots were influential and sometimes chosen as emperors, and the Shishman dynasty ruled it from the mid 13th century. Michael Shishman threw off Serbian overlordship and was chosen tsar in 1323. In 1365 Hungarian crusaders occupied the Tsardom of Vidin, until Vladislav I of Wallachia drove them out in 1369 and Vidin was returned to Ivan Stratsimir.

After the Ottomans took Vidin in 1396 they made it a sandjak. Austrian forces held it for nine months from October 1689 during the Great Turkish War, and many Muslim houses and shops were destroyed; of 3,000 buildings, only 200 to 300 survived. Late in Ottoman rule Osman Pazvantoğlu's breakaway state centred on it. Vidin joined the Principality of Bulgaria after the liberation of 1878, and Serbian armies besieged it unsuccessfully in 1885 and 1913.

Vidin keeps two medieval fortresses, Baba Vida, built between the 10th and 14th centuries, and Kaleto. Its other monuments include the Orthodox churches of St Pantaleimon and St Petka, both of the 17th century, the Vidin Synagogue of 1894 and the Osman Pazvantoğlu Mosque and library. The theatre of 1891 was the first Bulgarian theatre in a European model. The New Europe Bridge, finished in 2013, joins the town to Calafat in Romania, replacing a ferry. Nearby are the Belogradchik Rocks and the Magura Cave with prehistoric paintings.
vidisha: Vidisha lies in the eastern Malwa region of Madhya Pradesh, 62.5 km northeast of the state capital Bhopal, in the fork of the Betwa and Bes rivers, about 9 km from Sanchi. The surrounding land has fertile black soil and low hills. The city was formerly known as Bhelsa, Besnagar and Bhaddalpur, and was renamed Vidisha in 1956. Its name is said to derive from the nearby river Bes, mentioned in the Puranas, and the Ramayana refers to Vidisha under the rule of Shatrughna, the youngest brother of Rama.

Besnagar, 3 km from the present city on the west side of the river, became an important trade centre in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE and is mentioned in the Pali scriptures. It flourished under the Shungas, Nagas, Satavahanas and Guptas. Ashoka was governor of Vidisha during his father's lifetime, and Ceylonese chronicles say his first wife, Devi, was the daughter of a merchant of Vedisagiri. The Heliodorus Pillar was erected by Heliodorus, ambassador of the Indo-Greek king Antialcidas, in the court of Bhagabhadra, in front of a temple of Vāsudeva. Its Brahmi inscription dedicates it as a Garuda standard to Vāsudeva.

In the medieval period Besnagar was called Bhelsa and became known for the temple of the sun god Bhillasvamin, first named in an inscription of 878 CE. Iltutmish is said to have destroyed the temple in the 1230s. Alauddin Khalji sacked the city in 1293 and Bahadur Shah of Gujarat in 1532, after which it passed to the Malwa Sultans, the Mughals and the Scindias. Under British rule it lay in the princely state of Gwalior, and the Quit India Movement in Madhya Pradesh began there in August 1942.

Vidisha is the administrative headquarters of Vidisha district and a Jain pilgrimage centre; Bhaddalpur is believed to be the birthplace of Shitalanatha, the tenth tirthankar. Its monuments include the Heliodorus Pillar, known locally as Kham Baba, the remains of the Bijamaṇḍal temple of the late Paramara period, and the tomb of Lohangi Pir. The 2011 census counted 155,951 inhabitants. Agriculture is the main economic activity.
vidkun-quisling: Quisling was born in Fyresdal, in Telemark, the son of the pastor and genealogist Jon Lauritz Qvisling and Anna Caroline Bang, daughter of a Grimstad ship-owner. He first came to international prominence as a close collaborator of the explorer Fridtjof Nansen. In January 1922 he arrived in Kharkiv to help the League of Nations relief effort during the Russian famine, and his report on the mismanagement and a death toll of about ten thousand a day attracted aid. He later served as a Norwegian diplomat in the Soviet Union, where he also managed British diplomatic affairs for a time. He returned to Norway in December 1929 with a plan called Norsk Aktion, which proposed radical constitutional change.

Quisling was defence minister in the Agrarian governments of Peder Kolstad and Jens Hundseid from 1931 to 1933, though he was neither an Agrarian nor a friend of Kolstad. In 1933 he founded the fascist Nasjonal Samling, or National Gathering. He gained some popularity through attacks on the political left, but the party won no seats in the Storting. In the summer of 1935 he told opponents that heads would roll once he achieved power, which damaged the party's image, and several high-ranking members, including his brother Jørgen, resigned. In 1939 he supported Hitler and toured German and Danish cities, where he was well received.

During the German invasion on 9 April 1940 Quisling attempted the first radio-broadcast coup d'état, but the Germans sought instead to persuade the recognised government to legitimise the occupation. Hitler appointed Josef Terboven Reichskommissar on 24 April, and Terboven forced Quisling to step down as party leader in June. After Quisling won Hitler over on 16 August, he formed a second government on 1 February 1942 as minister president, alongside Terboven's administration. On 12 March 1942 Norway officially became a one-party state, and criticism of the party was criminalised. His collaborationist government took part in Germany's war effort and deported Jews to concentration camps in occupied Poland.

Quisling turned himself in on 9 May 1945, and his trial opened on 20 August. He was found guilty of charges including embezzlement, murder and high treason, and was executed by firing squad at Akershus Fortress on 24 October 1945. Some criticised the sentence's legality, since no death sentence had been carried out in Norway since 1876. Nasjonal Samling was wiped out as a political force after 1945. The word quisling, coined by The Times in a leading article of 15 April 1940, became a synonym for traitor in several North European languages.
vidovdan-constitution: The Constitutional Assembly of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes was formed after the election of November 1920. Earlier plans for a constitution had existed, among them the Guidelines, the Corfu Declaration and the Geneva Declaration, but the process of adopting the Vidovdan Constitution exposed major political conflicts in the new state.

The constitution was approved on 28 June 1921, the Serbian Orthodox feast of St Vitus, Vidovdan, which gave it its name. A simple majority sufficed: of 419 representatives, 223 voted for, 35 against and 161 abstained. In favour were the Democratic Party, the People’s Radical Party, the Yugoslav Muslim Organization, the Alliance of Agrarians and Džemijet. The Yugoslav Social-Democratic Party, the Yugoslav Republican Party and Foreign Minister Ante Trumbić voted against. The Croatian Republican Peasant Party boycotted the assembly from the 1920 elections, and the Communist Party, the Slovenian People’s Party, the Croatian People’s Party and the Croatian Union left it.

The kingdom was a constitutional, parliamentary and hereditary monarchy with a unitary system. Legislative power was shared by the king and a unicameral National Assembly. The king could initiate and sanction laws, declare war and conclude peace, appoint judges and dissolve the assembly. Voting rights were limited by a high age threshold and did not extend to women; the constitution promised legislation on women’s suffrage, which was never enacted in the kingdom’s life. The ministers answered to both king and assembly, and the courts were independent.

Alternatives had been offered. The Croatian Republican Peasant Party adopted its own constitution for a neutral peasant republic of Croatia on 1 April 1921, and the Croatian Union proposed a confederation of six entities: Serbia, Croatia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Vojvodina and Slovenia.

On 30 June the People’s Radical Party’s journal Samouprava wrote that this year’s Vidovdan had restored an empire to Serbs. The Communists, persecuted since the Obznana of December 1920, responded with violence: a member of the Pelagićevci faction tried to assassinate the king on 29 June, and on 21 July Interior Minister Milorad Drašković was assassinated, leading to the Law on the Protection of the State in August. The constitution’s viability dominated the 1923 elections. After the 1925 elections Nikola Pašić offered the Croatian Peasant Party a place in the government, which accepted and recognised the constitution, and its leader Stjepan Radić was released from prison. The constitution remained in effect until King Alexander proclaimed his 6 January Dictatorship in 1929.
vidyapati: Vidyapati was born to a Maithil Brahmin family in the village of Bisapi, now Bisfi, in the present-day Madhubani district of northern Bihar. His name means master of knowledge. The exact date of his birth is uncertain, because his own works and those of his patrons give conflicting information. His father, Ganapati Thakkura, was said to be a great devotee of Shiva, and his great-grandfather Devaditya Thakkura had been minister of war and peace at the court of Harisimhadeva. He was a priest at the court of Raya Ganesvara, the reigning chief of Tirhut. He is recorded as having had two wives, three sons and four daughters.

Vidyapati worked in the courts of seven kings and two queens of the Oiniwar dynasty of Mithila. His first commission, from Kirttisimha, produced the Kirtilata, a long praise-poem in verse. Under Devasimha he wrote the prose story collection Bhuparikramana, and he became a close friend of Devasimha's heir Sivasimha. When Sivasimha came to the throne he granted Vidyapati his home village of Bisapi, calling him on the copper plate the new Jayadeva.

In 1406 Sivasimha went missing in a battle with a Muslim army, and Vidyapati and the court took refuge at the court of a king at Rajabanauli, in present-day Nepal. Sivasimha's chief queen, Lakhima Devi, then reigned for twelve years. Later Vidyapati served Padmasimha, writing mainly treatises on law and devotional manuals, and by about 1430 he had returned to Bisapi.

Vidyapati wrote in Sanskrit, Prakrit, Avahattha and Maithili. Between 1380 and 1406 he composed some five hundred love songs on Radha and Krishna in Maithili, a language that had not been used as a literary medium before him. They continued the tradition of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, but each song stands alone, and he preferred Radha's point of view to Krishna's. Court singers performed them, and they spread beyond the court. Although he wrote of Krishna, he was not a special devotee of Vishnu: he gave most attention to Shiva and Durga, and he is known for songs of Shiva and Parvati and for the Gosaunik Geet Jai Jai Bhairavi, sung at auspicious ceremonies in Mithila.

Bengali Vaishnavas such as Chaitanya and Chandidas adopted his Radha and Krishna songs as hymns, and the literary language Brajabuli developed from Maithili in the sixteenth century. Rabindranath Tagore imitated it in his Bhanusingha Thakurer Padabali of 1884. His influence has been compared to that of Dante in Italy and Chaucer in England. In Mithila his love songs are still sung at weddings.
vidyaranya: Vidyaranya's dates are unclear. Jackson places his birth between 1280 and 1285, while the records of the Sringeri Sharada Peetham give c. 1296 at Ekasila Nagara, present-day Warangal. He is thought to have been named Madhava before he was ordained a sannyasin, and he is usually identified with Madhavacharya. The Sringeri accounts make him the elder brother of Bharati Tirtha, his predecessor at Sringeri, and some sources even hold that the two were one person, though the Sringeri records treat them as two. Other accounts identify him with Madhava, brother of the Mimamsa scholar Sayana and a minister of the Vijayanagara Empire.

Epigraphic evidence shows that he headed the Sringeri matha from at least 1374 or 1375, succeeding Bharatitirtha, until his death in 1386, and the first genuine inscription naming him is dated 25 October 1375. According to tradition he helped found the Vijayanagara Empire about 1336, converting Harihara I and Bukka I back to the Hindu faith and serving them and Harihara II as minister.

Studies by Filliozat, Kulke and Wagoner conclude that he had no part in it: the texts telling the story date from the 16th and 17th centuries, the earliest inscriptions are silent, and his political role may come from confusion with Madhavamatrin, a minister of the Sangama brother Mallapa I. In his time the matha gained far more land and royal patronage, and Vidyaranya helped establish Shankara as a symbol of Advaita Vedanta and spread its monasteries, competing for royal favour with Srivaisnava groups.

The Pañcadaśī, his standard work on Advaita, has fifteen chapters in three sections called Viveka, Deepa and Ananda, and treats the five sheaths of the self and the relation of God, world and individual. The Jivanmuktiviveka, composed c. 1380, adds yogic disciplines from the Bhagavad Gita and Patanjali's Yoga Sutras to Shankara's path of knowledge. The Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, a survey of sixteen schools ascending towards Advaita, is often attributed to him as Madhava, though it may have been written by Cannibhatta.
vidzeme: Vidzeme is one of the Historical Latvian Lands. Its name means the Middle Land, and in Old Latvian orthography it was written Widda-semme. It lies in north-central Latvia, north of the Daugava River, with the Latvian capital Riga in its south-western part. In German it was sometimes called Livland, from the Latin Livonia. Most of its inhabitants are Latvians, and it is the most ethnically Latvian region of the country.

In ancient times the territory was inhabited by Latgalians and by Livs, who lived near the coast of the Gulf of Riga and along the lower Daugava and Gauja rivers. Until the German conquest of the 13th century the Daugava marked the boundary between the lands of the Livs and Latgalians on its right bank and those of the Semigallians and Selonians on its left. The most notable Latgalian region in today's Vidzeme was Tālava.

After the Livonian War, part of the Livonian Confederation on the right bank of the Daugava and the Patrimony of Riga passed to the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth as the Duchy of Livonia. Sweden invaded the region in 1600, 1617 and 1621. After the Truce of Altmark in 1629 Sweden acquired the western part of the Duchy of Livonia, roughly as far as the Aiviekste River, which has since formed Vidzeme's eastern border. Russia conquered Swedish Livonia in the Great Northern War and received it at the Treaty of Nystad in 1721. It created the Riga Governorate, renamed the Governorate of Livonia in 1796, which the local German Baltic nobility administered autonomously through a feudal Landtag.

After World War I the governorate was split between the newly independent Latvia and Estonia. The Soviet Union occupied Vidzeme from 1940, and Nazi Germany from 1941 to 1944. With the dissolution of the Soviet Union it became part of independent Latvia once more. Vidzeme is not an administrative unit, but Latvian law defines its territory by municipalities, among them Cēsis, Sigulda, Valmiera and Riga.
vienna: Vienna lies in north-eastern Austria at the easternmost extension of the Alps, on the eastern edge of the Vienna Woods and at the transition to the Pannonian Basin. The earliest settlement, on the site of the inner city, lay south of the meandering Danube, and the city now spans both banks. It is both a city and one of the nine states of Austria. The name is a Latinised form of the German Wien, which comes from the River Wien and first appears in the Salzburg Annals, recording a battle at a place called Wenia in 881.

In the 1st century the Romans set up the military camp of Vindobona, in the province of Pannonia, near the Danube to secure the frontier. Construction of the legionary camp began around 97 CE, and the settlement at its peak had about 15,000 people. The emperor Marcus Aurelius may have died here in 180. The city was rebuilt after a Germanic invasion and served as a seat of Roman government until the fifth century, when its people fled the Huns and the site was abandoned for several centuries.

In 1155 Vienna became the seat of the Babenbergs, who ruled Austria from 976 to 1246, and in 1221 it was granted city rights. In the 16th century the Habsburgs made it the seat of the emperors of the Holy Roman Empire, which it remained until the empire's dissolution in 1806, with only a brief interruption. With the formation of the Austrian Empire in 1804 it became the capital of that empire and of all its successor states.

As capital of Austria-Hungary from 1867 to 1918 it grew sharply, and in 1910 it had more than two million inhabitants and was the third-largest city in Europe after London and Paris. Under the Nazi regime 65,000 Jews were deported from Vienna and murdered, and about 130,000 fled.

Vienna is the capital and most populous city of Austria, with just over two million inhabitants. The historic centre was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001 and includes Baroque palaces and gardens and the Ringstrasse of the late 19th century. Beethoven, Haydn, Mozart, Schubert and Brahms were among the composers who worked there, and Sigmund Freud, the first psychoanalyst, lived there too. Since 1980 the city has been a United Nations headquarters city.
vienna-general-hospital: The hospital grew out of a poorhouse. In 1686, after the second Siege of Vienna, Dr. Johann Franckh donated property for a military hospital, and in 1693 Emperor Leopold I arranged the building of a large hospital, whose first ward, finished in 1697, housed 1,042 people. By 1724 it held 1,740, and the will of Ferdinand Baron von Thavonat, who left his estate to disabled soldiers in 1726, paid for its extension. When Emperor Joseph II visited on 28 January 1783, he found that it served people with connections more than the neediest. Professor Joseph Quarin, later its director, used a general hospital plan, and the new hospital opened on 16 August 1784.

A maternity ward, an orphanage and a lunatic asylum were attached to it. The Narrenturm, built in 1784 by Isidore Canevale, was the first building anywhere made to house mental patients: a five-part circular fortress with slit windows for 200 to 250 patients, known in Vienna as the Gugelhupf after its round shape, and today the seat of the Federal Pathological-Anatomical Museum. In the 19th century the hospital was the centre of the Viennese Medical School, where Ignaz Semmelweis made his observations on hygiene and Karl Landsteiner discovered the blood groups.

A synagogue for Jewish patients, built in 1903 by Max Fleischer, was devastated on Kristallnacht in 1938, after the Anschluss, and its remains became the Marpe Lanefesch Memorial in 2005. In 1939 the hospital was transferred to municipal administration.

In 1957 it was decided to build a new central hospital about half a kilometre from the old site. Work began in the summer of 1964, and the main building with two 22-storey bed towers holding 2,200 beds was officially opened in 1994. Costs rose from a projected 1 billion Schilling to about 4.5 billion euro in 2004 values, and with a bribery affair led to the AKH scandal, the largest building scandal in Austria. The old buildings now serve as a campus of the University of Vienna, and the new hospital is the city's university hospital and the site of the Medical University of Vienna.
vienna-secession: The Vienna Secession, also called the Union of Austrian Artists, was founded on 3 April 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann, Joseph Maria Olbrich and others, who resigned from the Association of Austrian Artists, the Künstlerhaus, in protest against its support for traditional styles. Otto Wagner joined shortly afterwards. The name came from the Munich Secession of 1892. Its stated aims included contact with artists outside Austria, opposition to artistic nationalism, renewal of the decorative arts and a Gesamtkunstwerk, a total art uniting painting, architecture and the decorative arts. The group began with fifty members and elected Klimt its president, with Rudolf von Alt, aged eighty-five, as honorary president.

Olbrich's domed exhibition building of 1897 to 1898, with a frieze over the entrance, became the symbol of the movement and was the first dedicated gallery of contemporary art in Vienna. Between 1899 and 1903 it showed works by Monet, Degas, Renoir and other French artists. The 14th exhibition in 1902, designed by Hoffmann, was dedicated to Beethoven, with a statue by Max Klinger and Klimt's Beethoven Frieze. The group's magazine was Ver Sacrum.

Disputes arose after Hoffmann and Moser founded the Wiener Werkstätte in 1903. Members divided between those who put painting first and those who wanted equal treatment for the decorative arts. When a proposal to buy the Galerie Miethke was lost by one vote, Klimt, Hoffmann, Moser and others resigned on 14 June 1905, and Klimt formed the Kunstschau in 1906.

The Secession continued to hold exhibitions after 1905. Its building was destroyed under the Nazi regime as a symbol of degenerate art and rebuilt after the Second World War; Hoffmann rejoined in 1945 and was president from 1948 to 1950. Wagner's later work, such as the Austrian Postal Savings Bank of 1903 to 1906, and Hoffmann's Stoclet Palace in Brussels moved away from floral Art Nouveau towards geometric forms and the beginnings of modernism. Art Nouveau is named after the Vienna Secession in several languages of the former Austro-Hungary, such as Polish secesja and Czech secese, and the movement influenced Młoda Polska.
viet-cong: Viet Cong is a contraction of Việt Nam cộng sản, meaning Vietnamese communist, a term that acquired a derogatory sense by the late 1940s. After the Geneva Accords of 1954 about 90,000 Viet Minh were evacuated to the North, while 5,000 to 10,000 cadres stayed in the South. Ngo Dinh Diem announced in July 1955 that the election on reunification would not be held, and within a few months his campaign had driven the communists into remote swamps. An assassination campaign began in April 1957.

The Communist Party of Vietnam approved a people's war on the South in January 1959, and Group 559 was set up in May to maintain the Ho Chi Minh trail. The National Liberation Front was created on 20 December 1960 at Tân Lập village in Tây Ninh Province as a united front meant to draw in non-communists. Many core members were southern Viet Minh regroupees trained in the North.

The movement grew quickly: an estimated 300,000 members were enrolled in affiliated associations by early 1962, and its first victory over South Vietnamese forces came at Ấp Bắc in January 1963. It used guerrilla and regular units together with a network of cadres. It also used terror as a standard tactic, and death squads killed at least 37,000 civilians, according to the data available, which mostly cover 1967 to 1972.

In January and February 1968 some 80,000 fighters struck more than 100 towns in the Tet Offensive, including a raid on the United States embassy in Saigon and a massacre of about 3,500 residents at Huế. The hoped-for uprising did not come, and the offensive cost the movement heavily; Trần Văn Trà said about 75,000 were killed or wounded. In June 1969 the front and an urban alliance were merged into the Provisional Revolutionary Government.

After the fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 the Provisional Revolutionary Government moved into government offices, but authority over the South was given to the People's Army of Vietnam. People tainted by association with the old government were sent to re-education camps despite protests from non-communist members. The front and the alliance were later merged into the Vietnam Fatherland Front.

Its character was disputed. Opponents of American involvement said it was an insurgency native to the South, with chairman Nguyễn Hữu Thọ not a communist. Anti-communists said it was a front for Hanoi, and Trà's memoirs record that he followed orders from the party's military commission in Hanoi.
viet-minh: The Viet Minh, officially the League for Independence of Vietnam, was founded on 19 May 1941 at Pác Bó in Cao Bằng province by Ho Chi Minh. The Indochinese Communist Party set it up as a united front to achieve independence, the first step in a communist revolutionary project, and presented it as a broad coalition. Võ Nguyên Giáp commanded its military side, and Lê Duẩn and Phạm Văn Đồng were among the other founders. Non-communists also joined, including the Democratic Party and the Socialist Party, as did most Buddhists. Many Catholics, Cao Đài and Hòa Hảo followers first supported it but later split.

During the Second World War the Viet Minh fought the Japanese occupiers with support from the Republic of China and later the American Office of Strategic Services. At the end of 1944 it claimed 500,000 members. After the collapse of Japanese authority and the abdication of Emperor Bảo Đại, Ho Chi Minh proclaimed the Democratic Republic of Vietnam on 2 September 1945. French and British forces attacked in the south from 23 September, and talks with France broke down in December 1946, leading to nearly ten years of war.

The French pushed the Viet Minh out of Hanoi, but their encirclement of the Việt Bắc base in late 1947 failed to defeat it. In 1950 the newly communist People's Republic of China provided bases and heavy weapons, and the Viet Minh took control of many rural areas. On 7 March 1951 it merged with the National United League of Vietnam to form the Vietnamese United Front, which people still called the Viet Minh.

After its victory at Điện Biên Phủ, France entered negotiations, and the Geneva Conference divided Vietnam at the 17th Parallel, with the Viet Minh army withdrawing to the North. Civil administration of North Vietnam passed to it on 11 October 1954, and Ho Chi Minh became prime minister. The promised unification elections of 1956 never took place, and Viet Minh cadres left in the South later took up an insurgency.

The United Front became the Vietnam Fatherland Front on 10 September 1955, today regarded as the modern incarnation of the Viet Minh. Its Vietnam Liberation Army, founded in 1944, is today the People's Army of Vietnam. Cambodian and Laotian movements, among them the Khmer Việt Minh and the Pathet Lao, received training and support from it.
viet-nam-quoc-dan-dang: In late 1925 a group of young Hanoi intellectuals led by the teacher Phạm Tuấn Tài and his brother Phạm Tuấn Lâm founded the Nam Đồng thư xã, a publishing house that printed works on Sun Yat-sen and the 1911 Revolution and ran a free school teaching the Vietnamese alphabet to workers. French harassment and censorship ruined it, and by the autumn of 1927 the group turned to direct political action. The party was formed at a meeting in Hanoi on 25 December 1927, three years before the Indochinese Communist Party. It advocated democratic socialism and aimed to overthrow the colonial system by force and set up a democratic republic.

French intelligence estimated that by early 1929 it had about 1,500 members in 120 cells, mostly students, minor merchants and low-level officials around the Red River Delta. After the labour recruiter Hervé Bazin was shot on 9 February 1929, the French blamed the party and rounded up between three and four hundred men; 78 were sentenced to five to twenty years. Học then argued for a general uprising. Early on 10 February 1930 about 40 soldiers of the Fourth Régiment de Tirailleurs Tonkinois at Yên Bái, with around 60 party civilians, attacked their French officers, killing five, but the remaining 550 Vietnamese soldiers helped put the mutiny down within hours.

Survivors fled to Yunnan, where the party worked as a section of the Chinese Kuomintang. After Japan's surrender in 1945 it briefly joined Ho Chi Minh's Viet Minh, but from 1946 the Viet Minh drove it from the Red River Delta and massacred thousands of its members and other nationalists.

After the Geneva Accords of 1954 most members moved south during Operation Passage to Freedom. Divided and without strong leadership, the party was repressed by President Ngô Đình Diệm, who imprisoned many members; officers linked to it took part in the failed paratrooper revolt of November 1960. The party remained in South Vietnam until the Fall of Saigon in 1975, and today it survives only among overseas Vietnamese.
vietnam: Vietnam lies on the eastern Indochinese Peninsula, with a total area of about 331,000 square kilometres, a coastline 3,444 kilometres long and land boundaries of 4,639 kilometres. At its narrowest point, in Quảng Trị province, it is as little as 50 kilometres across, and in the north it widens to around 600 kilometres.

The land is mostly hilly and densely forested, with level land covering no more than 20%. The Red River flows past Hanoi into the Gulf of Tonkin, and its delta, a plain of 15,000 square kilometres, has the highest population density of any region; its sediment advances the delta 60 to 80 metres into the South China Sea every year.

Humans lived in what is now Vietnam as early as the Paleolithic, and Homo erectus fossils dating to around 500,000 BCE have been found in caves in the north. By about 1,000 BCE wet-rice cultivation in the Ma River and Red River floodplains led to the Đông Sơn culture, known for its bronze casting and elaborate bronze drums.

Vietnamese legends hold that the Hồng Bàng dynasty of the Hùng kings, first established in 2879 BCE, was the first state, known as Văn Lang. In 257 BCE the last Hùng king was defeated by Thục Phán, who formed Âu Lạc and proclaimed himself An Dương Vương. The Han dynasty annexed northern and central Vietnam, which were then under Chinese rule from 111 BCE until the first dynasty emerged in 939.

Successive monarchical dynasties absorbed Chinese influences through Confucianism and Buddhism and expanded southward to the Mekong Delta, conquering Champa. During most of the 17th and 18th centuries Vietnam was effectively divided into two domains, Đàng Trong and Đàng Ngoài. The Nguyễn, the last imperial dynasty, surrendered to France in 1883, and in 1887 the territory was integrated into French Indochina as three separate regions. The Viet Minh launched the August Revolution and declared independence in 1945. France returned and was defeated in the First Indochina War in 1954, after which Vietnam was divided into two parts.

The Vietnam War was fought between communist North Vietnam, supported by the Soviet Union and China, and anti-communist South Vietnam, supported by the United States. After the North Vietnamese victory in 1975 the country reunified as a communist state under the Communist Party of Vietnam. An ineffective planned economy, a Western trade embargo and wars with Cambodia and China crippled it further, and in 1986 the party launched the Đổi Mới reforms toward a socialist-oriented market economy. Vietnam joined the World Trade Organization in 2007. Its population was 96,208,984 in the 2019 census; the Kinh make up 85.32% of it, and 54 ethnic groups are officially recognised.
vietnam-war: Vietnam had been under French control as part of French Indochina since the 1880s. After the French defeat in the First Indochina War, Vietnam's independence was affirmed at the 1954 Geneva Conference, which divided the country at the 17th parallel. The communists under Ho Chi Minh took power in North Vietnam, while an anticommunist regime under Ngô Đình Diệm took control of South Vietnam with United States backing. The North Vietnamese supplied and eventually directed the Viet Cong, a communist front in the south that intensified a guerrilla war from 1957. The war was at once a postcolonial war of national liberation, a theatre of the Cold War and a civil war. In 1963 Diệm was killed in a US-backed military coup.

After the Gulf of Tonkin incident of August 1964, the US Congress passed a resolution that gave President Lyndon B. Johnson authority to increase the military presence without declaring war. On 8 March 1965, 3,500 US Marines landed near Da Nang, the start of the ground war, and deployment rose to 536,000 by 1969. The Tet Offensive of 1968 was a tactical defeat for the communists but contributed to growing American opposition to the war. Richard Nixon began Vietnamization from 1969, in which an expanded South Vietnamese army took over the fighting as US forces withdrew. Fighting spilled into Laos and Cambodia.

After the Paris Peace Accords of 1973 the last American forces left, but fighting continued. In March 1975 North Vietnamese forces opened an offensive in the Central Highlands, and the South Vietnamese army collapsed. Saigon fell on 30 April 1975, after the largest helicopter evacuation in history, Operation Frequent Wind.

North and South Vietnam were merged in July 1976 as the Socialist Republic of Vietnam. Estimates of the dead vary widely. About 58,220 US service members died, and estimates run from 275,000 to 310,000 Cambodians and 20,000 to 62,000 Laotians. The war was marked by atrocities, among them the massacres at Huế and Mỹ Lai, and some 20 percent of South Vietnam's jungle was sprayed with toxic herbicides, which led to significant health problems. Political repression and flawed economic policies after the war precipitated the flight of the Vietnamese boat people, of whom about 250,000 perished at sea. In the United States the war gave rise to Vietnam syndrome, an aversion to overseas military involvement.
vietnamese-alphabet: For centuries before the Latin script, Vietnam used Literary Chinese for government papers, scholarship and scripture. Indigenous writing with Chinese characters began around the ninth century, and from the 12th century some Vietnamese words were written in chữ Nôm, which supplemented Chinese characters with characters invented from Chinese radicals.

The Latin script began with Jesuit missionaries. From as early as 1620, Francisco de Pina and other missionaries used it to transcribe Vietnamese as an aid to learning the language. Alexandre de Rhodes continued the work and, building on earlier dictionaries by Gaspar do Amaral and António Barbosa, compiled a Vietnamese–Portuguese–Latin dictionary, printed in Rome in 1651. Its spelling is largely derived from Portuguese, with some French influence, while the use of gh and gi came from Italian.

The modern alphabet has 29 letters, including seven that carry diacritics: ă, â, ê, ô, ơ, ư and đ. Five further marks show tone. Vietnamese has six tones in the standard northern dialect, one of them unmarked, and the marks are placed on the vowel. In the south the hỏi and ngã tones have merged, leaving five.

Because the spelling was fixed centuries ago and the spoken language has changed, the match between letters and sounds is somewhat complicated: one letter can stand for several sounds, and different letters for the same sound. The letters i and y, for example, are mostly equivalent, and efforts since the late 20th century to standardise their use, including a decision by the Ministry of Education in 1984, have had limited effect.

For about 200 years the script was used within the Catholic community, where texts in chữ Nôm remained more widespread. In 1910 the French colonial administration enforced it. Historians stress other causes too: the Nguyễn emperors promoted it, and an imperial decree of Emperor Thành Thái in 1906 let parents choose between a curriculum in Literary Chinese and one in the Latin script. The historian Liam Kelley argues that neither the French nor the revolutionaries could have spread it to village level alone.

The French abolished the Confucian examination system in 1917 and set up schools that taught Vietnamese in the script, with hundreds of thousands of primary textbooks. Since the 1920s most Vietnamese have used it. Historian Pamela A. Pears argues that it cut Vietnamese readers off from traditional Hán Nôm literature.
vietnamese-fatherland-front: The Front stands in a line of Vietnamese popular fronts. The Anti-Imperialist Alliance was founded on 18 November 1930, and Hồ Chí Minh founded the League for the Independence of Vietnam, the Viet Minh, on 19 May 1941. The Vietnamese National Popular League, or Liên Việt, followed on 29 May 1946, and in 1951 it merged with the Viet Minh as the Vietnamese National Popular Front under Tôn Đức Thắng. In 1955 the Vietnam Fatherland Front replaced it in the North, again with Tôn Đức Thắng as chairman.

In the South the National Liberation Front of South Vietnam was founded on 20 December 1960 under Nguyễn Hữu Thọ, and the Alliance of National, Democratic and Peace Forces on 20 April 1968 under Trịnh Đình Thảo. In February 1977, after reunification, the northern Front merged with these two southern fronts. The new Front brought together many smaller groups, including the Communist Party of Vietnam itself, the Vietnam General Confederation of Labour, the Ho Chi Minh Communist Youth Union and the Ho Chi Minh Young Pioneer Organization.

The Democratic Party of Vietnam, founded in 1944, and the Socialist Party of Vietnam, founded in 1946, were members until both were dissolved in 1988. The first chairman of the merged Front was Hoàng Quốc Việt, from 1977 to 1983, followed by Huỳnh Tấn Phát and then, from 1988 to 1994, Nguyễn Hữu Thọ, the former head of the National Liberation Front.

The constitution makes the Front an integral part of the political structure of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, and both the constitution and the laws give it a special role. It is meant to supervise the work of the government and its organisations, and because its base is mass participation and popular mobilisation it is presented as representative of the people. Some of the government's social programmes, among them poverty reduction, are carried out through the Front, which is also responsible for much of the state's policy on religion. It is led by a chairman and a secretary general.
vijay-stambha: Rana Kumbha raised the tower in 1448 after his army defeated the forces of the Sultanate of Malwa under Mahmud Khilji at the Battle of Sarangpur. Mahmud Khilji was held prisoner at Chittor for six months and then released for a ransom. Before the tower was finished the Rana also had to face the combined forces of Gujarat and Malwa, and these victories are recorded in inscriptions on the building. The tower stands within Chittor Fort in Chittorgarh, in present-day Rajasthan. The name of the architect, Sutradhar Jaita, and of his three sons who assisted him, Napa, Puja and Poma, are carved on the fifth floor.

The column is one hundred and twenty feet high. Each face measures thirty-five feet across at the base and seventeen and a half feet at the summit, just below the cupola, and the tower stands on a terrace forty-two feet square. Each of its nine storeys has openings on every face, and every doorway has a colonnaded portico. Inscribed slabs in the uppermost storey give a detailed genealogy of the rulers of Chittor and their deeds; they are ascribed to Atri, a scholar at Rana Kumbha's court, and his son Mahesh. Although the tower is dedicated to Vishnu, its top storey also carries an image of the Jain goddess Padmavati, a sign of the religious pluralism of its Rajput builders.

Colonel James Tod considered the tower one of the finest examples of Hindu Rajput architecture and judged it superior to the Qutub Minar. India Post has issued commemorative postage stamps showing the monument.
vijaya-champa: Vijaya, Sanskrit for victorious and also called Vijayapura, lay in the lowlands along the lower Côn River, in the south of what is now Bình Định Province, at modern An Nhơn. Near the river's estuary a well-protected harbour gave rise to Thị Nại, one of Champa's main ports, while the river into the western highlands carried trade with the hill peoples, who supplied luxury goods such as eaglewood for export. One of the larger rivers of Champa also made its soils more fertile than those of many other places.

The area was probably one of the earliest landfalls of the Cham people in what is now Vietnam, but its buildings suggest that it rose to importance only in the 11th or 12th century, and the earliest mention of Vijaya as a Cham city dates from about 1153 to 1184. In the 12th and 13th centuries it was drawn into wars with Angkor: Suryavarman II subdued it in 1145 and deposed Jaya Indravarman III, though the Khmer were defeated in 1149, and Jayavarman VII at times dominated the city.

A Yuan army under the Mongol commander Sogetu took Vijaya early in 1283; the Mongols were driven out, but the city was sacked. A Vietnamese army besieged it without success in the Battle of Vijaya in 1377, and in 1403 Vietnamese troops besieged the citadel for a month before a lack of food forced them back. The final attack in early 1471 came after almost 70 years without major fighting, and it is read as a response to Champa's request for Chinese help against Đại Việt. Vijaya was destroyed, while the southern principalities kept a status like that of a protectorate.

Unlike most Cham buildings, which used brick alone, Vijaya's combined stone and brick, which suggests influence from Angkor and a larger supply of labour. Its style was long dominant, and Cham architecture of the 12th to 14th centuries is classed as the Bình Định style. Many of its towers survive, among them the Cánh Tiên tower in the ruined citadel and the Dương Long towers, and the ruins of the Tây Sơn era Hoang De citadel lie within the old walls.
vijayalaya-chola: The ancient Chola kingdom, known from Tamil literature and from Greek merchants and geographers, faded after about 300 CE, a decline attributed to the invasion of the Kalabhras. The Cholas held on to their old capital of Uraiyur, while a branch ruled in the Telugu lands as chieftains of the Pallavas, the Telugu Chodas. Historians long could not trace Vijayalaya's ancestry. The Anbil and Velanjeri plates name a Sri Kantha before him, and the Velanjeri inscription calls his father Ottriyuran, read by some scholars as a title meaning lord of Thiruottriyur, near modern Chennai.

Around the middle of the 9th century the Pallavas and the Pandyas were fighting for supremacy in southern India. Vijayalaya used the opportunity to rise out of obscurity and take Thanjavur from Elango Mutharaiyar, the last ruler of the Mutharaiyar dynasty, with the help of a Muttaraiyar lieutenant, Sattan Paliyilli. He ruled the region north of the river Kaveri, and it is said that in 852 he fought and defeated the Pandyas.

His rise alarmed the Pallava king Nandivarman III, who called on the Pandyan king Varagunavarman II, then his subordinate ally, to suppress him. Varaguna led an expedition into the Chola country and reached the north bank of the Kaveri near Thanjavur. Vijayalaya, by then old and an invalid, lost his kingdom to the Pandyas and became a tax-paying king under them, though the Cholas who came after him conquered the Pandya kingdom.

The Tiruvalangadu plates record that Vijayalaya made Thanjavur his capital and built there a temple to the goddess Nisumbhasudani, a form of Durga, and the Kanyakumari inscription says that he renovated the city. A Solesvara temple at Narttamalai in Pudukkottai is also attributed to him. He took the title Parakēcarivarmaṉ, great son who is a lion to his enemies, and the Chola kings after him used the title Parakēcari. He was succeeded by his son Aditya Chola I, who laid the foundation of the imperial Chola state.
vijayanagara-empire: Before the empire's rise, the Seunas of Devagiri, the Kakatiya dynasty of Warangal, the Pandyan Empire of Madurai and the Hoysalas of Belur had all been raided or annexed by the Delhi Sultanate under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq. The short-lived Kampili kingdom in the Tungabhadra basin fell to Tughluq forces around 1327 to 1328. The brothers Harihara I and Bukka Raya I of the Sangama dynasty founded the kingdom in 1336. By 1374 Bukka Raya I had defeated the chiefdom of Arcot, the Reddys of Kondavidu and the Sultan of Madurai, and held Goa and the Tungabhadra-Krishna doab.

The empire reached its peak under Krishna Deva Raya (1509 to 1529), who took Raichur in 1520 and Gulbarga from the Deccan sultanates and won the Kalinga region from the Gajapatis of Odisha. After the death of Achyuta Deva Raya in June 1542, the regent Salakaraju Tirumala seized power, had the boy Venkata I killed and invited the Sultan of Bijapur to sit on the throne symbolically. The nobility's anger began a civil war in 1542 to 1543. In January 1565 the united Deccan sultanates defeated Rama Raya's army at the Battle of Talikota, though the empire lasted until 1646.

The emperor was assisted by a cabinet of ministers headed by a prime minister, the Mahapradhana, and all high officers had military training. The economy rested on agriculture: cotton fed a large textile industry, betel, areca and coconut were the chief cash crops, and spices came from the Malnad hills. The capital was a centre of trade in gems and gold, and temple building employed thousands of masons and sculptors.

The founders were devout Shaivas who also made grants to Vishnu temples, and the later Saluva and Tuluva kings were Vaishnava by faith. Visitors recorded that the emperors tolerated all religions. Administration and court used Kannada, while Telugu gained literary prominence under the last emperors, especially Krishnadevaraya. At the Mahanavami festival the king received gifts and tribute from subordinate rulers and reviewed their armies on the last day.

The capital's ruins near modern Hampi are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Vijayanagara architecture combined Chalukya, Hoysala, Pandya and Chola forms, with tall gateway towers called rajagopurams and pillared halls, built in hard local granite. Carnatic music took its classical structure in this era. The Mahanavami ceremonies passed to successor states, and Raja Wodeyar I held Dasara at Srirangapatna in 1610, from which the modern Mysore Dasara developed. Knowledge of the empire rests on inscriptions, excavations and the accounts of visitors such as Domingo Paes, Fernão Nunes, Niccolò de' Conti and Abdul Razzaq.
vijayawada: Vijayawada lies on the banks of the Krishna River at an altitude of 11 m (36 ft) above sea level, flanked by the Eastern Ghats and the Indrakeeladri Hills. Three canals that leave the north side of the reservoir behind the Prakasam Barrage, the Eluru, Bandar and Ryves canals, flow through the city. The climate is tropical wet and dry, with the hottest weather in May and the coolest in January, and rain from both the south-west and north-east monsoons.

The name is explained by several legends. In one, the goddess Durga killed the demon Mahishasura and rested here, so that the place became the land of victory, from vijaya, victory, and wada, place. In another, the hero Arjuna of the Mahabharata prayed on the Indrakeeladri hill and received the weapon Pashupatastra from Shiva; one of Arjuna's names is Vijaya. The place was called Vijayavatika before it became Vijayawada.

Bezawada, as the city was then known, is said to have been founded around 626 CE by the Paricchedi kings, and it was ruled by Madhava Varma, one of the kings of the Vishnukundina dynasty. The Chinese Buddhist scholar Xuanzang stayed there for a few years around 640 CE to copy and study the Abhidhamma Pitaka, the last of the three baskets of the Pali canon, the scriptures of Theravada Buddhism.

The Mogalrajapuram hills hold five rock-cut temples built between the fourth and ninth centuries, and some of the caves can be attributed to the Vishnukundina dynasty. The Akkana Madanna Caves at the foot of Indrakeeladri Hill are a monument of national importance. In the modern period the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation was constituted on 1 April 1888, the same year the Vijayawada Junction railway station was established, and a line to Hyderabad was laid in 1889. Andhra Cements, founded in 1937, was the first cement factory in Andhra Pradesh.

Vijayawada is the second most populous city of Andhra Pradesh, with 1,021,806 people at the 2011 census, most of them Telugu speakers and Hindus, with Muslim, Christian and Jain minorities. It is a trading centre, notable for the mango market at Nunna, and an important rail and road junction. Its Hindu festivals include Durga Pooja and a boat festival, the Theppotsavam, on the Krishna during Dussera, centred on the Kanaka Durga Temple on Indrakeeladri hill. Kondapalli toys, handmade wooden toys from a suburb of the city, received a geographical indication in 2007.
viking-age: Many theories are put forward for the Viking expansion, and the will to explore likely played a major role. England, Wales and Ireland were divided into warring kingdoms and vulnerable, while the Franks were well defended. Overpopulation is one proposed cause, though some scholars reject it. Others point to growing urbanism and trade, as wealth moving along the routes of the expanding Islamic world drew Scandinavians to rich towns such as the wich towns of Anglo-Saxon England. Political centralisation in Scandinavia, especially in Norway, may have pushed people out, and advances in sailing, including larger sails, tacking and round-the-clock voyages, made distant targets possible.

The best-known beginning is the attack of 8 June 793 that destroyed the abbey on Lindisfarne, though Judith Jesch has argued that the age began between 700 and 750, since earlier contacts are likely. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle also records three Norwegian boats landing at Portland in 789.

Voyaging from Denmark, Norway and Sweden, Norse people settled in the British Isles, Ireland, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy and the Baltic coast, and briefly in Newfoundland. In the east they travelled along the Dnieper and Volga routes, where they were known as Varangians. They raided Iona in 794 and monasteries in Gaelic Ireland from 795, and from 840 built fortified camps called longphorts, the first at Dublin and Linn Duachaill. Their kingdoms and earldoms included the Kingdom of the Isles, Orkney, York, the Danelaw, Dublin, Normandy and Kievan Rus'.

In 844 a fleet appeared at the mouth of the Tagus, and in 959 an expedition under Björn Ironside and Hásteinn burned the mosque at Seville. In the 11th century the Norse homelands were unified into larger kingdoms.

Most of the age was pagan, and Scandinavia was Christianised towards its later part, with early centres in Denmark. Longships and the broader knarr, used for trade, gave the Norse a formidable reputation. Important trading ports included Ribe, Hedeby, Kaupang, Birka and Dublin.

The Icelandic sagas are seen as characteristic works of the time, and Old Norse shaped later languages. More than a thousand Old Norse words entered Standard English, among them sky, skin, window, law and sister, and many place names in eastern and north-eastern England are Danish.
vikings: The Viking Age is taken to run from the earliest recorded raid by Norsemen in 793 to the Norman conquest of England in 1066. In England it began on 8 June 793, when Norsemen destroyed the abbey on the island of Lindisfarne. The Northumbrian scholar Alcuin of York declared that never before had such an atrocity been seen, and medieval Christians could find no explanation for the suffering save the wrath of God.

The Vikings raided, traded, acted as mercenaries and settled over a wide area. Early raiders probably returned home, but later Vikings settled in the British Isles, the Faroe Islands, Iceland, Greenland, Normandy and the Baltic coast, and along the Dnieper and Volga routes, where they were known as Varangians. Vikings under Leif Erikson reached North America and set up short-lived settlements at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland. Two Vikings ruled England: Sweyn Forkbeard claimed the throne from 1013 to 1014, and his son Cnut the Great was king from 1016 to 1035. By the late 11th century the Church was legitimising royal dynasties, and the three kingdoms of Denmark, Norway and Sweden were taking shape.

Viking society was divided into thralls, karls and jarls, a structure described in the Eddic poem Rígsþula and confirmed by archaeology. Most Vikings were farmers, fishermen, craftsmen and traders. They spoke Old Norse and wrote inscriptions in runes, usually short and formulaic, so most contemporary written sources come from Christian and Islamic communities outside Scandinavia, often by authors who had suffered from Viking activity. They followed the Old Norse religion for most of the period and became Christians over the 8th to 12th centuries.

Their longships had a long, narrow hull and shallow draught, with oars to complement the sail, which let crews land in shallow water. Scandinavia used little coinage outside trading centres such as Ribe and Hedeby, so exchange rested on the weight and purity of silver, measured with small portable scales.

The Vikings influenced Old English, and so Modern English. The Normans descended from Vikings given overlordship of the Duchy of Normandy in the 10th century. Not until the 1890s did scholars outside Scandinavia begin to reassess Viking artistry, technology and seamanship. There is no evidence that Viking warriors wore horned helmets, a costume element that first appeared in the 19th century.
vikram-samvat: According to popular tradition, King Vikramaditya of Ujjain established the era after defeating the Śakas. The Jain text Kalakacharya Kathanaka tells that King Gandharvasena of Ujjain abducted a nun, Sarasvati, sister of the monk Kalakacharya. The monk sought help from the Śaka ruler in Sistan, who defeated Gandharvasena. The defeated king's son Vikramaditya later drove the Śakas from Ujjain and began a new era to mark the event. Colonial scholarship accepted this theory, but later inscriptions and study suggest it has no historical basis.

The era beginning in 57 BCE was first known by other names: Krita in inscriptions of 343 and 371, the era of the Malava tribe in 424, or simply Samvat. The earliest inscription calling it Vikrama is from 842, found at Dholpur and dated 20 April 842. The earliest to link it with a king named Vikramaditya dates from 971. Some authors hold that Vikramaditya was a figure of tradition or a title taken by a later king, such as Chandragupta II or Yashodharman, who renamed the era.

Vikram Samvat is lunisolar, like the Hebrew and Chinese calendars. A common lunar year has 354 days, and a leap month, the adhika masa, is added roughly seven times every 19 years so that festivals and crop rituals stay in season. Each month has two fortnights: the waxing, bright shukla paksha and the waning, dark krishna paksha. Days are counted in tithis, each the time the angle between the Moon and the Sun grows by 12 degrees. The year count is usually 57 ahead of the Gregorian one, and 56 ahead from January to March or April.

Hindus, Sikhs and Pashtuns have used the calendar. In north India the lunar year begins with the new moon of Chaitra, the beginning of Chaitra Navaratri, while Vaisakhi marks the solar new year in Punjab and other regions, and in Gujarat the new year falls on the first day of the bright fortnight of Kartika. Under Islamic rule the Hijri calendar became official, and under British rule the Gregorian calendar was adopted. Buddhist and Jain inscriptions continued to use eras based on the Buddha or Mahavira.

The Rana dynasty of Nepal made Vikram Samvat the official calendar in 1901, which began as 1958 VS. Nepal's new year starts on the first day of Baisakh, around 13 to 15 April, and is a public holiday. In India the reformed Saka calendar is the official one, except for traditional festival dates; the Hindi preamble of the Indian constitution dates its adoption of 26 November 1949 as Samvat 2006.
vikramaditya-i: Vikramaditya was one of several sons of Pulakeshin II; the later Chalukyas of Kalyani made him a son of Pulakeshin's son Adityavarman, a statement that can be dismissed as inaccurate. Pulakeshin was defeated and probably killed when the Pallavas invaded Vatapi around 642, and the history of the next decade is unclear. The throne may have passed to Adityavarman, his son Abhinavaditya and then another brother, Chandraditya, whose widow Vijaya-Bhattarika appears to have acted as regent for their minor son.

During that regency Vikramaditya seems to have risen as supreme commander of the army and ruler in practice. His inscriptions say that he recovered the regal fortune of his father, which had been concealed by three kings. The historian K. A. Nilakanta Sastri took these to include his brothers and supposed a partition of the kingdom, but there is no evidence of one; D. C. Sircar and others hold that he fought the Pallavas as a subordinate of his brothers and took the throne only after their deaths. His Gadval inscription of about 674, dated to his twelfth regnal year, places his accession about 655.

With the help of his maternal grandfather, a king of the Western Ganga dynasty, Vikramaditya ended a Pallava occupation that had lasted thirteen years. He gave his loyal younger brother Jayasimhavarma the viceroyalty of Lata in southern Gujarat. Against the Pallava kings Mahendravarman II and Paramesvaravarman I he allied himself with the Pandyas, and by 670 he had a military camp at Malliyur, west of Kanchipuram. Chalukya records claim that he defeated Paramesvaravarman I and took Kanchi but did not destroy it; the writer Anirudh Kanisetti holds that the city was sacked.

Chalukya records place him in camp at Uragapura on the south bank of the Kaveri river on 25 April 674. At Peruvalanallur he met Paramesvaravarman I and a Pandya king, and Pallava and Pandya records alike claim that the Chalukyas were defeated there. Pallava inscriptions also speak of the destruction of the city of Ranarasika, an epithet of Vikramaditya, but several historians question whether Vatapi was sacked a second time; Chalukya records credit his son Vinayaditya and grandson Vijayaditya with defeating the invaders.

Vikramaditya bore titles that advertised his military power, among them Rana-rasika, lover of war, Anivarita, unopposed, and Raja-malla, royal wrestler. He was married to the Western Ganga princess Gangamahadevi. Under him the Chalukya kingdom recovered most of the territory it had controlled under Pulakeshin II. He died in 680 and was succeeded by his son Vinayaditya.
vikramashila: Vikramashila was founded by the Pala king Dharmapala, who ruled from 783 to 820 CE, in the late 8th or early 9th century. It was established, in a supposed response to a decline in the quality of scholarship at Nalanda, as one of three most important Buddhist mahaviharas of its time, along with Nalanda and Odantapuri.

According to Tibetan sources, five great mahaviharas stood out in the Pala period: Vikramashila, the premier university of the era, Nalanda, Somapura, Odantapura and Jagaddala. They formed a network under state supervision, and great scholars moved easily from one to another. The monastery is known mainly through Tibetan sources, especially the writings of the monk historian Tāranātha of the 16th and 17th centuries.

Vikramashila had more than one hundred teachers and about one thousand students. According to the scholar Sukumar Dutt, it had a more clearly delineated hierarchy than other mahaviharas: an abbot, six gate scholars, one for each gate, great scholars, about 108 scholars, about 160 teachers including the scholars, and about 1,000 resident monks.

Philosophy, grammar, metaphysics and Indian logic were taught, but the most important branch of learning was Buddhist tantra, and the monastery employed tantric preceptors, the first of them Buddhajñānapāda. Tāranātha lists the gate scholars at its peak under King Chanaka as Ratnākaraśānti, Vāgīsvarakīrti, Ratnavajra, Jñanasrimitra, Naropa and Prajñākaramati. Atisha Dipankara, a founder of the Sarma traditions of Tibetan Buddhism, was among its scholars.

The site, at Antichak village near Kahalgaon in Bhagalpur district, was excavated by B. P. Sinha of Patna University in 1960–69 and by the Archaeological Survey of India in 1972–82. It revealed a square monastery with sides of 330 metres and 208 cells, with a cruciform stupa about 15 metres high at its centre, a library building and many votive stupas.

The stupa's walls carry terracotta plaques of Buddhist deities and scenes of daily life. Most of the library's manuscripts were lost after the raids of Bakhtiyar Khalji's forces and through decay, but some were found in Nepal and Tibet, where monks fled; one in the British Library names the monastery as its place of production.
vikramavardhana: His knightly name, according to the Pararaton, was Raden Gagak Sali. His mother was Hayam Wuruk's younger sister Iswari, Princess of Pajang, and his father Singhawardhana, Prince of Paguhan; of his two younger sisters, Nagarawardhani would later marry his rival. He himself held the title Bhre Mataram. As a boy of no more than 12 he was married to his cousin Kusumawardhani, Princess of Kabalan, then no more than 7, and the Nagarakretagama of 1365 already records them as married. The marriage made him heir apparent.

The rivalry began in the 1370s, when Wijayarajasa, husband of Rajadewi, proclaimed himself king with the regnal name Bhatara Parameswara ring Pamotan. Hayam Wuruk ruled the Western Court, Kedhaton Kulon, and Wijayarajasa the Eastern Court, Kedhaton Wetan, backed by Hayam Wuruk's son by a concubine. After Wijayarajasa died in 1388 and Hayam Wuruk in 1389, that son, Bhre Wirabhumi, took the eastern throne. Refusing to recognise him, Vikramavardhana gave the title Bhre Lasem to Kusumawardhani although his sister held it, so that each court had its own Princess of Lasem.

By the Pararaton's account he withdrew to religious life in 1400 and returned to court, renewing the feud with Bhre Wirabhumi, in 1401. Both courts dealt with the Chinese and received envoys separately, and Admiral Cheng Ho of the Ming dynasty visited Java in 1405. When the Regreg War broke out, Chinese envoys at the eastern court were killed by accident. In 1415 the Ming records noted that he had taken the name Hyang Wisesa, Yang-wei-hsi-sha in Chinese.

He ruled until 1429 and, as the Pararaton records, was deified at Lalangon, with his memorial sanctuary at Paramawiśesapura. He was followed by a queen regnant whose identity historians still debate: Kusumawardhani, if she was then alive, or their daughter Suhita. His eldest son, Hyang Wekasing Sukha, died in 1399, and a second son, Bhre Tumapel, in 1427. The youngest, Dyah Kertawijaya, reigned after Suhita as Wijayaparakramawardhana. Historian J. Noorduyn argued that all four children were Kusumawardhani's.
viktor-chernov: Viktor Mikhailovich Chernov was born on 19 November 1873 in Kamyshin, in Saratov Governorate on the Volga. His father, Mikhail Chernov, came from a peasant serf family and became a school teacher and later a district treasurer. His mother died when he was an infant. His political awakening in the late 1880s came through his elder brother Vladimir. He was briefly detained and questioned in 1890, and in autumn 1891 he moved to Dorpat to continue his studies. In 1899 he arrived in Zurich among the Russian émigrés, then moved to Berne.

In 1900, after the death of the populist Pyotr Lavrov in Paris, Chernov co-founded the Agrarian Socialist League at Lavrov's grave with Mikhail Gots and veteran populists. In his essay of that year, The Immediate Task of the Revolutionary Cause, he argued for a party uniting the industrial workers and the toiling peasantry, with the proletariat as vanguard and the peasantry as the mass force.

He held that the toiling peasantry, who lived by their own labour, stood closer to the proletariat than to the capitalist. By the end of 1901 the Southern and Northern Unions and the League merged into the Socialist Revolutionary Party, and Chernov and Gots edited its newspaper, Revoliutsionnaia Rossiia.

After the exposure of Evno Azef in 1908 as a long-term police agent who had headed the party's Combat Organization, Chernov, who had defended him, saw the party demoralised. When the First World War began he led the internationalist wing and took part in the Zimmerwald Conference in 1915. He returned to Petrograd on 8 April 1917 and served as Minister of Agriculture in the coalition government from May to September, where Kadet ministers and later Alexander Kerensky blocked his law transferring land to local committees.

Chernov was elected President of the Russian Constituent Assembly, which convened in January 1918. In his opening address he set out land socialisation and a policy of peace, between the Bolsheviks and the counter-revolution. After a single session of about 13 hours the Bolsheviks dispersed it. Harassed by the Cheka, he went into hiding and left Russia in 1920, living in exile mainly in Europe and later in New York, where he wrote and criticised the Soviet regime. He died there in New York on 15 April 1952.

The historian Oliver H. Radkey credits him with a splendid mind and powers of social analysis, but also a weakness of will that limited his effectiveness as a leader. Chernov himself admitted to being more a theorist and a man of the writing table and platform than a professional politician.
vila-velha: Vila Velha, whose name means Old Village, lies on the Atlantic coast of the state of Espírito Santo in south-eastern Brazil, about 10 km south of the state capital, Vitória, with which it forms part of the Greater Vitória Metropolitan Area.

The terrain is mostly flat, the municipal seat standing about 4 m above sea level, and the 32 km of coastline is almost entirely lined with beaches. Several hills rise from the plain, among them Morro da Penha at 154 m, which carries the Penha Convent, and Morro do Moreno at 164 m, which preserves a remnant of the Atlantic Forest, the original vegetation of the area.

In the 16th century the area was contested by three Indigenous groups: the Goitacá from the south, the Aimoré from the interior and the Tupiniquim from the north. On 23 May 1535 the Portuguese Vasco Fernandes Coutinho, grantee of the Captaincy of Espírito Santo, landed at the present-day Prainha, which the Indigenous people called Piratininga, from the caravel Glória with 60 men. He founded the Vila do Espírito Santo, now Vila Velha, so named because it was the Sunday of Pentecost. The settlement became the captaincy's capital, and the seat was later transferred to Vitória.

Agriculture sustained the town for much of its history and declined in the 20th century, giving way to commerce, tourism and industry. The chocolate factory Garoto was founded there in August 1929. The port terminal is one of the largest in south-eastern Brazil. Theatre has been part of the town since the colonial period: plays written by Jesuits were performed in the late 16th century, among them Na Visitação de Santa Izabel of 1597 by Father Joseph of Anchieta.

Vila Velha is the oldest city in the state and holds several historic landmarks, including the Church of Our Lady of the Rosary, the Fort of São Francisco Xavier de Piratininga and the Santa Luzia Lighthouse.
