The Penha Convent, one of the oldest churches in Espírito Santo, was begun around 1558 under Friar Pedro Palácios and was designated a national cultural heritage site by the heritage institute Iphan in 1943.
Its high altar, built around 1800 in the Rococo style, has over 200 pieces of 19 types of marble. The city has about half a million inhabitants, and its anniversary on 23 May is also a state holiday.
vilayet: The word vilayet is Ottoman Turkish, a loanword from the Arabic wilāya, an abstract noun formed from the verb waliya, to administer. In Arabic it meant province, region or administration in a general sense, but after the Tanzimat reforms the Ottoman term was fixed on specific areas in a defined hierarchy. The reform movement was initiated by the Ottoman Reform Edict of 1856.

The Danube Vilayet was formed in 1864 as an experiment under the reformer Midhat Pasha, and a vilayet law expanded the system, though it was not until 1884 that it was applied to all of the empire's provinces. The Ottoman Empire had already begun to modernise its administration and regularise its eyalets in the 1840s. Writing in the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1911, Vincent Henry Penalver Caillard claimed that the reform was intended to give the provinces more local self-government but in fact centralised more power with the sultan and local Muslims at the expense of other communities.

Each vilayet was governed by a vali appointed by the sultan, who acted as his representative and was notionally the supreme head of administration in the province. Military administration was entirely separate, though the vali controlled local police. His council included a secretary, a comptroller, a chief justice and directors of foreign affairs, public works, and agriculture and commerce, each nominated by the respective ministers in Istanbul; the comptroller answered directly to the finance minister.

A separate vilayet council had four elected members, two Muslims and two non-Muslims. The hierarchy ran from vilayet to sanjak, kaza and nahiye, under a mutasarrif, a kaymakam and a mudür, down to the muhtar of the village. Similar councils at lower levels included the heads of the millets, the local religious communities.

In the mid-1870s there were vilayets such as Adrianople, the Danube, Bosnia, Salonica, Janina, Aidin, Konya, Syria, Baghdad, Basra, Yemen and Tripolitania, together with special cases such as Mount Lebanon and the Principality of Samos. By 1905 the empire had lost administrative control over Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia, Crete and Cyprus, though all remained under nominal Ottoman sovereignty, as did Egypt. Jerusalem, because of its importance to three monotheistic religions, was an independent sanjak linked directly to the Minister of the Interior.

The Sharifate of Mecca coexisted with the Hejaz vilayet without being subordinate to it. In 1917 there were twenty vilayets, such as Baghdad, Beirut, Aleppo and Trebizond, alongside independent sanjaks. The early Republic of Turkey continued to use the term, and its 1927 census counted 63 vilayets, until it renamed them il in the late 1920s. The term also passed into Albanian, Bulgarian, French and Judaeo-Spanish.
viljandi: Viljandi lies on the north-western shore of Lake Viljandi, in a primeval valley, between the Estonian cities of Pärnu and Tartu. It is the capital of Viljandi County. Its symbol is a white rose, and 720 white roses were planted before the city hall for the anniversary in 2003. The first records of settlement near the town date to the fifth millennium BCE, and the earthen stronghold is first mentioned in 1154 in the commentaries to al-Idrisi's world atlas Geography.

In the twelfth century a permanent settlement emerged around the stronghold, which became the economic centre of the ancient Sakala district. In 1211 the hillfort of the Estonians was besieged by a joint army of Germans, Latvians and Livonians. The Livonian Sword Brethren, later the Livonian Order, started a powerful Order centre in place of the wooden stronghold in 1224, and the following year Grand Master Volquin led the building of Viljandi Castle on the site of the hillfort. It was one of the largest castles of the Baltic region, a commander was appointed to it from 1248, and it was rebuilt and modernised over the next two hundred years.

In the thirteenth century a medieval town arose on the north side of the stronghold, with the Hamburg-Riga town bylaws, first recorded in 1283. In the first half of the fourteenth century Viljandi joined the Hanseatic League, as an important stop for merchants travelling to and from Russia. In 1481 Ivan III of Russia besieged the castle but could not take it. The decline began in the Livonian War, and in 1560 the forces of Knyaz Andrey Kurbsky of Muscovite Russia seized and demolished the town and the stronghold. They were destroyed again in the Polish–Russian War of the early seventeenth century, and under Swedish rule the town bylaws were cancelled. They were restored in 1783, when Catherine II's reforms made Viljandi a district town.

Viljandi has about 17,000 inhabitants. The ruins of the castle lie in a park, and the town belongs to the international city league the Hanse. It is sometimes called the cultural capital of Estonia, partly because of the Viljandi Culture Academy, and the Viljandi Folk Music Festival is held each summer. The newspaper Sakala was founded there in 1878, and the railway station opened in 1897.
villefranche-sur-mer: Villefranche-sur-Mer lies on the French Riviera, immediately east of Nice below Mont Boron, Mont Alban and Mont Vinaigrier. Its name means Free City on Sea in Old French. The bay is one of the deepest natural harbours of the Mediterranean, reaching 98 metres between the Cape of Nice and Cap Ferrat, and it gives safe anchorage to large ships in easterly winds. Offshore it extends into an undersea canyon. The town's limits climb the surrounding hills to 577 metres at Mont-Leuze.

The site has been settled since prehistoric times, when Celto-Ligurian tribes farmed the hills. The Greeks and later the Romans used the harbour as a stop on the way to settlements in the western Mediterranean, and after Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul the Romans extended the Via Aurelia through the settlement of Montolivo. In 1295 Charles II, Duke of Anjou and Count of Provence, persuaded the people of Montolivo and its surroundings to settle nearer the coast, to protect the area from pirates. He established Villefranche by charter as a free port, with tax privileges and port fee rights that lasted well into the 18th century.

By 1388 East Provence had passed to the Duchy of Savoy after the disputed succession to Queen Joan I of Naples. In 1543 Franco-Turkish armies sacked and occupied the town after the siege of Nice, and Duke Emmanuel Philibert then built a citadel, in 1557, and a fort on Mont Alban. French forces occupied the town again in 1793, and the county of Nice remained part of the Napoleonic Empire until 1814. It was given to France in 1860 by treaty after a plebiscite.

The citadel now houses the town hall, a convention centre, three museums and an open-air theatre. The old harbour of la Darse dates from the 17th century, when it was built for the galleys of the Duke of Savoy, and today it is a marina and the site of an oceanographic observatory. The Rue Obscure, a passage under the harbour-front houses, dates from 1260. The Chapelle Saint-Pierre, from the sixteenth century, was restored in 1957 with murals by Jean Cocteau. The United States Sixth Fleet had its home port at Villefranche from 1948 to 1966.
villers-abbey: In 1146 twelve Cistercian monks and three lay brothers from Clairvaux came to Villers to found the abbey on land granted by Gauthier de Marbais. After two provisional sites, known as Villers I and Villers II, the present buildings were begun in the 13th century: the choir was finished by 1217, the crypt by 1240 and the refectory by 1267, while the church took 70 years and was completed by the end of the century.

The 13th century was the height of the abbey's fame. Contemporary accounts speak of about 100 monks and 300 lay brothers, perhaps an exaggeration, and its lands grew to some 100 square kilometres of woods, fields and pasture. Several members of the ducal house of Brabant were buried there, among them Duke Henry II, his wife Sophie of Thuringia and Duke John III, as was Juliana of Liège.

Decline came in the 16th century with the wider troubles of the Low Countries. Spanish tercios badly damaged the church and cloister in the campaign of 1544, and both were partly restored in 1587. Early in the 17th century Crisóstomo Henríquez wrote the abbey's history. Its monks and wealth dwindled through the 17th and 18th centuries, and it was abandoned in 1796 in the wake of the French Revolution.

In 1855 the railway between Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve and Charleroi was laid through the old abbey grounds. The Belgian state bought the site in 1893 and began to conserve it, and it was classed as a historic site in 1973. The cloister, refectory, kitchens, dormitories and brewing house survive with many outbuildings, and the ruined church, with its vaulting, arches and rose windows, is an example of Cistercian architecture. The ruins belong to the Walloon Region and are part of Wallonia's Major Heritage.
vilna-gaon: Elijah ben Solomon Zalman was born on 23 April 1720 in Sielec, then in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and now Syalyets in Belarus. His father was a rabbi. By nine he had begun to study Kabbalah, devoting several hours a day to the Zohar and the writings of Isaac Luria, and by ten he studied without teachers. By the age of twenty, rabbis were submitting their hardest legal problems to him. He married Chana, daughter of Yehuda Leib of Kaidan, who managed the household so that he could give himself wholly to study.

He wrote glosses on the Babylonian Talmud and the Shulchan Aruch, known as Bi'urei ha-Gra, a running commentary on the Mishnah, and commentaries on the Book of Proverbs and on Kabbalistic texts. None of his manuscripts was published in his lifetime. He favoured study of the literal meaning of a text and, like Maimonides, opposed pilpul, the sharp dialectical analysis of the schools. He often ruled according to his own reading of the Talmud, even against the Shulchan Aruch or established custom.

He supported secular studies that helped to understand the Torah. He wrote a book on mathematics, astronomy and geometry, Ayil Meshulash, and a Hebrew translation of Euclid's Elements was published in The Hague in 1780 with an introduction quoting his words. He condemned philosophy and metaphysics and opposed the study of the humanities in general. In Kabbalah he rejected the reception of revelations through a maggid, preferring to seek wisdom directly through study.

He held no official post and did not head a yeshiva. In the winter of 1767 he set up a beit midrash next to his home, where select scholars studied and brought him their questions. His students felt the gap between themselves and him so strongly that they refused to be called his students. The best known was Chaim of Volozhin, who founded the Volozhin Yeshiva and wrote Nefesh HaChaim, partly as a reply to Hasidism.

He opposed Hasidism, which he regarded as a deviation from the faith. His signature appears on the Vilna community's decree of excommunication against it in 1772, and he issued another in 1781. He refused to meet Shneur Zalman of Liadi, founder of the Chabad movement. Some of his followers later settled in Jerusalem. He died in Vilnius on 9 October 1797. In 2020, the 300th anniversary of his birth, the Lithuanian Parliament declared the Year of the Vilna Gaon.
vilnius: Vilnius lies at the confluence of the Vilnia and Neris rivers in southeastern Lithuania, 312 km from the Baltic Sea and the main Lithuanian seaport, Klaipėda. The city covers 402 km2, of which 68.8 per cent is green space. Its name comes from the river Vilnia, an old Lithuanian name meaning ripple, which was transferred to the city. The name first appears in Latin letters of Grand Duke Gediminas in 1323, in the form Vilna, and in 1325 as Wilno, a form still used in Polish. The Lithuanian form Vilnius was recorded around 1600 in the Postil of Mikalojus Daukša and became widespread during the national revival at the end of the 19th century.

The history of Vilnius goes back to the Stone Age. From at least 1323 until 1795 the city was the capital of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and from the 13th century until the mid-17th century the Vilnius Castle Complex was the residence of the Lithuanian monarchs. Magdeburg rights were granted in 1378, and a magistrate or city council, subordinate to the ruler, then governed it.

In 1517 the Italian princess Bona Sforza married the Lithuanian Grand Duke Sigismund I the Old, which strengthened the Italian influence on the city's Renaissance and Baroque architecture. Vilnius became an artistic centre of the Grand Duchy, attracting artists from across Europe. Under the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth it was noted for its multicultural population, which contemporary sources compared to Babylon. Before World War II and the Holocaust it was one of Europe's most important Jewish centres.

Later Vilnius was ruled by imperial and Soviet Russia, Napoleonic France, Imperial and Nazi Germany and interwar Poland, and it again became a capital of Lithuania in the 20th century. Before World War II Poles made up the majority of inhabitants, and the population exchange between Poland and Soviet Lithuania after the war changed that.

Vilnius is the capital and largest city of Lithuania and the most populous city in the Baltic states. Its Old Town, considered one of the largest and best-preserved in Europe, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1994. The Baroque style known as Vilnian Baroque is named after the city, which is the easternmost Baroque city and the largest north of the Alps. Around two thirds of its residents were Lithuanians in 2021.
vilnius-university: In 1568 the Lithuanian nobility asked the Jesuits to create an institution of higher learning in Vilnius or Kaunas. The following year Walerian Protasewicz, the bishop of Vilnius, bought several buildings in the city centre and established the college, which first enrolled students in 1570, 160 of them in its first year. A library was founded the same year, and Sigismund II Augustus donated 2,500 books to it.

Teaching was in Latin, in three divisions: humanities, philosophy and theology. The university was founded in 1579 as the Jesuit Academy of Vilnius by Stephen Báthory. It was the third oldest university, after the Cracow Academy and the Albertina, in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the only one in the Grand Duchy of Lithuania.

Vilnius University was prominent in the Baroque era. The Jesuits hired the architect Joannes Christophorus Glaubicius to repair its buildings and the Church of St. Johns, and he developed a Vilnius Baroque style. In 1753 Tomasz Żebrowski founded the first observatory in the Commonwealth, the fourth professional one in Europe.

In 1773 the Commission of National Education, the world's first ministry of education, took control of the academy and turned it into a modern university, and the language of teaching changed from Latin to Polish. After the failure of the November Uprising of 1830 to 1831 the university was closed and remained suspended until 1919, when it resumed as the Polish Stefan Batory University on 28 August with the authorisation of Józef Piłsudski.

In October 1939 Vilnius was transferred to Lithuania, and on 15 December the Lithuanian authorities closed the university and dismissed about 3,000 students. A new university named Vilniaus universitetas was created with Lithuanian as its language. Under the Nazi occupation all Jewish teachers and later all Polish and Jewish students were expelled, and nearly all the Jewish members of the university community became victims of the Holocaust. Under Soviet rule lecturers were arrested from 1945 until Stalin's death. On 12 June 1990 the Supreme Council of Lithuania approved a new statute declaring the university's autonomy.

The historic ensemble in the old town, with around thirteen courtyards, still serves its original educational role. The library, founded in 1570, is the earliest academic library in the Baltic region and holds over five million documents, including collections of old printed books and manuscripts, and its Central Library still works in its authentic 16th-century premises. The poet Czesław Miłosz, Nobel laureate in literature in 1980, was an alumnus.
vilshofen-an-der-donau: Vilshofen an der Donau lies at the confluence of the Vils, Pfudrach and Wolfach with the Danube, south of the Bavarian Forest, and is sometimes called the three-river town. Its height above sea level ranges from 309 to 457 metres. Here the Danube cut into the crystalline basement as the Bavarian Forest rose in the Late Tertiary and Quaternary, forming an impressive valley that continues far beyond Passau. Granite was quarried in the Vils valley nature reserve until the middle of the 20th century, and the abandoned quarries partly flooded, creating the Taferlsee.

The documented history of Vilshofen begins in 776, when a farm called Vilusa was donated to the Mondsee monastery. The Bishop of Passau was landlord of the Danube and Vils, and the Count of Ortenburg held Vilshofen as a fief. Count Heinrich I of Ortenburg raised it to a town in 1206, and a bridge over the Vils is reported in 1220. In 1241 Duke Otto II of Bavaria took the town by force after an inheritance dispute in the House of Ortenburg, making it a border town between Bavaria and the Prince-Bishopric of Passau. It finally passed to Bavaria in 1262 under a treaty negotiated by Duke Henry of Lower Bavaria with Bishop Rüdiger of Passau.

Emperor Ludwig the Bavarian confirmed the town charter in 1345, and a collegiate monastery was founded in 1376. The oldest town seal dates from 1434. In 1504 the town was defended successfully against attackers from the Palatinate and Bohemia in the Landshut War of Succession, and in 1536 a large fire destroyed 36 houses. Until 1972 Vilshofen was the seat of its own district.

Vilshofen is the largest town in the southeast of Bavaria and lies in the district of Passau, about 20 kilometres upstream of Passau. A Benedictine monastery was founded at Schweiklberg in 1904. The town lies on the Danube Cycle Path and is a port of call for river cruise vessels. In 2006 it marked the 800th anniversary of its elevation to a town. The brewer Josef Groll was born there in 1813.
vima-kadphises: His place among the Kushan kings is known from the Rabatak inscription, set up by Kanishka, which names Kujula Kadphises as Kanishka's great-grandfather, Vima Taktu as his grandfather and Vima Kadphises as his father. His name is written in Greek and in Kharosthi inscriptions, and he was known in Han dynasty China by a name of his own. He expanded Kushan territory in Afghanistan and north-west India, where he may have replaced the Indo-Scythian ruler Sodasa at Mathura.

The Kushans protected the Silk Road, along which silk, spices, textiles and medicine moved between China, India and the West, and sea trade with the Roman Empire brought back gold coins, Greek wine and slaves. Imported works of art are known from the Treasure of Begram. Roman historians tell of ambassadors from the kings of Bactria and India at the court of Trajan, bearing presents and letters in Greek, who may have been sent by Vima Kadphises or by Kanishka.

He was the first Kushan ruler to strike gold coins beside the existing copper and silver, most of the gold seemingly coming from trade with the Roman Empire. His coins follow the Roman weight standard of the 1st century, about eight grams, in three denominations: the double stater, the stater and the quarter stater, or dinara. The use of gold reflects the empire's prosperity as a centre of trade between Han China, Central Asia and Alexandria and Antioch in the West. Most of his coins bear on the reverse the Triratana, or possibly the Nandipada, with Shiva, often holding a Trishul, with or without his bull.
vimara-peres: Vímara Peres was a ninth-century nobleman who died in Galicia in 873. His father, Pedro Theon, who may have been a son of Bermudo I of Asturias, belonged to the Curia Regis of King Alfonso III and appears in January 867 confirming a royal charter together with other nobles, among them Count Rodrigo of Castile. Pedro took an active part in the Reconquista and was responsible for ousting and defeating the Vikings who invaded Galicia in 858. Vímara had a brother, Hermenegildo Peres. His name is believed to derive from Weimar, from the Old High German words for holy and standing water, and it survives in Portugal today as Guímaro.

Vímara was a vassal of Alfonso III of Asturias. He was sent to reconquer and secure from the Moors, the Arabs and Berbers who had occupied Visigothic Hispania, the western coastal fringe of Gallaecia, the area from the Minho River to the Douro River. It included Portus Cale, later Porto and Gaia, from which the name of Portugal emerged. The Kingdom of Asturias was divided into several counties, or royal provinces, and Portus Cale was one of them. In 868 Alfonso III named Vímara Count of Portugal after the reconquest of the region north of the Douro. He expelled the Moors and founded a fortified town under his own name, Vimaranis, which later became Guimarães, and the Portuguese call it the Cradle City.

Vímara Peres died in 873 at Vama, which has been identified either as Guimarães or as Bama in the territory of Touro, in A Coruña. Most historians agree that his son Lucídio Vimaranes succeeded him as governor of the county. Later Portuguese historians viewed his appointment in 868 as the earliest milestone in the history of the state of Portugal, although Portugal did not achieve independence until the twelfth century.
viminacium: Viminacium stood on the Roman road called the Via Militaris, in the valley of the Mlava river, which was rich in ore and grain. In Roman times its defences faced a southern branch of the Danube on the north and the Mlava on the west. Its position made it a hub of communications and trade as well as a defence of the Limes Moesiae, the northern frontier of the empire, and a place where eastern and western cultures met. The archaeological site covers 450 hectares.

The town began as a military camp. A legion may have been stationed there as early as the reign of Augustus, and in 33 or 34 CE a road was built linking Viminacium with Ratiaria in modern Bulgaria. Emperor Claudius garrisoned Viminacium, Oescus and Novae as camps for the Moesian legions, and the first legion attested at Viminacium is the Legio VII Claudia, which came from Dalmatia in 52. A civilian settlement grew up beside the camp. When Moesia was divided in 87, after Domitian's Dacian War, Viminacium became the capital of Moesia Superior.

It was one of the most important Roman cities and military camps from the first to the fourth century, and at its height it is believed to have held 40,000 inhabitants. As provincial capital it also became a metropolitan archbishopric, presumably from about 300 to about 400. The Notitia Dignitatum records that part of the Roman Danube fleet was anchored there. Huns devastated the city in the fifth century, but it was rebuilt by Justinian. It was destroyed completely with the arrival of the Slavs in the sixth century.

The first archaeological excavation in Serbia began at Viminacium in 1882, led by the architect Mihailo Valtrović, whose only help was twelve prisoners. Miloje Vasić, the first trained Serbian archaeologist, continued the work in the mid-1890s, and Queen Draga Obrenović donated 100 gold ducats to it.

The legionary camp was a rectangle of 442 m by 385 m. The amphitheatre, with 12,000 seats, was one of the largest in the Balkans. More than 16,000 graves have been found, the most at any Roman archaeological site, and over 700 objects of silver and gold have come from the tombs. Frescoes in tombs of the fourth century are valued as Roman art. Skeletons show an average life span of 35 years, and some skulls were deliberately elongated in childhood, a practice then thought beautiful.
vinayak-damodar-savarkar: Savarkar was born on 28 May 1883 into a Marathi Hindu Chitpavan Brahmin family in Bhagur, a village in Nasik district of the Bombay Presidency. He began his activism as a high school student. In 1903 he and his brother Ganesh founded the Mitra Mela, an underground revolutionary organisation that became the Abhinav Bharat Society in 1906, with the aims of overthrowing British rule and reviving Hindu pride. Lokmanya Tilak helped him obtain the Shivaji Scholarship of 1906 for law studies in London. There he associated with India House in Highgate and published books advocating complete independence by revolutionary means; British authorities banned his book The Indian War of Independence.

Arrested in 1910 over his involvement with India House and deported to India, Savarkar was tried before a special tribunal; one charge was abetment of the murder of the Nasik Collector A. M. T. Jackson. In July 1911 he was transported to Port Blair and imprisoned in the Cellular Jail. His first clemency petition, of 30 August 1911, was rejected. He was released on 6 January 1924 after a series of such petitions but was restricted to Ratnagiri District until 1937. At Ratnagiri jail he wrote Essentials of Hindutva.

As president of the Hindu Mahasabha, which endorsed the idea of India as a Hindu Rashtra, Savarkar supported the British war effort in the Second World War and criticised the Quit India movement of 1942. After Gandhi's assassination on 30 January 1948 he was arrested on 5 February and charged with murder, conspiracy and abetment, but he was acquitted for lack of sufficient evidence. The Kapur Commission later concluded that he was involved. On 1 February 1966 he renounced medicines, food and water, and he died on 26 February 1966 in Bombay.

In Essentials of Hindutva Savarkar described a Hindu as a patriotic inhabitant of Bharatavarsha, beyond religious identity, and described Hinduism, Jainism, Sikhism and Buddhism as one and the same. He outlined a Hindu Rashtra as Akhand Bharat, a united India across the subcontinent. He opposed the caste system and untouchability, and ate with dalits in public. Historians including Rachel McDermott, Leonard A. Gordon, Ainslie Embree, Frances Pritchett and Dennis Dalton state that he promoted an anti-Muslim form of Hindu nationalism. He wrote 38 books in English and Marathi and has been called one of the most divisive figures in Indian politics.
vincas-mickevicius-kapsukas: Mickevičius was born in Vilkaviškis, in Suvalkija, then part of Congress Poland in the Russian Empire, to a family of wealthy farmers who were Lithuanian patriots in the years of the tsarist ban on Lithuanian print. In 1895 his brother Juozas brought him into Sietynas, a society that printed books in East Prussia and smuggled them into Lithuania. He was expelled from the Sejny Priest Seminary after a year for illegal political work, and from Jelgava Gymnasium in 1901 for keeping banned press. He took his pen name Kapsukas from Vincas Kapsas, a pen name of Vincas Kudirka, founder of Varpas.

Escaping arrest, he studied philosophy, sociology and political economy at the University of Bern from 1901 to 1903 and edited Varpas and Ūkininkas in Tilsit. In 1903 he moved from the Lithuanian Democratic Party to the Lithuanian Social Democratic Party, where he belonged to the wing that wanted an independent Lithuania in a federation with Poland, Belarus, Ukraine and Latvia.

During the Revolution of 1905 he organised peasant demonstrations and strikes. Arrested in December 1905, he escaped from a prison hospital in Suwałki in 1906, was caught again in May 1907 and, once identified as the escapee, sentenced in 1909 to a further 8 years of katorga; Alexander Kerensky was among his defenders. Released under the amnesty of 1913 into exile in Siberia, he escaped, met Vladimir Lenin in Kraków in 1914, and spent the war years editing socialist papers in Scotland and the United States.

In 1917 he joined the Bolsheviks in Petrograd and edited Tiesa. On 8 December 1918 the Vilnius Soviet made him chairman and foreign minister of the Provisional Revolutionary Workers' and Peasants' Government of Lithuania, which proclaimed the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic on 16 December. Its support came mostly from urban workers and farm labourers, while most farmers backed the Council of Lithuania, and he warned Lenin that recruiting more Lithuanians to the Red Army would cost his government support. By August 1919 Polish and Lithuanian forces had driven the Soviets from almost all of Lithuania and Belarus.

From late 1921 he lived in Moscow, sat on the executive committee of the Comintern from 1923 and wrote more than 50 works and around 2,000 articles. He died in a Moscow hospital on 17 February 1935, officially of complications of tuberculosis; his wife Elena Domicėlė Tautkaitė was executed in 1937 for Trotskyist activities. Unmentionable in public under Stalin, he was honoured after 1953, and Marijampolė and Vilnius University bore his name until 1989.
vincent-auriol: Vincent Jules Auriol was born on 27 August 1884 in Revel, Haute-Garonne, the only child of a baker. He took a law degree and began work as a lawyer in Toulouse. A committed socialist, he co-founded the newspaper Le Midi Socialiste in 1908. In 1914 he entered the Chamber of Deputies as a Socialist for Muret, and he was mayor of Muret from 1925 to 1947. After the party split in December 1920, he refused to join the new SFIC and became, with Léon Blum, a leader of the remaining SFIO. He became its leading spokesman on financial questions, and he chaired the Finance Committee of the Chamber from 1924 to 1926.

As Minister of Finance in Blum's government of 1936–1937, Auriol devalued the franc by 30 per cent against the dollar, which led to capital flight. He was Minister of Justice in the next government, under Camille Chautemps. On 10 July 1940 he was one of the 80 deputies who voted against the extraordinary powers given to Philippe Pétain. He was placed under house arrest until he escaped to the Resistance in October 1942, and he reached London in October 1943. He represented the Socialists at the Free French Consultative Assembly and France at the Bretton Woods conference in July 1944. After the war he served in Charles de Gaulle's provisional government and presided over the Constituent Assemblies.

On 16 January 1947 the National Assembly elected Auriol the first President of the Fourth Republic, with 452 votes against 242 for Auguste Champetier de Ribes. His presidency was relatively weak, like the office under the Third Republic. Strikes in 1947 escalated into violence, and the government deployed 80,000 reservists. The war in Indochina and unrest in Morocco, Madagascar, Algeria and Tunisia marked the period. France joined the Council of Europe and NATO as a founding member, and the Monnet Plan was put into effect. Auriol did not seek re-election, and René Coty succeeded him on 16 January 1954. There had been eighteen governments in his seven years.
vincent-of-saragossa: Vincent is also known as Vincent Martyr, Vincent of Huesca or Vincent the Deacon. He was born at Huesca, near Zaragoza, in the latter part of the 3rd century; it is believed that his father was Eutricius and his mother Enola, a native of Osca. He spent most of his life in Zaragoza, where he was educated and ordained to the diaconate by Bishop Valerius, who sent him to preach throughout the diocese. Because Valerius suffered from a speech impediment, Vincent acted as his spokesman.

When the Roman Emperor Diocletian began persecuting Christians in Spain, Vincent and Valerius were brought before the governor, Dacian, in Valencia and imprisoned. The earliest account of Vincent's martyrdom is a poem by Prudentius in his Peristephanon. Offered release if he would consign Scripture to the fire, Vincent refused. He was stretched on the rack, his flesh torn with iron hooks, and burned on a red-hot gridiron, and he died in prison on a floor strewn with broken pottery. The gridiron story is perhaps adapted from the martyrdom of Lawrence, another son of Huesca. Valerius was exiled.

According to legend, ravens protected his body from vultures until his followers could recover it, and his remains were taken to what is now Cape St. Vincent. King Afonso I of Portugal had them exhumed in 1173 and brought by ship to Lisbon Cathedral; the transfer appears on the coat of arms of Lisbon. Three elaborated hagiographies, all based on a lost 5th-century Passion, circulated in the Middle Ages, and their Acts have been described as rather freely coloured by the imagination of their compiler.

His tomb in Valencia became the earliest centre of his cult, and veneration spread from Zaragoza to Oviedo, Béziers, Narbonne and Castres, where relics arrived in 863. A church built for him in Visigothic Iberia was razed in 711, and its materials went into the Great Mosque of Córdoba. His feast day is 22 January. He is patron of Valencia, Zaragoza and Portugal, and is shown as a deacon in a dalmatic. The island of São Vicente in Cape Verde and Saint Vincent in the Caribbean were named for him because they were first sighted on his feast day.
vincent-oge: Ogé was one of the children of Jacques Ogé, a white Frenchman, and Angélique Ossé, who held a contract to supply meat to the Dondon markets; the family's coffee plantation was worked by enslaved labourers. In 1768, at the age of eleven, he was sent to Bordeaux and apprenticed to a goldsmith for about seven years. Back in the colony in 1775 he settled in Cap-Français as a commission agent in the coffee trade for his uncle Vincent, later co-owning a merchant schooner and subletting properties to the colonial elite. By 1788 he owed 60,000 to 70,000 livres and moved for a time to Port-au-Prince.

In 1788 he went to France to buy goods and to bring his family's lawsuits before the Conseil du Roi. In Paris he embraced the Revolution. When absentee planters rejected his proposals in August 1789, he joined a group of free people of colour led by the lawyer Étienne de Joly. By October 1789 he was an officer in the Paris militia and had joined the Society of the Friends of the Blacks. On his secret journey home in 1790 he consulted the British abolitionist Thomas Clarkson in London and landed by way of Charleston, South Carolina.

In October 1790 he and Jean-Baptiste Chavannes, a non-commissioned officer of the colonial militia, demanded that Governor Philibert François Rouxel de Blanchelande and the colonial assembly apply the March law. Their followers, many of them former militiamen, repulsed a first force of about 600 militia, but a second force of 1,500 under Colonel Cambefort routed them. The two fled to Spanish Santo Domingo. On 20 November 1790 Ogé and 23 rebels, Chavannes among them, surrendered at Hinche on Spanish guarantees of safety, but the Spanish handed them to the French. After a trial at Cap-Français, Ogé was executed in Blanchelande's presence and his head was displayed on a pike.

Six months later enslaved rebels under Dutty Boukman rose, beginning the Haitian Revolution, and they often cited Ogé's execution as a reason to keep resisting. Historians have judged him very differently: C. L. R. James called him a man whose gifts were unsuited to his task, while the poet George Boyer Vashon praised him in an 1853 poem. Admired in 19th-century Haiti, where his memory served the mulatto elite, he came to be seen there as a minor figure.
vincent-van-gogh: Vincent Willem van Gogh was born on 30 March 1853 in Groot-Zundert, in the predominantly Catholic province of North Brabant. He was the oldest surviving child of Theodorus van Gogh, a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church, and Anna Cornelia Carbentus. His grandfather, also named Vincent, was a prominent art dealer, and three of that grandfather's six sons became art dealers. His younger brother Theo was born on 1 May 1857. Van Gogh was taught at home, then sent to boarding school at Zevenbergen and in 1866 to the middle school in Tilburg, where he was deeply unhappy. He returned home in March 1868 and later wrote that his youth was "austere and cold, and sterile."

As an adult he began painting at an elementary level. In early 1882 his uncle Cornelis Marinus, owner of a gallery in Amsterdam, commissioned drawings of The Hague but was twice disappointed. Theo gave him money for materials in August 1882. From early 1883 Van Gogh worked on multi-figure compositions, and he destroyed several large paintings made at Nuenen; The Potato Eaters and its companion pieces are the only ones to survive. In November 1885 he travelled to Antwerp and later to Paris, where he met Émile Bernard and Paul Gauguin. His colours grew brighter, and his style was fully realised during his stay in Arles in 1888, when he painted series of olive trees, wheat fields and sunflowers.

The correspondence with Theo is the most comprehensive primary source on his work. It includes more than 600 letters from Vincent to Theo, and most of what is known of his theories of art is recorded in them.

Van Gogh suffered from psychotic episodes and delusions. His friendship with Gauguin ended after a confrontation with a razor, when he severed part of his own left ear. He spent time in psychiatric hospitals, including one at Saint-Rémy, and then moved to the Auberge Ravoux in Auvers-sur-Oise, where he came under the care of Dr Paul Gachet. On 27 July 1890 he shot himself in the chest and died two days later.

His reputation grew steadily among artists and critics after exhibitions in the late 1880s. Theo died in January 1891, and Theo's widow Jo van Gogh-Bonger took charge of the paintings and letters. Memorial exhibitions were held in several cities, and in 1896 the young Henri Matisse was introduced to Van Gogh's work and turned to bright colours. The Fauves and German Expressionists later took up elements of his style.
vincenzo-i-gonzaga: Vincenzo Gonzaga was born on 21 September 1562, the only son of Guglielmo Gonzaga, Duke of Mantua, and Archduchess Eleanor of Austria. His maternal grandparents were the Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand I and Anna of Bohemia and Hungary. In 1582 he killed James Crichton, a Scottish polymath employed at his father's court, in cold blood, out of jealousy.

He married Margherita Farnese in 1581; the marriage was childless and ended in divorce. On 29 April 1584 he married his first cousin Eleonora de' Medici, the daughter of Francesco I de' Medici and Joanna of Austria. They had six children, among them Francesco, Ferdinando and Vincenzo, who each ruled as duke, and two daughters who married Henry II, Duke of Lorraine, and the Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand II.

Vincenzo ruled the Duchy of Mantua and the Duchy of Montferrat from 1587 to 1612 and was crowned fourth Duke of Mantua on 22 September 1587, with a ceremony at which the highest authorities of the duchy paid homage, followed by a ride through the city streets. He was a major patron of the arts and sciences, and turned Mantua into a vibrant cultural centre.

The composer Claudio Monteverdi became a viol player and cantor in his music chapel in 1590, and in 1602 Vincenzo appointed him master of music after the death of Benedetto Pallavicino. He also employed the painter Peter Paul Rubens and was a friend of the poet Torquato Tasso. A small book published at Verona in 1589 imagines an ideal gallery in which he stands as a colossus above all other collectors.

The astronomer Giovanni Antonio Magini, tutor to Vincenzo's sons, worked on an Atlas of Italy begun in 1594, which is dedicated to Vincenzo, who allowed maps of the Italian states to be brought to him. In the winter of 1603 to 1604 Galileo visited the court seeking a post and was offered a salary, but could not agree terms, and Vincenzo gave him a gold chain and two silver dishes. On 20 July 1588 Emperor Rudolf II granted him the right to an escutcheon of Austria, and in 1608 he agreed to marry his heir Francesco to Margaret of Savoy to warm relations between Mantua and Turin.

Vincenzo died on 9 February 1612. His son Francesco succeeded him and ruled until his own death on 22 December of that year, when Ferdinando became duke. Vincenzo created the Order of the Redemptor, or of the Most Precious Blood, approved by Pope Paul V on 25 May 1608, and was a Knight of the Golden Fleece. His spendthrift habits are considered to have accelerated Mantua's economic and cultural decline.
vincenzo-scamozzi: Vincenzo Scamozzi was born in Vicenza on 2 September 1548. His father, Gian Domenico Scamozzi, was a surveyor and building contractor and was his first teacher, instructing him in the principles of Sebastiano Serlio. Scamozzi visited Rome in 1579 and 1580 and moved to Venice in 1581. In 1599 and 1600 he travelled to the German Empire and France, and he left a sketchbook of his impressions of French architecture, which was first published in 1959.

Scamozzi worked mainly in Vicenza and the Republic of Venice. When Andrea Palladio died in 1580 he inherited several unfinished projects and brought them to completion. They included the Villa Capra, called La Rotonda, near Vicenza, where he finished the structure and added stables, and the facade of the church of San Giorgio Maggiore in Venice, completed in 1607 to 1611. He also finished Jacopo Sansovino's Library of San Marco.

In Venice he was invited to design the Procuratie Nuove on Piazza San Marco. It was built as housing for the Procuratorate of San Marco and presented as a unified palace front continuing the facade of Sansovino's library, with an added upper floor. He adapted a rejected project of Palladio's for the Doge's Palace. Eleven bays were completed in his time, and Baldassare Longhena, his only pupil, later extended them along the south side of the square. Scamozzi also remodelled the Teatro Olimpico in Vicenza in 1584 and 1585, and built the Teatro all'antica at Sabbioneta for Duke Vespasiano I Gonzaga in 1588 to 1590.

Scamozzi's influence spread through his two-volume treatise L'idea dell'architettura universale, published with woodcut illustrations at Venice in 1615, one of the last Renaissance works on the theory of architecture. For parts of his treatment of Vitruvius he relied on Daniele Barbaro's commentary of 1556. He included many of his own plans and elevations, some as built, some as they should have been built, and some as idealised projects, aware that such treatises had become a means of self-promotion.

The treatise appeared a year before his death and came too late to help his own career. His practice is sometimes seen as a source of the neo-Palladian architecture introduced by Inigo Jones, and Rudolf Wittkower called him one of the intellectual fathers of neo-classicism. His earlier book on the antiquities of Rome, published in 1583, was put together quickly, and over half its images were copied from a volume published by Hieronymus Cock in Antwerp in 1551.
vindhya-range: The Vindhyas are not a single range in the geological sense: they are a discontinuous chain of ridges, hill ranges, highlands and plateau escarpments, and the term is defined by convention. Today it mainly means the escarpment and its hilly extensions north of the Narmada River in Madhya Pradesh, forming the southern wall of the Malwa plateau. Its western end lies in Gujarat, joined to the Aravalli Range near Champaner. In the east it divides into a southern chain meeting the Satpura Range in the Maikal Hills and a northern chain continuing as the Bhander Plateau and the Kaimur Range, with a branch across Bundelkhand known as the Panna range. It averages roughly 300 to 650 metres in height.

Older texts used the name more widely, for hills between the Indo-Gangetic Plain and the Deccan, extending to the Godavari in the south and the Ganges in the north. Some Puranas apply it to what is now called the Satpura Range. Ancient texts mention three ranges in Central India, Vindhya, Rksa and Pariyatra, among the seven clan mountains of Bharatavarsha. The Greek geographer Ptolemy called the range Vindius or Ouindion and described it as the source of the Narmada and the Tapti.

Several ancient texts treat the Vindhyas as the southern boundary of Āryāvarta, and they remained the traditional dividing line between northern and southern India, though it is debated whether they marked a cultural boundary or only the southern limit of the settled societies then known. They were long considered inaccessible and dangerous because of dense vegetation and the tribes living there, and the Mahabharata places the Nishadas and other peoples in their forests. A legend tells that the mountain grew until it blocked the sun, and the sage Agastya asked it to lower itself so that he could cross south; it promised never to grow again.

Tributaries of the Ganga-Yamuna system, among them the Chambal, Betwa, Ken and Parbati, rise in the Vindhyas and drain their northern slopes, while the Narmada and Son drain the southern. Their highest point is Sad-bhawna Shikhar, 752 metres above sea level, in the Damoh district. A temple to Vindhyavasini, a fierce form of the goddess Shakti, stands at Vindhyachal in Uttar Pradesh. The Vindhyan Supergroup is one of the largest and thickest sedimentary successions in the world, and the Vindhya basin has yielded what may be the earliest known multicellular eukaryote fossils, perhaps 1.6 to 1.7 billion years old.
vindolanda: The fort lies on a hill near the village of Bardon Mill, where it guarded the Stanegate, the Roman road from the River Tyne to the Solway Firth. The name is probably Celtic, meaning white lawn or similar, and an altar records a group called the Textoverdi, who may have been the native people of the area. Archaeologists divide the site into nine periods: five successive forts of wood and turf, buried up to 4 metres deep in waterlogged, oxygen-free soil that has preserved large amounts of organic material, and later stone forts above them.

The first unit, the Cohors I Tungrorum from Gallia Belgica, arrived after Gnaeus Julius Agricola's conquest of the north and built the first timber fort, dated by Samian ware and a coin of Vespasian. One tablet, a troop roster, records 746 men and 6 centurions, of whom 295 men and one centurion were then at Vindolanda, 15 of them sick and 10 out of action with conjunctivitis. The cohort returned in or after 105, and a large timber building may have housed Hadrian while he oversaw the first stages of his wall in 122. Around 128 the Tungrians moved to the new fort of Vercovicium, Housesteads.

In the 210s a new stone fort was built for the Cohors IV Gallorum equitata, with a civilian settlement, or vicus, to the west, and most of the remains visible today belong to this period or later. Fort and village were largely abandoned about 285 for reasons unknown, the fort was rebuilt about 300 without its village, and it was roughly repaired about 370. There is no evidence that Roman occupation ended suddenly in 410.

Eric Birley bought the house at Chesterholm in the 1930s, and his sons Robin and Anthony and later his grandson Andrew Birley continued the summer excavations. Besides some 850 ink tablets, finds include over 160 boxwood combs, most of a military tent and the largest known group of Roman shoes. The Vindolanda Trust, a charity founded in 1970, runs the site and its museum, which has reconstructed buildings in its gardens.
vindonissa: Vindonissa stood on the peninsula between the Aare and the Reuss. Its name comes from a Gaulish place-name built on windo-, white. People lived there long before Roman rule: excavations along the western edge of the camp found a few funeral pyre graves of the late Bronze Age, around 1000 to 800 BCE. The first settlement was a fortified village of the Helvetii in the 1st century BCE, protected by a wood and earth wall about 350 metres long, with a trench up to 7 metres deep, across the narrow neck of the peninsula.

The site came under Roman control either after Julius Caesar's conquest of the Helvetii in 58 BCE or after the conquest of the Alps in 15 BCE, when a small guard-post was set up there. The camp covered about 20 hectares inside a wooden and earthen wall 1.8 kilometres long, with wooden gates, low watchtowers and a double ditch. Thermal baths were added in an expansion around 30.

The Legio XIII Gemina was stationed there until 44 or 45. Its successor, the Legio XXI Rapax, rebuilt the camp with stone fortifications, and after that legion looted the countryside in 69 it was replaced by the Legio XI Claudia. By 72 the wall had become a stone rampart 3.6 metres thick with massive gates and a single ditch.

A large peristyle house of the Flavian period near the principia is thought to have been the home of a senior officer of the 11th legion. Its later Mediterranean-style kitchen with a raised hearth is one of the few known in the north-west of the empire, and the finds show imported olive oil, wine, fish sauces and oysters. After the legions left, Vindonissa was a civilian settlement and later a bishop's seat.

Systematic excavation began in 1896. The remains of the camp are listed as a heritage site of national significance, and the amphitheatre, with seats for about 10,000, is the largest Roman one in present-day Switzerland. A Roman underground canal 2 kilometres long still brings water to the fountain of Königsfelden Monastery, and a small museum in the town of Brugg shows finds from the camp.
vinschgau: The Vinschgau, also called Vintschgau or the Vinschgau Valley, is the upper part of the Adige valley in the western part of the province of South Tyrol. It runs west to east from the Merano basin at Partschins up the river to the Reschen Pass. The Ötztal Alps in the north, part of the Alpine crest, separate it from the upper Inn Valley, and the valley is further confined by the Sesvenna Alps in the west and the Ortler Alps in the south.

Side valleys include the Suldental, the Matscher Tal and the Schnalstal. It has the largest cluster of alpine megafans in the Alps, among them Gadria, which divides the valley at Laas, and Malser Haide, which runs 11 kilometres down the upper valley; their origin is inferred to be mainly catastrophic, following deglaciation.

The names Vinschgau and Val Venosta come from the Celtic, or Rhaetian, Venostes tribes mentioned on the ancient Tropaeum Alpium. Under Charlemagne a Frankish Gau was established in 772. It is first mentioned in a deed of 1077, when King Henry IV of Germany granted the estates of Schlanders in pago Finsgowe to Bishop Altwin of Brixen; the medieval name was Finsgowe.

Its position within the central eastern Alps gives it a warm climate with little rain, about 400 millimetres a year, so fields, meadows and apple orchards are irrigated. Vines are also grown, notably Vernatsch for light summer reds and Lagrein for winter. 08 percent Ladin.

The Vinschgau District, set up in 1962, has 13 cooperating municipalities, with Schlanders (Silandro) as its capital; others include Glurns, Mals, Latsch and Prad. Naturns, Plaus and Partschins belong geographically to the lower valley but are politically linked to the neighbouring Burggrafenamt district.
violeta-chamorro: Violeta Barrios Torres was born on 18 October 1929 in Rivas, near the Costa Rican border, into a wealthy and conservative family with large landholdings and cattle. She attended school in Rivas, Granada and Managua and then American schools in Texas and Virginia, returning home in June 1947 when her father was diagnosed with terminal lung cancer. She met Pedro Joaquín Chamorro Cardenal in 1949, and they married in December 1950 and had five children. In 1952 he inherited the newspaper La Prensa, which became a voice of opposition to the Somoza regime, and he was frequently jailed or exiled; she followed him abroad or visited him in jail for about a decade.

After her husband's assassination in 1978 she took over La Prensa. When Daniel Ortega led the Sandinista guerrillas into Managua in July 1979, she was with them and represented the Democratic Union of Liberation on the Junta of National Reconstruction. She resigned on 19 April 1980, when the junta moved in a more radical direction and signed agreements with the Soviet Union, and returned to the newspaper, which went on criticising the government despite threats and forced shutdowns.

From 1987 a group of fourteen parties worked together, and by 1989 Ortega had agreed to free, monitored elections. The National Opposition Union chose Chamorro as its candidate after five rounds of voting. Her platform promised to end the civil war and military service, and she won the election on 25 February 1990 despite polls favouring Ortega.

Chamorro was sworn in on 25 April 1990, the first time in more than five decades that a government had peacefully surrendered power to the opposition. She abolished conscription on the day she took office, cut the army by half to three quarters within weeks and demobilised the Contras. She also granted unconditional amnesties for political crimes. Her administration tackled hyperinflation that had at one point exceeded 13,000 per cent, with a programme of privatisation and a new currency, the córdoba oro.

In 1995 a constitutional crisis arose over reforms that reduced presidential power, which she at first refused to publish. She left office on 10 January 1997, and in July 1997 founded a foundation to support peace initiatives. She moved to Costa Rica in October 2023 and died in San José on 14 June 2025, aged 95.
viracocha: Viracocha is the creator and supreme deity of pre-Inca and Inca mythology in the Andes. According to the myth he had human appearance and was generally considered bearded, and he ordered the construction of Tiwanaku. His epithets include Ticsi Viracocha, Contiti Viracocha and Viracocha Pachayachachi, meaning teacher of the world. For the Inca the Viracocha cult was more important than the sun cult, and he was followed in the pantheon by Inti, the Sun.

The meaning of the name is uncertain. In Quechua tiqsi means origin or beginning, wira fat and qucha lake or sea. A reading as fat or foam of the sea has been discarded for grammatical reasons since at least Inca Garcilaso. Max Uhle proposed that the name could mean lake of origin and of the end of all things, and some linguists suggest a borrowing from Aymara Wila Quta, blood lake, from sacrifices of camelids at Lake Titicaca.

In the myth recorded by Juan de Betanzos, Viracocha rose from Lake Titicaca, or sometimes from the cave of Paqariq Tampu, in a time of darkness to bring forth light. He made the sun, moon and stars. His first creation, brainless giants, displeased him and he destroyed them with a flood. He then made humans from smaller stones by breathing into them and scattered them across the world.

He wandered the earth disguised as a beggar, teaching the basics of civilization and working miracles, and many refused his teachings. In the end he disappeared across the Pacific by walking on the water and was expected to reappear in times of trouble. In another legend a flood called Unu Pachakuti lasted 60 days and 60 nights and he saved two beings, Manco Cápac and Mama Uqllu, who founded the Inca civilization carrying a golden staff.

Spanish chroniclers equated Viracocha with the creator. Bartolomé de las Casas wrote that the word means creator of all things, and Juan de Betanzos wrote that Viracocha may be said to be God. Using the word God in place of Viracocha is seen as the first step in evangelizing the Incas.

The chroniclers also described Viracocha as a white, bearded god, first done by Pedro Cieza de León in 1553. The whiteness is not mentioned in the authentic native legends of the Incas, and most modern scholars have considered the white god story a post-conquest Spanish invention. Bearded men appear on Moche pottery made long before the Spanish arrived. Local legend at Ollantaytambo sees a 140-metre rock formation on Cerro Pinkuylluna as a figure of Wiracochan, a messenger of Viracocha.
viracocha-inca: Wiraqucha Inka, in the hispanicised spelling Viracocha, was the eighth Sapa Inka of the Kingdom of Cuzco and the third of the Hanan dynasty. His reign is dated from about 1410 to 1438. He was not the son of his predecessor Yawar Waqaq, although he was presented as such because he belonged to the same Hanan dynasty. His original name was Hatun Tupaq Inca; he was renamed after the creator deity Wiraqucha after seeing visions of the god in Urcos.

His wife was Mama Runtu, and their sons included Inca Roca, Tupac Yupanqui, Pachacuti and Capac Yupanqui. With Curi chulpa he had two more sons, Inca Urco and Inca Socso. Spanish writers recorded events of his life, among them Juan de Betanzos, whose account lies closest to the original indigenous ones, the Jesuit Bernabe Cobo and Miguel Cabello Balboa, who describes him as a warlike and valiant prince. As a young man he is said to have declared that once on the throne he would conquer half the world.

The chronicler Sarmiento de Gamboa states that Wiraqucha was the first Inca to rule the territories he conquered, while his predecessors had merely raided and looted them. His captains Apu Mayta and Vicaquirau subdued the area within eight leagues of Cusco.

According to Cobo, the Chanka offensive came in 1438. Wiraqucha was advised to leave Cusco before the attack and went to Caquia Xaquixahuana, taking his sons Inca Urco and Inca Socso. His son Cusi Inca Yupanqui, later the emperor Pachakuti, refused to abandon Cusco and the House of the Sun. He stayed with his brother Inca Rocca and six other chiefs, and together they defeated the Chankas. The spoils were offered to Wiraqucha to tread on, but he declined and said that Inca Urco should do so as his successor. Inca Rocca later killed Urco, and Wiraqucha died of grief at Caquia Xaquixahuana.
virata: Virata was the king of Matsya in the Mahabharata and the titular character of its fourth book, the Virata Parva, which recounts the Pandavas’ year of incognito exile in his kingdom. The epic is a composite work revised and interpolated over many centuries, the oldest parts of the surviving text perhaps dating to near 400 BCE, and its manuscripts differ, the Southern recension being longer.

He is described as born from a portion of the celestial Maruts. He married Sudeshna, daughter of King Suta of Kekaya, and had two sons, Shankha and Uttara, and a daughter, Uttara. Her brother Kichaka became commander-in-chief of the Matsya army. The Southern edition gives him an earlier wife, Suratha of Kosala, and a son named Shveta. In the Adi Parva he appears at the svayamvara of Draupadi, and he was defeated by Sahadeva in his conquests before Yudhishthira’s Rajasuya sacrifice, yet attended it and gave 2,000 elephants.

In the Virata Parva he unknowingly shelters the Pandavas. Yudhishthira becomes Kanka, his court companion, Bhima the overseer of the kitchen, Arjuna the dance instructor Brihannala, Nakula a stable hand, Sahadeva a cattle keeper, and Draupadi a maid to Queen Sudeshna. The translator J. A. B. van Buitenen describes Virata as a somewhat comical and ineffectual figure, a cattle baron more interested in his livestock than in statecraft, while Kichaka effectively controls the palace.

When Bhima kills Kichaka, Virata is shaken and fears reprisals. The Trigartas under King Susharman then raid Matsya; Virata mobilises the whole army, is captured, and is rescued by Bhima. Meanwhile the Kauravas raid 60,000 cattle from the north, and his son Uttara, with Arjuna as charioteer, is sent against them. Virata wrongly credits Uttara with the victory and in anger throws dice at Yudhishthira, wounding his nose. Two days later the Pandavas reveal themselves. Virata offers his daughter to Arjuna, who proposes her marriage to his son Abhimanyu, and the wedding takes place at Upaplavya.

In the Kurukshetra War Virata was one of seven commanders of Yudhishthira’s army; Sahadeva favoured him as commander-in-chief but he was outvoted in favour of Dhrishtadyumna. He fought Bhagadatta, attacked Bhishma and clashed with Ashwatthama, Jayadratha and Shalya. When Drona killed his son Shankha he fled the field, and he was finally killed by Drona. His funeral was conducted with full honours, Yudhishthira made offerings to his spirit, and according to the Svargarohana Parva he ascended to heaven and rejoined the Maruts.
virbhadra-singh: Virbhadra Singh was born on 23 June 1934 at Sarahan, in Shimla district, into the royal Rajput family of Bushahr. He was the 122nd titular Raja of Bushahr from 1947 until 1971, when the 26th Amendment to the Constitution of India abolished the privy purses of the princes and ended official recognition of their titles. He was still known by the honorific Raja Sahib.

He was educated at Colonel Brown Cambridge School in Dehradun and at St. Edward's School and Bishop Cotton School in Shimla, and took a BA Honours degree at St. Stephen's College, Delhi. In 1954 he married Ratna Kumari, princess of Jubbal, who died in 1983; in 1985 he married Pratibha Singh, princess of Keonthal, who was herself later elected to the Lok Sabha from Mandi.

Singh first entered the Lok Sabha in 1962 and was returned in 1967, 1971, 1980 and 2009. He served in the governments of Indira Gandhi and Manmohan Singh: as Deputy Minister for Tourism and Civil Aviation in 1976-1977, Minister of State for Industries from 1980 to 1983, Minister for Steel from May 2009 to January 2011, and then minister for Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises until June 2012.

In state politics he entered the Himachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly at a by-election in October 1983 for Jubbal-Kotkhai, later sitting for Rohru and from 2012 for Shimla rural. He was first Chief Minister from April 1983 to March 1990, again from December 1993 to March 1998, and from March 2003; between 1998 and 2003 he was Leader of the Opposition. He led the Congress to victory in November 2012 and resigned after the party lost its majority in 2017.

His career was shadowed by corruption cases. A case registered in 2009 by the state Anti-Corruption Bureau led to his resignation from the Union Cabinet on 26 June 2012; he and his wife were acquitted that December. In 2015 the Central Bureau of Investigation filed a case alleging assets disproportionate to his income while a union minister.

Singh suffered a cardiac arrest on 5 July 2021 at Indira Gandhi Medical College, Shimla, after testing positive for COVID-19 a second time in June, and died of multiple organ failure on 8 July 2021, still sitting as the member for Arki. The state observed three days of mourning, and he was cremated with full state honours at Rampur Bushahr on 10 July. Over 21 years in office he remained the longest-serving Chief Minister of Himachal Pradesh.
virgil: Biographical information about Virgil comes chiefly from ancient vitae, or lives, prefixed to commentaries on his work by Probus, Donatus and Servius. The life given by Donatus is thought to reproduce closely a lost life by Suetonius. Some of this evidence relies on allegory and on inferences drawn from his poetry, so details of his life are considered somewhat problematic.

According to the vitae, Publius Vergilius Maro was born on 15 October 70 BCE in the village of Andes, near Mantua in Cisalpine Gaul, in what is now northern Italy. His ancestry is uncertain, and scholars have proposed Etruscan, Celtic, Venetic, Ligurian or Greek origins. Most sources say his father was an employee of an apparitor named Magius, whose daughter he married. Phocas and Probus give his mother's name as Magia Polla. Confusion between the family name Magius and the noun magus, 'magician', probably contributed to the medieval legend that Virgil was a magician.

The commentators say Virgil began school at five and later went to Cremona, Milan and finally Rome to study rhetoric, medicine and astronomy, which he abandoned for philosophy. His admiring references to Asinius Pollio and Cinna have led scholars to infer that he was for a time associated with the neoteric circle of Catullus. According to the Catalepton, he began to write poetry while in the Epicurean school of Siro in Naples. A group of small works attributed to him by the commentators, the Appendix Vergiliana, is considered spurious by modern scholars, with the possible exception of some short pieces.

The Eclogues are ten poems in dactylic hexameter, roughly modelled on the pastoral poetry of the Hellenistic poet Theocritus. Eclogues 1 and 9 address the land confiscations and their effects on the Italian countryside. Eclogue 4, addressed to Asinius Pollio and called the Messianic Eclogue, uses the imagery of a golden age in connection with the birth of a child whose identity has been debated. Virgil is credited with establishing Arcadia as a poetic ideal. Modern scholars largely reject attempts to draw his biography from the characters of the poems.

His works revolutionised Latin poetry almost from publication, and the Eclogues, Georgics and above all the Aeneid became standard school texts. Ovid parodied the opening of the Aeneid, Lucan wrote an anti-Virgilian epic, and Statius and Silius Italicus engaged closely with him. Servius, a commentator of the 4th century CE, based his work on that of Donatus. Augustine of Hippo confessed that he had wept at reading the death of Dido. In the Divine Comedy Dante presents Virgil as his guide through Hell and most of Purgatory.
virgin-gorda: Virgin Gorda lies at about 18 degrees 30 minutes north and 64 degrees 30 minutes west and covers about 8 square miles, or 21 square kilometres. After Tortola and Anegada it is the third-largest of the British Virgin Islands, and it is the second most populous. The main commercial and residential area is Spanish Town, on the south-western part of the island. At the southern end the Baths is an unusual geological formation: huge granite boulders lie in piles on the beach, forming grottoes open to the sea. Granite is an intrusive rock formed deep underground, and it becomes visible only after long erosion removes the overlying material, after which weathering breaks it into rounded boulders.

The earliest known settlers were the Taíno, also called Arawak, who migrated from South America between 100 and 300 CE; evidence of their settlements has been found at Spanish Town. In the fifteenth century the Carib people displaced them. Christopher Columbus sighted the island in 1493 on his second voyage and is said to have named it Virgen Gorda, Spanish for fat virgin, because its profile on the horizon looks like a fat woman lying on her side. The Spanish claimed it with the other Virgin Islands but never settled it. The island was formerly called Paneston or Peniston, a corruption of Spanish Town.

In the sixteenth century North Sound served as a strategic anchorage for the British Navy. Sir John Hawkins visited in the 1560s with the young Francis Drake aboard, and Drake anchored there in 1585 before his raid on Santo Domingo. In 1595 twenty-six ships anchored in North Sound under Hawkins and Drake, and used the large hill at Bitter End to practise for their attack on San Juan. Both admirals died on that voyage, and Bitter End may be the last place on British soil where they set foot. In 1631 the Dutch West India Company funded a settlement, set up by Joost van Dyk, to mine copper.

North Sound, called Gorda Sound in the past, lies at the north-eastern end and is bordered by four islands and connected reef systems that keep over 3,000 acres of water calm. The most notable ruin on the island is the old copper mine. The Baths and the sound make it one of the main tourist destinations of the British Virgin Islands, and ferries from Tortola, St. Thomas and St. John serve it.
virgin-lands-campaign: In September 1953 a Central Committee group of Nikita Khrushchev, two aides, two Pravda editors and an agricultural specialist met to assess the Soviet agricultural crisis. The Soviet Union had endured a famine in the early 1930s, and earlier in 1953 Georgy Malenkov had won credit for reforms that raised procurement prices, cut taxes and encouraged individual peasant plots. Khrushchev, irritated at this, proposed his own plan: the ploughing of 13 million hectares of uncultivated land by 1956, in the Volga's right bank, the northern Caucasus, Western Siberia and northern Kazakhstan. Molotov, Malenkov and Kaganovich opposed it as not feasible.

Rather than offer incentives to existing collective-farm workers, Khrushchev advertised the venture as a socialist adventure for Soviet youth, and in summer 1954 some 300,000 Komsomol volunteers went. The first harvest was 65 percent above the average of 1949 to 1953, and by the start of 1955 some 200,000 tractors had arrived, 425 new state farms had been created and 30 million hectares had been ploughed. Khrushchev then raised his target to between 28 and 30 million hectares. In 1955 drought cut Kazakhstan's harvest by 35 percent; 1956 brought the largest harvest in Soviet history to that point, and 1957 a failure.

In 1960 a new administrative unit, Tselinny Krai, was formed from five provinces of northern Kazakhstan, and its capital Akmolinsk was renamed Tselinograd. Yields declined after 1958, and in 1963 Khrushchev ordered 60 new fertilizer factories, yet the record of 1956 was never matched.

Housing and food shortages drove many workers away, and 14,000 of the 24,000 specialists sent to Kazakhstan between 1957 and 1960 left. Machinery, repair shops and grain storage were short. The land received 200 to 350 millimetres of rain a year, wind caused erosion, and grain on 83 percent of the cropland in 1958 and 1959 depleted the soil.

The campaign increased grain production and eased food shortages in the short term. From 1954 to 1960 the sown area of the Soviet Union grew by 46 million hectares, 90 percent of the increase from the campaign. Its wide swings, the failure to surpass 1956 and the decline after 1959 mark it as a failure, and it fell short of Khrushchev's aim of overtaking American grain output by 1960.

It left an environmental disaster of soil erosion on the Kazakh steppe and considerably changed the region's demographics. It also marked a permanent shift in the economy of northern Kazakhstan, where wheat was sown on almost twice as many hectares in 1998 as in 1953. A minor planet, 2111 Tselina, was named in 1979 for the 25th anniversary of the campaign.
virginia: Virginia, officially the Commonwealth of Virginia, lies between the Atlantic coast and the Appalachian Mountains and borders Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina, West Virginia and Maryland. Central Virginia lies mostly in the Piedmont, the foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains, and the Shenandoah Valley holds the state's most productive farmland. Hampton Roads is the site of the region's main seaport and of Naval Station Norfolk.

Hunter-gatherers are estimated to have reached Virginia about 17,000 years ago, and Daugherty's Cave was in regular use as a rock shelter by 9,800 years ago. Farming spread in the late Woodland period, between 500 and 1000 CE. In the 1500s the native population within the present boundaries reached about 50,000. From the 1570s some thirty tribes of Tsenacommacah consolidated under Wahunsenacawh, commonly called Chief Powhatan, forming the Powhatan Confederacy, which governed more than 150 settlements with about 15,000 people in 1607. Three-quarters of the native population died of smallpox and other Old World diseases during that century.

In 1607 the London Company founded the Colony of Virginia, the first permanent English colony in the New World, which gave the state its nickname of the Old Dominion. Enslaved people from Africa and land taken from displaced native peoples fed the plantation economy and also fuelled conflict. The first General Assembly met in July 1619 and is the oldest lawmaking body in North America. Virginians fought in the American Revolution. In the American Civil War the state government in Richmond joined the Confederacy, while many north-western counties stayed loyal to the Union, which led to the separation of West Virginia in 1863.

The capital is Richmond and the most populous city is Virginia Beach; more than a third of the state's people live in Northern Virginia. The 2020 census counted 8,631,393 residents. The state's motto is Sic Semper Tyrannis, Thus Always to Tyrants. Eight Virginians have been President of the United States, including four of the first five, which gave it the name Mother of Presidents. It is governed under its seventh constitution, approved in 1970.
virginia-declaration-of-rights: The Declaration was adopted unanimously by the Fifth Virginia Convention at Williamsburg on 12 June 1776, as a document separate from the Constitution of Virginia, which followed on 29 June 1776. George Mason drafted ten articles at about 20 to 26 May 1776, and three more were added in committee, in the handwriting of Thomas Ludwell Lee, though their author is unknown. James Madison proposed liberalising the clause on religious freedom, and the convention made further changes. Patrick Henry persuaded it to delete a ban on bills of attainder.

Mason based his draft on the English Bill of Rights of 1689 and the writings of John Locke. Edmund Pendleton proposed the phrase when they enter into a state of society, which let slave holders support a declaration of universal rights that would be understood not to apply to slaves, who were not part of civil society. Mason owned over 100 slaves at the time.

The Declaration has sixteen articles on the rights that pertain to the people of Virginia as the basis and foundation of government. Article 1 holds that all men are by nature equally free and independent and have inherent rights, namely life and liberty, with the means of acquiring property, and pursuing happiness and safety. Articles 2 and 3 say that all power derives from the people and that a majority has a right to reform, alter or abolish an inadequate government. Article 4 rejects hereditary offices and exclusive privileges.

Articles 5 and 6 call for separate legislative, executive and judicial powers and for frequent, certain and regular elections. The later articles limit the government's powers and establish rights to confront accusers and to a speedy trial by an impartial jury, protection against self-incrimination, excessive bail and cruel and unusual punishments, and a ban on general warrants. Article 12 is the first codification of the right to a free press, and Article 16 holds that all men are equally entitled to the free exercise of religion.

The Declaration was incorporated into the Virginia Constitution in 1830 as Article I, and a slightly updated version remains in it. The Committee of Five is thought to have drawn on it for the Declaration of Independence in June 1776, and Madison was influenced by it when drafting the Bill of Rights, introduced in September 1789 and ratified in 1791.

Before the American Civil War, the delegates of Virginia's western counties at the Wheeling Convention cited it against the state's Ordinance of Secession, arguing that a change in the form of government needed a referendum. This set in motion the events by which the western counties became the separate state of West Virginia.
viriathus: Little is known about Viriathus. The only reference to the location of his native tribe is by the Greek historian Diodorus Siculus, who says he came from the Lusitanian tribes of the ocean side. He belonged to the warrior class of the ruling elites, and Livy described him as a shepherd who became a hunter and then a soldier. The Romans knew him as dux of the Lusitanian army or as its protector. Ancient writers describe a man of great physical strength and an excellent strategist, faithful to the treaties he made.

Appian says he was one of the few who escaped when the Roman governor Servius Sulpicius Galba massacred the young Lusitanian warriors in 150 BCE, after luring them to give up their weapons under a treaty.

After the massacre the Lusitanians rebelled and waged war for three years, meeting many failures, until Viriathus appeared and offered himself as leader. When a Roman force under the praetor Caius Vetilius surrounded Lusitanian warriors, he proposed an escape plan and was made their commander. At Tribola he defeated Vetilius, killing 4,000 of 10,000 soldiers, and further Roman armies were defeated. He also inspired the Numantine people and some Gauls to rebel.

Polybius called the conflict the War of Fire, and many authors regard Viriathus as the model of the guerrilla fighter. After an ambush near Sierra Morena, the Roman general Quintus Fabius Maximus Servilianus was released in exchange for a treaty recognising Lusitanian rule over the land they held, and the Senate declared Viriathus a friend of the Roman people.

Quintus Servilius Caepio, who succeeded his brother Servilianus, thought the treaty dishonourable, and the Senate authorised him to harass Viriathus and finally to declare war. According to Appian, Caepio bribed Audax, Ditalcus and Minurus, whom Viriathus had sent as an embassy to make peace, and they killed him in his sleep. The Lusitanians kept fighting under Tautalus. Viriathus became an enduring symbol of Portuguese nationality and independence, and Luís Vaz de Camões praises his deeds in Os Lusíadas.
viroconium-cornoviorum: The site lies about 8 km east-south-east of Shrewsbury, near the end of Watling Street, the main Roman road across Britannia from Dubris (Dover). It guarded the valley of the River Severn where it comes out of Wales and the route south to the Wye valley. Its name is a Latinised form of a Common Brittonic place name reconstructed as *Uiroconion, the city of *Uirokū, a man's name meaning man-wolf; the Cornovii's original capital of that name was the hillfort on the Wrekin.

The first post held a cohort of Thracian auxiliaries during the campaigns of the governor Publius Ostorius Scapula. Legio XIV Gemina replaced it with a larger legionary fortress ahead of the invasion of Wales, and after Gnaeus Julius Agricola took that legion north in 80, Legio XX Valeria Victrix held the fortress until it moved to Deva Victrix (Chester) in the late 80s. The civilian settlement around the fort then grew into a town, and an unfinished legionary bath house became its forum.

The colonnaded forum, begun in the 120s, carried a dedicatory inscription to Emperor Hadrian dated to 130. The town came to cover more than 70 ha and is estimated to have had over 15,000 people, which made it the fourth-largest Roman settlement in Britain. Between 165 and 185 the forum burned down with neighbouring shops and houses and was rebuilt.

Urban life went on into the 5th century; the Cunorix Stone, a gravestone in partly Latinised Primitive Irish probably of 460-475, dates from then. Between 530 and 570 the old basilica was demolished and replaced by 33 timber-framed buildings on rubble platforms, built to Roman measurements, perhaps on a bishop's initiative. The site was probably abandoned peacefully in the later 7th or early 8th century, and in 656 Oswiu's conquest made the area part of the Wreocensæte, a sub-kingdom of the Angles.

A corner of the city is now the village of Wroxeter.
