English Heritage cares for the remains as Wroxeter Roman City, with a small museum; they include the Old Work, part of the baths' frigidarium and the largest free-standing Roman ruin in England. Most of the town is still buried but has been mapped by geophysical survey and aerial archaeology, and a reconstructed Roman villa opened in February 2011.
virunum: The town's full name was Municipium Claudium Virunum. It may have taken its name from the hilltop settlement on the Magdalensberg, widely believed to have been the royal capital of the pre-Roman Celtic kingdom of Noricum. It stood on a flood-proof terrace on the main route from the Adriatic to the Danube, with a branch to the Amber Road, and its territory covered about 9,000 square kilometres of central and lower Carinthia and parts of Styria. The city had the Latin Right, and its council, magistrates and dual mayors are known in part by name.

Virunum was the seat of the provincial governor until the middle of the 2nd century. After the Marcomannic Wars the administration moved to Ovilava, now Wels, though the province's finances stayed in Virunum, and when Emperor Diocletian divided Noricum it became the capital of Noricum mediterraneum. It was a bishop's see from 343. Unfortified and on a flat valley floor, the city was probably partly or wholly left by its people for nearby hills such as the Ulrichsberg, and in the 5th century Teurnia is named as the capital of Noricum.

The city covered about one square kilometre on a checkerboard plan. Digging began in the 18th century, with systematic excavations from the end of the 19th century to 1931 and again from the end of the 20th, which uncovered the amphitheatre. Finds include the forum and Capitolium, a Dionysus mosaic of almost 30 square metres, a sanctuary of Jupiter Dolichenus, inscriptions from two Mithraea, votive plates from a temple of Nemesis and an early Christian church. On the slope of Töltschach Hill stood an amphitheatre and the only Roman theatre with a stage known in Noricum.

Roman stones from Virunum are built into the Prunnerkreuz, a small shrine of 1692 put up by Johann Dominikus Prunner, who believed the town had been called Sala. Virunum is today a Catholic titular see, and in summer its amphitheatre is used for historical re-enactments with the Carinthian State Museum.
visayas: The Visayas are one of the three principal geographical divisions of the Philippines, along with Luzon and Mindanao. They lie in the central part of the archipelago, mostly around the Visayan Sea, which is also considered the northeast extremity of the Sulu Sea. The region has a land area of 71,503 km2 and consists of seven large and several hundred smaller islands, among them Guimaras, Biliran, Siquijor, Panaon and Bantayan. Palawan, Romblon and Masbate may also be included, since their populations identify as Visayan.

The origin of the name is unknown. A possible first documented use is by the Song-era Chinese maritime official Zhao Rugua, who wrote of the Pi-sho-ye raiding the coasts of Fujian and Penghu in the late 12th century. The Spanish first called the Visayans Pintados, the painted ones, for their full-body tattooing. In his Sucesos de las Islas Filipinas of 1609, Antonio de Morga described them as skilful in navigation and eager for war and raids for plunder, which they called mangubas.

After the Magellan expedition was defeated at the Battle of Mactan by Lapu-Lapu, King Philip II of Spain sent Miguel López de Legazpi to colonise the islands. Many of the local kingdoms began to convert to Christianity, and Spanish and Mexican conquistadors received encomiendas, chiefly on Panay and Cebu; Cristóbal Sánchez, for example, held about 3000 Cebuano tributaries. Resistance followed, including the Tamblot Uprising of 1621 to 1622 and the Bohol Rebellion led by Francisco Dagohoy, which lasted from 1744 to 1829. During the Philippine Revolution the short-lived Federal State of the Visayas took Iloilo City as its capital.

The Visayas are divided into four administrative regions, Western Visayas, Central Visayas, Eastern Visayas and the Negros Island Region, with sixteen provinces. Cebu City, Bacolod and Iloilo are among the largest cities. The main languages are Cebuano, Hiligaynon and Waray, with Aklanon, Kinaray-a and Capiznon also widely spoken; Cebuano alone has about 20 million speakers. The Sinulog festival in Cebu City, the Ati-Atihan in Kalibo and the Dinagyang in Iloilo City, all held in January, honour the Santo Niño.
visegrad: Visegrád is a castle town in Pest County, north of Budapest on the right bank of the Danube in the Danube Bend. The name is of Slavic origin and means acropolis, literally upper castle or upper settlement; in Czech and Slovak it is Vyšehrad, and in German Plintenburg. A fortification on Sibrik Hill, just to the north, was built in the first half of the 4th century as part of the Roman frontier along the Danube. The Roman army abandoned it in the early 5th century.

In the 10th and 11th centuries the fortification, rebuilt as a castle, became a regional centre of the new Hungarian state, and the name Visegrád first appears in 1009. The Mongol invasion of 1242 destroyed it, and the town was rebuilt a little to the south, with a new fortification system built by King Béla IV in the 1240s and 1250s. King Charles I made Visegrád the royal seat in 1325.

In 1335 Charles hosted a two-month congress with the Bohemian king, John of Luxembourg, and the Polish king, Casimir III. It was crucial in creating peace between the three kingdoms and an alliance between Poland and Hungary against Habsburg Austria, and another congress followed in 1339. Sigismund moved the royal seat to Buda between 1405 and 1408, and Matthias Corvinus later used Visegrád as a country residence.

The palace was laid out on a square plan of 123 by 123 metres under Louis I and Sigismund, and between 1477 and 1484 Matthias Corvinus had it reconstructed, with Italian Renaissance decoration used for the first time in Europe outside Italy. The Ottomans took Visegrád in 1544, after which the palace fell into ruins and was covered by earth by the 18th century. Excavation began in 1934. The Upper Castle and the Solomon Tower, a hexagonal 13th-century residential tower, are open to visitors.
On 15 February 1991 Václav Havel, Lech Wałęsa and József Antall met there and founded the Visegrád Group, alluding to the meeting of 1335. Visegrád was granted town privileges again in 2000.
visegrad-group: The name refers to the Congress of Visegrád of 1335, where Charles I of Hungary, Casimir III of Poland and John I of Bohemia agreed to create new commercial routes bypassing Vienna, a staple port that required goods to be offered for sale in the city. The congress also confirmed Czech sovereignty over the Duchy of Silesia. A second congress in 1339 decided that if Casimir died without a son, as happened in 1370, Louis I of Hungary, son of Charles I, would become King of Poland.

From the 16th century large parts of the later members' territories came under the Habsburg monarchy, until Austria-Hungary dissolved in 1918. After 1945 the three countries became Soviet satellite states: the Polish People's Republic, the Hungarian People's Republic and the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. Communism fell in central and eastern Europe in 1989.

The group was founded on 15 February 1991 at a meeting in Visegrád of Václav Havel, president of the Czech and Slovak Federative Republic, Lech Wałęsa, president of Poland, and József Antall, prime minister of Hungary. Its aim was to move away from communism and carry out the reforms needed for full membership of Euro-Atlantic institutions such as NATO and the European Union. After Czechoslovakia dissolved in 1993, the Czech Republic and Slovakia became separate members, raising the number from three to four. All four joined the European Union on 1 May 2004, achieving the group's main goal, and the Schengen Area in 2007.

After 2004 the group concentrated on cultural cooperation and on expert-level work on topics such as infrastructure. In 2011 Poland's defence minister announced a Visegrád EU Battlegroup, which stood on standby in 2016, and a patent institute was created by an agreement signed in Bratislava on 26 February 2015.

The International Visegrád Fund is the group's only institutionalised form of cooperation. It supports regional non-governmental initiatives to strengthen ties among people and institutions in Central and Eastern Europe, and Ukraine has been one of its largest recipients. The group has also served as a model: the Craiova Group of Bulgaria, Romania and Serbia, established in 2015, was inspired by it. Its members share a close trading relationship with Germany, particularly in car manufacturing, and the group's networking among public servants and civil society actors has outlasted changes of government.
viseslav-of-serbia: Višeslav is known from the De Administrando Imperio, compiled in the mid-10th century under the Byzantine emperor Constantine VII, which drew on a Serbian source among others. It tells of an unnamed 7th-century Serbian ruler who led his people from the north to the Balkans under the protection of Emperor Heraclius and founded a hereditary rule, the throne passing to the first-born son. The names of this prince's descendants are unknown until Višeslav, whom the work spells Boïsesthlabos. Since the 19th century historians have divided between reading the name as Višeslav, greater glory, and as Vojislav, war glory.

Višeslav ruled around 780, as a contemporary of the Frankish ruler Charlemagne. Serbia was then a Slavic principality in the western Balkans, subject to the Byzantine Empire and bordering on Bulgaria in the east; its ruler bore the title archon of Serbia, and its exact borders are unclear. The Serbs were organised into župe, confederations of village communities roughly equivalent to counties, each headed by a hereditary župan who answered to the ruler and served in his army. Although the work gives only Višeslav's name, it records that the Serbs of that time were allied to the emperor and at war with the neighbouring Bulgars.

Višeslav was succeeded by his son Radoslav and then by his grandson Prosigoj, one of whom most likely ruled during the revolt of Ljudevit of Lower Pannonia against the Franks between 819 and 822. His great-grandson Vlastimir began his rule in April 830 and is the oldest Serbian ruler shown on a fresco. The dynasty, known in historiography as the Vlastimirović dynasty, ruled the Principality of Serbia until around 960. An illustration of Višeslav appears in Kosta Mandrović's work of 1885, and a street in the Čukarica neighbourhood of Belgrade bears his name.
vishnu: Vishnu is a Rigvedic solar deity, but he does not figure prominently in the Rigveda compared with Indra and Agni: only five of its 1,028 hymns are dedicated to him. Some scholars, among them F. B. J. Kuiper and Jan Gonda, argue that he must have been a more important figure than his infrequent appearances suggest. He rose to prominence in the Brahmana layer of the Vedas in the mid-first millennium BCE. In the last centuries BCE and the early centuries CE he was identified with local traditions and deities, particularly the Bhagavata deities Vasudeva-Krishna and Gopala-Krishna and the Pancharatra deity Narayana, and became a divinity of the highest rank, equivalent to the Supreme Being.

Vishnu is the Supreme Being within Vaishnavism and the preserver in the Trimurti, the triad that includes Brahma and Shiva. His name means all pervasive. In Vaishnava belief he creates, protects and transforms the universe, and he is depicted sleeping on the coils of the serpent Shesha in the primeval ocean of milk with his consort Lakshmi. Whenever the world is threatened with evil he descends as an avatar to restore the cosmic order and protect dharma. The Dashavatara are the ten primary avatars, of which Rama and Krishna are the most worshipped.

In iconography he has dark blue, blue-grey or black skin and is usually shown with four arms, wearing jewels. When he descends as Rama and Krishna, Lakshmi appears as Sita and Radha or Rukmini. His mount is the eagle Garuda.

Vishnu is the main subject of the Vaishnava Puranas, of which the most important are the Bhagavata Purana, Vishnu Purana, Nāradeya Purana, Garuda Purana and Vayu Purana. The Tamil Sangam literature, mostly from the early centuries CE, reveres him as Mayon, the dark one. Ideas about Vishnu became important to the Bhakti movement, which swept India after the 12th century. The Alvars, Tamil Vaishnava poet-saints, sang his praises as they travelled and established temple sites such as Srirangam, and their poems were compiled as the Divya Prabhandham.
vishnuvardhana: Originally a Jain known as Bitti-deva, Vishnuvardhana governed parts of Gangavadi under his elder brother, King Veera Ballala I, and succeeded him on his death in 1108. The Cholas had destroyed Jain temple complexes around Talakadu, and his first great campaign was to recover the parts of Gangavadi occupied by the Cholas. The historian Kamath suggests that the Chola governor Adigaiman, a Vaishnava who may have been badly treated by King Kulothunga Chola I, helped him, while Sastri holds that Vishnuvardhana defeated Adigaiman before winning his support.

By about 1117 he had also defeated the Chengalvas, the Kongalvas and the Nidugal Chola ruler Irukkavela, and the Nolambas, the Kadambas of Banavasi and Goa, the Alupas of Mangaluru and the Santaras of Hosagunda accepted him as overlord. Inscriptions record his crossing of the Nilgiris and call him master of Kerala, and he took the titles Talakadugonda, Lord of Talakad, and Nolambavadi gonda.

He then turned north against his overlord, the Western Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI, fighting at Kannegala around 1118 and Hallur around 1120, but by the Krishna River around 1122 he was defeated by the Sinda chief Achugi and had to accept Chalukya overlordship for a time. After Vikramaditya's death he retook Hanagal, Uchchangi and Bankapura by about 1140 and reached Lakkundi. The historian Majumdar holds that he performed the Tulapurusha ceremony, a mark of sovereignty, around 1131.

Vishnuvardhana later came under the influence of Ramanujacharya, who gave him the name by which he is known, though his queen Shantala Devi and his family remained devotees of Jainism. To mark his victories over the Cholas he built Jain temples at Kambadahalli and Shravanbelgola as well as the Chennakesava Temple at Belur, also called the Vijayanarayana temple; Shantaladevi built the smaller Kappe Chennigaraya temple within its complex. The temples of Belur and Halebidu have been accorded UNESCO World Heritage Site status. Kannada writers flourished under his patronage: the mathematician Rajaditya wrote the Vyavaharaganita, and according to E. P. Rice the poet Nagachandra wrote the earliest surviving Jain Ramayana in Kannada, the Ramachandra charita purana.
visigothic-code: In the first centuries of Visigothic rule, Romans and Goths lived under different laws. The earliest known Visigothic laws, the Code of Euric, were compiled by about 480, and the Breviary of Alaric, based on Roman imperial law and meant for the Roman majority, was promulgated at a gathering of nobles in Toulouse on 2 February 506. King Leovigild attempted a revised code for both peoples, and after the Visigoths gave up Arianism for Catholicism at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, King Reccared issued laws that applied equally to both.

The code itself was begun by King Chindasuinth in the second year of his reign, 642–643, but his text had been hastily written, and the version his son Recceswinth published was edited by Braulio of Zaragoza. Later kings, Wamba, Erwig, Egica and perhaps Wittiza, added laws of their own; Erwig's revision at the Twelfth Council of Toledo in 681 included 28 new laws dealing with Jews.

The code is arranged in twelve books, from the lawmaker and the conduct of trials through marriage, inheritance, contracts, crimes, theft, violence, fugitives and boundaries to physicians, the dead and merchants from overseas. It fused Roman and Germanic law, abolished the separate laws for romani and gothi so that all subjects became hispani, and absorbed much of the Catholic Church's canon law, which gives it a strongly theocratic tone. Women could inherit land and titles, manage property apart from their husbands, make wills if they had no heirs, testify in court from the age of 14 and arrange their own marriages from 20. Its last book is directed against heretics and Jews.

The laws stayed in force long after the kingdom fell. Monastic charters in 10th-century Galicia refer to them, and under Muslim rule Christians were allowed their own law in return for paying the jizya, so the code probably remained the authority of Christian magistrates. After Ferdinand III of Castile took Córdoba he ordered it observed and translated, inaccurately, as the Fuero Juzgo. Its Occitan translation, the Llibre Jutge of about 1050, is among the oldest texts in that language. Samuel Parsons Scott's English translation of 1910 was severely criticised.
visigoths: The Visigoths emerged from the Gothic tribes, probably descended from the Thervingi, whose name may mean forest people. Gothic tradition, on which the account of their origins largely rests, places the Goths' beginnings in Scandinavia, with a migration south-east to the Black Sea, though archaeology does not support that legend.

The name Visigoths was apparently coined by the writer Cassiodorus about 507, on the model of Ostrogoths, from the older tribal name Vesi, which is Gothic for good. Until then they were called simply Goths. They spoke an eastern Germanic language that was distinct by the 4th century. They had been Christianized while still outside the empire, but adopted Arianism rather than the Nicene version followed by most Romans, who considered them heretics.

In 376 the Gothic leader Fritigern asked the Eastern Roman Emperor Valens to let his people settle south of the Danube, seeking refuge from the Huns. Famine followed, and the Romans abused the Goths, even forcing them to trade away their children, which led to revolt and six years of plundering in the Balkans.

At the Battle of Adrianople in 378 the Roman army was slaughtered and Valens was killed. Alaric I led the Visigoths from 395. In 397 Arcadius named him military commander of the eastern Illyrian prefecture, and the sack of Rome in 410 followed. In 418 Honorius settled the Visigoths in Gallia Aquitania, where a kingdom grew with its capital at Toulouse, and they later expanded into Hispania.

Defeat by the Franks under Clovis I at the Battle of Vouillé in 507 ended Visigothic rule in Gaul, but the kingdom endured in Spain and Portugal. King Liuvigild (568 to 586) failed to unite Arian and Catholic subjects, and Reccared I converted to Catholicism, a step confirmed at the Third Council of Toledo in 589. The kingdom collapsed in 711 after defeat by an Umayyad army at the Battle of Guadalete, where King Roderic was killed.

The Visigothic Code, set in writing in 654 under Chindasuinth, abolished separate laws for Romans and Goths, so that all subjects became hispani, and it protected the property rights of married women. Surviving churches include San Pedro de la Nave, and Reccopolis, founded by Liuvigild to honour his son Reccared, is an archaeological site. The Treasure of Guarrazar, twenty-six votive crowns and gold crosses from the royal workshop in Toledo, shows the high point of Visigothic goldsmithery. After 711 the Kingdom of Asturias arose under Pelagius, marking the start of the Reconquista.
visoko: Visoko lies between Zenica and Sarajevo where the Fojnica joins the Bosna, in a fertile basin ringed by the foothills of the Central Bosnian mountains. The name comes from the Slavic adjective visok, high, and refers to the fortress of Visoki on Visočica hill, first mentioned in a charter of Ban Tvrtko I in 1355. Before that the region around the valley was commonly called simply Bosna, and the settlement below the fortress was known as Podvisoki, below Visoki. Traces of settlement go back to the 5th millennium BCE, and at Okolište one of the largest Neolithic settlements of the Butmir culture in south-eastern Europe was found, with perhaps 3,000 people.

The Daesitiates inhabited the area in antiquity, and the Roman Empire established its rule in 9 CE. The Visoko basin is considered the nucleus of the Bosnian state, which emerged around 1000. Podvisoki, Mile, Biskupići and Moštre together formed the Visoko valley, where many charters were written. Podvisoki, protected by the fortress, was long the main trade centre of medieval Bosnia. At Mile the Rusag, the assembly, met; Tvrtko I was buried there beside his uncle Stjepan II Kotromanić, and Ban Kulin's Plate, dated 1193, was found at Biskupići.

The Ottoman Empire conquered the area around 1463, and the modern town took shape then, its founder being Ajas-beg, a local who had converted to Islam. Up to 1477 he built a hammam, a school, an aqueduct, a bridge over the Bosna, a madrassa and a dervish tekke. Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878. On 11 November 1911 a fire burned down the upper town and the main street, about 450 buildings in all, and rebuilding began in 1912 in brick and tile in a traditional Bosnian style.

Six national monuments of Bosnia and Herzegovina stand in Visoko, among them the Old town of Visoki, Mile, the Okolište settlement and the Franciscan monastery of Saint Bonaventure. Šerefudin's White Mosque, by the architect Zlatko Ugljen, received the Aga Khan Award for Architecture in 1983. Visoko has long been known for leather, and before the Bosnian War it was the largest exporter of textiles and leather in socialist Yugoslavia. In 2005 Semir Osmanagić claimed that Visočica and nearby hills concealed pyramids; scientific investigation found no pyramid.
vistula: The Vistula is 1,047 km long and the longest river draining into the Baltic Sea. It rises at Barania Góra in the Silesian Beskids, at 1,220 metres above sea level, and flows through Kraków, Sandomierz, Warsaw, Płock, Toruń, Bydgoszcz and Gdańsk. Near the sea it forms a wide delta, the Żuławy Wiślane, whose channels include the Nogat. Its basin covers 193,960 km2, of which 168,868 km2 lies in Poland. The river took its present shape within the last 14,000 years, after the Scandinavian ice sheet withdrew, and it gives its name to the last glaciation of northern Europe, the Vistulian or Weichselian.
The name first appears in Pomponius Mela in 40 CE and as Vistla in Pliny in 77 CE; Ptolemy wrote Ouistoula. It is often derived from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to ooze or flow slowly.

In the first millennium BCE large parts of the basin were occupied by the Iron Age Lusatian and Przeworsk cultures. Roman authors included the western part among the lands of Magna Germania, and Ptolemy in the 2nd century CE described the river as the border between Germania and Sarmatia. Slavs settled the estuary in the 7th and 8th centuries.

West Slavic Polish tribes formed small dominions from the 8th century, and the ninth-century document of the Bavarian Geographer lists the Vistulans in southern Poland, with Kraków and Wiślica as their main centres. Polish legend ties the river to the beginnings of the state: according to Jan Długosz, Princess Wanda, daughter of King Krak, drowned herself in it rather than marry a German prince.

For centuries the Vistula was one of Poland's main trading arteries, carrying salt, timber, grain and building stone between the 10th and 13th centuries. The Teutonic Knights, invited in 1226 by Konrad I of Masovia, controlled the lower river in the 14th century and captured Gdańsk castle in 1308. In the 15th century Gdańsk became a great centre of trade. Grain shipped on the river rose from 14,000 in 1491 to 310,000 in 1618, and Gdańsk, at the river's end, became the wealthiest and largest centre of crafts in the country.

The river is associated with Polish culture and national identity, flows through the two main cities, Kraków and Warsaw, and gives the phrase Land on the Vistula, which can mean Poland. It is navigable from the Baltic to Bydgoszcz, though navigation upstream is limited. Severe floods over the centuries sometimes depopulated land in the delta, which had to be resettled.
vistula-lagoon: The Vistula Lagoon is a brackish lagoon on the Baltic Sea roughly 90 kilometres long, 10 to 24 kilometres wide and up to 5 metres deep, separated from the Gdańsk Bay by the Vistula Spit. It is the mouth of a few branches of the Vistula River, notably the Nogat and Szkarpawa, and of the Pregolya River. The Kursenieki, a nearly extinct ethnic group, lived on the Vistula Spit by the lagoon, and the surrounding area was inhabited by Poles, Germans and Kursenieki.

The earliest version of its name was recorded by Wulfstan of Hedeby at the end of the 9th century as Estmere, an Anglo-Saxon rendition of the Old Prussian Aīstinmari, meaning the lagoon or sea of the Aesti. In the first half of the 13th century deeds of the Teutonic Order call it in Latin Mare Recens, fresh sea, in contrast to the Baltic, the Mare Salsum. By 1288 the form Recenti Mari Hab corresponds with the German Frisches Haff. Its Russian name since 1946 is Kaliningradskiy zaliv, Kaliningrad Bay.

From the first half of the 13th century the lagoon was part of the State of the Teutonic Order. In 1454 King Casimir IV Jagiellon incorporated the region into the Kingdom of Poland at the request of the anti-Teutonic Prussian Confederation. After the peace treaty of 1466 the western part belonged to the Polish provinces of Royal Prussia and Greater Poland, and the eastern part was a Polish fief held by the Teutonic Knights and Ducal Prussia.

After the First Partition of Poland the territory formed part of the Kingdom of Prussia, which became part of the German Empire in 1871. From 1920 to 1939 it was split between Germany and the Free City of Danzig. In 1945 the western part, 43.8 percent, became part of Poland and the eastern part fell to the Soviet Union. That winter refugees from East Prussia crossed the frozen lagoon on their way west after the Red Army reached its coast near Elbing on 26 January. Attacked by Soviet aircraft, thousands were killed or fell through the broken ice.

The lagoon is divided between Poland, with Elbląg, Tolkmicko, Frombork and Krynica Morska, and Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast, with Kaliningrad, Baltiysk and Primorsk. Kaliningrad and Baltiysk are major seaports on it. It is an Important Bird Area of Poland.
visvaldis: The date of Visvaldis's birth is unknown, and his origins are unclear: some scholars think he was a son of Barys Davidavič, prince of Polotsk, and a Latgalian mother. The Livonian Chronicle of Henry calls him king. He was married to a daughter of the Lithuanian duke Daugerutis, which made him an ally of Lithuania as well as a vassal of the Principality of Polotsk. His seat was the Jersika hillfort on the River Daugava, the waterway that the newly arrived German crusaders also sought to control.

He first appears in the record in 1203, when he and the Lithuanians attacked the newly founded city of Riga. Between 1203 and 1208 they raided Livonian lands again and again, trying to win full control of the River Daugava. In 1209 Bishop Albert of Riga led German crusaders and an allied Livonian army against Jersika. They met little resistance, plundered the Jersika hillfort and took his wife prisoner. Visvaldis escaped, but he had to surrender, give his kingdom to the Bishopric of Riga and receive part of it back as a fief.

His feudal charter, which names him "Vissewalde, rex de Gercike", is the oldest such document to survive in Latvia. Because he still supported the Lithuanians, the German knight Meinhard from Koknese destroyed Jersika castle again in 1214. In later years his lands were divided again and again between Bishop Albert and the Livonian Brothers of the Sword. The date of his death is unknown and probably falls between 1230 and 1239; the chronicle describes the Jersika hillfort as abandoned in 1239.
vita-karoli-magni: Einhard received advanced schooling at the monastery of Fulda some time after 779. Word of his learning reached Charlemagne, who sent him to the Palace School at Aachen in 791. He found employment at the Frankish court about 796 and stayed for some twenty years, holding a position that has been likened to that of a modern minister of public works and receiving responsibility for many of the king's abbeys. He wrote the biography after he had left Aachen, while living at Seligenstadt.

The date of the work is uncertain. The will printed at its end shows that it was written after Charlemagne's death in 814, and the first reference to it is a letter to Einhard from Lupus of Ferrières, dated to the middle of the 9th century.

The work has 33 chapters. It begins with the genealogy of the Merovingian family, passes to the rise of the Carolingian dynasty, and briefly describes the kingship of Pepin the Short and the years of joint rule between Charlemagne and Carloman. A large part then goes through Charlemagne's wars. Einhard presents the conquests as justified and even righteous, and is often vague on how the campaigns went, giving instead the reasons they began and how they ended.

Einhard next describes Charlemagne's appearance and character at length, stressing his piety and moderation. He also discusses the king's children, and appears to explain that Charlemagne never let his daughters marry because he loved them too much to be parted from them. His short account of the rebellion of Pepin the Hunchback has been seen by many historians as revisionism, since much more is known about Pepin than Einhard says.

The last part covers the imperial coronation on Christmas Day 800, Charlemagne's death and will, and the succession of Louis the Pious. Einhard states that Charlemagne would not have entered the church that day had he foreseen the pope's design. Most modern historians conclude that Charlemagne must have known of the plan long beforehand.

Historians have traditionally described the work as the first biography of a European king. Einhard imitated the style of the Roman biographer Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, author of the Lives of the Caesars, and followed especially his life of the emperor Augustus.

Most medieval biographies recorded only the good deeds of their subjects, with embellishment. Einhard's is considered for the most part trustworthy, and the British historian Thomas Hodgkin wrote that almost all real knowledge of Charles the Great derives from Einhard and that the work is one of the most precious literary bequests of the early Middle Ages.
vitcos: The ruins, known locally as Rosaspata, stand on a ridge above the meeting of two small rivers and the village of Pucyura, in the Vilcabamba District of La Convención Province. The Vilcabamba region is very rugged, falling from the north-eastern slopes of the Andes to the Amazon Basin through snow-covered mountains, forest and deep river canyons. The Incas had occupied it since about 1450, with major centres at Vitcos, Machu Picchu, Choquequirao and Vilcabamba. At 2,980 metres Vitcos is higher and cooler than Vilcabamba, at 1,450 metres, and closer to the highland setting the Incas knew.

After winning the Battle of Ollantaytambo in January 1537, Manco Inca Yupanqui withdrew to Vitcos. In July 1537 Rodrigo Orgóñez, sent by Almagro with 300 Spaniards and many Indian allies, sacked it and took many prisoners, but Manco escaped, and he escaped again in 1539 from a raid by Gonzalo Pizarro, which captured his principal wife. Manco then built up Vilcabamba as a more remote refuge, but Vitcos remained a royal residence and a place of ceremonies, above all at the nearby shrine of Ñusta Hisp'ana.

In 1570 two Roman Catholic friars allowed to settle nearby led their congregation in an attack that damaged the shrine; one was expelled and the other killed, accused of poisoning Emperor Titu Cusi Yupanqui. His brother Tupac Amaru was more hostile to the Spaniards, and after his supporters killed an envoy of the viceroy, Francisco de Toledo, two armies of more than 300 Spaniards and 2,000 allies invaded. In June 1572 they took Vitcos, Vilcabamba and Tupac Amaru, ending the Neo-Inca State.

Its location was forgotten after the conquest. Hiram Bingham, searching for Vilcabamba in 1911, found the site by following the conquistadors' descriptions and mapped it briefly before going on to find Vilcabamba itself. The palace has an upper group of eight large rooms in four back-to-back pairs within a common outer wall, and below a terrace wall a lower group of a dozen or more buildings round a courtyard. In the 1980s Vincent Lee described more than thirty buildings and structures on the hill between Vitcos and Chuquipalta, among them kalankas, storehouses and a large usnu.
viti-levu: The name Viti Levu means Great Fiji. The island is 146 kilometres long and 106 kilometres wide. Fiji lies in a tectonically complex area between the Australian and Pacific plates, and earthquakes and volcanic eruptions account for the rugged terrain. A mountain range running north to south divides the island into roughly equal halves, and the forested centre includes the nation's highest peak, Mount Tomanivi, also called Mount Victoria, at 1,324 metres. Heavy rain falls on the eastern side, which has Fiji's tropical moist forests. The western side, colloquially called the burning west, lies in the range's rain shadow and is drier, with tropical dry forests and sugar cane.

Viti Levu is believed to have been inhabited longer than Vanua Levu, the island to its north. According to oral tradition, the first Melanesian settlers landed at Vuda Point and founded Viseisei as Fiji's oldest settlement, though archaeological evidence contradicts this account. Many of the ancestors of the Indo-Fijians, who are concentrated in the west, came to the island from India as indentured workers between 1879 and 1916. Indigenous Fijians predominate in the east, except in the cities, which are more mixed.

Viti Levu holds the capital and largest city of Fiji, Suva, and a large majority of the country's people. Other important towns spread along the coast include Ba, Lautoka, Nadi, Nausori, Rakiraki and Sigatoka. Eight of Fiji's fourteen provinces lie on the island. A single major road runs around its perimeter, and Nadi International Airport on the north-west side is the principal airport of Fiji. The island is the only known home of the Giant Fijian long-horned beetle, one of the world's largest insects.
vitoria-espirito-santo: Vitória lies on a small island within a bay where several rivers meet the sea, on the south-eastern coast of Brazil. The municipality of 93 square kilometres has the main island, another 34 islands and a mainland portion; there were originally 50 islands, many of them joined to the largest by landfill. It borders Serra, Cariacica and Vila Velha, and with them forms Greater Vitória. The central massif of the island, Morro da Fonte Grande, rises to 308.8 metres. The climate is tropical, and the city lies in the domain of the Atlantic Forest.

Vila Velha, the first capital of the Captaincy of Espírito Santo, suffered constant attacks from Tupi-Guarani-speaking and possibly some Macro-Jê-speaking indigenous peoples, and from the French and Dutch. The Portuguese therefore chose an island near the mainland, called Guanaani by some of the native peoples. Vila Nova do Espírito Santo was founded there on 8 September 1551 and later renamed Vitória, in memory of a victory won by the captaincy's holder, Vasco Fernandes Coutinho, against the Goytacaz. The city was built on the highlands, which produced narrow streets, and fortresses guarded the exposed lowlands along the coast.

Vitória became a city on 24 February 1823, but its isolation on an island held back its growth. From 1894, during the coffee cycle, landfills in the lower parts changed the shape of the island, new neighbourhoods were settled, public steps joined them to the high ground, old houses were pulled down and sanitation improved. A bridge to the mainland opened in 1927 and the first harbour pier followed in 1941. By 1970 the port ranked among the most important in the country and industrialisation began; the modernisation led to the disappearance of almost all traces of the colonial and imperial periods.

Vitória is the capital of the state of Espírito Santo and the smallest of the 27 Brazilian capitals by area. Its population was 322,869 in 2022, within a metropolitan area of more than 1,880,828. It has two major ports, the Port of Vitória and the Port of Tubarão, and its economy rests on port activity, trade, industry and services, with the steelmaker ArcelorMittal Tubarão and the mining company Vale among its main firms. The Chapel of Santa Luzia, built in the 16th century, is the oldest building in the municipality. The city also administers the islands of Trindade and Martim Vaz, 1,100 kilometres off the coast.
vitus-bering: Vitus Jonassen Bering was born in the Danish port town of Horsens and was baptised in the Lutheran church there on 5 August 1681. His father, Jonas Svendsen, was a customs inspector and churchwarden, and his mother was Anne Pedderdatter. He was named after a maternal great-uncle, Vitus Pedersen Bering, a chronicler at the royal court. The family was reasonably secure financially, and two of his elder half-brothers attended the University of Copenhagen.

Vitus instead signed on as a ship's boy at the age of 15. Between 1696 and 1704 he sailed to India and the Dutch East Indies and completed naval officer training in Amsterdam. He later claimed, with some supporting evidence, to have served on Danish whalers in the North Atlantic and to have visited European colonies in the Caribbean and on the eastern seaboard of North America.

In 1704 Bering enrolled in the navy of Tsar Peter I, where Admiral Cornelius Cruys helped him to a commission as sub-lieutenant. He reached the rank of second captain by 1720. He apparently fought in no sea battles but commanded several vessels on risky missions, and in the last years of the Great Northern War his duties were mostly lightering. On 8 October 1713 he married Anna Christina Pülse at Vyborg; they had nine children, of whom four survived childhood.

Bering was not promoted when the war ended in 1721. After his sister-in-law married a rear-admiral in 1724, he retired to save face, was promoted to first captain on retirement, and rejoined the navy later that year. On 29 December 1724, by the old calendar, Peter I ordered him to lead the First Kamchatka Expedition, to map the lands visited and establish whether Asia and America shared a land border. His lieutenants were Martin Spanberg and Aleksei Chirikov, and the party travelled overland and by river to Okhotsk. He later proposed a more ambitious second expedition, to sail east in search of North America, which involved 600 people at the outset.
vix-grave: The grave lies near the village of Vix, about 6 km north of Châtillon-sur-Seine in the department of Côte-d'Or. It belongs to a Celtic complex of the Late Hallstatt and Early La Tène periods centred on Mont Lassois, a steep, flat-topped hill crowned by a fortified settlement with ditches and walls up to 8 m thick. In the sixth and fifth centuries BCE the settlement appears to have controlled a trading point where the Seine crossed the land route from the Mediterranean to northern Europe. In 2006 a hall measuring 35 by 22 m, likened to an early Greek megaron, was found at its centre.

Maurice Moisson found the mound, which he and René Joffroy excavated early in 1953. Under a tumulus of earth and stone once 40 m across and 6 m high, a wooden chamber 3 m square held a body laid in the box of a cart whose wheels had been taken off and set beside it. She was between 35 and 40 years old at death. Her jewellery included a 480-gram gold torc, fibulae and bracelets of slate and amber. Drinking cups from Etruria and Attica lay with the krater, and one dated to about 525 BCE gives the earliest date the burial can have.

The krater weighs 208.6 kilograms, holds 1,100 litres and was made of seven or more pieces bearing Greek letters, so it was probably carried to Burgundy in parts and assembled there; it may have been made at Sybaris. Its neck carries a frieze of eight four-horse chariots, each followed by a hoplite, and its lid a bronze statuette of a veiled woman. Some scholars link it to gift exchange between Mediterranean wine traders and northern elites. The identification of the dead as a woman has been questioned since a reexamination by Bettina Arnold in 1991, and an osteological analysis by Knüsel in 2002 concluded that the individual was likely female, with some androgynous features.

Research on and around Mont Lassois resumed in 1991 under Bruno Chaume, and the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research reopened the mound in 2019. A reconstruction of the grave and the original finds are displayed in the museum at Châtillon-sur-Seine, from which the gold torc was stolen on 24 July 2026.
vizier: The word vizier is believed to derive from the Arabic wazara, to bear a burden, from the Semitic root W-Z-R. The Quran describes Aaron as the wazir, or helper, of Moses. Proto-Shi'a leaders such as al-Mukhtar and Abu Salama adopted the title wazir al Muhammad, helper of the family of Muhammad. Another view takes it from the Pahlavi vichir, meaning a decree and later a judge, but historians of Islamic administration such as S. D. Goitein reject this and hold the word to be purely Arabic. The Abbasid caliphs gave the title wazir to a minister formerly called katib, or secretary, who had become the representative and successor of the dapir, the official scribe of the Sasanian kings.

The office arose under the first Abbasid caliphs and spread across the Muslim world. The 11th-century legal theorist al-Mawardi distinguished two types: the wazir al-tanfidh, a vizier of execution with limited powers who carried out the caliph's policies, and the far more powerful wazir al-tafwid, with delegated authority over civil and military affairs. The first could be a non-Muslim or even a slave; the second had to be a Muslim well versed in the Shari'a. Women were barred from the office.

In al-Andalus the Umayyad caliphs of Córdoba appointed a varying number of viziers as department heads and councillors, as many as 29 at once in 1008, though the senior office was that of the chamberlain, the hajib. The Spanish word alguacil derives from the title. In the Ottoman Empire the Grand Vizier was often the de facto ruling prime minister, second only to the sultan and leader of the Divan, the Imperial Council. Some Ottoman provincial governors, as in Bosnia and Herzegovina, also held the title of vizier.

The title was used for chief ministers in many other states, among them Fatimid Egypt, Muslim Iran, where the prime minister was styled Vazir-e A'zam, the Husainid beylik of Tunisia, the Sultanate of the Maldives, Durrani Afghanistan, and the Bengal Sultanate, as well as by many princes in India. In Tunisia ministers included the Wazir al-Bahr, minister of the sea, and the Wazir al-Qalam, minister of the pen. Wazir remains the standard Arabic word for a government minister, and Waziri is a highly regarded chieftaincy title in much of northern Nigeria, where most emirs have one as a high-ranking adviser.
vlachs: The word Vlach, with many variants such as Wallachian, Vlah and oláh, comes from the name of a Celtic tribe, the Volcae, adopted into Proto-Germanic as *Walhaz, meaning "stranger". In Gothic it came to mean "foreigner" or "Romance-speaker" and later "shepherd" or "nomad". Medieval Romanians called themselves rumân or român, from the Latin romānus, and Aromanians use armãn or rãmãn. Today the term refers chiefly to speakers of Aromanian, Megleno-Romanian and Istro-Romanian south of the Danube, in Albania, Bulgaria, northern Greece, North Macedonia and eastern Serbia.

Their origins are disputed. Proponents of Daco-Roman continuity hold that the ancestors of the Vlachs and Romanians descend from Dacians and survived in the lower Danube basin in the Migration Period. The other theory holds that Romanians and Vlachs were one group of Eastern Romance speakers whose origins lie in the southern Balkans, with early Romanian speakers moving north from the 12th century.

In medieval sources Vlach was an exonym, and it could also refer to other peoples, so it ranked, in the words of the Serbian historian Sima Ćirković, with names such as Greek, Serb or Latin. In 976 Vlachs fought and killed David of Bulgaria between Prespa and Kastoria. Around 1000 they were present in large numbers on the Chalcidice peninsula, where they were known for cheese and meat products. In 1020 the Archdiocese of Ohrid was founded with responsibility for the spiritual care of all the Vlachs, and in 1027 many Vlachs recruited from Macedonia served in the Byzantine army that tried to recapture Sicily.

Between 1105 and 1109 correspondence between Emperor Alexios I Komnenos and Patriarch Nicholas III Kyrdiniates mentions 300 Vlach families serving the monks of Mount Athos, who were expelled after the patriarch complained about their pasturing. The traveller Benjamin of Tudela was one of the first to use the word for a Romance-speaking people, placing them in the mountains of Thessaly. In 1330 Stefan Dečanski gave Vlach pastures and katuns along the Drim and Lim rivers to the Visoki Dečani monastery. Transhumant pastoralism took hold only between the 14th and the 19th centuries.

Vlach shepherds drove flocks through the mountains of central and eastern Europe, and groups were found as far north as Poland and Moravia and as far west as Dalmatia, where Slavs called them Vlasi or Valaši. As national states appeared in the area of the former Ottoman Empire, new borders divided the summer and winter habitats of many transhumant groups. Ilona Czamańska notes that research on Vlach origins was long dominated by political issues. Some researchers have also raised concern about the denial of Vlach descent of various groups and personalities.
vlad-the-impaler: Vlad was the second legitimate son of Vlad II Dracul, who took his nickname from membership of the Order of the Dragon, a fraternity founded by Sigismund of Luxemburg, King of Hungary, to halt the Ottoman advance. Dracula is the Slavonic genitive, meaning the son of Dracul. In modern Romanian dracul means the devil, which added to his reputation.

The historian Radu Florescu writes that Vlad was born in Sighișoara, where his father lived from 1431 to 1435. In 1442 Vlad and his younger brother Radu were held as hostages in the Ottoman Empire to secure their father's loyalty. In 1447 his father and eldest brother Mircea were murdered after John Hunyadi invaded Wallachia and installed Vladislav II as voivode.

Vlad took Wallachia briefly with Ottoman support in October 1448, but Vladislav returned and Vlad fled by 7 December. After exile in Moldavia and Hungary he invaded Wallachia with Hungarian support in 1456, and Vladislav died during the invasion. Vlad purged the boyars and came into conflict with the Transylvanian Saxons, whose villages he plundered, impaling the captives, which gave him his epithet.

When Mehmed II demanded personal homage, Vlad had the sultan's two envoys captured and impaled. In January 1462 he attacked Ottoman territory, massacring tens of thousands of Turks and Muslim Bulgarians. He tried to capture the sultan at Târgoviște on the night of 16 to 17 June 1462. The Ottomans withdrew, but many Wallachians deserted to Radu.

In late 1462 Matthias Corvinus, King of Hungary, had Vlad captured. To justify this to Pope Pius II and the Venetians he produced letters said to be Vlad's, which most historians regard as forged. Vlad was held at Visegrád from 1463 to 1475 and released at the request of Stephen III of Moldavia. He was reputedly made to convert to Roman Catholicism. After fighting with Corvinus's army in Bosnia, he regained Wallachia in his last attempt to hold the throne, but Basarab Laiotă returned with Ottoman support. Vlad was killed in battle near Snagov before 10 January 1477.

Stories of his cruelty circulated in his lifetime, and courtiers of Corvinus promoted them after his arrest. The poet Michael Beheim wrote a poem about him that was performed at the court of Emperor Frederick III in 1463, and such books were among the first bestsellers in German-speaking lands. Some in his region regarded him as a folk hero for opposing the Ottomans. His name is linked to Bram Stoker's vampire Count Dracula of 1897, although Stoker's notes do not name Vlad directly. Stoker learned of vampires from Emily Gerard's article on Transylvanian superstitions, published in 1885. Tursun Beg called him Kazıklı Voyvoda, the Impaler Lord.
vladikavkaz: Vladikavkaz is the capital of North Ossetia-Alania in Russia. It lies in the south-east of the republic at the foothills of the Caucasus, on the Terek River. The Russian name literally means "ruler of the Caucasus", while the Ossetian name Dzæudžyqæu means "Dzaug's settlement". The Soviet period gave it other names: in 1931 it was renamed Ordzhonikidze after the Soviet leader Sergo Ordzhonikidze, who established Soviet power in the region during the Civil War; in 1944, after the deportation of the Chechens and Ingush, it became Dzaudzhikau; in 1954 it was Ordzhonikidze again. In 1990 it took the double name Vladikavkaz in Russian and Dzaudzhikau in Ossetian.

The city was founded in 1784 as a Russian fortress at the entrance to the Darial Gorge, to serve as an outpost on the routes between Russia and Georgia. Accounts differ on the site: it is said to stand near the Ingush village of Zaur, while many other sources place it on the Ossetian village of Kapkai. The Georgian Military Highway, linking it with Georgia across the mountains, was built in 1799, and a railway connected it to Rostov-on-Don and Baku in 1875. Under the Russian Empire it was the administrative seat of the Vladikavkazsky Okrug of the Terek Oblast.

It was the capital of the Mountain Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which existed from 1921 to 1924 and covered most of modern Chechnya, North Ossetia and Kabardino-Balkaria. In February 1919 the anti-Communist Volunteer Army under General Anton Denikin seized the city, and the Red Army expelled it in March 1920. In early November 1942 German forces tried unsuccessfully to take it and left North Ossetia in January 1943.

Vladikavkaz is one of the most populous cities of the North Caucasus. It is an industrial and transport centre producing processed zinc and lead, machinery, chemicals, clothing and food. Trams have run since 1904. The Mukhtarov Mosque, built in 1906, dominates the city, and the Georgian Military Road begins there. Most residents are Eastern Orthodox, with a minority following Sunni Islam and followers of the Ossetian folk religion Uatsdin.
vladimir-ii-monomakh: Vladimir was the son of Vsevolod Yaroslavich, who reigned as Grand Prince Vsevolod I of Kiev from 1078 to 1093. In 1046 Vsevolod had made a diplomatic marriage to a relative of the Byzantine emperor Constantine IX Monomachos, from whom Vladimir probably took his nickname Monomakh. The Primary Chronicle names his mother only as a Greek princess. A later story that he defeated Constantine and was given the name in a peace settlement is impossible, since the emperor died in 1055. The name first appears in a eulogy in the Kievan Chronicle and on his seal.

As a young prince Monomakh ruled in Smolensk and Chernigov and led 13 campaigns in the name of his father. In 1068 he allied himself with the Cuman chief Bilge-Tegin. After 1094 his chief patrimony was Pereyaslav, though he also controlled Rostov, Suzdal and other northern provinces, where he founded several towns, notably the one named Vladimir. His quarrel with his cousin Oleg began when Oleg made peace with the Polovtsians to retake Chernigov, and it continued among their descendants.

Monomakh initiated three princely congresses, at Lyubech in 1097, Vytachiv in 1100 and Dolobsk in 1103, to unite the princes against the steppe by allowing each princely branch to keep its patrimony. Between 1103 and 1111 the Rus princes raided the Polovtsians every year. In 1107 Monomakh defeated the Cuman khan Boniak, and in 1111, with Sviatopolk II, he led the army that defeated a Cuman force at the river Salnitsa, probably near modern Izium. These victories drew the Cumans into the steppes and prevented new raids. His Instruction states that he conducted 83 campaigns and made peace with the Polovtsians 19 times.

When Sviatopolk II died in 1113, the people of Kiev revolted, attacking officials, wealthy citizens and Jews. The ruling circles invited Monomakh, the most liked prince, to take the throne. He lowered the rate of interest on loans and issued decrees that prohibited usury, banned the enslavement of merchants indebted through accident, regulated the status of bondsmen and restricted the power of the boyars.

His statute was included in the revised Russkaya Pravda. He wrote his Instruction to Children about 1117, a didactic and autobiographical work that condemns princely strife and promotes the idea of a unified state. He was buried in Saint Sophia Cathedral. Later generations remembered his reign as a golden age, before Rus was torn apart by internal struggles after the death of his son Mstislav in 1132.
vladimir-lenin: Vladimir Ilyich Ulyanov was born in Simbirsk on 22 April 1870 (10 April O.S.), the third of eight children. His father, Ilya Nikolayevich Ulyanov, came from a family of former serfs and rose to be Director of Public Schools for the province, a post that carried hereditary nobility. Lenin took up revolutionary socialist politics after his brother's execution in 1887 and was expelled from Kazan Imperial University for protesting against the Tsarist government. In late 1893 he moved to Saint Petersburg and rose to a senior position in a Marxist cell. Arrested for sedition in 1897, he argued in prison that industrial capitalism had created a proletariat that would overthrow Tsarism. He was exiled to Siberia, where he married Nadezhda Krupskaya.

In 1903 Lenin took a key part in the split of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party and led the Bolshevik faction. After the failed Revolution of 1905 he campaigned for the First World War to be turned into a Europe-wide proletarian revolution. He returned to Russia after the February Revolution of 1917 and helped lead the October Revolution, in which the Bolsheviks overthrew the Provisional Government.

His government at first shared power with the Left Socialist Revolutionaries. The Constituent Assembly elected in November 1917 gave the Bolsheviks about a quarter of the vote; it met in January 1918 and was forcibly disbanded. By 1919 Mensheviks and Socialist Revolutionaries had been expelled from the soviets and Russia was a one-party state. The government redistributed land, nationalised banks and large industry, left the First World War by a treaty conceding territory, and won the Russian Civil War. Opponents were suppressed in the Red Terror, in which tens of thousands were killed or interned. In 1921 Lenin encouraged economic growth through the New Economic Policy.

Lenin fell seriously ill in 1921, suffered strokes in May and December 1922, and died at Gorki on 21 January 1924. Joseph Stalin succeeded him as the pre-eminent figure in the Soviet government. His interpretation of Marxism, first called Leninism by Martov in 1904, became the basis of Marxism-Leninism and a model for later Communist-led states. Supporters see him as a champion of revolutionary socialism and internationalism, while critics accuse him of establishing a totalitarian dictatorship that carried out mass killings and political repression.
vladimir-mayakovsky: Vladimir Vladimirovich Mayakovsky was born on 19 July 1893 in Baghdati, in the Kutais Governorate of Georgia, then part of the Russian Empire. His father, a local forester, belonged to a noble family. At home the family spoke Russian, but with friends and at school Mayakovsky spoke Georgian. At fourteen he took part in socialist demonstrations. His father died suddenly in 1906, and his widowed mother moved the family to Moscow.

In December 1912 his first published poems appeared in the Futurist manifesto A Slap in the Face of Public Taste, signed with Velemir Khlebnikov, David Burlyuk and Alexey Kruchenykh, which called for throwing Pushkin, Dostoyevsky and Tolstoy off the steamboat of modernity. In December 1913 the Futurists toured 17 cities in riotous readings that police often stopped; the tour cost Mayakovsky and Burlyuk their places at the Art school. He met Osip and Lilya Brik in July 1915 and recited A Cloud in Trousers to them, dedicating it to Lilya.

During the Russian Civil War he produced agitprop posters for the Communist Party, and he edited the art journal LEF. His work showed support for the Bolsheviks and admiration for Lenin, but his relationship with the Soviet state was complex. Works that satirised it, such as the plays The Bedbug and The Bathhouse of 1929, met with scorn from the state and literary establishment.

Futurism rejected traditional poetry in favour of formal experiment and welcomed the social change promised by modern technology. Mayakovsky's verses of 1913, with words split into pieces and staggered across the page and peppered with street language, were considered unpoetic. His idea was to create a democratic language of the streets. A Cloud in Trousers of 1915 treated love, revolution, religion and art from the viewpoint of a spurned lover.

He died on 14 April 1930 by his own hand, and about 150,000 people attended his funeral. After his death his publications were cancelled for a time, until Joseph Stalin wrote in 1935 that he was the best and most talented poet of the Soviet epoch. Boris Pasternak said the official canonisation dealt him a second death.
vladimir-minorsky: Vladimir Fyodorovich Minorsky was born on 5 February 1877 in Korcheva, in the Tver Governorate, northwest of Moscow on the upper Volga, a town now submerged beneath the Ivankovo Reservoir. His father was Feodor M. Minorsky and his mother Olga, née Golubitsky. He was a gold medallist of the Fourth Grammar School in Moscow, entered Moscow University in 1896 to study law and graduated in 1900. He then spent three years at the Lazarev Institute of Oriental Languages preparing for a diplomatic career, and in 1902 he made his first trip to Qajar Persia, where he collected material on the Ahl-i Haqq religion.

In 1903 Minorsky entered the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs. He served as a diplomat in Persia, at the Tabriz Consulate-General and then the Legation in Tehran, from 1904 to 1908, and in Saint Petersburg from 1908 to 1912. In 1911 he took part in the Four-Power Commission that delimited the Turco-Persian border, and he published a monograph on the Ahl-i Haqq, for which the Imperial Society of Natural Sciences in Moscow awarded him a gold medal. His surveys in Persia supplied material for his Materials for the Study of the East of 1915. From 1915 to 1917 he was chargé d'affaires at the Russian Legation in Tehran.

The Bolshevik Revolution of 1917 made a return to Russia difficult, and in 1919 he moved to Paris, where he worked at the Russian Embassy and used his knowledge of Middle Eastern affairs during the Versailles and Trianon peace settlements. From 1923 he lectured at the École nationale des langues orientales vivantes. In 1932 he became lecturer in Persian at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London, Reader in 1933 and Professor of Persian in 1937, and he retired in 1944.

Minorsky published over 200 books and articles, among them Studies in Caucasian History (1957), A History of Sharvan and Darband in the 10th-11th Centuries (1958) and Medieval Iran and its Neighbours, a reprint of his articles that appeared in 1982. He is best known for his contributions to the history of Iran and of peoples such as the Persians, Lurs and Kurds. He became a Corresponding Fellow of the British Academy in 1943 and received an honorary doctorate from the University of Brussels in 1948. He died on 25 March 1966. Although he never returned to Russia, his ashes were interred in the Novodevichy Cemetery, and the bulk of his personal library was given to Leningrad.
vladimir-the-bold: Vladimir Andreyevich was born on 15 July 1353, the son of Andrei Ivanovich, Prince of Novgorod, and a grandson of Ivan Kalita. At the age of five he inherited Serpukhov, Borovsk and a third part of Moscow from his brother. Because his cousin Dmitry of Moscow was also a child, both princes were tutored by Metropolitan Alexis, who arranged a treaty binding Vladimir to loyalty to his Muscovite cousin. His byname refers to his many military exploits in Dmitry's wars.

Under that treaty Vladimir helped Dmitry fight Tver in 1375, the Livonian Knights in 1379, Ryazan in 1385 and the Republic of Novgorod in 1392. He married a daughter of Algirdas of Lithuania in 1371 but still supported Dmitry against the Lithuanians. In 1374 he built the first oaken kremlin at Serpukhov, and in 1377 he sacked the Severian towns of Trubchevsk and Starodub. When Tokhtamysh invaded two years after Kulikovo, Vladimir defeated his force near Volokolamsk.

It is not clear why he quarrelled with his cousin in 1388. They made peace the same year, but after Dmitry's death and the accession of his son Vasily I, Vladimir had to leave Serpukhov for Torzhok. A year later he returned and made a treaty with Vasily that gave him Volokolamsk and Rzhev, which he later exchanged for Gorodets, Uglich and Kozelsk while giving up his claims to Murom and Tarusa.

He died in 1410 and was buried in the Archangel Cathedral. His seven sons continued the line of the princes of Serpukhov until 1456. His granddaughter Maria of Borovsk married Vasily II and was the mother of Ivan the Great, who drove the last princes of Serpukhov into Lithuania. The last of Vladimir's male-line descendants died in 1521.
vladimir-the-great: Vladimir was the illegitimate youngest son of Sviatoslav I of Kiev by his housekeeper Malusha, and her brother Dobrynya was his tutor and most trusted adviser. Sviatoslav made him ruler of Novgorod in 970 and gave Kiev to his legitimate son Yaropolk. After Sviatoslav was killed by the Pechenegs in 972, Yaropolk's war against his brother Oleg in 977 sent Vladimir abroad, where he gathered a Varangian army. He returned, took Polotsk by force after its prince Rogvolod refused him his daughter Rogneda, and slew Yaropolk by treachery to become prince of all Kievan Rus'.

Vladimir widened his father's domain: he seized the Cherven towns from Poland in 981, suppressed a Vyatichi rebellion, subdued the Yatvingians in 983, conquered the Radimichs in 984 and campaigned against the Volga Bulgars in 985. He remained a pagan and raised a temple on a hill in Kiev to six gods, among them Perun, Stribog, Dazhd'bog and Mokosh. A mob killed the Christian Fyodor and his son Ioann, whom later tradition counted as the first Christian martyrs in Rus'.

According to the Primary Chronicle, missionaries and then envoys examined Islam, Latin Christianity, Judaism and Byzantine Christianity, and those sent to Constantinople were won over by its worship. In 988, after taking Chersonesus in Crimea, he sought the hand of Basil II's sister Anna and was baptised there with the name Basil. Arab sources tell it differently: the emperor, facing a revolt of Bardas Sclerus and Bardas Phocas, asked for help, and Vladimir sent 6,000 troops in exchange for a marriage and his own conversion.

Back in Kiev he destroyed pagan monuments and built churches, among them the Church of the Tithes in 989. He set his twelve sons over the subject principalities, founded schools, introduced ecclesiastical courts and, according to the chronicles, abolished capital punishment. In 1014 his son Yaroslav the Wise stopped paying tribute; Vladimir began gathering troops but fell ill and died at Berestove, near Kiev, in 1015.

The Orthodox and Catholic churches canonised him, and his feast day is 15 July (28 July in the older calendar). Byzantine sources barely mention his baptism, and some historians conclude that the canonical story took shape in the 1040s, when a Rus' church equal to the Byzantine one was wanted. Folk ballads call him Krasno Solnyshko, the Fair Sun. The town of Volodymyr in north-western Ukraine was founded by him, and St Volodymyr's Cathedral in Kyiv is dedicated to him.
vladislaus-ii-of-hungary: Vladislaus was born in Kraków on 1 March 1456, the eldest son of Casimir IV, King of Poland and Grand Duke of Lithuania, and Elizabeth of Austria. He was his father's heir in Poland and Lithuania, and the historian Jan Długosz was his tutor. In 1468 George of Poděbrady, the Hussite king of Bohemia, offered to make him heir, needing Casimir's support against rebellious Catholic nobles and Matthias Corvinus of Hungary. After George died on 22 March 1471, the Bohemian Diet elected the fifteen-year-old Vladislaus at Kutná Hora on 27 May, and he was crowned in Prague on 22 August.

Matthias occupied Moravia, Silesia and both Lusatias, so Vladislaus ruled only Bohemia proper. In the Peace of Olomouc in 1479 the lands of the Bohemian Crown were divided on those lines. Vladislaus's attempt to strengthen the Catholics provoked a rising in Prague in September 1483, and in March 1485 the Diet at Kutná Hora confirmed the right of nobles and commoners to adhere freely to Catholicism or Utraquism. Having come without an army, he relied on the nobles, and the Diet became the most influential body of state.

After Matthias died on 6 April 1490, the Diet of Hungary elected Vladislaus king on 15 July, since most barons preferred him because his rule in Bohemia suggested he would respect their liberties. He was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 18 September and settled in Buda. His brother John Albert and Maximilian of Austria both invaded but gave up their claims, and in the Peace of Pressburg of 7 November 1491 he acknowledged the Habsburgs' right to inherit Hungary and Bohemia if he died without a son.

He did not continue Matthias's centralising policy. Decisions were made in the Royal Council and he accepted them with the word Dobrze, Polish for Very well, which gave him his Hungarian nickname. Unable to pay Matthias's Black Army, he dissolved it on 3 January 1493, while the Ottomans raided the southern border.

Vladislaus died at Buda on 13 March 1516. His ten-year-old son Louis succeeded him in both kingdoms, having been crowned in Hungary in 1508 and in Bohemia in 1509. In 1500 the Bohemian Diet adopted a land constitution that limited royal power, known as the Vladislav land order, and he oversaw the building of Vladislav Hall at Prague Castle from 1493 to 1502.
vladislaus-iii-duke-of-bohemia: Vladislaus Henry was born around 1160, the second son of Duke Vladislaus II of Bohemia by his second wife, Judith of Thuringia, and so the younger brother of Ottokar I. In the struggles within the Přemyslid dynasty he supported Ottokar when he seized the Bohemian duchy in 1192, and Ottokar, with the consent of Emperor Henry VI, made him margrave of Moravia; he had been Prince of Brno and Znojmo since 1191. The brothers never paid the sum the emperor demanded, and in June 1193 the Imperial Diet at Worms deposed them in favour of their cousin, the Prague bishop Henry Bretislaus. Vladislaus spent the following years at Prague Castle under the duke's suspicious eye.

After the deaths of Henry VI and Bretislaus in 1197 he was released and elected duke on 22 June, with his brother present. Faced with a rising in Ottokar's favour, he abdicated on 6 December. The two armies were encamped facing each other when the brothers met and agreed that Ottokar would take the throne, though without imperial approval, and Vladislaus the hereditary title of a near-autonomous Moravia. His renunciation helped to end the destructive dynastic wars of the Přemyslids, which had lasted more than twenty-five years since their father's death, and he was the last ruler of Bohemia to hold the title of duke.

In Moravia he worked closely with his brother. He had the rival claimant Prince Spytihněv III of Brno blinded and installed his own confessor, Daniel Milík, as Bishop of Prague, the first investiture by a reigning prince in Bohemia. The Golden Bull of Sicily of 1212 acknowledged his status as a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1205 Vladislaus founded the Cistercian abbey of Velehrad as the family monastery and burial place of the Moravian margraves. He married a woman named Heilwida, or Hedwig, of unknown origin, and died childless at his court in Znojmo on 12 August 1222. He was buried at Velehrad, and Moravia passed back to King Ottokar I, who granted it to his younger son Vladislaus II.
vladivostok: Vladivostok stands around the Golden Horn Bay on the southern extremity of the Muravyov-Amursky Peninsula, about 45 kilometres from the border between China and Russia and 134 kilometres from the border with North Korea. Its name means Lord of the East or Ruler of the East, from the Slavic word for to rule and the Russian word for east. The area was historically part of Outer Manchuria. Some modern Chinese historians claim a Chinese settlement stood on the site around 600 CE under the name Yongmingcheng.

Russia gained the territory from Qing China under the Treaty of Aigun, confirmed by the Convention of Peking, and the city was founded as a military outpost on 2 July 1860. The first civilian settler, the merchant Yakov Lazarevich Semyonov, arrived in 1861. In the early 1870s the main naval base of the Siberian Military Flotilla was moved there from Nikolaevsk-on-Amur, which set off a construction boom. The first urban plan, by Mikhail Lubensky, dates from 1868, and the railway station was completed in 1894. The Trans-Siberian Railway, finished in 1905, linked Moscow with Vladivostok, Russia's most important Pacific port.

From the late 1890s to the early 1920s half of the population was Asian, the Chinese being the largest group, followed by Koreans and Japanese. The Chinese quarter, called Millionka, held up to 50,000 people at its peak. Koreans moved to the area in large numbers after Japan annexed Korea in 1910, and by 1915 about 10,000 lived in the city. Their enclave, Sinhanch'on, became a hub of the Korean independence movement and hosted the first Korean provisional government, the Korean Independence Army Government. On the orders of Joseph Stalin both quarters were liquidated and their residents deported between 1936 and 1938.

After the Russian Revolution of 1917, White Russian and Allied forces occupied Vladivostok in 1918. The last of them, from Japan, were not withdrawn until 1922, and the Red Army took the city the same year. By then it was in decline, and its population had fallen to 106,000. Under the New Economic Policy of 1923 to 1925 the commercial port reopened and became the most profitable in the country.

Vladivostok is the administrative centre of Primorsky Krai and the largest Russian port on the Pacific Ocean. It is the home of the headquarters of the Pacific Fleet of the Russian Navy and the starting point of the Trans-Siberian portion of the Eurasian Land Bridge. Its population passed 500,000 in the 1970s and reached a high of over 648,000 in 1992. More than 90 per cent of residents declare Russian ethnicity, though minorities of Koreans and Chinese remain.
vladko-macek: Vladimir Maček was born on 20 June 1879 in Kupinec near Jastrebarsko, south-west of Zagreb, to a Slovene father and a mother of Croatian and Polish descent. He studied law at the University of Zagreb, opened a practice in Sv. Ivan Zelina in 1908 and joined the Croatian Peasant Party at its founding. In the First World War he served as an Austro-Hungarian reserve officer, was wounded at the Battle of Kolubara in November 1914 and was decorated for bravery.

After the war he became a close associate of Stjepan Radić. In 1925, after the party joined the Peasants International, he was arrested by the Yugoslav authorities and elected to the National Assembly while in jail, and was released that July when the party entered the government.

Maček became party leader on 13 August 1928 and soon emerged as a main opponent of King Alexander, who had him sentenced in 1933 to three years in jail for treason; he was freed after the king's assassination in 1934. He sought to turn Yugoslavia from a unitary state dominated by Serbs into one in which Croatian statehood would be restored, and his coalition, though it lost the elections of 1938, remained strong. The Cvetković–Maček Agreement with Dragiša Cvetković in August 1939 created the Banovina of Croatia, which took in Croatia and large parts of present-day Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The Banovina collapsed with Yugoslavia in the Axis invasion of April 1941. Nazi Germany saw him as the ideal leader of the new Independent State of Croatia, but he twice refused the post of prime minister. In October 1941 he was interned in the Jasenovac concentration camp, and from March 1942 he was held under house arrest until the fall of Ante Pavelić's regime in May 1945. His party split as members joined the Ustaše or Tito's Partisans, both of whom he opposed. He went into exile in France and then the United States, helped found the International Peasants' Union in 1947 and died in Washington, D.C., on 15 May 1964. His remains were buried in Zagreb's Mirogoj cemetery in 1996.
vlastimir: Vlastimir descended from the unnamed ruler who had led the Serbs to the Balkans in the 7th century under the protection of Emperor Heraclius. His great-grandfather Višeslav, a contemporary of Charlemagne, is the first Serbian monarch known by name; Radoslav and then Prosigoj, Vlastimir's father, followed him. The Serbs were organised in župe, communities headed by local župans who owed the prince aid in war. To the east the Bulgarian Empire was conquering one Slavic neighbour after another, and the Byzantine emperor, nominal overlord of the Serbs, was bound by a thirty-year peace with Bulgaria signed in 815.

According to the historian Živković, Vlastimir succeeded his father around 830. He united the nearby Serbian tribes, most likely in alarm at the Bulgarian advance, and Emperor Theophilos probably encouraged the Serbs to resist it. Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus writes that Serbs and Bulgarians had lived at peace until Presian I invaded to force the Serbs into subjection. The Serbs, fighting in forests, gorges and hills, held out for three years; Presian lost many men and gained no land. The war ended with the death of Theophilos in 842, which released Vlastimir from his obligations to the Empire.

Vlastimir's standing rose after the victory, and he expanded to the west, into Bosnia and Hum. Around 847 or 848 he married his daughter to Krajina, son of Beloje, župan of Trebinje, and raised Krajina's title to archon; their son Hvalimir later ruled Travunia. Historians read the marriage as a sign that he stood at the head of the Serbian rulers.

Vlastimir was followed by his three sons, Mutimir, Strojimir and Gojnik. Soon after his death they defeated an invasion by Boris I of Bulgaria, capturing Boris's son Vladimir and 12 great boyars. He is the founder of the Vlastimirović dynasty, the first Serbian dynasty, and a street in Novi Sad bears his name.
vlissingen: Vlissingen lies on the island of Walcheren in the south-west of the Netherlands, in a strategic position between the Scheldt and the North Sea. A fishermen's hamlet is said to have arisen at the estuary of the Scheldt around 620 CE. The Counts of Holland, Flanders and Zeeland had the first harbours dug, and the town received city rights in 1315. The origin of the name is unclear, though most scholars connect it with the word fles, bottle. One story tells that Saint Willibrord landed with a bottle whose contents did not diminish when he shared them with beggars. Another traces it to a ferry house with a bottle as its sign.

Over the centuries Vlissingen became a hub of fishing, especially herring, of commerce, privateering and the slave trade. The first reliable records are a charter of 1247, when the town had a church and an infirmary, and one of 1264 that mentions a castle. In 1294 Floris V, Count of Holland, bought the town and began its development, and the harbour was extended in the mid-15th century, financed by a local herring monopoly.

In the mid-16th century the Eighty Years' War and the punitive taxes of the Duke of Alba brought poverty. In April 1572 the townspeople rose, expelled the Flemish garrison, fired on ships bringing reinforcements and hanged a Spanish nobleman in front of the town hall. By the Treaty of Nonsuch of 1585 English garrisons were stationed here and at Brill, until the towns were sold back to the Dutch in 1616.

In the 17th century the roadstead was a main harbour of the Dutch East India Company, and ships from Vlissingen sailed for the Dutch colonial outposts. The town declined in the 18th century and suffered badly in the Napoleonic Wars. After 1870 new docks, the Walcheren canal, the railway and the shipyard De Schelde revived it. British Commandos of the 4th Special Service Brigade liberated the heavily shelled and flooded city on 3 November 1944.

Vlissingen is rebuilt after the war, and in the 1960s the seaport and industrial area of Vlissingen-Oost developed. It is noted for the yards on the Scheldt where most ships of the Royal Netherlands Navy are built. Its English name Flushing was already in use in the 17th century, when Samuel Pepys used it in his diaries. The Dutch colonial village founded in 1645 in what is now Queens, New York City, was first called Vlissingen and became Flushing, and a village in Cornwall was named after the town by Dutch engineers.
vlore: Vlorë lies on the Bay of Vlorë in south-western Albania, on the eastern side of the Strait of Otranto, surrounded by the foothills of the Ceraunian Mountains. The bay forms a natural harbour, which gave the site a significant place in antiquity as a base for trade. The name comes from the ancient Greek Aulon, meaning channel or glen, first recorded in the 2nd century CE by Lucian and Ptolemy. The Albanian form Vlorë developed by a sound change, rhotacism, from Vlonë, while the Italian Valona and the Turkish Avlonya come from the Greek name.

The coast of Vlorë was among the Illyrian sites with pre-urban activity from the 11th to 10th centuries BCE, and Greek colonists are traditionally believed to have founded Orikos, Thronion and Aulon on these shores. A large fortified port town, inhabited from the 6th century BCE to the 2nd century CE, lies partly submerged at Triport to the north-west; it may have been moved to the site of the modern city. Aulon was an important port of the Roman Empire, in the province of Epirus Nova, and became an episcopal see in the 5th century.

In the 11th and 12th centuries Vlorë figured in the conflicts between the Byzantine Empire and the Norman Kingdom of Sicily. A Venetian fleet attacked it in 1321, and from 1346 to 1417 it was the capital of the Principality of Valona, at first a vassal of the Serbian Empire. The Ottomans captured it in 1417; Albanian rebels freed it in 1432, but it returned to Ottoman rule and became a sanjak centre under the name Avlonya. Venice held it briefly from 1690 to 1691.
