A Jewish community, settled with Ottoman support from 1426 and enlarged by exiles from Spain after 1492, numbered some 2,600 people in the censuses of 1506 and 1520, and traded between Europe and Ottoman cities.

On 28 November 1912, during the First Balkan War, Ismail Qemali headed the Albanian Declaration of Independence at Vlorë, and the city became Albania's first capital. Italy occupied it in 1914 and again in 1939, and under Enver Hoxha's communist government after the Second World War the port was leased to the Soviet Union as a submarine base until the break of 1961.

Vlorë is the third most populous city of Albania and the seat of Vlorë County. It is a major seaport and commercial centre, and its Museum of Independence stands in the 19th-century building where the founders of Albania signed the declaration. The Castle of Kaninë and the archaeological sites of Amantia and Oricum lie in the municipality. The city belongs to the cultural region of Labëria, known for polyphonic music that UNESCO has recognised.
vltava: The Vltava rises from the confluence of two rivers, the Teplá Vltava, which is longer and begins at Kvilda in the Bohemian Forest at an elevation of 1,174 m, and the Studená Vltava, which comes from Bavaria. With the Teplá Vltava it is 431.3 km long. It flows south-east along the Bohemian Forest and then north across Bohemia, through Český Krumlov, České Budějovice and Prague, and joins the Elbe at Mělník at 156 m.

Its basin drains 28,089.9 square kilometres, over half of Bohemia and about a third of the Czech Republic. Its waters ultimately reach the North Sea. The river is commonly called the Czech national river. Both the Czech name Vltava and the German Moldau are believed to come from old Germanic words meaning wild water. It appears as Fuldaha in 872 and as Wlitaua in the Chronica Boemorum of 1125.

Hydrologically the Elbe upstream of Mělník is a tributary of the Vltava, since the Vltava has the longer course, greater discharge and larger basin. The combined river is nonetheless called the Elbe for historical reasons, because at the confluence the Elbe runs in a straight line down the main valley while the Vltava meets it at a right angle.

Through Prague the river is crossed by 21 bridges, and its water was used for drinking until 1912, when the Vinohrady Water Tower stopped pumping. Since the 1930s nine hydroelectric dams have been built on the river south of Prague, among them Lipno, Orlík, Slapy and Štěchovice. The Štěchovice reservoir covers the site of St John's Rapids.

The basin has flooded many times, and markers along the banks show the water line for floods in 1784, 1845, 1890, 1940 and, highest of all, 2002. The flood of August 2002 killed several people and left Charles Bridge, the oldest bridge in Prague, seriously weakened.

Vessels of up to 1,000 tonnes can navigate between Mělník and Prague, and smaller craft can go upstream as far as České Budějovice. The stretch near Český Krumlov is popular for water tourism. In Jewish folklore the mystic Judah Loew ben Bezalel made the golem out of clay from the banks of the Vltava to defend the Prague ghetto. Bedřich Smetana's symphonic poem Vltava, often called The Moldau, is among the best-known works of Czech classical music and describes the river's course through Bohemia. The minor planet 2123 Vltava is named after the river.
vo-nguyen-giap: Võ Nguyên Giáp was born in Quảng Bình province, Annam, French Indochina, into a relatively comfortable peasant family. His father, a minor official and committed nationalist who had taken part in the Cần Vương movement in the 1880s, was arrested by the French colonial authorities in 1919 and died in prison a few weeks later. In 1924, at the age of thirteen, Giáp left home to attend the Quốc Học, a French-run lycée in Huế. He was expelled after two years for taking part in protests, and joined the underground Tân Việt Revolutionary Party, which introduced him to communism.

He was arrested in 1930 for taking part in student protests and served 13 months of a two-year sentence in Lao Bảo Prison. He studied law, worked as a history teacher in Hanoi and wrote for revolutionary newspapers. He had no military training before the Second World War.

On 3 May 1940, after the French outlawed the Indochinese Communist Party, Giáp went into exile in China and joined Ho Chi Minh. His wife, left behind, was arrested and sentenced to fifteen years, and in 1943 he was told that guards in Hanoi's central prison had beaten her to death. In 1942 he and about forty men moved back into Vietnam and settled in caves near Vu Nhai, forming the basis of the Viet Minh. On 25 December 1944 he led successful attacks on the French outposts at Khai Phat and Na Ngan.

He served as military commander of the Viet Minh and the People's Army from 1941 to 1972, as minister of defence in 1946 to 1947 and from 1948 to 1980, and as deputy prime minister from 1955 to 1991. He turned a disorganised band of rebels into a light-infantry army with artillery and advanced logistics, and won the decisive victory at Dien Bien Phu in 1954. In the Vietnam War he commanded the army during the Tet Offensive of 1968 and the Easter Offensive of 1972, and he was the principal architect of the Ho Chi Minh trail through Laos and Cambodia. He oversaw the campaigns in Cambodia in 1978 and against China in 1979.

Giáp resigned as defence minister in 1980 and left the Politburo in 1982. He wrote extensively on military theory, including People's Army, People's War and We Will Win. He died on 4 October 2013 at Central Military Hospital 108 in Hanoi, aged 102, and was given a state funeral on 12 and 13 October, before burial in his home province of Quảng Bình. Several Vietnamese cities renamed prominent streets after him.
vogelsberg: The Vogelsberg lies in the county of Vogelsbergkreis, around 60 kilometres north-east of Frankfurt, between the towns of Alsfeld, Fulda, Büdingen and Nidda. The Fulda valley separates it from the Rhön Mountains, and to the south-west lies the low-lying Wetterau. The high central plateau, the Oberwald, stands 600 to 773 metres high and is entirely wooded. The main peaks, the Taufstein at 773 metres and the Hoherodskopf at 763 metres, lie in the High Vogelsberg Nature Park. Numerous rivers rise here and flow outwards in all directions, among them tributaries of the Schwalm, Lower Fulda, Kinzig, Nidda and Ohm. A section of the Rhine-Weser watershed runs over the range.

The Vogelsberg is the largest contiguous volcanic region in Central Europe, covering 2,500 square kilometres. It is not a single shield volcano but many overlapping volcanoes, whose basalt terraces descend from the Oberwald in stepped rings. Volcanic activity in the region began about 20 million years ago and ended about 7 million years ago, and in the Vogelsberg itself it was mainly active between 18.5 and 10 million years ago, with a peak 17 to 15 million years ago. Tropical weathering afterwards turned volcanic rock into red clays, in places forming bauxite and iron ore, which were mined over a long period. Basalt is still quarried for gravel and building stone.

Springs in the eastern Vogelsberg were enclosed in 1876 to supply water pipes to Frankfurt. Excessive withdrawal later dried up springs, caused cracks in buildings and subsidence of the ground, because the particular hydrogeological and ecological situation was not understood.

Parts of the Oberwald are protected, and the beech wood in the Taufstein Nature Reserve has been left to manage itself since 1906. The massif has stone runs of basalt and tuff, raised bogs and ancient woodland. Groundwater from the Vogelsberg supplies the Rhine-Main region, with about two thirds of the water pumped by the Upper Hessian Water Companies going to Frankfurt. The area is known for hiking, cycling and winter sports at Herchenhainer Höhe and Hoherodskopf, which is the tourism centre.
vogt: Church protectors existed in Roman times: a Synod of Carthage in 401 asked the emperor to provide defensores for the churches, though Pope Gregory I later confined that office to the clergy. Under the Merovingians lay representatives of the churches appeared as agentes, defensores and advocati, and the idea drew on the Old German Munt, or guardian. A Capitulary of about 790 ordained that the higher clergy should have advocates, and under the Carolingians bishops, abbots and abbesses had to appoint one in every county where they held property, choosing men familiar with the law.

The church advocate, or advocatus ecclesiae, ran the courts on church lands, including high justice, defended the church with arms and led its men in war, receiving revenues in return. At first the office was neither hereditary nor for life, but after the Carolingian period it passed to powerful nobles who treated church estates as their own, appropriating tithes and oppressing those they were meant to protect. Councils from the ninth century and warnings from Rome in the twelfth sought to curb them. The Hirsau formulary of 1075 confirmed Count Adalbert of Calw as hereditary advocate of that abbey, a model copied across Germany.

Emperors also appointed Vögte to govern lands, castles and towns under their own lordship: a Stadtvogt for a city, a Landvogt for rural estates, a Burgvogt for a castle, and a Reichsvogt often seated in an imperial city.

In Austria abbeys of the 13th and 14th centuries bought back their advocacies in alliance with the Babenberg and early Habsburg dukes. Several small land Vögte survived in the Swabian Circle until 1806, and in the Old Swiss Confederacy cantons appointed Landvögte to shared territories until the office was abolished in 1798. Elsewhere the word took other paths: avoué in France, the advowson, a right of presentation to a benefice, in England, the wójt as hereditary head of a town in medieval Poland, and in modern Dutch voogd, a legal guardian.
vojvodina: In the Neolithic the Starčevo and Vinča cultures flourished in the area. Under Roman rule, Sirmium (modern Sremska Mitrovica) was one of the four capital cities of the empire, and six emperors were born in or near it. Syrmia belonged to the province of Pannonia and the Banat to Dacia, while Bačka lay outside the empire and was held by the Sarmatian Iazyges. After the Romans, Goths, Huns, Gepids and Avars ruled the area, and Slavs settled there in the 6th and 7th centuries. The region belonged to the Principality and Kingdom of Hungary from the 10th century until the 16th.

After the Hungarian defeat at Mohács in 1526, the Serb mercenary leader Jovan Nenad created a short-lived state with Subotica as its capital and proclaimed himself Serbian Emperor; Hungarian nobles defeated his troops in 1527 and he was assassinated. Ottoman rule then lasted until the Treaty of Karlowitz of 1699 and the Austrian conquest of 1716, confirmed at Passarowitz in 1718. Serbs who settled in the Habsburg lands received rights in exchange for serving in the Military Frontier, and Germans were settled from Swabia and Bavaria to repopulate the land.

At the May Assembly in Sremski Karlovci in 1848 the Serbs declared the Serbian Vojvodina, an autonomous region of the Austrian Empire, and war between Serbs and Hungarians followed, with atrocities against civilians on both sides. In 1849 the emperor made it the crown land of the Voivodeship of Serbia and Banat of Temeschwar, which lasted until 1860. After 1867 it returned to Hungarian administration. The 1910 census counted 34% Serbs, 28% Hungarians and 21% Germans.

On 25 November 1918 an assembly of 757 deputies at Novi Sad proclaimed the union of Banat, Bačka and Baranja with the Kingdom of Serbia, and on 1 December 1918 the region became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. From 1929 to 1941 it formed part of the Danube Banovina. In the Second World War Hungary annexed Bačka and Baranya and the Independent State of Croatia took Syrmia. Axis authorities killed about 50,000 people there, mostly Serbs, Jews and Roma, and the Jewish population was almost completely killed or deported. Vojvodina is today an autonomous province of Serbia, with about 1.7 million inhabitants and Novi Sad as its administrative centre.
volcae: The Volcae were not a single tribe but, in Venceslas Kruta's description, a people or group of peoples of composite character and marked mobility. Modern scholarship places their formation in central Europe, though the exact area is disputed: Kruta sets it in Bohemia and Moravia, Karl Strobel in Thuringia and north-eastern Bavaria. Caesar records a section of the Tectosages still living around the Hercynian forest in the mid-1st century BCE. Most Celtologists derive the name from a Gaulish word uolcos, hawk or falcon. Borrowed into Germanic as *walhaz, it later came to mean speakers of Celtic and then Romance languages.

In the 4th century BCE the grouping, led by the Tectosages, spread into the central Danube basin. Some settled in southern Pannonia between the Drava and the Sava, where the name survived in the Volcae Paludes, the marshes of the Volcae, and were later absorbed into the Scordisci. In 279 BCE a band of Tectosages joined the expedition of Brennos against Greece, which forced Thermopylae and advanced on Delphi. After its failure part of them crossed into Asia Minor about 277 BCE in the service of Nicomedes I of Bithynia and became one of the three peoples of the Galatian confederation, beside the Tolistobogii and the Trocmi.

Other bands moved west across the upper Rhine into Gaul in the first half of the 3rd century BCE as two confederations. In 218 BCE they tried in vain to stop Hannibal crossing the Rhône. In the 2nd century BCE the smaller Arecomici held Languedoc around Nemausus, while the Tectosages pushed towards the upper Garonne and Tolosa. Kruta links these mobile groups with the Gaesatae, mercenaries in Cisalpine Italy from the mid-3rd century BCE.

Strabo, following Posidonius, held that the Galatian Tectosages came from Tolosa; modern scholars reverse this and treat the western and eastern bands as offshoots of the central European core. An ancient tradition going back to Timagenes said that the gold seized when the consul Quintus Servilius Caepio stormed Tolosa in 106 BCE was plunder from Delphi under a curse, the Gold of Tolosa. Posidonius rejected the story and held the treasure to be local. The arrival of the Volcae brought Danubian material into southern Gaul and contributed to the Latènisation of the region, which went on without a break over a largely native material culture.
volga: The Volga is 3,531 kilometres long and drains about 1,360,000 square kilometres, almost entirely within Russia. It rises at Volgoverkhov'e in Tver Oblast, in the Valdai Hills north-west of Moscow, and runs east past Tver, Yaroslavl, Nizhny Novgorod and Kazan before turning south past Samara, Saratov and Volgograd. Below Astrakhan it spreads into a delta of as many as 500 channels and smaller rivers and enters the Caspian Sea, an enclosed body of water, so the river reaches no ocean. Its main tributaries are the Kama, the Oka, the Vetluga and the Sura. It freezes over most of its length for three months each year.

The Volga–Oka region has been occupied for at least 9,000 years. In antiquity the river marked the boundary between the Cimmerians and the Scythians, and later between the Scythians and the Massagetae. Names for it survive from several peoples: Scythian Rahā, Herodotus's Oaros, and Turkic Itil, which gave modern forms such as the Tatar İdel. In the first millennium Slavic, Finno-Ugric, Scandinavian, Baltic and Turkic peoples lived along it, and Alans settled the Middle Volga between the 6th and 8th centuries.

The river was a trade route linking Scandinavia and the Slavic lands with Volga Bulgaria, Khazaria, Persia and the Arab world. Volga Bulgaria flourished where the Kama joins the Volga, and Khazaria controlled the lower stretches. Cities such as Atil, Saqsin and Sarai were among the largest of the medieval world. The Mongols founded the Golden Horde on the lower river, and its successor khanates of Kazan and Astrakhan were conquered by the Russians in the 16th century.

Catherine the Great invited foreigners to settle the region in 1763, and Germans responded in the largest numbers. In 1941 the remaining Volga Germans, about 400,000, were deported and many were forced into labour camps. During the Second World War the Battle of Stalingrad was fought on the river's bend, where Volgograd now stands.

The Volga is widely regarded as the national river of Russia, and its place in Russian literature and folklore is shown in the name Mother Volga. Soviet-era dams formed some of the largest reservoirs in the world, and building them involved the forced resettlement of many people and the flooding of the town of Mologa and of several monasteries. Canals connect it to the Black Sea, the Azov, Baltic and White seas, and Moscow.
volga-germans: Catherine II, born a German princess in Stettin, deposed her husband Peter III in 1762 and took the Russian throne. She issued manifestos in 1762 and 1763 inviting non-Muslim, non-Jewish Europeans to settle, become Russian subjects and farm Russian land while keeping their language and culture. The first drew little response; the second improved the terms and attracted colonists. The settlers lived along the Volga around Saratov and kept their churches, which were Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic, Moravian and Mennonite. They were also exempt from military service, a right revoked in the later nineteenth century. In the late eighteenth century nomadic Kazakhs raided their settlements amid the disorder of Pugachev's Rebellion.

Towards the end of the nineteenth century Russia pursued a policy of Russification, eroded the settlers' special rights and reinstated conscription, which especially harmed the pacifist Mennonites. Many emigrated to the United States, Canada, Brazil and Argentina. In the United States they settled in the Dakotas, Kansas and Nebraska, where they succeeded in dryland farming. In Argentina they founded many villages, and today descendants celebrate festivals such as the Kerb.

After the Russian Revolution the Volga German Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was established in 1924, with its capital at Engels, and lasted until 1941. After the German invasion of 22 June 1941, the Soviet government decided to deport the whole German population from the republic and from the Saratov and Stalingrad oblasts to Siberia and Kazakhstan, as a precaution, with about half going to each. The Central Committee issued its resolution on 12 August, and the republic was abolished on 7 September 1941. The operation was finished at the end of September.

Possessions were confiscated. Able-bodied men and later women were forced into labour columns, the Trudarmee, in forests and mines under conditions similar to the Gulag. Robert Conquest estimated that about one third did not survive the camps in the first stage. Historians debate whether the deportations were a genocide, some classing them as ethnocide, since the question is whether destroying non-Russians was intentional. The Volga Germans never returned in their old numbers and were not allowed to settle in the area for decades. After the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, many emigrated to Germany under its law of return. 28 August is the unofficial Day of Mourning and Memory of Russian Germans.
volga-tatars: The name Tatar has a long and complicated history and was once an umbrella term for different Turkic and Mongolic tribes. Today it mostly refers to the Volga Tatars, who became its main bearers after the founding of the Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which lasted from 1920 to 1990 and is now Tatarstan. Their ethnogenesis is still debated, but their history is usually connected to the Kipchak Tatars of the Golden Horde (1242 to 1502) and to its predecessor, Volga Bulgaria, whose adoption of Islam, in 922, is marked each year in Tatarstan.
After the Golden Horde collapsed, the ancestors of the modern Tatars formed the Khanate of Kazan (1438 to 1552), which lost its independence to Russia in the Siege of Kazan in 1552.

Tatars have been subjects of Russia since 1552. Russian authorities began a policy of converting Muslim Tatars in that year, and many were forcibly baptised under Ivan the Terrible in the sixteenth century; forced conversions continued under later rulers until the mid-eighteenth century. This produced the Kryashens, an Orthodox Christian group of Tatars, of whom 34,882 identified themselves as such in the census of 2010. The Tatar Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic of 1920 was the first successful Tatar formation since the Khanate of Kazan.

Several subgroups are distinguished. The largest are the Kazan Tatars, followed by the Mishar Tatars, who differ mainly in dialect. The Kasimov Tatars formed in the Qasim Khanate and fought in the troops of Ivan the Terrible, including at the conquest of Kazan.

The Tatar language belongs to the Kipchak-Bulgar branch of the Kipchak languages and has two main dialects, the central Kazan dialect, which is the literary language, and the western Mishar dialect. Until the early 1900s Tatars used a local variant of Türki as their literary language, and Ğabdulla Tuqay (1886 to 1913) is often considered the founder of the modern literary language.

Most Tatars are Sunni Muslims. Their celebrations include Islamic and ancient Turkic feasts as well as Nowruz. The best known is Sabantuy, a harvest festival that dates from pre-Islamic times and is now a national holiday in Tatarstan, with wrestling and horseback riding. Tatars make up 53.6 percent of the population of Tatarstan; about a third of all Tatars live there and the rest elsewhere in Russia, and there are diasporas abroad, including the Finnish Tatars, descended from Mishar Tatar merchants who settled in Finland in the late 1800s and early 1900s.
volga-trade-route: The route was established by the Varangians who settled in north-western Russia in the early 9th century. About 10 km south of the point where the Volkhov River enters Lake Ladoga they founded a settlement called Ladoga, in Old Norse Aldeigjuborg. Archaeological evidence suggests Rus trading along the Volga as early as the end of the 8th century.

The earliest and richest finds of Arabic coins in Europe come from present-day Russia, notably Timerevo in the district of Yaroslavl. A hoard at Petergof near Saint Petersburg holds twenty coins bearing graffiti in Arabic, Khazar runic, Greek and Old Norse runic, the last accounting for more than half, and the latest of the coins dates to 804–805.

From Aldeigjuborg the Rus travelled up the Volkhov to Novgorod, then across Lake Ilmen and along the Lovat River. A portage of about 3 kilometres took their boats to the sources of the Volga. Traders carried furs, honey and slaves through lands held by Finnic and Permian peoples to the Volga Bulgars, and on to the Khazar Khaganate, whose capital Atil was a busy entrepot on the Caspian shore. From there they crossed the sea to the caravan routes to Baghdad.

Vikings trafficked captives taken in raids in eastern Europe along the route, selling them to Muslim merchants for silver dirhams and silk. The Arabic term for such slaves, saqaliba, did not mean only Slavs, since the captives included Finno-Ugric peoples. The silver hoards of Scandinavia, such as the Spillings and Sundveda hoards, reflect this trade, which functioned from at least 786 until 1009.

The route lost its importance by the 11th century, owing to the decline of silver output in the Abbasid caliphate, and the Dnieper route to the Byzantine Empire gained weight. Yngvars saga víðförla describes a Swedish expedition into the Caspian launched about 1041 by Ingvar the Far-Travelled. It was unsuccessful, and Scandinavians made no later attempts to use the route.

Written accounts survive from Muslim writers. About 885–886 ibn Khordadbeh described Rus merchants taking beaver hides, black fox pelts and swords to the Black Sea and the Caspian, paying a tithe to the Byzantine ruler and to the ruler of the Khazars.

In 921–922 Ahmad ibn Fadlan joined a diplomatic delegation from Baghdad to the Volga Bulgars. He described Rus merchants who, on landing, offered food and drink to a wooden stake with a human face and asked it to send them a merchant with many dinars and dirhems. Scholars have disputed whether ibn Khordadbeh's phrase a kind of the Saqaliba shows the Rus to have been Slavs or Scandinavians.
volgograd: Volgograd lies on the western bank of the Volga and covers 859.4 square kilometres. It is the administrative centre and largest city of Volgograd Oblast, divided into eight districts. The city stands at the east end of the Volga–Don Canal, opened in 1952 to link the two great rivers of southern Russia, and is a major railway junction. Its climate is a hot-summer continental one with cold winters and low rainfall spread through the year.

The fortress of Tsaritsyn, named after the Tsaritsa River, stood near the mouth of that river and soon became the nucleus of a trading settlement. At the start of the 17th century its garrison numbered 350 to 400 people, and in 1607 it rebelled for six months against the troops of Tsar Vasili Shuisky. The Streltsy stationed there were paid to defend the Volga trade route from the Cossacks, though some joined the Cossacks themselves. The railway link to Moscow in 1871 connected the isolated area to the rest of the empire, and by the 1890s the economy rested on grain, naphtha, fish and salt.

Tsaritsyn came under Bolshevik control in November 1917, fell briefly to the White Army in mid-1919 and returned to Bolshevik control in January 1920. On 10 April 1925 it was renamed Stalingrad in honour of Joseph Stalin, then General Secretary of the Communist Party, for his role in its defence. Under Soviet rule minorities were targeted: the only Jewish school in the area was closed in 1926, and the synagogue was closed in 1929 after a campaign begun in 1928. The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, consecrated in 1918, was closed in 1929, used as a motor depot and demolished in 1932.

The Battle of Stalingrad, the largest and bloodiest battle of the Second World War, earned the city the title of Hero City. On 10 November 1961 Nikita Khrushchev's administration renamed it Volgograd, after the river, as part of de-Stalinization. The change was controversial because of the city's importance as a symbol of resistance, and proposals to restore the old name were floated in 1984 but not accepted.

Volgograd has a little over one million inhabitants and remains an industrial city, with shipbuilding, oil refining, steel and aluminium production and heavy machinery. The Mamayev Kurgan memorial complex, the hill where some of the most intense fighting took place, is dominated by The Motherland Calls, an 85-metre statue. The Panorama Museum preserves Gerhardt's Mill in its bombed-out state, and Pavlov's House, another surviving monument of the battle, stands nearby. The Alexander Nevsky Cathedral was rebuilt as a replica and consecrated in 2021.
volhynia: Volhynia is a historic region lying between south-eastern Poland, south-western Belarus and north-western Ukraine. Its borders are not clearly defined. In Ukraine it corresponds roughly to Volyn Oblast, Rivne Oblast, the western part of Zhytomyr Oblast and the northern parts of Khmelnytskyi and Ternopil oblasts. Geographically it occupies the northern areas of the Volhynian-Podolian Upland and the western part of the Polesian Lowland along the Pripyat valley, in the basins of the Western Bug and the Pripyat. Its alternative name, Lodomeria, comes from the city of Volodymyr, once the capital of the medieval Volhynian Principality. Important cities include Lutsk, Rivne, Kovel and Volodymyr.

The Primary Chronicle names the tribes of the Dulebes, Buzhans and Volhynians. Volhynia may have belonged to Kievan Rus' as early as the 10th century. In 983 Vladimir the Great appointed his son Vsevolod as ruler of the Volhynian principality, and in 988 he founded the city of Volodymer. From the late 12th century Volhynia was closely tied to the neighbouring Principality of Galicia, and the two were united on several occasions under Roman the Great from 1199, though they broke apart.

The Hungarian king Andrew II took the title King of Galicia and Lodomeria, which Hungarian kings used up to 1918. After the Galicia-Volhynia state broke up about 1340, Poland took western and Lithuania eastern Volhynia. After 1569 Volhynia was a voivodeship within the Lesser Poland Province of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth.

After the Third Partition of Poland in 1795 most of Volhynia became the Volhynian Governorate of the Russian Empire, which forcibly liquidated the Ukrainian Greek Catholic Church and transferred its buildings to the Russian Orthodox Church. 7 percent Germans. The Peace of Riga of 1921 divided Volhynia between Poland and the Soviet Union.

In World War II most of the region's Jewish population of about 460,000 was shot in the Holocaust, mainly between August and October 1942, and in 1943 up to 100,000 Poles in Volhynia were massacred by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army.

The Soviet Union annexed Volhynia to Soviet Ukraine after World War II, and most of the remaining ethnic Poles were expelled to Poland in 1945. Ethnic Germans were also expelled. Since the dissolution of the Soviet Union in the 1990s Volhynia has been an integral part of Ukraine. The territory that still carries the name is Volyn Oblast. The Peresopnytsia Gospel is counted among its important relics.
voline: Vsevolod Eikhenbaum was born on 23 August 1882 into an educated Russian Jewish family from Voronezh. His parents were both doctors, and he and his brother Boris were taught French and German as well as Russian by foreign tutors. He studied law at Saint Petersburg State University, but in 1904 he left to work full time for the Socialist Revolutionary Party, tutoring workers and setting up a library and study groups. In the 1905 revolution he witnessed Bloody Sunday, took part in founding the Saint Petersburg Soviet and was arrested for a Kronstadt uprising. Arrested again in 1907 and deported to Siberia, he escaped to France, where he met the anarchists Sébastien Faure and Apollon Karelin and by 1911 had become an anarchist himself.

He fled to the United States in 1915, joined the Union of Russian Workers and wrote for its paper Golos truda, and returned to Petrograd in July 1917 to promote anarcho-syndicalism, calling for workers' control. After the October Revolution he criticised the Bolsheviks, warning of their authoritarian tendencies, and moved to Ukraine, where he helped found the Nabat Confederation of Anarchist Organisations. On 18 November 1918 he drew up its declaration of principles, written to suit anarchist communists, individualists and syndicalists alike. In 1919 the Nabat moved to Huliaipole and became a central part of the Makhnovshchina, the movement of Nestor Makhno.

There Volin joined its Cultural-Educational Commission, edited its publications and chaired its Military Revolutionary Council. On 14 January 1920 he was arrested while ill with typhus and handed to the Cheka, with orders from Leon Trotsky to execute him. Appeals by anarchists and by the Bolshevik Victor Serge led to his death sentence being commuted, and he was freed in October 1920 under the Starobilsk agreement, refusing an offer of the post of People's Commissar for Education in Ukraine. He was imprisoned again in Moscow, took part in a hunger strike in July 1921 and was then deported from Soviet Russia.

In exile in Berlin and then Paris he contributed to Sébastien Faure's Anarchist Encyclopedia and to anarchist papers in several languages, and in 1927 criticised the Platform as contradicting decentralisation. He completed The Unknown Revolution in Marseille in 1940 and went into hiding after the Nazi invasion of France and the establishment of the collaborationist French State because of his Jewish heritage and his politics. He died of tuberculosis in a Paris hospital on 18 September 1945, and his ashes were buried at the Père Lachaise Cemetery near those of Makhno. Victor Serge called him a man of absolute probity and exceptional rigour of thought.
volkhov-river: The Volkhov is 224 kilometres long and drains a basin of 80,200 square kilometres. It is the only outflow of Lake Ilmen and runs north into Lake Ladoga, the largest lake in Europe, as the second largest tributary of Ladoga. It belongs to the basin of the Neva and passes Veliky Novgorod, the towns of Kirishi, Volkhov and Novaya Ladoga, and the historically important village of Staraya Ladoga. It is navigable over its whole length, and freezes up in late November and breaks up in early April. Several etymologies of the name have been proposed, none universally accepted; the philologist Max Vasmer doubted a link with the Russian volkhv, a pagan priest.

Despite its modest size the Volkhov has played a large part in Russian history. Its role in trade came from its position as the only river penetrating deep into inland Russia that flows north towards the Baltic, rather than south towards the Caspian or Black Seas. In the mid-9th century it was a heavily populated trade artery of the Varangian-dominated Rus' Khaganate, and a vital part of the route linking northern Europe to the Orient by way of the Volga and of the Dnieper, the route from the Varangians to the Greeks.

Viking commercial vessels entering the river anchored at the trade emporium of Aldeigja, now Ladoga, and then rowed upstream past rapids guarded by fortified settlements at Novye Duboviki and Gorodishche. Another outpost lay at Kholopy Gorodok, 13 kilometres north of Veliky Novgorod, or rather Holmgard, which was founded near the point where the river leaves Lake Ilmen. Most of these sites were small stations for refitting and resupply, and such settlements are likely to have given the country its Norse name of Gardariki. The river carried a significant part of the trade between Novgorod and Western Europe. From 1941 to 1944 the stretch north of Novgorod separated Soviet troops on the right bank from German troops on the left.

The level of the river is regulated by the dam of the Volkhov hydroelectric plant, the first Soviet regional hydroelectric dam, opened on 19 December 1926 under the GOELRO plan about 25 kilometres upstream from the mouth. The dam also eased navigation in the lower river, once known for its rapids. The Siversov Canal joins the upper Volkhov to the Msta, bypassing Lake Ilmen, and the Ladoga Canal joins the lower part to the Neva, the Syas and the Svir, bypassing Lake Ladoga. A figure of the Volkhov stands among the allegorical monuments to four major rivers of Russia on the rostral columns of the Old Saint Petersburg Stock Exchange.
volodymyr-shcherbytsky: Shcherbytsky was born on 17 February 1918 in Verkhnodniprovsk. He joined the Komsomol in 1931, studied at the Dnipropetrovsk Chemical Technology Institute and graduated in 1941, the year he joined the Communist Party. After the German invasion he was mobilized into the Red Army, served in chemical units on the Transcaucasian Front and left the service in December 1945 as a captain. From 1948 he was a party functionary in Dniprodzerzhynsk, where he succeeded Leonid Brezhnev as regional party boss in November 1955. He became chairman of the Ukrainian Council of Ministers in 1961 and was shifted to Dnipropetrovsk in 1963, but Brezhnev restored him to that post in 1965.

In May 1972 Petro Shelest was recalled to Moscow amid a broader attack on the nationally minded Ukrainian intelligentsia, and the Central Committee elected Shcherbytsky first secretary. He belonged to Brezhnev's Dnipropetrovsk clan and had joined the Politburo in April 1971. The first year brought a purge in which 5 percent of the party's members were removed and leading intellectuals, among them Viacheslav Chornovil and Ivan Svitlychnyi, were arrested. Under him meetings of the Ukrainian party were conducted in Russian, Ukrainian education was scaled back and political prisoners were often re-arrested.

After the Chernobyl disaster of 1986 Gorbachev ordered him to hold the International Workers' Day parade in Kyiv. Political groups opposed to him formed from 1987, and in December 1987 he publicly acknowledged the Holodomor for the first time, blaming the famine on drought. In July 1989 coal miners in the Donbas struck, some demanding his resignation. On 20 September 1989 he lost his Politburo seat, and he was removed as first secretary, officially because of old age, and replaced by Vladimir Ivashko.

Shcherbytsky died on 16 February 1990, the day before his 72nd birthday and the day he was due to testify about Chernobyl before the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR. The official cause was pneumonia, although it was alleged that he shot himself. He was buried at the Baikove Cemetery in Kyiv. The writer Oles Honchar called him the most loyal Russifier, while he is also credited with supporting monuments to Ukrainian Cossacks and the football manager Valeriy Lobanovsky. Under decommunization laws streets named for him in Dnipro and Kamianske were renamed in 2015 and 2016.
volodymyr-vynnychenko: Vynnychenko was born on 28 July 1880 in the village of Vesely Kut, in the Kherson Governorate of the Russian Empire, to a peasant family; his father had been a serf. At the Yelyzavetgrad gymnasium he joined a revolutionary organisation, wrote a revolutionary poem and was jailed for a week and excluded. In 1900 he joined the Revolutionary Ukrainian Party and enrolled in law at Kiev University, but he was expelled for his activities. He was arrested several times, and in 1902 he published his first novel, Beauty and Strength. After a third arrest in 1906 he fled abroad, living from 1907 to 1914 in cities including Lemberg, Vienna, Geneva and Paris. In 1911 he married Rosalia Lifshitz, a French Jewish doctor.

He returned to Kiev in 1917 and, after the February Revolution, headed the General Secretariat of Ukraine, an executive body under the Russian Provisional Government. He resigned on 13 August in protest and formed a second government, confirmed by Alexander Kerensky on 1 September. The Ukrainian People's Republic proclaimed its independence on 22 January 1918. Bolshevik forces under Mikhail Muravyov took Kiev, and the government retreated to Zhytomyr and signed a treaty with Germany. Hetman Pavlo Skoropadsky seized power in April 1918, and Vynnychenko left Kiev. He headed the Ukrainian National Union and, after forming the Directorate, helped organise a revolt that succeeded; he returned to the capital on 19 December 1918 to restore the republic.

Critics often say that the mistakes of Vynnychenko and Mykhailo Hrushevsky cost the republic its independence, since both opposed creating an army and refused Symon Petliura's requests to use his volunteers as its core. Unable to restore order or end his disagreement with Petliura, Vynnychenko stepped down on 10 February 1919 and emigrated. In 1920 he travelled to Moscow to seek agreement with the Bolsheviks, but after four months of negotiation he accused them of Great Russian chauvinism.

Vynnychenko spent thirty years in Europe, in Germany and then France. His works were published in eleven volumes in the 1920s, and in 1928 he published the science fiction novel The Solar Machine. In 1934 he moved to Mougins, near Cannes, where he farmed a homestead and wrote on his philosophy of happiness, Concordism. He refused to cooperate with the Nazis during the German occupation of France and was held in a concentration camp, which badly affected his health. He died in Mougins in 1951. He is recognised as a leading Ukrainian modernist writer; his works were banned in Soviet Ukraine from the 1930s to the mid-1980s.
volodymyr-zatonsky: Volodymyr Petrovych Zatonsky was born on 27 July 1888 in the village of Lysets in Podolia Governorate, the son of a volost clerk. He graduated from Kyiv University in 1912 and taught physics at the Kyiv Polytechnic Institute. He joined the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party as a Menshevik in 1905 and went over to the Bolsheviks in March 1917, sitting on their Kyiv Committee, and he was one of the founders of the Communist Party (Bolshevik) of Ukraine.

Zatonsky took part in the fight against the Central Rada. When the Red Army took Kyiv in 1918 he narrowly escaped execution as a counter-revolutionary, saved, by his own account, only by a mandate from Vladimir Lenin. Early in 1918 he led the Soviet Ukrainian delegation to the peace talks at Brest-Litovsk, and from 19 March to 18 April he chaired the All-Ukrainian Central Executive Committee. From November 1918 he was people's commissar of education and worked to close the Kamyanets-Podilsky State University, which he saw as a centre of Symon Petliura's forces.

He sat with Vladimir Antonov-Ovseyenko and Joseph Stalin on the Revolutionary Military Council of the Kursk group that planned the Soviet campaign in Ukraine, and in 1921 received the Order of the Red Banner for his part in suppressing the Kronshtadt mutiny.

In 1922 he signed the treaty founding the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics for the Ukrainian SSR. He headed the education ministry again from 1923, the political directorate of the Ukrainian Military District from 1924 to 1926 and the people's commissariat of state inspection from 1927 to 1932. In 1933 he succeeded Mykola Skrypnyk in charge of education and became chief editor of the Ukrainian Soviet Encyclopedia. He was a full member of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences from 1929.

On 3 November 1937 Zatonsky was arrested at a cinema with his family, and his wife, the physician Elena Zatonskaya, was arrested days later. He was charged with membership of an anti-Soviet Ukrainian National Center, although he had been loyal to Stalin. On 29 July 1938, after a trial of twenty minutes, he was sentenced to ten years without the right of correspondence, a euphemism for death, and shot the same day. He was rehabilitated in 1956.
vologases-vi: Vologases VI, in Parthian Walagash and in New Persian Balāsh, succeeded his father Vologases V as king in about 208. His rule was unquestioned for a few years, until his brother Artabanus IV rebelled, most likely in about 213. Artabanus conquered much of the empire, including Media and Susa, while Vologases seems to have kept only Seleucia, where he minted coins. By 216 Artabanus controlled most of the empire and was acknowledged as supreme ruler by the Roman Empire.

The Roman emperor Caracalla tried to exploit the quarrel. He asked Vologases to send two refugees, a philosopher named Antiochus and a certain Tiridates, who was possibly an Armenian prince or an uncle of Vologases, hoping for a pretext to invade the Parthian Empire. To the surprise of the Romans, Vologases sent both men to Caracalla in 215 and so denied him the pretext. That Caracalla addressed Vologases rather than Artabanus shows that the Romans still regarded him as the dominant king at that time. Caracalla turned instead to an invasion of Armenia under a freedman named Theocritus, which ended in disaster. He then asked Artabanus for his daughter in marriage, an offer that Artabanus declined.

By then Artabanus was the dominant king, and Vologases ruled a small principality centred on Seleucia until 221/2. In 224 Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian dynasty, defeated and killed Artabanus, which ended the Parthian Empire. Coins of Vologases continue to appear in Mesopotamia until 228, and Ardashir must have driven him out or defeated him there soon after that year.
volos: Volos lies on the Greek mainland about 170 kilometres north of Athens and 140 kilometres south of Thessaloniki, at the innermost point of the Pagasetic Gulf and at the foot of Mount Pelion, which Greek tradition made the land of the Centaurs. It is the only outlet to the sea from Thessaly. West of the city are the Neolithic settlements of Dimini and Sesklo; Sesklo has the remains of the oldest acropolis in Greece, dated to 6000 BCE.

Demetrias was founded in 293 BCE by Demetrius Poliorcetes, King of Macedon. Iolcus was known in myth as the home of Jason, who sailed on the Argo with the Argonauts in quest of the Golden Fleece. The mound of Kastro in western Volos was a Bronze Age settlement, with a Mycenaean palace complex where a few Linear B tablets have been found. The Slavic tribe of the Belegezites settled in the area in the 7th century.

The city reappears in 1333 under the name Golos, captured by the Byzantine general John Monomachos; the name is of Slavic origin and is thought to come from a word for barren. Thessaly fell under Serbian rule in 1348, returned to Byzantine rule for about twenty years after 1373, and was conquered by the Ottomans under Bayezid I. Volos was definitively Ottoman only in 1423. The Venetians under Francesco Morosini took the fortress in 1665, but the Ottomans recovered it.

In April 1827 the Greek fleet under the philhellene Frank Abney Hastings captured five Ottoman ships in the harbour and forced the garrison out, yet the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832 left Volos outside the new Greek state. It joined the Kingdom of Greece in November 1881 with the rest of Thessaly, when it had only 4,900 people, and grew rapidly as merchants, craftsmen and sailors moved in. Refugees arrived in the 1920s from Ionia, Pontus, Cappadocia and Eastern Thrace. Under the Axis occupation the local rabbi, Moshe Pesach, and the Greek authorities saved about 700 members of the Jewish community from deportation.

Volos is the capital of the Magnesia regional unit and the seat of the University of Thessaly, founded in 1984. It had 85,803 people in 2021. Much of the city was rebuilt after catastrophic earthquakes in 1955, and some neoclassical buildings of the late 19th and early 20th centuries survive, among them the Archaeological Museum of Volos of 1909. It is a major port, with ferry connections to the Sporades islands, and an industrial centre known for steel and cement.
volta-redonda: Volta Redonda is a municipality in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, covering 182.81 square kilometres at 350 to 707 metres above sea level and lying 130 kilometres from the city of Rio de Janeiro. Its name, Portuguese for Round Turn, comes from the round curve of the Paraíba do Sul river around which the city was built. It borders Barra Mansa, Barra do Piraí, Pinheiral, Piraí and Rio Claro, and with Barra Mansa and Pinheiral it forms a conurbation. It is the economic centre of the South Fluminense region.

In 1744 the first explorers named the curve of the Paraíba do Sul river Volta Redonda, and large farms were installed in the region. Between 1860 and 1870 navigation on the river between Resende and Barra do Piraí had its golden period, and the Dom Pedro II railroad was built at Barra do Piraí and Barra Mansa. The village of Santo Antonio de Volta Redonda began to grow in 1875, but after the freeing of slaves in 1888 the Vale do Paraíba declined, and its agriculture never recovered in a very satisfactory way.

The cycle of industrialisation began in 1941, when the site was chosen, in the middle of the Second World War, for the steel mill of the Companhia Siderúrgica Nacional (CSN). It marked the base of Brazilian industrialisation, and labourers from many regions of the country came to work there. The mill opened in 1946. A symbol of national pride, it embodied the protectionist policies that prevailed in Latin American economies between the Second World War and the debt crisis of the 1980s. It was privatised in 1993 and is now known as the Presidente Vargas Steelworks.

Volta Redonda had 261,563 inhabitants at the 2022 census. Because of its steel it is known as Cidade do Aço, Portuguese for City of Steel, although its economy now rests largely on services and trade as well as industry. A school of industrial engineering and metallurgy of Fluminense Federal University opened there in 1961, and other universities followed.
voltaic-pile: The voltaic pile built on Luigi Galvani's discovery in the 1780s that a circuit of two metals and a frog's leg can make the leg respond. Its invention can be traced to an argument between Galvani and Volta. In 1794 Alessandro Volta demonstrated that two metals and brine-soaked cloth or cardboard arranged in a circuit also produce an electric current. Volta taught at the University of Pavia from 1778 to 1819, and many of his instruments are kept in its University History Museum, although the piles on display are not original: those lent for the centenary of the invention were lost in a fire.

In 1800 Volta stacked several pairs of alternating copper (or silver) and zinc discs, separated by cloth or cardboard soaked in brine, which increased the total electromotive force. When the top and bottom contacts were joined by a wire, a current flowed through the pile and the wire. This was the first true battery, giving a continuous charge.

Because Volta believed the electromotive force arose at the contact between the two metals, his piles had one extra copper disc at the top and one extra zinc disc at the bottom. Each zinc, electrolyte and copper cell generates 0.76 V with a brine electrolyte, and the voltages of the cells add.

Humphry Davy showed that the electromotive force was caused by a chemical reaction, not by the voltage difference between the two metals. Michael Faraday, building on Volta's work, proposed two laws of electrochemistry that conflicted with the beliefs Volta had laid down thirty years earlier, and the words electrode and electrolyte are his.

On 20 March 1800 Volta wrote to the Royal Society in London to describe the technique. William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle used the pile to discover the electrolysis of water in 1800. Davy and Andrew Crosse were among the first to build large piles; Davy's 2000-pair pile of 1808 for the Royal Institution served to demonstrate carbon arc discharge and to isolate barium, calcium, boron, strontium and magnesium, after he had found sodium and potassium in 1807. Batteries related to Volta's, such as the Daniell cell and the Grove cell, powered the 19th-century electrical industry until the dynamo arrived in the 1870s.
voltaire: François-Marie Arouet, later known as Voltaire, was born in Paris, the youngest of five children of François Arouet, a lawyer and minor treasury official, and Marie Marguerite Daumard, whose family was of the lowest rank of the French nobility. He gave his birth date as 20 February 1694, claiming to be the illegitimate son of a nobleman, but his birth is dated to 21 November 1694, with a baptism on 22 November. The Jesuits educated him at the Collège Louis-le-Grand from 1704 to 1711, where he was taught Latin, theology and rhetoric.

Voltaire's play Artémire flopped in 1720, and he turned to an epic poem about Henry IV of France, La Henriade. Denied a licence to publish it, he went north in August 1722 to find a publisher outside France, and in the Netherlands he was impressed by the openness and tolerance of Dutch society. The poem was printed clandestinely in Rouen, and when copies were smuggled into Paris it was an instant success. His play Mariamne failed in 1724 but did better in a reworked version in April 1725.

In early 1726 Guy Auguste de Rohan-Chabot had Voltaire beaten by servants after a quarrel about his name change. When Voltaire challenged him to a duel, the powerful Rohan family had him imprisoned without trial in the Bastille on 17 April 1726. Fearing indefinite imprisonment, he asked to be exiled to England instead, and on 2 May he was escorted from the Bastille to Calais and embarked.

He was one of the first authors to be commercially successful internationally, and wrote more than 20,000 letters and 2,000 books and pamphlets. In February 1778 he returned to Paris for the first time in over 25 years, partly for the opening of his tragedy Irène, and died there on 30 May 1778. The Church had refused him a Christian burial because he would not retract his criticism, so friends buried him secretly at the Abbey of Scellières.

Voltaire produced plays, poems, novels, essays, histories and scientific expositions. His best-known work is the novella Candide (1759), which ridicules Gottfried Leibniz's belief that this is the best of all possible worlds. His History of Charles XII (1731), The Age of Louis XIV (1751) and Essay on the Customs and the Spirit of the Nations (1756) set aside diplomatic and military narrative for customs, social history and the arts and sciences, and treated Europe as a whole.
volturno: The Volturno, in Latin Volturnus, a name taken from volvere, to roll, is a river in south-central Italy, 175 km long. It rises in the Abruzzese central Apennines of Samnium near Castel San Vincenzo, in the province of Isernia, Molise, flows south-east to its junction with the Calore Irpino near Caiazzo, runs south to Venafro and turns south-west, past Capua, to enter the Tyrrhenian Sea at Castel Volturno, north-west of Naples. Its main tributaries are the San Bartolomeo, Lete, Torano, Rivo Tella, Titerno, Calore Irpino and Isclero.

The river has always had considerable military importance. The Romans founded the colony of Volturnum at its mouth in 194 BCE, probably preceded by an older, possibly Etruscan, port of Capua. A fort had already been placed there during the Roman siege of Capua to serve, with Puteoli, for the provisioning of the army, and Augustus placed a colony of veterans there. The Via Domitiana crossed the river at this point, and at Capua the Via Appia and the Via Latina joined just north of the bridge. In 554 the Byzantine general Narses defeated a Frankish-Alamannic army near the river during the Gothic War.

In 1860, after Giuseppe Garibaldi's invasion of southern Italy, Francis II of the Two Sicilies fled from Naples and took up a defensive position on the south bank of the Volturno. On 1 and 2 October the Piedmontese troops and those of Garibaldi inflicted a defeat on the Neapolitan forces at the battle of the Volturno, which led to the fall of Capua. In World War II the river gave its name to the Volturno Line, a German defensive position in Italy.
volubilis: Volubilis stands on a ridge below the Zerhoun mountain, above the valley of the Khoumane and its small tributary, the Fertassa, overlooking a fertile alluvial plain north of Meknes. The area has been inhabited for some 5,000 years, and by the third century BCE the Carthaginians had a presence there, shown by the remains of a temple to the Punic god Baal and by pottery and stones inscribed in Phoenician. The origin of the name is unknown, but it may be a Latinisation of the Amazigh word Walilt, meaning oleander, which grows along the valley.

The city lay within the kingdom of Mauretania, which became a Roman client state after the fall of Carthage in 146 BCE. Its magistrates kept the Carthaginian title of suffete long after Punic rule ended. In 25 BCE Augustus placed Juba II of Numidia on the Mauretanian throne; Juba, educated in Rome and married to Cleopatra Selene II, built up Volubilis as a second capital. Roman rule expanded the city from about 12 to about 42 hectares, and olive oil made it prosperous: fifty-eight oil-pressing complexes have been found, and some of the grandest mansions had their own presses. The city fell to local tribes around 285 and was never retaken by Rome.

It remained inhabited for centuries, with residents still bearing Latin names in the sixth and seventh centuries. By the time the Arabs arrived in the eighth century the city had converted to Islam and was inhabited by the Awraba, a Berber tribe. Idris I, a descendant of Muhammad who had fled Syria after the Battle of Fakhkh in 787, was proclaimed imam there. He was assassinated at Volubilis in 791 on the orders of Harun al-Rashid, and his son Idris II moved to Fes, which removed the city's last political importance.

About half of the site was excavated by the French between 1912 and 1955, and some buildings, among them a basilica and a triumphal arch, were restored or reconstructed. The Decumanus Maximus, lined with porticoes and shops, and the grand houses with mosaics still in place on their floors can be seen. Volubilis is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, described as an exceptionally well preserved example of a large Roman colonial town on the fringes of the Empire.
volunteer-army: The Volunteer Army began to form in November or December 1917 at Novocherkassk under General Mikhail Alekseyev and General Lavr Kornilov. Its first supporters were volunteering officers, cadets, students and Cossacks; of the first 3,000 recruits only twelve were ordinary soldiers, and some of the officers resented serving as privates. Its creation was announced on 27 December 1917 (9 January 1918 in the modern calendar). Alekseyev became its overall leader and Kornilov commander-in-chief, with General Alexander Lukomsky as chief of staff and General Anton Denikin commanding the 1st Division. A Special Council at headquarters included civilian politicians such as Peter Struve, Pavel Milyukov, Mikhail Rodzianko, Sergey Sazonov and Boris Savinkov.

In early February 1918 the army numbered more than 3,600 men. The Red Army's advance forced it to retreat from Rostov-on-Don to the Kuban, a march known as the Ice March, but most Kuban Cossacks did not support it, and only a unit of 3,000 under General Viktor Pokrovsky joined it on 26 March, raising it to 6,000. Its attempt to take Yekaterinodar between 9 and 13 April was a disaster, and Kornilov was killed by an artillery shell. Denikin took over the remnants.

In June 1918 Colonel Mikhail Drozdovsky brought 3,000 men, and on 23 June the army began the Kuban Offensive with the support of General Pyotr Krasnov. By September it numbered 30,000 to 35,000 men and took the name Caucasus Volunteer Army. In the autumn Britain, France and the United States increased their aid, and the southern White forces combined as the Armed Forces of South Russia under Denikin. In June 1919, after capturing the Donbas, Tsaritsyn and Kharkov, Denikin began to advance on Moscow, the main blow being assigned to the Volunteer Army of 40,000 under General Vladimir May-Mayevsky.

Its efficiency fell over the summer through heavy losses and the conscription of peasants and captured Red soldiers, and in October 1919 a Red Army counteroffensive defeated it decisively. In early 1920 it was reduced to a corps of 5,000 under General Alexander Kutepov, and on 26 and 27 March 1920 its remnants were evacuated from Novorossiysk to the Crimea, where they merged with the army of General Pyotr Wrangel.

Its officers had been out of politics before the revolution and could not judge or organise the political struggle. The army proclaimed a fight against the Bolsheviks, after which a Constituent Assembly would choose a form of government, and this did not give most of the population an idea they could understand. Its propaganda service, OSVAG, was headed by the biologist S. Chakhotin.
vorarlberg: Vorarlberg borders Germany by way of Lake Constance, Switzerland and Liechtenstein, and its only Austrian neighbour is Tyrol, to the east. The state is largely mountainous: two thirds of it lies above 1,000 metres, and about 37 per cent is forest. Its main rivers are the Ill, which runs through the Montafon and Walgau valleys into the Rhine, the Rhine itself, the Bregenzer Ache and the Dornbirner Ach. The name means in front of the Arlberg, a mountain whose own name is recorded from 1218 and is thought to come from the Arlen bushes, the mountain pines. Its nickname is Ländle, the small land.

Before the Romans, two Celtic tribes lived in the area: the Raeti in the highlands and the Vindelici around Lake Constance and the Rhine valley. Brigantion, the modern Bregenz, was an important Vindelici settlement founded around 500 BCE, and the first settlements around it date from about 1500 BCE. The Romans conquered the region in 15 BCE and made it part of the province of Raetia, with the towns of Brigantium and Clunia, the modern Feldkirch. Alemannic tribes took it about 450 CE.

The much larger County of Tyrol was the frame of reference for the small district west of the Arlberg, which tried to detach itself from it. In 1861 Vorarlberg was raised to a crown land with its own state parliament. Walser migrants from the Swiss canton of Valais settled in its valleys, and in the 19th century some were invited to come under Austro-Hungarian rule.

The capital is Bregenz, though Dornbirn and Feldkirch have larger populations. Vorarlberg has 397,094 inhabitants (2020) and is divided into four districts: Bregenz, Dornbirn, Feldkirch and Bludenz. It is the only Austrian state whose local dialect is Alemannic rather than Austro-Bavarian, which ties it culturally to German-speaking Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Baden-Württemberg more than to the rest of Austria. Hydroelectric power and seasonal Alpine transhumance, the droving of livestock between valley and high pasture, are long-standing parts of its economy.
vorma: The Vorma is 30 kilometres long. It leaves Lake Mjøsa at the village of Minnesund, on a southern shore formed by a terminal moraine left when the retreating ice paused about 9,400 years ago, and runs through the town of Eidsvoll to the Glomma just north of Årnes. The river has cut through the moraine's clay, sand and gravel, leaving steep banks where many tributaries fall in cascades, until it met a harder intrusive sill of the Oslo Graben at Eidsvoll, where it forms the Svanfoss.

The same glacial deposits dammed a side valley to form Lake Hurdalssjøen, which drains into the Vorma at Eidsvoll through the Andelva. Its name is said to come from its being a warm river that never froze, while the Glomma and the Gudbrandsdalslågen routinely freeze in winter. Where it meets the Glomma lies the Funnefoss, a fall of 10 metres.

In the days when travel by boat was much easier than by land, the meeting of Minnesund and the Vorma at Eidsvoll was an ancient ting, the assembly place of Romerike. The Eidsivating, founded according to tradition by Halvdan Svarte, served all the Opplands and Viken, and Saint Olav held a ting there and built a church at the site in 1017.

In 1795 a landslide blocked the river at Disen for 111 days and dried its bed completely, and a channel was cut around it to prevent a major flood downstream. At the Svanfoss south of Eidsvoll, where the level of Lake Mjøsa is regulated, a lock 6 metres wide and 60 metres long opened in 1906, lifting boats 3 metres past the fall.
voronet-monastery: The age of the monastic site is not known. A legend tells that Stephen the Great, at a moment of crisis in a war against the Ottoman Turks, went to the hermit Daniel at his skete in Voroneț and asked for advice. Daniel told him not to give up the fight and, after victory, to build a monastery dedicated to Saint George. The inscription over the original entrance, now in the exonarthex, records that Voivode Stephen, son of Bogdan, began the church on 26 May, a Monday after Pentecost, and finished it in September 1488.

The monastery is said to have been built in three months and three weeks to commemorate the victory at the Battle of Vaslui. The tomb of Saint Daniel the Hermit, its first abbot, lies in the monastery.

The church of Saint George is built on a triconch plan, with three apses, a chancel, a naos with its tower and a pronaos. Its small windows and the pointed or shouldered arches of its inner doorframes are Gothic. In 1547 the Metropolitan Bishop of Moldavia, Grigorie Roșca, added the exonarthex at the west end and had the exterior walls painted; an inscription at the left of the entrance records this.

The doors of the exonarthex have rectangular frames, which point to a transition from Gothic to Renaissance, and the west façade has no openings at all, probably because Roșca meant it for frescoes. The church is known for its exterior frescoes of bright, intense colours, with hundreds of well-preserved figures set against a background of azurite blue, known as Voroneț blue. On the north façade the original decoration remains, rows of enamelled ceramic discs showing the rampant lion and aurochs head of the Moldavian arms and creatures such as two-tailed mermaids.

Voroneț had a school of calligraphy in which priests and monks learned to read, write and translate religious texts. It produced two notable copies of Romanian translations of the Bible, the Codex of Voroneț, found in 1871, and the Psalter of Voroneț, found in 1882, now held at the Romanian Academy. The monastery was deserted soon after 1775, when the Habsburg monarchy annexed the northern part of Moldavia, and a monastic community returned in 1991. Because of its frescoes it is often called the Sistine Chapel of the East, and it is one of the Painted churches of Moldavia on UNESCO's World Heritage list.
vortigern: Vortigern is known from sources written long after the 5th century, and scholars contest his existence. The name is also spelt Vortiger, Vortigan and Voertigern, and appears in Welsh as Gwrtheyrn and in Old English as Wyrtgeorn. In Brittonic the name means something like Great King or Overlord, from elements meaning over and king, and it has occasionally been suggested that it was a title rather than a personal name.

The Historia Brittonum gives his genealogy: his father was Vitalis, his grandfather Vitalinus and his great-grandfather Gloui, probably an eponym linking him with Glevum, the civitas of Gloucester. It names four sons, Vortimer, Pascent, Catigern and Faustus. The inscription on the Pillar of Eliseg, a mid-9th century stone cross at Llangollen, gives the Old Welsh spelling Guarthi[gern] and says he married Sevira, daughter of Magnus Maximus. Some historians, including Nikolai Tolstoy and David Dumville, regard this as doubtful tradition or propaganda of the Powys dynasty.

The cleric Gildas, writing in the late 5th or early 6th century, condemned a proud tyrant who, with his council, let the Saxons into Britain like wolves into a fold to beat back the peoples of the north. The earliest surviving manuscript does not name Vortigern, but two Continental manuscripts do. David Dumville argued in 1977 that these texts may be superior, and some historians note that the Welsh name resembles a word play on proud tyrant.

Bede, in the 8th century, supplied the name, called him king of the British people and gave Hengist and Horsa as the Saxon leaders. The Historia Brittonum, compiled probably in the early 9th century, is more hostile and accuses him of incest, oath-breaking and treason. It tells how he granted Thanet to the Saxons as foederati, then the rest of Kent in return for marriage to Hengest's daughter.

Accounts of his end differ. One tradition says he took refuge in North Wales, and the Llŷn Peninsula has a valley called Nant Gwrtheyrn, once with a barrow known as Vortigern's Grave. Other reports place his death in a castle on the River Teifi in Dyfed, or in a tower at The Doward in Herefordshire.

His story stayed well known in later centuries. He appears in two Jacobean plays, and his meeting with Rowena was painted by William Hamilton in 1793. The play Vortigern and Rowena, promoted in 1796 as a lost work of William Shakespeare, was a forgery by William Henry Ireland and was performed at Drury Lane on 2 April 1796.
vosges: The Vosges run north-north-east from the Burgundian Gate to the Börrstadt Basin and form the western boundary of the Upper Rhine Plain. Together with the Palatine Forest on the German side of the border they make a single low mountain range of around 8,000 square kilometres. The range is divided from south to north into the Higher Vosges, whose rounded summits are called ballons in French, the sandstone Middle Vosges and the Lower Vosges, a sandstone plateau between 300 and 560 metres high. After the Grand Ballon come the Storkenkopf at 1,366 metres and the Hohneck at 1,364 metres.

The Vosges and the Black Forest across the Rhine were both formed by uplift beside the Rhine Graben, and they are alike in geology and in their forested lower slopes. Westerly winds bring heavy rain and snow to the western slope, while the Alsatian plain beneath the range is much drier, and vineyards on the eastern slope climb to about 400 metres.

In Latin the massif was called Vosago mons, Vosego silva or Vogesus mons, a name extended to the vast woods of the region; German speakers later called it Vogesen or Wasgenwald. Forests were cleared over the centuries for farming and livestock and for early industry, including charcoal works, glassworks and water mills. In the mining valley of the Lièpvrette, Saxon miners settled. Castles, mostly ruined, stand on the Alsatian slopes, and at Sainte Odile survives the Mur Païen, a dry-stone wall that archaeologists are divided on whether the Romans built or whether it is older.

From 1871 to 1918 the range formed the main border between France and the German Empire, running from the Ballon d'Alsace to Mont Donon. It saw almost continuous fighting in the First World War. In October 1944 the U.S. 442nd Regiment, composed of second-generation Japanese Americans, fought a fierce battle on the mountain to rescue the cut-off 1st Battalion of the 36th Infantry, the Lost Battalion, and suffered 800 casualties.

The French department of Vosges is named after the range. Two nature parks lie within it, the Northern Vosges Regional Nature Park, established in 1976, and the Ballons des Vosges Nature Park, established in 1989. The Northern Vosges park and the Palatinate Forest park across the border form a cross-border UNESCO biosphere reserve.
voting-rights-act-of-1965: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) barred denial of the vote on account of race, color or previous condition of servitude and empowered Congress to enforce it. Congress passed the Enforcement Acts in the 1870s, criminalizing obstruction of voting and providing federal supervision of elections, but in 1875 the Supreme Court struck down parts of them in United States v. Cruikshank and United States v. Reese. After 1877 enforcement became erratic, and in 1894 Congress repealed most of the provisions.

Case-by-case litigation by the Department of Justice had failed to overcome the resistance of state officials, and Congress concluded that a comprehensive new law was needed. The bill was introduced on 17 March 1965 as S. 1964 by the Senate majority leader Mike Mansfield and minority leader Everett Dirksen, who had drafted it with Attorney General Katzenbach. Dirksen agreed to back it after learning of the police violence against marchers at Selma on Bloody Sunday.

Section 2 prohibits any state or local government from imposing voting rules that restrict the vote on account of race, color or membership in a language minority group. The act also outlaws literacy tests and similar devices. Its special provisions apply to jurisdictions with a history of discrimination, chiefly through the Section 5 requirement that they obtain approval from the attorney general or a federal court before changing any voting rule.

The Senate passed the bill on 26 May 1965, the Republican Party voting 30 to 2 and the Democratic Party 47 to 17. The House of Representatives followed on 9 July, the Republican Party voting 112 to 23 and the Democratic Party 221 to 62. President Lyndon B. Johnson signed it on 6 August 1965.

The effect was immediate. By the end of 1965 a quarter of a million new Black voters had been registered, a third of them by federal examiners. In Alabama the share of adult African Americans registered rose from 19.3 percent in 1964 to 61.3 percent in 1969, and in Mississippi from 6.7 percent to 66.5 percent.

In South Carolina v. Katzenbach, decided on 7 March 1966, the Supreme Court held the act a constitutional means of enforcing the Fifteenth Amendment. Congress amended it in 1970, 1975, 1982, 1992 and 2006, extending the special provisions each time one of them was due to expire, and in 1970 it created a nationwide ban on literacy tests. In Shelby County v. Holder (2013) the Court nullified the preclearance requirement for the covered jurisdictions, reasoning that it was obsolete.
vratislaus-ii-of-bohemia: Vratislaus II was the son of Bretislaus I and Judith of Schweinfurt. When his father died in 1055 he became duke of Olomouc, while his older brother became Duke of Bohemia as Spytihněv II. The two fell out and Vratislaus was exiled to Hungary. With Hungarian assistance he regained Olomouc, was reconciled with his brother and succeeded him as duke of Bohemia when he died in 1061. His younger brothers Conrad and Otto held Brno and Olomouc, following the Přemyslid tradition of entrusting Moravia to younger brothers, and the youngest, Jaromír, entered the church.

Popes Alexander II and Gregory VII confirmed Vratislaus in the privilege of wearing the mitre and tunic, yet he supported Emperor Henry IV in the Investiture Controversy and in the Saxon rebellions. He joined Henry in 1075 and they defeated the rebels at the First Battle of Langensalza on 9 June. At Flarchheim his contingent enabled the imperial army to overcome the rebels of Rudolf of Rheinfelden, and he seized Rudolf's golden lance, which was afterwards carried before him on state occasions. He won again at Mailberg in 1082, and in thanks Henry granted him the title of king in 1085.

He often quarrelled with his brother Jaromír, Bishop of Prague. In 1063 Vratislaus founded a diocese at Olomouc, which Jaromír ignored, and in 1070 he created the Vyšehrad Chapter, endowed independently of the Prague bishop. In 1080 he asked Rome for permission to use the Slavonic liturgy and was refused. He joined Henry's Italian campaign of 1081 and entered Rome with him in 1083. He held Lower Lusatia from 1075 to 1086 but never received Meissen and Lusatia as promised, and after 1088 he gave Henry no military aid, though he stayed loyal.

His last years were taken up with dynastic quarrels. When Otto died in 1086 Vratislaus gave Olomouc to his son Boleslaus, which Conrad took as an act against his interests. The army sent against Conrad under another son, Bretislaus, turned on him. Vratislaus named Conrad his heir, and together they attacked Bretislaus, who fled to Hungary. Vratislaus died of a hunting wound on 14 January 1092 and was buried in the Church of St Peter and Paul at Vyšehrad. His reduction of the Prague bishop's power strengthened the Bohemian crown, and his policy towards the Empire was followed in the 12th century.
vryburg: Vryburg lies halfway between Kimberley, the capital of the Northern Cape, to the south and Mahikeng, the capital of North West Province, to the north, where the N18 and N14 roads meet. The township of Huhudi, Tswana for running water, lies just south of the town. Vryburg stands on the Cape to Cairo Railway, the line linking Cape Town and Kimberley with Mahikeng, Botswana and Zimbabwe, and is served by its own airport.

The republicans of Stellaland called themselves Vryburgers, free citizens, and the town took its name from them. Its site, first named Endvogelfontein, was renamed Vryburg on 15 November 1882. In December the newly laid out plots were shared among the volunteers by lottery, and by February 1883 some 400 farms had been set up on land taken from native tribes. On 16 August 1883 G. J. van Niekerk proclaimed the Republic of Stellaland with himself as its first and only president; by 1884 the town had about 20 houses.

Stellaland split between those who supported annexation by the Cape Colony, as Cecil Rhodes proposed, and those who wanted independence. The London Convention of February 1884 made it a British protectorate, with the Reverend John McKenzie as Commissioner to British Bechuanaland. During the Second Boer War the British built a concentration camp at Vryburg for Boer women and children. In 1904 the London Missionary Society founded the Tiger Kloof Native Institute south of the town, whose stone church is a national monument.

Vryburg is the seat of the Dr Ruth Segomotsi Mompati District Municipality and became part of North West Province when the nine provinces were created in 1994. Its district is South Africa's largest producer of beef, chiefly from Bonsmara cattle, and also grows maize and peanuts. The Theiler Museum, 8 km west of the town, holds equipment of the veterinarian Sir Arnold Theiler.
vryheid: Vryheid is a coal mining and cattle ranching town in northern KwaZulu-Natal. Its name is the Afrikaans word for freedom, while its original name, Abaqulusi, recalls the abaQulusi clan of the local area. Its Zulu names are eFilidi and iFilidi. The town stands on the Transnet Coalline.

Boer farmers living in the Vryheid area helped King Dinuzulu defeat his rival chief Zibhebhu in a struggle over the Zulu succession. In return the Zulu king ceded to them land along the banks of the Mfolozi River. On 5 August 1884 the Boers formed the Nieuwe Republiek, or New Republic, with Vryheid as its capital, and its sovereignty was recognised by Germany and by Portugal. The republic was later incorporated into the South African Republic. At the end of the Second Boer War the town and its surrounding area were absorbed by the British into the Natal colony. The general Louis Botha, who became the first Prime Minister of the Union of South Africa, represented the district of Vryheid in parliament.

In 2016 and 2017 the town suffered water shortages, after pumps and pipelines had been allowed to fall into disrepair. Many residents had to collect water from communal tanks supplied by the municipality, and three sewage treatment plants stopped working, polluting the Besterspruit and the Klipfontein Dam. Outbreaks of diarrhoea followed, and another struck in 2019.

Vryheid has the Roman Catholic Benedictine Inkamana Abbey. Its church known as Die Moeder Gemeente, the Mother Congregation, has been listed among notable churches and cathedrals in Africa. In 2007 Inkamana High School and Vryheid Comprehensive Secondary School were recognised as historic schools and given funding to become academies focused on mathematics, science and technology. Hoërskool Vryheid teaches in both Afrikaans and English, and Hoërskool Pionier in Afrikaans.
vseslav-of-polotsk: Vseslav Bryachislavich was the son of Bryachislav Izyaslavich, Prince of Polotsk and Vitebsk, and so a great-grandson of Vladimir I of Kiev and Rogneda of Polotsk. He took the throne of Polotsk in 1044 on his father's death and married around 1060. Because his father had never been prince in Kiev, he was excluded from the grand princely succession as an izgoi. As the only major prince in Rus not descended from Yaroslav, he was, in the words of Simon Franklin and Jonathan Shepard, an outsider from within.

Unable to secure Kiev, which Yaroslav's three sons held, he began to pillage the northern lands of Kievan Rus. In 1065 he besieged Pskov but was thrown back, and in the winter of 1066 to 1067 he pillaged and burnt Novgorod the Great, taking the bell and other objects from its Cathedral of Holy Wisdom to decorate his own cathedral of the same name in Polotsk. The attack forced the young Mstislav to flee from Novgorod to his father Iziaslav in Kiev. The Yaroslavichi joined forces, sacked Minsk and defeated Vseslav on the Nemiga River on 3 March 1067.

In June he was captured during peace talks, when Iziaslav broke his oath, and was imprisoned in Kiev. In the Kiev Uprising of 1068, after a defeat by the Kipchaks on the Alta River, the crowd freed Vseslav from prison and proclaimed him grand prince of Kiev, and Iziaslav fled to Poland.
