Iziaslav returned with an army after seven months and retook the throne, and Vseslav fled back to Polotsk. After several years of struggle he secured Polotsk in 1071. In his last thirty years his chief enemies were Vsevolod Yaroslavich and Vsevolod's son Vladimir Monomakh.

Vseslav died on 24 April 1101, the Wednesday before Good Friday according to the Primary Chronicle, and was buried in the Cathedral of Holy Wisdom in Polotsk, the oldest stone building in Belarus. He had six sons, among them Gleb, Prince of Minsk, Davyd, Prince of Polotsk, and Sviatoslav, Prince of Vitebsk. He had a reputation for sorcery: the Primary Chronicle says that he was conceived by sorcery and born with a caul on his head. The 12th-century Tale of Igor's Campaign depicts him as a werewolf who rode like a wolf from Kiev to Tmutarakan and heard the bells of Polotsk from Kiev.
vsevolod-i-of-kiev: Vsevolod Yaroslavich was the fifth and favourite son of Yaroslav I the Wise and Ingigerd Olafsdottir. A seal from his last years names him Andrei in Greek, which implies that his baptismal name was Andrew. To back an armistice with the Byzantine Emperor Constantine IX Monomachos in 1046, his father married him to a Byzantine princess, who according to tradition was called Anastasia or Maria. Their son bore the emperor's family name, Monomakh, which suggests she belonged to his close family, though no contemporary evidence attests the relationship. After her death in 1067 he married a Kypchak princess, Anna Polovetskaya.

On his father's death in 1054 Vsevolod received the towns of Pereyaslav, Rostov and Suzdal and the township of Beloozero. With his elder brothers Iziaslav and Sviatoslav he formed a princely triumvirate that fought the steppe nomads and compiled the Russkaya Pravda, the first law code of the state. He made peace with the Cumans, who first appeared in Europe in 1055, but they invaded his principality in 1061 and routed him. In 1068 they defeated the three brothers on the Alta River, after which the citizens of Kiev rose in rebellion and proclaimed Vseslav their grand prince.
In 1073 Vsevolod and Sviatoslav forced Iziaslav to flee Kiev. Sviatoslav died in 1076, and Iziaslav was killed in battle in a campaign against Oleg Sviatoslavich, who had allied with the Cumans.

Vsevolod took the Kievan throne as his father's only surviving son, uniting Kiev, Chernigov and Pereyaslavl, and put his eldest son Vladimir Monomakh in charge of Chernigov. The Primary Chronicle complains that the people no longer had access to the prince's justice and that judges became corrupt and venal. It also says he followed the advice of young councillors instead of his old retainers.

According to Vladimir Monomakh's Autobiography he spoke five foreign languages. He lost most of his battles, and Vladimir did most of the fighting. In his last years Vsevolod was gravely ill and Vladimir presided over the government. His daughter Eupraxia of Kiev married Emperor Henry IV.
vsevolod-the-big-nest: Vsevolod III Yuryevich was the tenth or eleventh son of Yuri Dolgoruky, who founded the town of Dmitrov to commemorate the site of Vsevolod's birth. Nikolai Karamzin began the speculation that his mother Helene was a Greek princess, because after her husband's death she took Vsevolod to Constantinople; other scholars such as Alexander Kazhdan regard this as speculative. Vsevolod spent his youth at the chivalric court of the Komnenoi and returned to Rus' in 1170.

In 1173 two Smolensk princes captured Kiev and Vsevolod with it. Ransomed a year later, he took the side of his brother Mikhalko against the powerful boyars of Rostov and Suzdal, and when Mikhalko died in 1176, Vsevolod succeeded him in Vladimir. He promptly subjugated the boyars and raided the Volga states, notably Volga Bulgaria. He installed puppet rulers on the throne of Novgorod and married his daughters to princes of Chernigov and Kiev. In 1180 and 1187 he punished the princes of Ryazan by ousting them from their lands, and in 1207 he burned Ryazan and Belgorod to the ground. In the latter part of his reign Kievan matters concerned him little, and he concentrated on building up Vladimir.

Vsevolod's wife Maria Shvarnovna, whose origins are disputed, devoted herself to works of piety and founded several convents, and the Russian church glorified her as a saint. They had at least fourteen children, which earned him the nickname Big Nest. Before his death he divided his territories between his sons, with the second-oldest, Yuri, receiving the largest share. He died on 12 April 1212 and was buried in the Assumption Cathedral in Vladimir. Four of his sons later succeeded him as grand princes of Vladimir, and immediately after his death a war of succession (1212–1216) broke out between them.
vuk-brankovic: Vuk Branković was born in 1345 into a Serb noble family. His father, Branko Mladenović, who died before 1365, received the high court title of sevastokrator from Emperor Stefan Dušan and governed Ohrid. His grandfather Mladen was župan of Trebinje under King Stefan Milutin and vojvoda under King Stefan Dečanski. Later chronicles claimed that the family descended from Vukan Nemanjić, a son of Stefan Nemanja. After their father's death Vuk and his brothers Grgur and Nikola Radonja withdrew to the valley of Drenica in central Kosovo.

Vuk took advantage of the death of King Vukašin at the Battle of Maritsa in 1371 to conquer Sjenica, Zvečan and part of the Lim valley. In the same year he married Mara, daughter of Prince Lazar Hrebeljanović, the most powerful Serbian magnate, which brought him lands in Kosovo and Lazar's support, though he had to acknowledge Lazar as his feudal senior. When Lazar and King Tvrtko I of Bosnia divided the lands of Nikola Altomanović in 1373, Vuk received Raška, with the old capital Ras, and lands in Polimlje. After Đurađ I Balšić died on 13 January 1378 he captured Prizren, Peć and the area of Metohija.

At its height his realm stretched from Sjenica in the west to Skopje in the east, with Pristina and Vushtrri as capitals and the mining settlements of Trepča, Janjevo and Gluhavica among its towns. In the Battle of Kosovo in 1389 he fought alongside his father-in-law Lazar. Lazar died there with most of his army, but Vuk survived and kept his army. He then planned action against the Ottomans together with King Sigismund of Hungary, and he refused to fight on the Ottoman side at Rovine in 1395 or Nicopolis in 1396. The Ottomans attacked him in 1395 and 1396 and seized his land, giving most of it to Prince Stefan Lazarević.

Vuk was imprisoned and died in an Ottoman prison on 6 October 1397. Priština and Vučitrn were left to his sons as Ottoman vassals. One son, Đurađ Branković, succeeded his maternal uncle Stefan Lazarević as Despot of Serbia and ruled from 1427 to 1456. A Serbian folk tradition, told in epic poems, says that Vuk betrayed Lazar at Kosovo to make himself supreme ruler of Serbia. Modern Serbian historians reject this, though Momčilo Spremić has said that a betrayal remains possible.
vulcanization: Vulcanization is a range of processes for hardening rubbers. The term first referred only to the treatment of natural rubber with sulfur and heat, which remains the most common practice, but it has grown to cover synthetic rubbers hardened by other means, such as silicone rubber cured at room temperature and neoprene cured with metal oxides. It works by forming cross-links between sections of the polymer chain, which increases rigidity and durability and changes mechanical and electrical properties. Like the curing of other thermosetting polymers, it is generally irreversible.

In sulfur vulcanization, some carbon-hydrogen bonds next to double bonds are replaced by chains of sulfur atoms that link one polymer chain to another. The number of sulfur atoms in a bridge affects the finished rubber: short cross-links give better heat resistance, while longer ones give good dynamic properties but less heat resistance.

The word was suggested by William Brockedon, a friend of Thomas Hancock, who obtained the British patent, and refers to the god Vulcan, associated with heat and sulfur in volcanoes. In ancient Mesoamerican cultures rubber was made into balls, sandal soles, elastic bands and waterproof containers, and was cured with sulfur-rich plant juices.

In the 1830s Charles Goodyear tried to make rubber tires that did not turn soft and sticky in heat. His announced formulas repeatedly failed because the hardening he saw came from the heating itself. In 1839 he dropped a mixture of rubber and sulfur into a hot frying pan, and the rubber stayed firm and hardened further as the heat rose. Hancock took out a British patent on 21 November 1843, eight weeks before Goodyear's American patent of 30 January 1844. Accounts differ on whether Hancock had examined samples of Goodyear's rubber.

Most rubber products are vulcanised, which greatly improves their lifespan, function and strength. Examples include hoses, shoe soles, toys, erasers, shock absorbers, conveyor belts and bowling balls, and above all tires, for which sulfur vulcanization of natural rubber and styrene-butadiene rubber is used.
vushmgir: Vushmgir, whose name means quail catcher in the local Caspian Iranian dialects, was a son of Ziyar of the Arghich tribe and spent his early life in Gilan, then ruled by the Alids. His religion is uncertain: he is most commonly thought to have been a Zaydi Shiite Muslim, but he has also been described as a Zoroastrian, at least in his earlier years. After his brother Mardavij conquered Tabaristan from Makan ibn Kaki, Vushmgir became governor of Amol.

When Mardavij was murdered by his Turkish troops in 935, the Daylamite and Gilite troops pledged themselves to Vushmgir at Ray. That year he defeated a Samanid army and Makan, who had invaded Tabaristan together, and took Gorgan; he then acknowledged Samanid overlordship and handed Gorgan to Makan. At the Battle of Iskhabad against the Samanid governor Abu 'Ali ibn Muhtaj he fled the field, and Makan was killed.

Losing Ray in 943, when two of his officers went over to the Buyid Hasan, he fled to the Samanid court of Nuh I. With 30,000 Samanid troops under Qaratakin he retook Gorgan in 945, and by 947 had driven his rival al-Hasan ibn al-Fairuzan from Tabaristan. From 948 Hasan, by then called Rukn al-Dawla, fought him for Tabaristan and Gorgan, which changed hands several times until a treaty of 955 left him in Tabaristan. In 958 he briefly occupied Ray, Rukn al-Dawla's capital.

He was killed by a boar during a hunt in December 967, shortly after a Samanid army had arrived for a joint campaign against the Buyids. His eldest son Bisutun succeeded him, although the Samanid army tried to put another son, Qabus, in power. A third son had died before him in 964, in fighting over Hausam.
vyachko: Vyachko, called Vetseke in the Chronicle of Henry of Livonia, held the fortress of Koknese some 100 kilometres up the Daugava when Bishop Albert of Buxhoeveden and the crusaders were settling on the Gulf of Riga. The chronicle says its people included Latgallians and Selonians, a Germanic colony and some Slavic peoples. His principality is believed to have been subject to Polotsk, but that did not shield him from the crusaders or the Lithuanians, and he offered Albert half of his land and fort in return for protection against the Lithuanians.

In 1208 the Livonians of Lielvārde, answering his raids, took Koknese and put him in chains. Albert had the fort and his wealth restored, received him in Riga with gifts and sent him back with armed men and masons to strengthen it.

When the bishop prepared to sail to Germany, Vyachko had these men murdered and sent their horses and arms to Grand Prince Vladimir of Polotsk, urging him to take the weakly held Riga. The crusader fleet, held at Dünamünde by a contrary wind, turned back; the Russians burned Koknese and fled, and the crusaders took revenge on the Latgallians and Selonians hiding in the woods.

After the Estonian rising of 1223 against the crusaders, the Novgorod Republic gave Vyachko money and 200 men to establish himself at Tartu. By 1224 it was the last centre of resistance in south Estonia, held by the local Ugandi and fighters from Sakala and neighbouring provinces. A first siege after Easter was abandoned after five days.

On 15 August 1224 the crusaders returned, reinforced by Christian Latvian and Livonian troops; Vyachko refused free passage while he awaited relief from Novgorod. When the fortress fell everyone inside was killed, and he died with his Russian mercenaries, by Henry's account dragged from a last stronghold. The relief army turned back at Pskov. Soviet historians later presented the defence as a sign of friendship between the Russian and Estonian peoples.
vyazma: Vyazma lies on the Vyazma River about halfway between Smolensk and Mozhaysk, and it is the administrative centre of Vyazemsky District in Smolensk Oblast. The river's name comes from the Russian word vyaz', meaning bog or swamp. Throughout its history the town helped defend Russia against invasions from the west aimed at Moscow, and it is today a major railway junction on the line from Moscow to Smolensk.

The territory around Vyazma was rapidly developed in the 12th century, and a fortified settlement was built in the late 12th or early 13th century. The chronicles first mention it under the year 1230, when it was given as an appanage to Andrey Vladimirovich. It became an important administrative centre of the Principality of Smolensk and a centre of trade and crafts, and from the late 13th century of a separate appanage principality. In 1403 the Lithuanians expelled the local princes to Moscow, where they became service princes and took the name Vyazemsky. A Russian army under Daniil Shchenya captured the town in 1494, and the Treaty of Deulino of 1618 confirmed it as Russian after the devastation of the Time of Troubles.

A kremlin wall with six towers was built from 1631 to 1634, and the Spasskaya Tower survives. During the Russo-Polish War of 1654–1667 the town was the main stronghold in the struggle for Smolensk, and Tsar Alexis lived there in the winter of 1654–1655 to escape the plague.

On 22 October 1812 Russian forces under Mikhail Miloradovich and Matvey Platov attacked the rear guard of the retreating French army, under Marshal Louis-Nicolas Davout, near Vyazma. The French lost 6,000 men and 2,500 were taken prisoner, while the Russians lost around 2,000. In October 1941 four Soviet armies were surrounded west of the town by German forces, who occupied it from 7 October 1941 to 12 March 1943. The Germans ran camps there, Dulag 184 and Dulag 230, where tens of thousands of prisoners are estimated to have died, and 117 Jews were shot in December 1941. The town was heavily damaged and rebuilt, and a memorial complex stands outside it on the Moscow–Minsk highway.
vyborg: Vyborg lies on the Karelian Isthmus near the head of Vyborg Bay, 130 kilometres north-west of St Petersburg and 38 kilometres south of the Russian border with Finland. Its Swedish name Viborg may be interpreted as "holy fort", from vi, "sacred", and borg, "fortress" or "city"; the Finnish Viipuri adapts it. The area was a trading centre on the western branch of the Vuoksi River, since dried up, and was inhabited by Karelians, a Balto-Finnic people who came under the domination of Novgorod and Sweden. Wider settlement is generally dated from the 13th century, when Hanseatic traders began travelling to Novgorod.

Vyborg Castle was founded in 1293 during the Third Swedish Crusade by the marshal Torkel Knutsson, on the site of an older Karelian fort that was burned. It was the first centre for the spread of Christianity in Karelia and was fought over for decades by Sweden and the Republic of Novgorod. The Treaty of Nöteborg in 1323 recognised it as Swedish. King Eric of Pomerania chartered its trade privileges in 1403, and it withstood a long siege in the Russo-Swedish War of 1496 to 1497.

Tsar Peter the Great captured the town in the Great Northern War in 1710, and the Treaty of Nystad of 1721 confirmed the transfer. Sweden developed Fredrikshamn as a substitute port, and Vyborg's diocese moved to Borgå. The naval Battle of Vyborg Bay was fought on 4 July 1790. Alexander I incorporated the town into the Grand Duchy of Finland. The Saimaa Canal, opened in 1856, linked eastern Finland to the sea and benefited its trade. Vladimir Lenin lived in the town for a period in 1917.

After Finnish independence, the town was held by the Red Guards until the White Guard captured it on 29 April 1918; between 360 and 420 civilians were killed in the Vyborg massacre. In 1939 its population was slightly under 75,000, with minorities of Swedes, Germans, Russians, Romani, Tatars and Jews. Alvar Aalto built the Vyborg Library there. Over 70,000 people were evacuated during the Winter War, and the Moscow Peace Treaty gave the town to the Soviet Union; about 10,000 remaining Finns were evacuated in haste, so that practically the whole Finnish population was resettled elsewhere in Finland.

Vyborg is the administrative centre of Vyborgsky District in Leningrad Oblast, Russia. The 2021 census recorded 72,530 inhabitants. The town lies 245 kilometres east of Helsinki, near the point where the Saimaa Canal enters the Gulf of Finland, and in 2010 it was given the status of City of Military Glory.
vytautas-magnus-university: After Lithuania became an independent republic in 1918, its State Council decided to re-establish Vilnius University. Because Vilnius was later under Polish administration and the Lithuanian government had moved to Kaunas, the decision could not be carried out. Higher Courses of Study were set up in Kaunas at the beginning of 1920, and on 13 February 1922 the Cabinet of Ministers decided to found the University of Lithuania there. It opened on 16 February 1922, and on 12 April the President confirmed its statute and six faculties: Theology-Philosophy, Humanities, Law, Mathematics and Sciences, Medicine, and Technical Studies.

An Agricultural Academy grew out of the agronomy and forestry sections in 1924, and a Veterinary Academy out of the veterinary section of the medical faculty in 1936. On 7 June 1930, the 500th anniversary of the death of Vytautas the Great, the university took his name.

In 1940 the university helped to re-establish Vilnius University: the faculties of Humanities and Law moved there in the winter, and Mathematics and Sciences in the summer. Soviet occupation that summer forced it to be called the University of Kaunas. The Provisional Government restored the name of Vytautas Magnus in summer 1941, after the German invasion of the Soviet Union. The German occupation government closed it in March 1943, after Lithuanians refused to form an SS battalion.

Soviet authorities reopened it in autumn 1944 with four faculties, and closed it in the autumn of 1949 after the Faculty of Philosophy was transferred to Vilnius. On 31 October 1950 it was reorganised into the Kaunas Polytechnic Institute and the Kaunas Medical Institute. A law of 4 July 1989 re-established it, and the first academic year began on 1 September 1989 with faculties of Economics, Humanities and Sciences. It was then the second university in Soviet-occupied Lithuania and the first higher school independent of governmental institutions.

After 1989 academic freedom was its guiding principle, with a common programme in the humanities and general education for the first two years from 1990. In 1991 it was the first in Lithuania to adopt a system of Bachelor's, Master's and doctoral levels. Students are admitted to fields of study rather than specialisations and make their final choice after two years. In 1993 it formed Lithuania's first Research and Study Association with ten research institutes. Its subdivisions include faculties of Economics and Management, Humanities, Law and Catholic Theology, a Music Academy and a Botanical Garden. It has about 8,800 students, a student council and some thirty student clubs and corporations.
vytautas-the-great: Vytautas was the son of Kęstutis and his wife Birutė and a cousin and childhood friend of Jogaila. His uncle Algirdas and his father Kęstutis had ruled Lithuania jointly, Algirdas the east and Kęstutis the west, which was chiefly responsible for defence against the Teutonic Order. After Algirdas died in 1377 and Jogaila succeeded him, a struggle for power followed. Kęstutis seized Vilnius in 1381 but was arrested with Vytautas and found dead a week later, and whether he died naturally or was murdered is still debated. Vytautas escaped in 1382, sought help from the Teutonic Order and for years switched between the Order and Jogaila.

After the Union of Krewo in 1385 made Jogaila king of Poland, Vytautas attacked Vilnius in 1389 and allied again with the Order. In 1392 Jogaila offered to make him regent in place of the unpopular Skirgaila. In the Astrava Treaty Vytautas recovered all his father's lands, including Trakai, and in practice held all the Grand Duke's power. The Union of Vilnius and Radom in 1401 recognised him as Grand Duke for his lifetime, with Jogaila as Supreme Duke, and with the title to pass to the Polish king at his death.

He sought to control Ruthenian lands and helped the Golden Horde's khan Tokhtamysh. In 1398 his army attacked part of the Crimea, so that Lithuania spanned the Baltic to the Black Sea, and he brought Karaim and Tatar families, 388 of them Karaim, to guard castles and bridges. A crusade against the Mongols ended in crushing defeat at the Vorskla River in 1399. In 1410 he commanded the forces of the Grand Duchy at Grunwald, a decisive Polish-Lithuanian victory over the Teutonic Order.

By the Peace of Thorn of 1411 Vytautas received Samogitia for his lifetime, and it was returned to Lithuania in perpetuity by the Treaty of Lake Melno after a war in 1422. He helped create the Union of Horodło of 1413, which gave Lithuanian Christian nobles the same rights as the Polish szlachta. At the Congress of Lutsk in January 1429 Sigismund of Hungary proposed that Vytautas be crowned King of Lithuania, which caused a crisis with Poland. Vytautas died at Trakai Island Castle on 27 October 1430, ending the affair, and was buried in the Cathedral of Vilnius. In modern Lithuania he is revered as a national hero, and Vytautas Magnus University is named after him.
vytenis: Vytenis is first mentioned in 1292, during his father’s invasion of Masovia, when an army of 800 men reached as far as Łęczyca and he fought in the Battle of Trojanów. After his father’s death, about 1295, he became Grand Duke. He was soon involved in succession disputes in Poland, supporting Boleslaus II of Masovia, married to a Lithuanian duchess, Gaudemunda, against Władysław I of Poland. In Ruthenia he recaptured lands lost after the assassination of Mindaugas and took the principalities of Pinsk and Turov.

Crusading against pagan Lithuania and Samogitia intensified in the 1290s as the Teutonic Knights and the Livonian Order conquered the Prussians and other Baltic tribes. During his reign a network of defensive castles was built along the Neman and Jūra rivers, matched by Teutonic castles on the opposite bank, and the Teutonic Knights organised some 20 raids into Samogitia, seeking a corridor to link up with the Livonian Order. He acted to undermine Samogitian nobles, some of whom considered resettling in Prussia as vassals of the Knights, and Gediminas appears to have helped him control them.

In 1297 disagreements between the Archbishop of Riga, the burghers and the Livonian Order grew into war. Vytenis offered help to the citizens, with vague promises of conversion to Christianity, invaded Livonia, destroyed Karkus castle and defeated the Order at the Battle of Turaida, killing the Land Master Bruno and 22 knights. He then led eleven campaigns into Prussia between 1298 and 1313, in one of which the entire population of Brodnica was massacred. A Lithuanian garrison guarded Riga until 1313, when the townspeople gave the castle to the Order. Around 1307 Polatsk was annexed, and in 1312 he invited Franciscan friars to maintain a Catholic church at Navahrudak for German merchants.

Vytenis died without an heir, in circumstances that are not known. He is last mentioned in September 1315 during the unsuccessful siege of Christmemel. Russian historians long claimed he was struck by lightning, but this was a mistranslation of Teutonic propaganda that Gediminas had killed his master and usurped the throne. His only known son, Žvelgutis, possibly died before him, and Gediminas, his brother, became Grand Duke, under whom Lithuania became a major military and political power in Eastern Europe.
